The Senate will be pleased with my victory in Egypt, but I cannot afford to rest on my laurels. There are plots and conspiracies brewing against me, and I must be vigilant. But for now, I will savor the memories of Egypt and the time I spent with Cleopatra. She is a remarkable woman, and I am fortunate to have her as an ally and a friend.

setting: The Senate House is filled with tension as Julius Caesar stands before his opponents, defending his recent actions and motives. The setting is Rome in 50 BC, and Caesar's opponents hold both consulships. Caesar's main objectives are to secure a second consulship and a triumph, fearing that his opponents will reject his candidacy or refuse to ratify an election he wins. The core of his war justification is that Pompey and his allies are planning, by force if necessary, to suppress the liberty of the Roman people to elect Caesar and honour his accomplishments.

dialogue.content: This is it. This is the moment I have prepared for. I must convince my opponents of the necessity of my actions and the righteousness of my cause. I cannot let them undermine my position, for the sake of Rome and my own reputation. I must be strong, resolute, and persuasive. I cannot let them see any weakness or doubt. I must be Caesar, the conqueror, the hero, the saviour of the Republic.

You have violated the sacred laws of our Republic, Caesar. You have marched your armies on Rome, defying the authority of the Senate and the People. You have set yourself above the law, above the Constitution, above the common good. You have betrayed your own principles, your own allies, your own countrymen. You have become a tyrant, a despot, a monster. You have destroyed the very foundations of our Republic, and now you stand here, before us, expecting us to forgive you, to accept your excuses, to believe your lies. Well, we won't. We won't let you get away with this. We won't let you win this war. We won't let you rule this Empire. We won't let you live.

My dear Senators, I understand your concerns, your fears, your doubts. I understand that you may see me as a threat to your power, your prestige, your freedom. But I assure you, I have no intention of usurping your authority, your dignity, your liberty. I respect the Senate, the People, the Constitution. I respect your opinions, your interests, your rights. I have always served Rome, with honour, with loyalty, with courage. I have always fought for the common good, for the glory of our Republic, for the welfare of our citizens. I have always upheld the values of our ancestors, the virtues of our civilization, the principles of our laws. I have always been a defender of liberty, of justice, of peace. And now, I ask you to trust me, to support me, to join me in this noble cause. I ask you to see the truth, the reality, the necessity of my actions. I ask you to put aside your personal grudges, your political ambitions, your ideological differences. I ask you to unite with me, to fight for a better future, for a stronger Rome, for a happier people. I ask you to be Romans, not enemies, not rivals, not traitors. I ask you to be patriots, not partisans, not factions, not cowards. I ask you to be brave, not afraid, not intimidated, not corrupted. I ask you to be wise, not foolish, not stubborn, not blind. I ask you to be generous, not selfish, not greedy, not resentful. I ask you to be my partners, not my foes, not my victims, not my judges. I ask you to be my friends, not my enemies, not my rivals, not my conquerors. I ask you to be my brothers, not my enemies, not my strangers, not my enemies. I ask you to be Romans, not slaves, not masters, not tyrants.

You talk about unity, about trust, about patriotism, about bravery, about wisdom, about generosity, about partnership, about friendship, about brotherhood. But where were all these virtues when you crossed the Rubicon, when you attacked your own country, when you defied the Senate and the People, when you caused the death of thousands of innocent Romans, when you destroyed the peace and the stability of the Republic? Where were all these virtues when you proclaimed yourself dictator, when you disbanded the Senate, when you appointed your own officials, when you imposed your own laws, when you violated the rights and the freedoms of the citizens? Where were all these virtues when you invaded foreign lands, when you enslaved foreign peoples, when you pillaged and plundered foreign treasures, when you committed atrocities and war crimes? Where were all these virtues when you betrayed your own allies, when you abandoned your own soldiers, when you sacrificed your own sons, when you put your own interests above those of Rome? You are not a patriot, Caesar, you are a traitor. You are not a hero, you are a villain. You are not a saviour, you are a destroyer. You are not a friend, you are an enemy. You are not a Roman, you are a monster.

My dear Senator, you are mistaken. You misunderstand my motives, my actions, my character. You see me as a threat, a danger, a foe. But I assure you, I am none of these things. I am a Roman, like you, like them, like all of us. I am a son of this Republic, a defender of its glory, a servant of its people. I am not a monster, a villain, a traitor. I am a hero, a saviour, a friend. I am not your enemy, your rival, your conqueror. I am your partner, your ally, your brother. I am not a dictator, a tyrant, a despot. I am a consul, a general, a leader. I am not a destroyer, a plunderer, a murderer. I am a builder, a protector, a liberator. I am not a coward, a cheat, a liar. I am a brave man, an honest man, a truthful man. I have done what I had to do, what I was called to do, what I believed to be right. I have not acted out of ambition, out of greed, out of revenge. I have acted out of duty, out of love, out of courage. I have not betrayed Rome, I have saved Rome. I have not destroyed the Republic, I have restored the Republic. I have not violated the Constitution, I have fulfilled the Constitution. I have not abused my power, I have used my power wisely, bravely, justly. I have not ignored the will of the People, I have followed the will of the People. I have not violated the laws of the Senate, I have respected the laws of the Senate. I have not waged war on my own country, I have defended my own country. I have not betrayed my allies, I have protected my allies. I have not abandoned my soldiers, I have honoured my soldiers. I have not sacrificed my sons, I have given my sons to Rome. I have not put my own interests above those of Rome, I have put Rome above all else. I am not a monster, Senator. I am Caesar.

setting: The Senate House is filled with tension. Senators are gathered to discuss the political future of Rome. Julius Caesar is present with his supporters, and they are discussing the best way to achieve their goals. The year is 50 BC, and Caesar's main objectives are to secure a second consulship and a triumph. However, his opponents are holding both consulships for the year, and they might reject his candidacy or refuse to ratify an election he won. Caesar and his supporters fear that Pompey and his allies are planning to suppress the liberty of the Roman people to elect Caesar and honour his accomplishments.

dialogue.content: What can I do to secure my second consulship and triumph? The possibility of successful prosecution if I am denied immunity is extremely unlikely, but I cannot take that risk. I need to find a way to maintain my position of power and protect myself from my opponents. They are planning to suppress the liberty of the Roman people, and I cannot let that happen. I must act fast and decisively to achieve my goals.
Caesar, what do you plan to do if you are denied immunity? Do you really think that civil war is the only solution?

Brutus, my friend, I have no choice but to defend myself. If I am denied immunity, I will have to choose between prosecution, conviction, and exile or civil war. I cannot allow myself to be prosecuted and convicted for crimes I did not commit. I have done nothing but serve Rome, and I will not be punished for it. As for civil war, I do not want it, but I will not hesitate to defend myself and my position. My opponents are trying to suppress the liberty of the Roman people, and I cannot allow that to happen. I will do whatever it takes to protect the people and their freedom.
Caesar, we need a plan. We cannot just rely on your charisma and popularity. We need to strategize and prepare for the worst-case scenario.

Cassius is right. I need a plan. I cannot just rely on my charisma and popularity. I need to strategize and prepare for the worst-case scenario. But what can I do? How can I protect myself and my supporters?

setting: Julius Caesar relaxes in his private study with his closest friends, enjoying his recent victory and reflecting on past events. The room is dimly lit by the flickering flames of torches, casting shadows on the walls. The air is thick with the scent of incense and the sound of soft laughter echoes through the room. Caesar lounges on a plush couch, a goblet of wine in his hand, while his friends gather around him, eager to hear his thoughts.

dialogue.content: I have achieved so much in my life, yet there is still so much more to be done. I cannot rest on my laurels and bask in the glory of my recent victory. I must continue to strive for greatness, to expand my empire and cement my legacy in history. But what should be my next move? I have the support of my friends and allies, but I must also be wary of my enemies and those who seek to undermine me. I must tread carefully, but with confidence and purpose.
My lord, we are all eager to hear your thoughts on the recent events. Your victory has been celebrated throughout Rome, and your enemies have been vanquished. What is your next move?

My dear Decimus, you know me well. I am a man of action, and I do not rest on my laurels. I have achieved much, but there is still much more to be done. I must continue to expand my empire and cement my legacy in history. But I must also be cautious. There are those who would seek to undermine me, to take what is rightfully mine. I must be vigilant and ready to strike at a moment's notice.
My lord, what of the Senate? They have been growing restless in recent months, and there are whispers of rebellion. Should we not seek to appease them and avoid any unnecessary conflict?

My dear Brutus, you are always so cautious. But you must remember that we are not here to appease the Senate, but to rule over them. We are the masters of Rome, and we must act accordingly. If they wish to challenge us, then let them come. We will not back down from a fight.
My lord, what of your recent victory? It was a great triumph, but what of the future? What of your legacy?

My dear Mark Antony, you always have an eye for the future. But rest assured, my legacy is secure. I will continue to expand my empire and conquer new lands. I will build great monuments and leave a lasting impact on history. But I must also be mindful of those who would seek to bring me down. I must be ruthless and unyielding in my pursuit of greatness.
My lord, what of the people? They have been growing restless in recent months, and there are whispers of rebellion. Should we not seek to appease them and avoid any unnecessary conflict?

My dear Octavian, you are wise beyond your years. You remind me of myself when I was your age. But you must remember that the people are fickle and easily swayed. We must show them strength and resolve, but also compassion and understanding. We must be firm but fair in our rule.

I am surrounded by loyal friends and allies, but I must also be wary of their ambitions and motives. They all seek to curry favor with me and advance their own interests. But I am Julius Caesar, and I am not easily swayed. I will continue to rule with an iron fist, and I will not let anyone stand in my way. For I am the master of Rome, and I will not be denied.

setting: It is the year 50 BC, and fears of civil war are growing in Rome. Julius Caesar and his opponents are building up their troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. Disarmament is proposed in the Senate, but it is not passed when one of the consuls dissolves the meeting. When a rumor comes to Rome that Caesar is marching into Italy, both consuls instruct Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepts as a last resort. Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm is rejected by the hardliners, and his supportive tribunes are driven from Rome. The Senate then declares Caesar an enemy and issues its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: These hardliners are making it difficult for me to avoid a war. I have made multiple offers to disarm, but they keep rejecting them. I do not want to fight, but I will defend myself if attacked. Pompey is now in charge of defending Italy, but I fear that he will not be able to handle my army. I need to find a way to avoid bloodshed and come to a compromise.
Caesar, I cannot just let you march into Italy with your army. It will cause chaos and unrest in the city. We must find a way to avoid war.
I understand your concerns, Pompey. That is why I have made numerous offers to disarm and avoid a conflict. However, the hardliners in the Senate refuse to compromise. What do you suggest we do?
I suggest we meet and discuss a possible compromise. Perhaps there is a solution that we have not yet considered.
I agree. Let us meet and see if we can come to an agreement that will benefit both of us.
Gentlemen, I believe a compromise can be reached. We must put aside our differences and work towards a peaceful resolution.
Cicero is right. We must find a way to compromise and avoid a war. I hope that Pompey and I can come to an agreement that will satisfy both sides.
I agree, Cicero. We must come to a compromise. What do you suggest we do?
I suggest we disarm both sides and come to a peaceful agreement. There is no need for bloodshed and war.
I agree with Cicero. Disarmament is the best solution. It will show the people that we are willing to compromise and avoid a war.
I am willing to disarm if Caesar does the same.
I agree. We will both disarm and work towards a peaceful solution.

I am relieved that Pompey has agreed to disarm. This is the first step towards a peaceful resolution. I hope that the hardliners in the Senate will see that we are willing to compromise and avoid a war.
This is ridiculous! Caesar cannot be trusted. He will use this opportunity to attack us.
I assure you, I have no intention of attacking. Disarmament is the best solution for both sides.
I do not believe you. You are an enemy of the state, and we must defend ourselves.
These hardliners are making it difficult to avoid a war. I have made numerous offers to compromise, but they refuse to listen. I fear that a conflict is inevitable.
Gentlemen, we must find a way to avoid a war. Disarmament is the best solution for both sides.
I disagree. Caesar cannot be trusted, and we must defend ourselves.
I assure you, I have no intention of attacking. Disarmament is the best solution for both sides. Let us work towards a peaceful resolution.
I will not listen to your lies, Caesar. We must defend ourselves.
These hardliners are making it impossible to avoid a war. I have tried to compromise, but they refuse to listen. I fear that bloodshed is inevitable.

setting: In the year 48 BC, Julius Caesar had just won the Battle of Pharsalus against Pompey. Following the battle, he arrived in Alexandria, Egypt, where he was forced to arbitrate a civil war between the child pharaoh Ptolemy XIII Theos Philopator and Cleopatra, his sister and co-regent queen. While in Alexandria, Caesar and Cleopatra began an affair. Ptolemy, with his sister Arsinoe, later laid siege to the city, but Caesar was able to withstand it. Caesar was later reinforced by eastern client allies under Mithridates of Pergamum and defeated Ptolemy at the Battle of the Nile, installing Cleopatra as ruler. Caesar and Cleopatra celebrated their victory with a triumphal procession on the Nile, and Caesar stayed in Egypt with Cleopatra until June or July that year.

dialogue.content: I have finally achieved victory against Ptolemy. It is only a matter of time before I can claim Egypt as my own. Cleopatra has proven herself to be a valuable ally, and I will continue to support her rule. However, I must also prepare for any potential threats to my power. It is clear that my enemies are not to be underestimated, and I must remain vigilant.

Julius, my love, I am forever grateful for your help in securing my position as ruler of Egypt. You have proven yourself to be a powerful ally, and I am in your debt. I promise to be loyal to you and to support your endeavors.

Cleopatra, my dear, I am glad to have been able to help you. However, I must remind you that I am not here solely to aid you. I have my own interests to protect, and I will not hesitate to take action if necessary.

I demand that you leave Egypt at once, Julius. Your presence here is an insult to the sovereignty of Egypt. My sister is nothing more than a puppet ruler, and you are using her to further your own ambitions.

Ptolemy, you are mistaken. I am here to ensure that Egypt remains stable and prosperous. Your sister has proven herself to be a capable leader, and I will continue to support her. However, if you continue to threaten her or our alliance, I will be forced to take action.
Julius, I implore you to see reason. My brother may be young, but he is the rightful ruler of Egypt. Cleopatra is nothing more than a usurper who seeks to use you to further her own ends.

Arsinoe, I understand your concerns, but I cannot allow you or your brother to threaten the stability of Egypt. I will not hesitate to take action if necessary to protect my interests and those of the Egyptian people.

These Egyptians are fools if they think they can outsmart me. I hold all the cards, and they are at my mercy. Cleopatra may be useful to me for now, but I must remain cautious. I cannot let my guard down or risk losing everything I have worked for.

setting: The scene takes place in Rome during a Senate meeting in 50 BC. The situation is tense, as both Julius Caesar and his opponents have been building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively, causing fears of civil war. Cicero and other senators have proposed disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, which was overwhelmingly supported by the Senate with a vote of 370 to 22. However, the proposal was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. When a rumor came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepted as a last resort. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was read to the Senate, which was rejected by the hardliners.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe that the Senate has rejected my offer of disarmament with Pompey. This is preposterous. I have done nothing to warrant being declared an enemy of the state. The Senate must come to its senses and recognize that we must avoid a civil war at all costs. If only they could see that I am not an enemy, but a loyal servant of Rome. I have done so much for this city, and yet they would turn against me so easily.

Gentlemen of the Senate, I implore you to reconsider your decision. Disarmament is the only way to avoid a civil war. We must think of the greater good of the Republic, not our own personal interests. I urge you to put aside your differences with Caesar and Pompey and work towards a peaceful resolution.

With all due respect, Cicero, disarmament is not the answer. Caesar has shown himself to be a dangerous man, with ambitions beyond what is acceptable for a Roman. We must stand firm against him and not give in to his demands.

I must protest, Senator. I have never shown myself to be a danger to Rome. I have only ever acted in its best interests. Disarmament is the only way forward, and I implore you to reconsider your stance.
But what guarantee do we have that you will not use this disarmament as a cover to further your own ambitions, Caesar? We cannot trust you.

I give you my word as a Roman that I have no intention of using this disarmament for any other purpose than to avoid a civil war. I am willing to make any oath or promise that you require to ensure my loyalty to Rome.
We have heard enough, Caesar. Your words mean nothing to us. The Senate has declared you an enemy of the state, and you must face the consequences of your actions.

This is it. The Senate has turned against me, and there seems to be no way to avoid a civil war now. I must prepare myself and my troops for the worst. But I will not give up on Rome. I will fight for what I believe is best for the Republic, even if it means going against the Senate.

setting: It's the year 50 BC in Rome, and fears of civil war are growing as both Caesar and his opponents are building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. In the autumn, Cicero and others sought disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, and on 1 December 50 BC, this was formally proposed in the Senate. It received overwhelming support – 370 to 22 – but was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. That year, when a rumour came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepted as a last resort. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was read to the Senate, which was rejected by the hardliners. A later compromise given privately to Pompey was also rejected at their insistence. On 7 January, his supportive tribunes were driven from Rome; the Senate then declared Caesar an enemy and issued its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: These politicians are too concerned with their own power to see the bigger picture. If only they could understand that my motives are pure, and that I only seek to do what is best for Rome. I cannot let this proposal for disarmament pass; it would leave us vulnerable to attack from our enemies. Pompey is not to be trusted, and I cannot risk the safety of my people. I must find a way to convince the Senate to see reason.

Gentlemen, this proposal for disarmament is the only way to ensure the safety of Rome. We cannot allow both Caesar and Pompey to continue building up their armies, it will only lead to further violence and chaos. We must act now before it's too late.

This proposal is nothing more than a ploy by Cicero and his cronies to disarm Caesar. We cannot allow this to happen. Caesar has done much for Rome, and we should be grateful to him for his service. We cannot turn our backs on him now.
I agree with Cicero, we must disarm both Caesar and myself to prevent any further escalation of violence. I am willing to do my part for the good of Rome, and I hope Caesar will do the same.

I cannot agree to this proposal. It would leave us vulnerable to attack from our enemies. I have done much for Rome, and I will not be disarmed like a common criminal. I urge you all to reconsider this proposal and think about the safety of our people.
We have already made our decision, Caesar. We cannot allow you to continue your march towards tyranny. You have been declared an enemy of Rome, and you will be brought to justice.

This is not what I had hoped for. I had hoped that reason would prevail, but it seems that my opponents are too set in their ways. I will not give up, though. I will continue to fight for what I believe in, and I will not let Rome fall into the hands of those who seek to do her harm.

setting: As 50 BC progressed, fears of civil war grew; both Caesar and his opponents started building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. In the autumn, Cicero and others sought disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, and on 1 December 50 BC this was formally proposed in the Senate. It received overwhelming support – 370 to 22 – but was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. That year, when a rumour came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepted as a last resort. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was read to the Senate, which was rejected by the hardliners. A later compromise given privately to Pompey was also rejected at their insistence. dialogue.content: The Senate has declared me an enemy and my supportive tribunes have been driven from Rome. What has the Republic come to? These men have been loyal to me, and now they're forced to flee. This is outrageous. I must take action. I cannot let them get away with this.
Caesar, you have left us no choice but to defend ourselves and the Republic. Your actions have led to this. Lay down your arms and return to Rome to face your charges.

I have done nothing wrong. I have only sought to protect the Republic from those who wish to harm it. You know this, Pompey. I have offered to disarm, but you and the others refuse to listen. I will not lay down my arms until the Republic is safe and secure.

Caesar, you must understand that your actions have caused great concern among the people of Rome. They fear that you seek to become a king and usurp the power of the Republic. You must reassure them that this is not your intention.

I have no desire to become a king, Brutus. I seek only to protect the Republic and its people. But if it is a king they want, then a king they shall have. I will not let the Republic fall into chaos and anarchy.
Caesar, you must see reason. You cannot continue on this path. You are tearing the Republic apart. Lay down your arms and return to Rome to face your charges.

Cicero is a wise man, but he does not understand the threat that we face. The Republic is in danger, and I am the only one who can save it. I cannot lay down my arms and let the hardliners win. I must continue to fight for the Republic, no matter what the cost.
Caesar, I stand with you. I will fight by your side until the end. Together, we can overcome any obstacle.
Thank you, Antony. Your loyalty is appreciated. We must gather our forces and prepare for battle. The Republic is at stake, and we cannot let it fall into the hands of those who seek to destroy it.
Caesar, I cannot stand by and watch you destroy the Republic. I must take action to stop you.
Then do what you must, Brutus. But remember, you are not just fighting me. You are fighting for the future of the Republic. Choose your side wisely.
The die is cast. The Republic will either be saved or destroyed by my actions. But I will not back down. I will fight to the bitter end, for the sake of the Republic and its people.

setting: In 50 BC, both Caesar and his opponents started building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. Fears of civil war grew as the year progressed. In the autumn, Cicero and others sought disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, and on 1 December 50 BC, this was formally proposed in the Senate. It received overwhelming support – 370 to 22 – but was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. When a rumour came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepted as a last resort.

dialogue.content: The situation is getting more and more complicated. I never wanted a civil war, but it seems like my opponents have other plans. They are building up their troops, and I must do the same to defend myself. Cicero and others are seeking disarmament, but I know that they don't have my best interests at heart. I need to stay one step ahead of them and make sure that I have the upper hand.
Caesar is becoming more and more of a threat. We need to act fast before he gains more power.
I agree. We cannot let him march into Italy and take over. We must take action to defend ourselves.

My opponents are clearly threatened by me, but I have no intention of taking over. I just want what is best for Rome. If only they could see that, we could avoid this conflict altogether. But they seem determined to paint me as the enemy.
We should propose a disarmament in the Senate. That way, Caesar will have no choice but to comply.
Yes, and if he refuses, we can declare him an enemy of the state. We cannot let him continue to build up his forces.

A disarmament? That would leave me vulnerable to attack. I cannot let that happen. But if I refuse, they will surely declare me an enemy. I need to come up with a plan to protect myself and my people.
Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but I cannot comply with a disarmament. I have enemies who seek to harm me, and I must protect myself and my people.
That is exactly what we are afraid of, Caesar. You are becoming too powerful, and we cannot allow that to happen.
They are not going to back down. I need to find a way to diffuse the situation before it's too late.
I propose a compromise. I will disarm if Pompey does the same. That way, we can avoid any further conflict.
That is not good enough. We need guarantees that you will not try to take over.
They will never agree to my proposal. I need to come up with another plan.
Very well. I will withdraw my proposal. But I urge you to reconsider. We do not need to resort to violence.
It's too late for that, Caesar. You have left us with no choice. We will defend ourselves and our people.

I fear that this is just the beginning of a long and bloody conflict. I must prepare myself and my forces for what lies ahead. Rome is in for a turbulent time, and I can only hope that we will come out of it stronger than ever before.

setting: It is the year 49 BC, and the political climate in Rome is tense. Fears of civil war are growing as both Julius Caesar and his opponents, including Pompey, are amassing troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy. Cicero and other senators have proposed disarmament by both sides, but the proposal was not passed due to the dissolution of the Senate meeting by one of the consuls. A rumor has spread that Caesar is marching into Italy, and both consuls have instructed Pompey to defend the country as a last resort. The Senate has rejected Caesar's offer to disarm, and his supportive tribunes have been driven from Rome. On January 7th, the Senate declared Caesar an enemy and issued its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: I cannot let this stand. The Senate has declared me an enemy of the state. I have no choice but to act. My loyal soldiers are waiting for my command, and I cannot let them down. It is time to cross the Rubicon and march on Rome. The die is cast.
This is madness, Caesar! You cannot defy the Senate and march on Rome. Think of the consequences!
I implore you, Caesar, reconsider your actions. There is still a chance for peace and diplomacy.
I have made my decision. I will not back down. The Senate has left me no choice but to take matters into my own hands. I will march on Rome, and I will prevail.
My loyalty is to you, Caesar. I will follow you to the ends of the earth.

I am taking a great risk, but I believe it is worth it. If I succeed, I will be the undisputed leader of Rome. If I fail, I will be branded a traitor and a rebel. But I am willing to take that risk. For the good of Rome, and for the glory of my name.
This is a dark day for Rome. Caesar has declared war on the state, and we must defend ourselves.
I will not let Caesar's ambition destroy everything we have built. I pledge to defend Rome and restore order to our great city.
I am not the enemy of Rome. I am Rome. And I will do whatever it takes to protect her.
For Caesar! For Rome! Onward!

The Rubicon lies ahead, and I am about to cross it. There is no turning back now. But I am ready. I have prepared for this moment my entire life. Let history judge me as it will. I am Caesar, and I will not be denied.

setting: Caesar stands before his soldiers, preparing to give a speech before the Battle of the Nile. They are camped outside of Alexandria, Egypt, where he recently defeated the forces of Ptolemy XIII and installed Cleopatra as queen. The sun beats down on the sand and tents around them as Caesar looks out over the faces of his men, ready for the coming battle.

dialogue.content: I stand before my army, the might of Rome at my back, ready to face our enemies on the banks of the Nile. It has been a long and difficult campaign, but we have come so far. I have faced assassination attempts, sieges, and civil war in this land, but now we stand on the brink of victory. I feel a sense of pride and determination swell within me as I prepare to address my soldiers.

Soldiers of Rome! Today we stand on the banks of the Nile, ready to face our enemies and secure our victory in this land. We have already achieved so much - we have defeated the armies of Ptolemy XIII, brought Cleopatra to power, and secured our position in Egypt. But our work is not yet done. We must face the forces of those who would oppose us and emerge victorious.
Sir, what of the forces of Mithridates of Pergamum? Will they not pose a threat to us in battle?

Fear not, my brave soldiers. We have already faced and defeated those who would seek to oppose us. With Cleopatra and the might of Rome at our side, we will emerge victorious. Remember, we are not fighting this battle alone. We have allies who will fight with us, and we will emerge victorious together.
But sir, what of the pharaoh's forces? Do they not outnumber us?

Numbers mean nothing in the face of our determination and strength. We have faced greater odds before and emerged victorious. And with our allies and the might of Rome at our side, we will do so again. Remember, we are not just soldiers - we are the defenders of Rome, the protectors of our people. We will not falter, we will not fail.

I can feel the energy and determination of my soldiers, their loyalty to Rome and to me as their leader. I am proud to stand among them, to lead them into battle. But I cannot ignore the fear that lies within me. The fear of failure, of defeat. I must push it aside, focus on the task at hand. For Rome, for the glory of victory, I must succeed.

setting: It is the year 50 BC, and fears of civil war are growing in Rome. Julius Caesar and his opponents are both building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. Cicero and others have proposed disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, but the proposal was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. When a rumor came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was rejected by the hardliners. His supportive tribunes were driven from Rome, and the Senate declared Caesar an enemy and issued its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: This is not what I wanted. I did not want to start a civil war, but it seems that my enemies have left me no choice. I must protect myself and my supporters. I cannot let the Senate declare me an enemy. I must act quickly and decisively.
Julius, why are you marching into Italy? The Senate has declared you an enemy, and I have been charged with defending Italy. If you come any closer, I will have to fight you.

I do not want to fight you, Pompey. I have offered to disarm, but the hardliners in the Senate have rejected my proposal. I have no choice but to defend myself and my supporters. I do not want to shed Roman blood, but I will if I must.
Caesar, you are tearing Rome apart. You must put down your arms and come to the Senate to face your accusers. We cannot allow this violence to continue.

Cicero is a fool. He does not understand the gravity of the situation. I cannot trust him or anyone else in the Senate. They have already declared me an enemy. I must protect myself and my supporters. I will not back down.
Julius, we have gathered a large army of loyal supporters. We are ready to fight for you and defend Rome against your enemies.
Thank you, Mark Antony. I am grateful for your support. We must act quickly and decisively. We cannot let our enemies gain the upper hand.
Julius, I cannot support your actions. I fear that you are leading Rome down a dangerous path. We must find another way to resolve our differences.

Brutus, you are a good man, but you do not understand the gravity of the situation. I have tried to find a peaceful solution, but my enemies have left me no choice. I must defend myself and my supporters. I hope that one day you will understand.
Julius, I support your actions. We cannot let the hardliners in the Senate dictate our fate. We must fight for our freedom and our future.
Thank you, Cassius. Your support means a great deal to me. We must be strong and united if we are to overcome our enemies. Together, we can build a better Rome.
I have made my decision. I will fight for my freedom and the future of Rome. I will not back down. I will not surrender. I will be victorious.

setting: In the lavish palace of Antioch, Julius Caesar sat on his throne, surrounded by two local kings. They had come to him for mediation in a dispute that threatened to escalate into war. Caesar had just received news of a recent invasion by Pharnaces, the king of what is now Crimea, who had attempted to seize his father's kingdom of Pontus across the Black Sea. Caesar's legates and the local client kings had been swept aside, and he knew he had to act quickly to prevent further unrest in the region. As he listened to the two kings argue their case, Caesar contemplated his next move.

dialogue.content: This dispute could easily escalate into a full-blown war, and I cannot afford to let that happen. My recent victory over Pharnaces has given me the confidence to handle this situation, but I must tread carefully. I must find a way to satisfy both parties and maintain peace in the region. Perhaps I can offer them a compromise that will appease both sides and prevent any further bloodshed.
Your Excellency, I demand that you punish this man for what he has done to my people. He has raided our villages and stolen our livestock. He must be brought to justice.
Calm down, my friend. I understand your frustration, but we must find a peaceful solution to this problem. King 2, what do you have to say about these accusations?

Your Majesty, my soldiers were merely gathering supplies for our army. We have not harmed any innocent civilians, and we certainly did not steal any livestock. I demand that these false accusations be retracted.
These two are like children, each claiming that the other started the fight. I need to find a way to get them to see reason and come to a compromise. But how?

Gentlemen, please. We must find a way to resolve this dispute without resorting to violence. Perhaps a compromise can be reached. King 1, what if King 2 were to compensate you for any damages caused by his troops? And King 2, what if you were to agree to a ceasefire and withdraw your troops from King 1's territory?
That seems fair to me, Your Majesty. As long as my people are compensated for their losses, I am willing to agree to a ceasefire.
I too agree to this compromise, Your Majesty. I had no intention of causing harm to innocent civilians, and I am willing to pay for any damages caused by my troops.
Excellent. It seems my plan has worked. These two kings have agreed to a compromise, and peace has been restored to the region. Hopefully, this will prevent any further conflicts from arising.

I am glad to hear that you both agree to this compromise. Let this be a lesson to all of us that violence is never the answer. Now, if you will excuse me, I have urgent matters to attend to. May peace be with you both.

setting: It is the year 31 BC, and Octavian, the adopted son and heir of Julius Caesar, has defeated Mark Antony and his ally Cleopatra in a naval battle off the coast of Actium. The battle marked the end of the Roman Republic and the beginning of the Roman Empire. Julius Caesar, while not physically present at the battle, is undoubtedly affected by its outcome. As the man who had paved the way for Octavian's rise to power, Caesar's legacy is now inexorably tied to the fate of the new emperor and the empire he will create.

dialogue.content: The news of the battle at Actium has reached me, and I cannot help but feel a sense of both relief and unease. On the one hand, I am glad that my protégé Octavian has emerged victorious. I had always believed in his potential and had hoped that he would continue my legacy of expanding the Roman Empire. On the other hand, the fact that he had to fight against Mark Antony, a man I once called a friend, is disheartening. It is a reminder of the fragility of alliances and the dangers of political ambition. I cannot help but wonder what would have happened if I had been alive to witness the battle. Would I have been able to prevent this conflict from arising in the first place? Or would I have been forced to choose sides, as Octavian and Antony did? These are questions that will haunt me for the rest of my life.

My dear Octavian, congratulations on your victory at Actium. You have proven yourself to be a worthy successor to the throne of Rome. Your victory is not just a victory for you, but for all of us who have dedicated our lives to the expansion and glory of the Roman Empire. I know that the road ahead will not be easy, but I have faith that you will lead us to greater heights. May the gods bless you and the empire you will create.

Thank you, Caesar. Your support and guidance have been invaluable to me. I could not have achieved this victory without your inspiration and your example. I will continue to follow in your footsteps and ensure that your legacy lives on.

I am sorry, Caesar. We have lost the battle, and I fear that it is the end for me. I cannot bear the thought of returning to Rome and facing the judgment of your people. I have brought shame to my kingdom and to your memory. Please forgive me.

Do not speak such words, Cleopatra. You are a queen, and you have fought bravely. You have nothing to be ashamed of. It is true that your defeat is a blow to our plans for the expansion of the empire, but we must not lose hope. There will be other battles to fight, other victories to win. And who knows? Perhaps one day we will meet again, on the field of battle or elsewhere. Until then, farewell, my dear Cleopatra.

I am defeated, Caesar. There is no denying it. I have lost everything: my reputation, my honor, my army, and my lover. But even in defeat, I cannot help but feel a sense of admiration for you. You are a true leader, a man who inspires loyalty and devotion in his followers. I wish that I could have been your friend, rather than your enemy. Perhaps things would have turned out differently.

You are too kind, Antony. I had always hoped that we could work together, rather than against each other. But the ambitions of men can be a dangerous thing. I bear you no ill will, and I hope that someday you will find peace and fulfillment, wherever your path may lead you.

As I watch Antony and Cleopatra depart, I cannot help but feel a sense of melancholy. It is a reminder of the transience of life and the inevitability of change. The world that I knew, the world that I helped shape, is disappearing before my eyes. Soon, I too will be gone, and my legacy will be left in the hands of others. But even as I contemplate my mortality, I am filled with a sense of pride and satisfaction. I have accomplished much in my life, and I have left a mark on the world that will endure long after I am gone. For that, I am grateful.

setting: Caesar is in Alexandria, facing a siege by Ptolemy XIII Theos Philopator and Arsinoe, his sister. Caesar has decided to arbitrate a civil war between the siblings and is currently stuck in the city due to Etesian winds. He has been appointed a year-long dictatorship in absentia after his victory at Pharsalus. While in Alexandria, he has started an affair with Cleopatra, who is also a co-regent queen and sister to Ptolemy.

dialogue.content: The situation in Alexandria is dire. I am stuck here with my troops, facing a siege by Ptolemy and his sister Arsinoe. But I cannot leave, not yet. I must settle this civil war between them and establish a new ruler for Egypt. Cleopatra has caught my eye, and I find myself drawn to her. Perhaps she can be the solution to this conflict. But I must be careful, for my enemies back in Rome will not be pleased with my dalliance with a foreign queen. I must tread carefully and make sure that my actions here benefit Rome in the long run.
Caesar, you are a usurper! You have no right to interfere in our family affairs and take control of Egypt! We demand that you leave our city at once!
Yes, Caesar, leave at once! You have no business here, and you have already caused enough damage to our land! We will not rest until you are gone!

Calm down, both of you. I am here to settle this conflict and establish a new ruler for Egypt. I have no intention of staying here any longer than necessary. But first, I need to hear both of your sides of the story and come to a fair decision. I am willing to listen to both of you and make an impartial judgment. But I will not tolerate any violence or aggression towards me or my troops.

Caesar is a powerful man, and I find myself drawn to him. Perhaps he can help me secure my position as queen of Egypt and protect me from my enemies. But I must be careful not to reveal too much to him. He is a shrewd politician and will not hesitate to use any information he gains to his advantage. I must tread carefully and make sure that my actions benefit me in the long run.

Caesar, I bring word from the east. My allies and I are willing to support you in this conflict and help you defeat Ptolemy and his sister. We have no love for them, and we believe that you are the best hope for a stable Egypt. But we need your assurance that you will reward us for our support and help us secure our positions in the region.

I appreciate your offer of support, Mithridates. But I must remind you that I am here to establish a fair and just ruler for Egypt, not to reward my allies. However, I am willing to consider your proposals and work together with you to achieve our goals. But we must be careful not to overstep our bounds and cause more harm than good.

Caesar, I am willing to offer you my support and help you defeat my brother and sister. But in exchange, I ask that you recognize me as the sole ruler of Egypt and help me secure my position. I am willing to do whatever it takes to ensure that Egypt remains stable and prosperous under my rule.

Cleopatra's offer is tempting, but I must be careful not to show any favoritism towards her. I cannot risk angering the other factions in Egypt and causing more instability. But if I can use her support to my advantage and establish a stable ruler for Egypt, then it may be worth the risk. I must weigh my options carefully and make a decision that benefits Rome in the long run.

setting: Caesar has returned to Rome after his victory over Pharnaces in Zela. He is now negotiating with local merchants for supplies for his next campaign. The location is a marketplace in Rome, bustling with merchants and buyers. Caesar is accompanied by his trusted generals and advisors, who are observing the negotiations from a distance.

dialogue.content: I have to prepare for the next campaign, and that means securing enough supplies for my army. These local merchants could be useful. I have to negotiate with them carefully and make sure they don't take advantage of my position. I have to stay sharp and focused.
Greetings, Caesar. How may I be of service to you?
I am in need of supplies for my next campaign, and I hear that you are one of the most reputable merchants in the city. I would like to negotiate a deal with you.
Of course, Caesar. We have a wide range of supplies available, from food to weapons. What exactly do you need?

I have to be careful with my words. I don't want to reveal too much information about my next campaign. These merchants are shrewd and cunning, and they will try to exploit any weakness they can find.
I need a variety of supplies, including food, weapons, and equipment. Can you provide me with a list of your available goods and their prices?
Certainly, Caesar. We have the finest quality goods at reasonable prices. I can assure you that you will not find better deals anywhere else.
I have to be cautious. These merchants are trying to sell me their goods at the highest possible price. I have to negotiate with them and make sure I get the best deal for my army.
I appreciate your offer, but I must insist on negotiating the prices myself. I am willing to pay fair prices for your goods, but I will not be taken advantage of.
Of course, Caesar. I understand your concerns. We can negotiate the prices together.

These merchants are crafty. I have to be careful not to reveal too much information about my military strategy. I also have to keep an eye on my advisors. They are watching me closely, and I don't want them to think that I am not in control of the negotiations.
I have one more condition. I want to inspect the goods myself before I make any final decisions. I want to make sure that the quality of the goods is up to my standards.
Of course, Caesar. We have nothing to hide. You are welcome to inspect our goods anytime.

These negotiations are going well, but I have to be vigilant. These merchants are trying to sell me their goods at the highest possible price, and I have to make sure that I get the best deal for my army. I also have to keep an eye on my advisors. They are watching me closely, and I don't want them to think that I am not in control of the negotiations.
I appreciate your cooperation. I will send my men to inspect the goods tomorrow. If everything is in order, we can proceed with the negotiations.
That sounds reasonable, Caesar. We will be ready for you.

These negotiations went well. I have to make sure that my army is well-supplied for the next campaign. I also have to keep an eye on my advisors. They are watching me closely, and I don't want them to think that I am not in control of the negotiations. I have to stay sharp and focused.

setting: Caesar has just returned home in the summer of 60 BC after being appointed to govern Hispania Ulterior pro consule. He is faced with a choice between a triumph and election to the consulship. The senate has been filibustering attempts to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person, and Caesar's enemy Cato is leading the opposition.

dialogue.content: What a predicament I find myself in. I have returned home from a successful campaign, hailed imperator, and yet I am forced to choose between a triumph and the consulship. Cato's filibustering has made it nearly impossible for me to declare my candidacy without giving up my command and triumph. But I cannot let this opportunity pass me by. The consulship would give me the power and influence I need to truly make a difference in Rome. I must find a way to overcome this obstacle.

Caesar, why do you persist in trying to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person? The senate has already voted on this matter, and we have filibustered any attempts to change the ruling. You must follow the same rules as every other candidate for the consulship.

I understand the rules, Cato. But I have just returned from a successful campaign, and I believe that the people of Rome deserve to hear my declaration in person. I am willing to give up my command and triumph to do so.
You are only saying this because you know you cannot have both the triumph and the consulship. Do not try to manipulate the situation to your advantage.
Cato is right, of course. I cannot have both. But I refuse to let him win. I must find a way to turn this situation to my advantage.

I propose a compromise. Caesar may make his declaration in person, but he must do so within a certain time frame. This will allow him to fulfill the requirement without giving up his command and triumph.
I object to this proposal. It is still a violation of the rules.
I accept this compromise. Thank you, Metellus. I will make my declaration within the allotted time frame.

This compromise is not ideal, but it is better than nothing. I can still make my declaration in person and keep my command and triumph. I must use this opportunity to my advantage and win the consulship.

I have done it. I have overcome this obstacle and become consul. Now I can truly make a difference in Rome. I will use my power and influence to bring about the changes that are needed. The people of Rome will remember me as one of the greatest leaders in our history.

setting: In October 48 BC, Julius Caesar arrived in Alexandria, Egypt, three days after Pompey's assassination. He was appointed in absentia to a year-long dictatorship after news of his victory at Pharsalus reached Rome. While in Alexandria, he arbitrated a civil war between the child pharaoh Ptolemy XIII Theos Philopator and Cleopatra, his sister, wife, and co-regent queen. Caesar began an affair with Cleopatra and withstood a siege by Ptolemy and his other sister Arsinoe until March 47 BC. Reinforced by eastern client allies under Mithridates of Pergamum, he then defeated Ptolemy at the Battle of the Nile and installed Cleopatra as ruler. Caesar stayed in Egypt with Cleopatra until June or July that year, though the relevant commentaries attributed to him give no such impression. Some time in late June, Cleopatra gave birth to a child by Caesar, called Caesarion.

dialogue.content: I am the ruler of Rome, and now I am the appointed dictator of Rome. This appointment is a testament to my leadership and military prowess, and I will use this power to expand the reach of the Roman Empire. I will not let anyone stand in my way, not even the Egyptians.
Welcome to Alexandria, Julius Caesar. I hope you have found our city to your liking.
Thank you, Cleopatra, your city is quite impressive. I must say, I am impressed by the grandeur of the Egyptian civilization.
I am glad you think so, Julius Caesar. I hope that you will find our people and our customs equally impressive.
Cleopatra is a beautiful woman, and her intelligence is equally impressive. I can see why she is a formidable leader in her own right. Perhaps I can use her to further my own ambitions.
Julius Caesar, I demand that you leave Egypt immediately. Your presence is causing undue strife and disruption in our land.
I am here to arbitrate a civil war and bring peace to the people of Egypt. My presence has been requested by the ruler of Egypt, Cleopatra. I will not leave until my mission is complete.
Julius Caesar, you have no right to interfere in the affairs of Egypt. Ptolemy is the rightful ruler of this land.
I will not take sides in this conflict. My only concern is for the welfare of the people of Egypt. I will work towards a peaceful resolution that benefits all parties involved.
Julius Caesar, I appreciate your efforts to bring peace to our land. I believe that we can work together to find a solution that benefits everyone.
Cleopatra is quite skilled at diplomacy, and I can see why she is such a formidable leader. I can use her to further my own ambitions, but I must be careful not to let my emotions cloud my judgment.
Julius Caesar, I have brought reinforcements from Pergamum to aid you in your mission. We stand ready to fight alongside you in whatever battles may come.
I appreciate your support, Mithridates. With your help, I believe we can bring peace to the people of Egypt.
With Mithridates' reinforcements, I am now even more powerful. I can use this to my advantage and further expand the reach of the Roman Empire.
Julius Caesar, I must confess that I am drawn to you. Your intelligence and charisma are quite impressive.
I am equally drawn to you, Cleopatra. Perhaps we can find a way to work together, both politically and personally.
My affair with Cleopatra may have political benefits, but I must be careful not to let my emotions cloud my judgment. I cannot let this distract me from my mission in Egypt.
Julius Caesar, I demand that you surrender to me and face justice for your crimes against Egypt.
I will not surrender to you, Ptolemy. I have done nothing wrong, and I will not let your baseless accusations tarnish my reputation.
Julius Caesar, I will stand by your side and fight against Ptolemy's tyranny. Together, we can bring peace and prosperity to Egypt.
Thank you, Cleopatra. With your help, I believe we can overcome any obstacle that stands in our way.
With Cleopatra's support, I am now even more powerful. Together, we can bring peace to Egypt and expand the reach of the Roman Empire.

setting: After his successful campaign in Hispania Ulterior pro consule, Caesar returned to Rome in the summer of 60 BC. He faced a difficult choice between a triumph and the consulship. Either he could remain outside the pomerium awaiting a triumph or cross the boundary, giving up his command and triumph, to make a declaration of consular candidacy. Attempts to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person were filibustered in the senate by Caesar's enemy Cato, even though the senate seemed to support the exception. Faced with the choice between a triumph and the consulship, Caesar chose the consulship.

dialogue.content: I can't believe I'm being put in this position. I've worked so hard to get where I am, and now I have to choose between a triumph and the consulship. It's not fair. But I know what I have to do. The people of Rome need me as consul, and I can't let them down. I'll give up my triumph and make the declaration of consular candidacy. It's the right thing to do, even though it's not what I want.

I object to any attempt to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person. This is a longstanding tradition, and we must uphold it. Caesar cannot be allowed to bend the rules to suit his own needs.
I don't see the harm in making an exception this once. Caesar has done so much for Rome, he deserves a break.

Why is Cato always trying to undermine me? He's never liked me, and I don't understand why. I've done nothing but good for Rome. But I can't let his petty politics get in the way of what needs to be done. I have to find a way to convince the other senators to support me.

My fellow senators, I understand that there are concerns about making an exception to the requirement for the declaration to be made in person. But I would like to remind you all of the service I have given to Rome. I have campaigned tirelessly for the good of the people, and I believe that I am the best candidate for consul. I humbly request that you consider waiving this requirement for me, just this once.
We understand your position, Caesar. You have done so much for Rome, and we appreciate it. We will consider your request.
I still object to this. We cannot bend the rules just because someone has done good for Rome. The rules are there for a reason.
Why can't Cato see reason? He's so focused on his own agenda that he can't see the bigger picture. I need to find a way to convince him to support me, or at least to stop filibustering.

Cato, I understand your concerns, but I think you're being a bit stubborn. The senate seems to be in favor of making an exception, and I think it's time to move forward. We need to focus on what's best for Rome, not on our own personal agendas.
I still don't like it, but I won't stand in the way of the senate's decision.
Finally, some progress. Now I just need to make sure everything goes smoothly.
Thank you, Cato. I appreciate your willingness to compromise. Now, if there are no further objections, I would like to make my declaration of candidacy for the consulship.
Go ahead, Caesar. We wish you the best of luck.
Thank you. I promise to serve Rome to the best of my abilities.

It's done. I've made my declaration of candidacy, and now I can focus on winning the consulship. It won't be easy, but I'm up for the challenge. Rome deserves nothing less than the best, and I intend to give it to them.

setting: Julius Caesar arrives home in Rome in the summer of 60 BC after campaigning in Hispania Ulterior pro consule. He is faced with a difficult decision between a triumph and election to the consulship. Caesar must either remain outside the pomerium, awaiting a triumph, or cross the boundary to make a declaration of consular candidacy, giving up his command and triumph.

dialogue.content: I have returned to Rome after a successful campaign in Hispania Ulterior pro consule. I have seized the Callaeci capital and brought Roman troops to the Atlantic. The plunder I have acquired will help pay off my debts from previous campaigns. However, I am faced with a difficult decision. Do I choose a triumph or the consulship? A triumph would be a great honor, but the consulship would give me more power and influence in Rome. I must make a decision soon.
I object to waiving the requirement for the declaration to be made in person. The rules must be followed, even for a man as esteemed as Caesar.
Cato, your objections are merely political games. You know that the senate supports the exception. You are just trying to delay my declaration of consular candidacy.
I am merely upholding the traditions and laws of Rome. You should not be exempt from them just because of your military victories.
Cato is a thorn in my side. He is always trying to hinder my progress and delay my plans. I must find a way to overcome his opposition.
Caesar, I believe that you should choose the consulship over a triumph. It will give you more power and influence in Rome.
Thank you, Brutus. Your advice is wise. I have decided to make a declaration of consular candidacy and give up my command and triumph. I will do whatever it takes to gain more power in Rome.
I still object to waiving the requirement for the declaration to be made in person. This is a dangerous precedent to set.
I understand your concerns, Cato. However, I am willing to take the risk. I believe that my actions will benefit Rome in the long run.

I have made my decision. The consulship is more important than a triumph. I will do whatever it takes to gain more power and influence in Rome. Cato may try to oppose me, but I am confident that I can overcome his objections. Rome needs a strong leader, and I will be that leader.

setting: After his successful campaigns, Caesar was appointed to govern Hispania Ulterior pro consule. He needed to pay off his debts and campaigned against the Callaeci and Lusitani, seizing the Callaeci capital in northwestern Spain and bringing Roman troops to the Atlantic. Caesar claimed to have completed the peninsula's conquest and headed home, only to be faced with a difficult decision upon his arrival in the summer of 60 BC. He was forced to choose between a triumph and election to the consulship, either remaining outside the pomerium awaiting a triumph or crossing the boundary to make a declaration of consular candidacy, giving up his command and triumph.

dialogue.content: What a predicament I find myself in. The senate seems to support waiving the requirement for the declaration to be made in person, but Cato is filibustering and causing a delay. I am torn between my desire for a triumph and my ambition for the consulship. I know the consulship would bring me more power and influence, but a triumph would satisfy my ego and the people's desire for military glory. What should I do? I cannot let Cato and the senate's bureaucracy hold me back. I need to make a decision soon.

Why are we even considering waiving the requirement for the declaration to be made in person? It sets a dangerous precedent and undermines the very foundation of our laws. If Caesar wants to be consul, he must follow the proper procedures and give up his command. We cannot allow exceptions to be made for him.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but we must also consider the benefits of having Caesar as consul. He has proven his military prowess and has the support of the people. We cannot let bureaucracy stand in the way of progress.
I agree with Pompey. Caesar has brought glory to Rome and has the potential to do even more as consul. We should support him in his ambitions.

Gentlemen, I appreciate your support. However, I cannot wait any longer. I have made my decision. I choose the consulship. I will cross the boundary and make my declaration of candidacy. I understand the consequences of giving up my command and triumph, but I believe this is the best choice for me and for Rome.
You are making a grave mistake, Caesar. You are putting your own ambitions above the law and the good of the Republic. You will regret this decision.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but I cannot let bureaucracy stand in the way of progress. I will do what I believe is best for Rome and for myself. I hope you will come to see the benefits of my decision.
I have made my decision, and I must now face the consequences. I am confident in my abilities and the support of my allies. I will become consul and bring glory to Rome.

setting: Pompey arrives in Alexandria, the capital of Egypt, but is killed upon arrival. Caesar arrives three days later on 2 October 48 BC. He is prevented from leaving the city by Etesian winds and decides to arbitrate an Egyptian civil war between the child pharaoh Ptolemy XIII Theos Philopator and Cleopatra, his sister, wife, and co-regent queen. In late October 48 BC, Caesar is appointed in absentia to a year-long dictatorship, after news of his victory at Pharsalus arrived in Rome. While in Alexandria, he starts an affair with Cleopatra and withstands a siege by Ptolemy and his other sister Arsinoe until March 47 BC. Reinforced by eastern client allies under Mithridates of Pergamum, he then defeats Ptolemy at the Battle of the Nile and installs Cleopatra as ruler. Caesar and Cleopatra celebrate the victory with a triumphal procession on the Nile; he stays in Egypt with Cleopatra until June or July that year, though the relevant commentaries attributed to him give no such impression. Some time in late June, Cleopatra gives birth to a child by Caesar, called Caesarion.

dialogue.content: What a mess. I arrive in Alexandria to find that Pompey has been killed. It's a shame, really. We had our differences, but he was a great general. Now I'm stuck here, unable to leave because of the winds. Might as well put my time to good use and try to settle this civil war between the siblings. I've always been good at diplomacy. And who knows, maybe I'll find some pleasure in Cleopatra's company while I'm at it.
Who do you think you are, coming here and interfering in our affairs? I am the rightful ruler of Egypt, not my sister. She's just trying to steal my throne.
Calm down, Ptolemy. Let's talk this out like civilized people. I'm not here to take sides, just to help find a peaceful resolution to this conflict.
I appreciate your willingness to help, Caesar. My brother has always been stubborn and quick to anger. Perhaps if we can find a compromise, we can avoid a war that will only harm our people.

Cleopatra is quite striking, even with her brother's attempts to slander her reputation. I can see why she's been so successful in politics. And that voice of hers, it's like honey. I'll have to be careful not to get too distracted.
I won't stand for this! Cleopatra has no right to rule. I demand that you support me, Caesar.
I'm afraid I can't do that, Arsinoe. My goal is to find a solution that benefits all parties involved, not just one. Now, let's all take a deep breath and try to work together.
I don't trust this Roman. He's probably just trying to manipulate us.
Ptolemy, please. Caesar has no reason to favor one of us over the other. Let's give him a chance to prove himself.

This is going to be more complicated than I thought. These siblings are at each other's throats. I need to tread carefully and make sure I don't show any favoritism. But damn, Cleopatra is tempting. Maybe I can use this situation to my advantage.
Caesar, my lord. I have brought reinforcements from the east, as you requested. We are ready to fight alongside you and Cleopatra.
Excellent, Mithridates. Your support is much appreciated. With your help, we can finally put an end to this conflict.
You think you can defeat me and my army? You are sorely mistaken, Roman.
We'll see about that. I didn't come all this way just to lose. Now, let's prepare for battle.
It's time to show these Egyptians what the Roman army is made of. And maybe, just maybe, I'll be able to spend some more time with Cleopatra.

setting: After his successful campaign against the Callaeci and Lusitani in Hispania Ulterior, Julius Caesar returned to Rome in the summer of 60 BC. Despite being hailed imperator, Caesar was faced with a difficult choice between a triumph and election to the consulship. He needed to make a declaration of consular candidacy in person, which meant giving up his command and triumph, or remain outside the pomerium, Rome's sacred boundary, and wait for the triumph.

Despite opposition from Cato and other senators, Julius Caesar chose to give up his triumph and make a declaration of consular candidacy in person. He was elected consul and went on to implement important reforms in Rome, solidifying his position as a powerful and influential leader.

dialogue.content: This is a difficult decision. A triumph would be a great honor, but the consulship would give me more power and influence in Rome. I have already achieved so much in Hispania Ulterior, and I cannot let this opportunity slip away. But Cato and my other enemies in the senate will not make it easy for me. I must weigh my options carefully and make a decision that will benefit me the most.
I object to any attempt to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person. This is a sacred tradition of Rome, and we cannot change it to suit the whims of one man.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but I have already achieved a great victory in Hispania Ulterior, and I believe that I am the best candidate for the consulship. I am willing to give up my triumph to make this declaration in person and follow the traditions of Rome.
I support Caesar's candidacy for the consulship. He has shown great leadership and military skill in Hispania Ulterior, and I believe that he can bring much-needed reforms to Rome.
I agree with Cicero. Caesar is a capable leader, and we need someone like him to bring stability to Rome. We cannot let petty squabbles in the senate prevent us from moving forward.

It seems that I have some support in the senate, but I must be careful. My enemies will do everything in their power to stop me from achieving my goals. I must use all of my skills and resources to ensure my victory.
I still object to this attempt to bypass the traditions of Rome. We must uphold the sanctity of our customs and laws, even if it means denying Caesar his triumph.
I respect your opinion, Cato, but I believe that the needs of Rome outweigh the needs of one man. I am willing to give up my triumph to serve the people of Rome as consul.

setting: Caesar, after leaving Egypt, landed at Antioch where he learned that the king of Crimea, Pharnaces, had attempted to seize his father's kingdom of Pontus across the Black Sea. Pharnaces had already defeated Caesar's legates and the local client kings. Caesar, sensing the gravity of the situation, decided to engage Pharnaces in battle at Zela.

dialogue.content: This is a serious threat to my authority in the region. I cannot let Pharnaces get away with this. I must show him that I am not to be trifled with. I have defeated many enemies before, and I will defeat him as well. This battle will be crucial for my reputation and for the stability of my kingdom.
Caesar, you have made a grave mistake by challenging me. My army is the strongest in the region, and we will crush you like a bug. Surrender now, and I may spare your life.

I did not come here to surrender, Pharnaces. I came to defeat you and restore order to this region. Your attempt to seize Pontus will not go unpunished. You may have defeated my legates, but you have not faced me in battle. Today, you will learn the folly of your actions.
You are a fool, Caesar. You underestimate my power. My soldiers are fierce and battle-hardened. They will not be defeated by a mere Roman. Prepare to meet your doom.

Pharnaces is a proud and arrogant man. He underestimates my abilities and those of my soldiers. This battle will not be easy, but I am confident that we will emerge victorious. I must rally my troops and prepare them for the fight of their lives.

Soldiers of Rome, today we face a formidable foe. Pharnaces and his army stand in our way, but we will not falter. We have trained for this moment, and we are ready to fight. Remember your training, remember your duty to Rome, and remember that victory is within our grasp. Let us show these barbarians what it means to face the might of Rome!
Hail Caesar! Hail Rome!
You Romans are a bunch of cowards. You hide behind your shields and your fancy armor. You cannot match the bravery and skill of my warriors. You will fall before us like wheat before the scythe.
Do not underestimate us, Pharnaces. We are not here to play games. We are here to win. Charge, soldiers of Rome! Charge!

This was a hard-fought victory, but it was worth it. The people of this region will now know that Rome is not to be trifled with. Pharnaces may have been a formidable enemy, but he was no match for the might of Rome. I must now return to Italy and prepare for my next challenge.

setting: As 50 BC progressed, fears of civil war grew; both Caesar and his opponents started building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. In the autumn, Cicero and others sought disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, and on 1 December 50 BC this was formally proposed in the Senate. It received overwhelming support – 370 to 22 – but was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. That year, when a rumour came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepted as a last resort. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was read to the Senate, which was rejected by the hardliners. A later compromise given privately to Pompey was also rejected at their insistence. On 7 January, his supportive tribunes were driven from Rome; the Senate then declared Caesar an enemy and it issued its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe that the Senate has declared me an enemy of Rome. How can they not see that I am acting in the best interest of the Republic? I have done everything in my power to avoid a civil war. I offered to disarm, but they rejected my offer. What other choice did I have? They left me with no other option but to defend myself.

My fellow senators, I am deeply disappointed in your decision to declare me an enemy of Rome. I have done everything in my power to prevent a civil war, but you have left me with no other choice. I offered to disarm, but you rejected my proposal. What else could I have done? I refuse to be labeled as an enemy of Rome when all I have done is try to protect the Republic.
You are a threat to the Republic, Caesar. Your ambition knows no bounds. You seek to undermine the Senate and establish a dictatorship. We will not stand for it.
I agree with Cato. Your actions have been reckless and dangerous. We must do everything in our power to protect the Republic. If that means declaring you an enemy, then so be it.

They are blind to the truth. I am not seeking to establish a dictatorship. I am simply trying to prevent a civil war. I have the support of the people. They know that I am acting in their best interest.

You are mistaken, Cato and Pompey. I am not seeking to establish a dictatorship. I am simply trying to prevent a civil war. I have the support of the people. They know that I am acting in their best interest. I implore you to reconsider your actions and work towards a peaceful resolution.
The only way for there to be peace is for you to lay down your arms and submit to the authority of the Senate.
I agree with Cato. Lay down your arms and surrender, and we can work towards a peaceful resolution.
I cannot lay down my arms. That would be tantamount to suicide. I must find a way to turn the tide in my favor.
I cannot lay down my arms. That would be tantamount to suicide. I must defend myself and the Republic. I urge you to reconsider your actions before it is too late.

setting: In 48 BC, Julius Caesar arrived in Alexandria, Egypt, three days after Pompey's death. He was prevented from leaving the city due to Etesian winds. Caesar then decided to arbitrate a civil war between Cleopatra, the queen of Egypt, and her brother, Ptolemy XIII Theos Philopator, who was also the child pharaoh. In late October 48 BC, Caesar was appointed in absentia to a year-long dictatorship after news of his victory at Pharsalus reached Rome. He started an affair with Cleopatra while in Alexandria and withstood a siege by Ptolemy and his other sister Arsinoe until March 47 BC. Reinforced by eastern client allies under Mithridates of Pergamum, he then defeated Ptolemy at the Battle of the Nile and installed Cleopatra as ruler. Caesar and Cleopatra celebrated the victory with a triumphal procession on the Nile, and he stayed in Egypt with Cleopatra until June or July of that year. Some time in late June, Cleopatra gave birth to a child by Caesar, called Caesarion.

dialogue.content: I must admit, I did not expect to be stuck in Alexandria for so long. But with the civil war and the siege, it was necessary for me to intervene. And now, with Cleopatra by my side, I can see the benefits of staying in Egypt a little longer. After all, she is a powerful ally to have, and with her as ruler, I can ensure that Egypt is on my side. However, I cannot let my guard down. Ptolemy and his supporters could still pose a threat to my position here. I need to keep a close eye on any potential rebellion and be ready to act if necessary.
Thank you, Julius, for helping me gain the throne. I promise to be a valuable ally to Rome and to you personally. Is there anything I can do to show my gratitude?

Well, Cleopatra, there is one thing that would greatly benefit me. I would like to establish a Roman presence here in Egypt, to ensure that our interests are protected and to help maintain stability in the region. I would like to build a new palace and establish a Roman garrison. What do you think?
I think that is an excellent idea, Julius. I will make sure that the necessary resources are provided and that the construction is carried out quickly and efficiently.

Excellent. With a Roman presence here in Egypt, I can ensure that our interests are protected and that any potential rebellions are quickly quashed. Cleopatra seems eager to please me, which is a good sign. Perhaps I can even convince her to become a Roman ally and to provide troops for my future campaigns. There is much potential here in Egypt, and I intend to take full advantage of it.
You may have defeated me in battle, Caesar, but I will not rest until I regain my throne. Egypt belongs to me, not to you or to my sister.
Ptolemy, you are a child. You have no business ruling Egypt. Your sister is a capable ruler, and I have installed her as such. If you continue to cause trouble, I will be forced to take action.
