I will not be intimidated by you, Caesar. I have loyal supporters who will help me regain my rightful place.

This Ptolemy is quite a nuisance. I cannot allow him to cause any more trouble. Perhaps it is time to take more drastic action and eliminate him once and for all. But I must be careful. I do not want to upset the Egyptian people or cause a rebellion. I need to find a way to remove Ptolemy without causing too much unrest.
Julius, I have been thinking. I would like to offer you something that I think you will find very valuable.
What is it, Cleopatra? You have already done so much for me and for Rome.
I am willing to provide you with a fleet of ships, to help you in your future conquests. With my naval power at your disposal, you will be unstoppable.

This is a generous offer indeed. With a fleet of ships at my disposal, I can expand the Roman Empire even further. I must accept this offer, but I must also be careful not to rely too heavily on Cleopatra's support. I cannot afford to be seen as a puppet of the Egyptians.
Thank you, Cleopatra. Your offer is most generous, and I accept it with gratitude. We shall make a powerful team, you and I. Together, we can achieve great things.
I am honored to be your ally, Julius. I will do everything in my power to ensure our success.

With Cleopatra's support and the loyalty of the Egyptian people, I can achieve great things. The Roman Empire will be stronger than ever, and I will go down in history as one of the greatest leaders of all time. But there is much work to be done. I must continue to be vigilant, to watch for any potential threats, and to act quickly and decisively when necessary. But with Cleopatra by my side, I am confident that we can overcome any obstacle.

setting: After his successful campaign against the Callaeci and Lusitani, Julius Caesar returned to Rome in the summer of 60 BC, having been hailed as imperator. He faced a difficult choice between a triumph and election to the consulship, as he could only make a declaration of consular candidacy if he crossed the pomerium, giving up his command and triumph. Despite attempts to waive the requirement, Caesar's enemy Cato filibustered in the senate, making it difficult for him to declare his candidacy.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe this is happening. After everything I have done for Rome, they are making it so difficult for me to run for consul. Cato is making a fool of himself, filibustering in the senate. But I will not let him stop me. I must become consul, for the sake of Rome and for my own ambitions. I have come too far to give up now.

Julius Caesar, you have been given too much already. You have been hailed as imperator, and now you want to be consul as well? Have you no sense of propriety? We cannot simply waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person. It sets a dangerous precedent. You must choose between a triumph and the consulship.

I understand your concerns, Cato. But I have proven myself time and time again on the battlefield, and I have the support of the people. I will not be deterred by your filibustering. I will cross the pomerium and make my declaration of consular candidacy. And I will win, because I am the best candidate for the job.
But what about the debt you have accumulated from your campaigns, Caesar? How will you pay it off if you give up your command and triumph?

I have already seized enough plunder from my campaigns to pay off my debts. And besides, becoming consul will give me more opportunities to enrich myself. I will not let money stand in the way of my ambitions.
But what about the precedent this will set, Caesar? If we waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person, what will stop others from doing the same in the future?

I understand your concerns, but we must look to the future. I will be an excellent consul, and I will use my power to benefit Rome. This is not just about me, but about the future of our great republic.

I cannot wait to become consul. It will give me even more power and influence, and I will be able to shape Rome in my image. I will show them all what I am capable of. And once I am consul, there will be no stopping me.

setting: Caesar sits at the head of a long table in his tent in Antioch, surrounded by his top advisors. Maps of the Black Sea and the surrounding regions are spread out on the table before them, while quills scratch across parchment as they discuss their next move. There is a sense of urgency in the air as Caesar learns of Pharnaces' invasion of his father's kingdom of Pontus across the Black Sea. His legates and local client kings have been defeated, and Caesar must act quickly to ensure his own rule is not threatened. His advisors watch him closely, waiting for his command.

dialogue.content: This is a direct challenge to my authority. If I do not respond swiftly and decisively, others may see it as a sign of weakness. I cannot allow that to happen. Pharnaces must be defeated, and I must do it in a way that sends a message to anyone who would dare to challenge me. But how? My legions are stretched thin, and the Black Sea is a formidable obstacle. I need a plan.

Caesar, we have reports that Pharnaces is consolidating his power in Pontus. His army is growing stronger by the day, and he shows no signs of slowing down. We must act quickly if we hope to defeat him.

I am well aware of the situation, Brutus. I have been considering our options. The Black Sea is a formidable obstacle, but it can also be an advantage. Pharnaces has not yet established complete control over the region. We can use that to our advantage. I propose that we launch a surprise attack from the sea, catching him off guard and taking him by surprise.
But Caesar, our navy is not equipped for such an attack. It would take time and resources to prepare them, and we cannot afford to wait. We need to strike now, while Pharnaces is still weak.

I understand your concerns, Cassius, but we cannot afford to rush into this blindly. We must be strategic in our approach. I propose that we send a small, elite force to infiltrate his army and gather intelligence. We can use that information to plan our attack and ensure our victory.
Caesar, I have a suggestion. We could also try to enlist the support of the local tribes in the area. They have long resented Pharnaces' rule and may be willing to fight alongside us.

An excellent idea, Decimus. We will need all the allies we can get if we hope to defeat Pharnaces. I want you to send emissaries to the local tribes immediately and begin negotiations. Meanwhile, I will assemble a small, elite force to infiltrate Pharnaces' army. We will gather intelligence and plan our attack. Once we have a clear picture of his strengths and weaknesses, we will strike with all our might.

This plan will work. I can feel it. Pharnaces may have thought he could challenge me, but he has underestimated my power. I am Julius Caesar, conqueror of Gaul, and I will not be defeated by a petty king from Crimea. My victory over him will send a message to all who would dare to oppose me. Veni, vidi, vici.

setting: In 50 BC, tensions were high between Julius Caesar and his opponents as they both built up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy. Cicero and others proposed disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, but the proposal was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. When a rumour came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was rejected by the hardliners. On 7 January, his supportive tribunes were driven from Rome; the Senate then declared Caesar an enemy and issued its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: These hardliners are making it impossible for me to avoid a civil war. I've made offers to disarm, but they refuse to compromise. I don't want to fight Pompey, but it seems like they're forcing my hand. I must find a way to gather more support and show them that I am not their enemy.

I am willing to defend Italy, but I do not wish to engage in a civil war. Caesar has made offers to disarm, and I believe we should consider them. We must find a way to avoid senseless bloodshed and come to a peaceful resolution.

I agree with Pompey. We cannot continue down this path of violence and destruction. Caesar has shown that he is willing to compromise, and we must meet him halfway. Disarmament is the only way forward.
We cannot trust Caesar. He has already shown that he is a threat to the Republic. We must prepare for war and defend ourselves against his tyranny.
I agree. We cannot let Caesar continue to undermine our democracy. We must stand firm and show him that we will not back down.
I must find a way to convince them that I am not a threat to the Republic. Perhaps I can rally more support from the people. I will need to make a speech and appeal to their sense of reason.

My fellow Romans, I come before you today to address the concerns that have been raised about my intentions. I want to assure you that I am not a threat to the Republic. I have made offers to disarm, but they have been rejected by the hardliners. I urge you to consider the consequences of a civil war. We must find a way to come to a peaceful resolution and avoid senseless bloodshed.
Caesar is right. We don't want a civil war.
Don't be fooled by his words, fellow Romans. Caesar is a threat to our democracy. We must prepare for war and defend ourselves against his tyranny.
I agree. We cannot let Caesar continue to undermine our Republic. We must stand firm and show him that we will not back down.

It seems like the hardliners have already made up their minds. I must find a way to gather more support and show them that I am not their enemy. Perhaps I can reach out to other senators and try to find a compromise.

Senators, I implore you to consider the consequences of a civil war. We must find a way to come to a peaceful resolution. I am willing to compromise, but the hardliners refuse to meet me halfway. I ask you to consider the future of our Republic and find a way to avoid senseless bloodshed.
I agree with Caesar. We must find a way to avoid a civil war and come to a peaceful resolution.
I also agree. We cannot let our differences tear apart the fabric of our society. We must find a way to compromise and work together for the good of the Republic.
Don't be fooled by their words, fellow senators. Caesar is a threat to our democracy. We must prepare for war and defend ourselves against his tyranny.
I agree. We cannot let Caesar continue to undermine our Republic. We must stand firm and show him that we will not back down.

It seems like the hardliners are not willing to compromise. I must find a way to show them that I am not their enemy. Perhaps if I can win a decisive victory on the battlefield, they will be forced to reconsider their position.

I have offered to disarm, but the hardliners refuse to meet me halfway. I do not want to fight a civil war, but I cannot let them threaten the Republic. I ask you to support me in this struggle for the future of our democracy.
Caesar! Caesar! Caesar!
You will regret this, Caesar. We will not back down. We will defend the Republic against your tyranny.
I agree. We cannot let Caesar continue to undermine our Republic. We must stand firm and show him that we will not back down.

It seems like the hardliners have already made up their minds. I must prepare for war and gather more support. This will not be an easy fight, but I am willing to do whatever it takes to defend the Republic.

setting: After his praetorship, Caesar was appointed to govern Hispania Ulterior pro consule. He required military victory beyond the normal provincial extortion to pay off his debts. He campaigned against the Callaeci and Lusitani and seized the Callaeci capital in northwestern Spain, bringing Roman troops to the Atlantic and seizing enough plunder to pay his debts. Claiming to have completed the peninsula's conquest, he made for home after having been hailed imperator. When he arrived home in the summer of 60 BC, he was then forced to choose between a triumph and election to the consulship. Either he could remain outside the pomerium (Rome's sacred boundary) awaiting a triumph or cross the boundary, giving up his command and triumph, to make a declaration of consular candidacy. Attempts to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person were filibustered in the senate by Caesar's enemy Cato, even though the senate seemed to support the exception. Faced with the choice between a triumph and the consulship, Caesar chose the consulship.
Caesar ultimately chose the consulship over a triumph, crossing the sacred boundary and giving up his command. This decision would ultimately lead to his rise to power and his eventual assassination.

dialogue.content: I can't believe I have to make this choice. A triumph would be an incredible honor, but the consulship is the ultimate political power in Rome. I could achieve so much more with that position. But if I cross the boundary, I have to give up my command and my triumph. And what if I don't win the consulship? Then I'll have nothing. This is a difficult decision, but I have to choose the consulship. It's the only way to secure my power and influence in Rome.

Caesar, I urge you to reconsider. A triumph is a great honor, but the consulship is not guaranteed. If you give up your command and fail to win the election, you will have nothing to show for it. Think carefully before you make this decision.
I have thought carefully, Cato. The consulship is the ultimate power in Rome. I cannot pass up this opportunity. I understand the risks, but I am willing to take them.
But what about your troops? They will be disappointed if you give up your command and do not receive a triumph. They will question your loyalty to them and to Rome.
I will explain to them my decision. They will understand that I am putting the good of Rome above my personal glory. I trust that they will continue to support me.

Caesar, I understand your ambition, but please consider the consequences of your actions. The senate is already wary of your power and influence. If you give up your command and take the consulship, they may see it as a threat to the Republic.

I understand your concerns, Brutus. But the Republic needs strong leadership. With me as consul, I can ensure that Rome remains powerful and prosperous. I will do whatever it takes to secure the future of Rome.

Caesar, I understand your desire for power, but I urge you to think about the consequences of your actions. If you give up your command and take the consulship, you may be seen as a threat to the balance of power in Rome. This could lead to civil war.
I am aware of the risks, Pompey. But I am willing to take them for the good of Rome. I trust that the people will see the value of my leadership and support me in the election.

setting: The Senate House is filled with tension as Julius Caesar argues with his opponents about their attempts to suppress his candidacy. Caesar's main objectives are to secure a second consulship and a triumph, but his opponents – then holding both consulships for 50 BC – are wary of his ambitions. They fear that Caesar's growing power will threaten the liberty of the Roman people, and they are determined to stop him at all costs.

dialogue.content: These fools think they can stand in my way, but they underestimate my power and my resolve. I will not be denied my rightful place as consul of Rome, and I will not let anyone stand in the way of my triumph. They may try to suppress my candidacy, but they will not succeed. I will fight for what is mine, and I will emerge victorious.

Caesar, you have overstepped your bounds. You seek to become consul once again, but you have already served your time. We cannot allow you to continue to accumulate power at the expense of the Roman people.
Indeed, Caesar. Your ambitions are well-known, and we fear that you would use your position as consul to undermine the liberties of our great republic. We cannot allow that to happen.

You speak of my ambitions as if they are a bad thing. I have accomplished more for Rome than any of you ever could, and yet you seek to hold me back. You fear my power, and you fear the people's love for me. But I will not be deterred. I will fight for what is right, and I will not let anyone stand in my way.
You are mistaken, Caesar. We do not fear your power, but we do fear what you might do with it. Your actions have already shown that you care more about your own glory than the good of the people.
Indeed. Your conquests have brought glory to Rome, but at what cost? The people are tired of war and bloodshed. They want peace and prosperity, not endless conquests.

These fools do not understand the true nature of power. They think that they can hold me back with their words, but they are wrong. I have the love of the people, and that is a power that cannot be denied. I will use that power to achieve my goals, no matter what the cost.
You speak of peace and prosperity, but you forget that it was my conquests that brought us to this point. Without my leadership, Rome would be weak and vulnerable. You cannot deny the truth of that.
Your leadership has been nothing but a series of wars and conquests. What good is that if the people are suffering?
We do not deny your accomplishments, Caesar, but we cannot allow you to continue down this path. We must think of the good of the people, not just your own ambitions.
They are blind to the truth. They cannot see that I am the only one who can lead Rome to greatness. Without me, the republic will fall apart. I must convince them of that, no matter what it takes.

I understand your concerns, but you must understand that I am the only one who can lead Rome to greatness. Without me, the republic will fall apart. You cannot deny that. So let us put aside our differences and work together for the good of Rome.
You ask us to put aside our concerns, but what about yours? You seek power for its own sake, not for the good of the people. We cannot support such ambitions.
We cannot support you, Caesar. Your actions have already shown that you care more about your own glory than the good of the people. We must think of the good of Rome, not just your own ambitions.
They are not listening to reason. They are blinded by their own fears and prejudices. I must find a way to convince them of my true intentions, or all will be lost.

Listen to me, my friends. I seek power not for its own sake, but for the good of Rome. I have accomplished great things for our republic, and I will continue to do so if you give me the chance. Trust me, and I will not let you down.
We cannot trust you, Caesar. Your actions have already shown that you care more about your own glory than the good of the people. We must think of the good of Rome, not just your own ambitions.
We cannot support you, Caesar. Your ambitions threaten the very foundations of our republic. We must think of the good of Rome, not just your own glory.
They will not listen to reason. They are blinded by their own fears and prejudices. I must find a way to convince them of my true intentions, or all will be lost.

Very well. If you will not support me, then I will have to find another way. But mark my words, my friends. I will not be denied my rightful place as consul of Rome. I will fight for what is right, and I will not let anyone stand in my way.

setting: As 50 BC progressed, fears of civil war grew; both Caesar and his opponents started building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. In the autumn, Cicero and others sought disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, and on 1 December 50 BC this was formally proposed in the Senate. It received overwhelming support – 370 to 22 – but was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. That year, when a rumour came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepted as a last resort. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was read to the Senate, which was rejected by the hardliners. A later compromise given privately to Pompey was also rejected at their insistence. On 7 January, his supportive tribunes were driven from Rome; the Senate then declared Caesar an enemy and it issued its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: The Senate has declared me an enemy. I cannot believe this is happening. I have tried to compromise, to avoid bloodshed, but the hardliners have their minds set on war. They refuse to see reason. I must act quickly to protect myself and my supporters. I will not let them destroy all that I have worked for. But how? I must gather my forces and march on Rome. It is my only choice. Pompey and his allies have left me no other option.
Caesar has left us no choice. We must defend Rome against his aggression. I call on all loyal citizens to join us in this fight. We will not let him destroy the Republic.

I implore you, gentlemen, to reconsider. War is not the answer. We must find a way to resolve this conflict peacefully. Disarmament is the only way forward. We cannot afford to let our differences escalate into bloodshed.

Enough of this talk of disarmament! Caesar is a threat to the Republic. He must be stopped at all costs. We cannot allow him to seize power and destroy everything we hold dear. We must prepare for war, and we must do it now.

I cannot let Pompey and his allies paint me as a threat to the Republic. I have always acted in its best interests. But they will not listen to reason. They have already declared me an enemy. I must act quickly and decisively. My forces are ready. It is time to march on Rome.

My fellow Romans, do not be deceived by the lies of Pompey and his allies. Caesar is not a threat to the Republic. He has only ever acted in its best interests. We must stand with him in this time of crisis. We cannot let the hardliners destroy everything we hold dear.
Do not listen to this traitor! He speaks only lies and deceit. Caesar is a threat to the Republic and must be stopped. Join us in this fight, and we will defend Rome against his aggression.

The time has come. I will not let them destroy everything I have worked for. My forces are ready, and we will march on Rome. It is time to take back what is rightfully mine. The Republic will be restored, and I will not let anyone stand in my way.

setting: After his praetorship, Caesar was appointed to govern Hispania Ulterior pro consule. Deeply indebted from his campaigns for the praetorship and for the pontificate, Caesar required military victory beyond the normal provincial extortion to pay them off. He campaigned against the Callaeci and Lusitani and seized the Callaeci capital in northwestern Spain, bringing Roman troops to the Atlantic and seizing enough plunder to pay his debts. Claiming to have completed the peninsula's conquest, he made for home after having been hailed imperator. When he arrived home in the summer of 60 BC, he was then forced to choose between a triumph and election to the consulship: either he could remain outside the pomerium (Rome's sacred boundary) awaiting a triumph or cross the boundary, giving up his command and triumph, to make a declaration of consular candidacy. Attempts to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person were filibustered in the senate by Caesar's enemy Cato, even though the senate seemed to support the exception. Faced with the choice between a triumph and the consulship, Caesar chose the consulship.

dialogue.content: As I stand here, outside the pomerium, I am faced with a difficult choice. On one hand, I have the opportunity to claim a triumph for my conquest of Hispania Ulterior, bringing great honor to myself and my family. On the other hand, there is the chance to be elected as consul, the highest office in the Roman Republic, giving me the power to shape the future of Rome. I must weigh the benefits of each option carefully.

To claim a triumph would bring great glory to myself and my family, but it would mean giving up my command and delaying my chance to run for consul. The people of Rome would see this as a sign of weakness, that I am more concerned with my own personal glory than the future of our great Republic. No, I cannot afford to be seen as selfish or power-hungry. I must put the needs of Rome before my own desires.

Caesar, you claim to be a devoted servant of Rome, yet you hesitate to claim the honor that is rightfully yours. Is this not a sign of weakness? Do you not have the courage to claim the triumph that you have earned?

Cato, always the thorn in my side. He knows that I cannot claim a triumph without giving up my command, yet he continues to push me towards that option. He wants me to appear selfish and power-hungry, to discredit me in the eyes of the people of Rome. But I will not give him that satisfaction.

I am not hesitant, Cato. I am simply weighing my options carefully. I have always put the needs of Rome before my own personal desires, and I will continue to do so. I believe that running for consul is the best way for me to serve our great Republic.

Your words are empty, Caesar. You claim to put the needs of Rome first, yet you refuse to claim the triumph that you have earned. I fear that you are more concerned with your own personal reputation than the future of our Republic.

He is right about one thing - my reputation is important. But not for the reasons he thinks. If I am to gain the support of the people of Rome, I must appear strong and decisive. I cannot be seen as weak or unsure of myself. But at the same time, I must be careful not to appear too ambitious or power-hungry. It is a delicate balance that I must strike.

I assure you, Cato, that my only concern is the future of our great Republic. I believe that running for consul is the best way for me to serve Rome, and I will not be swayed by personal ambition or desire for glory. I ask for your support in this endeavor.

I cannot support a man who is unwilling to claim the honor that is rightfully his. The people of Rome will see through your empty words, Caesar. They will see that you are more concerned with your own personal gain than the future of our Republic.

He is a stubborn old man, but I cannot let him get the best of me. I must remain calm and composed, no matter what he throws my way. I know that I am the best candidate for consul, and I will do whatever it takes to win the support of the people of Rome. Even if it means giving up the chance to claim a triumph.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but I must do what is best for Rome. I will not be swayed by personal ambition or desire for glory. I ask for your support in this endeavor, but even if I do not have it, I will continue to fight for the future of our Republic.

setting: It is the year 50 BC, and Rome is under the dictatorship of Julius Caesar. Fears of civil war are growing as both Caesar and his opponents build up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. Cicero and others have proposed disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, but it was not passed when one of the consuls dissolved the meeting. When a rumor came to Rome that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepted as a last resort. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer that he and Pompey disarm was rejected by the hardliners. On 7 January, his supportive tribunes were driven from Rome; the Senate then declared Caesar an enemy and issued its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: The Senate has declared me an enemy. How dare they? I have done everything in my power to keep this country together. I have brought wealth and prosperity to Rome, and yet they still seek to undermine me. I will not stand for this. I must act quickly and decisively. I will not let them bring about my downfall. I will do whatever it takes to maintain my power. The people of Rome need me, and I will not let them down.
Caesar has become too powerful. He must be stopped. We cannot allow him to continue to act with impunity. We must take action now, before it is too late.
I agree with Pompey. Caesar has shown no regard for the law or for the will of the people. He has become a tyrant, and we cannot allow him to continue unchecked.

You dare speak of me in such a way? I have done more for Rome than any of you ever could. I have brought stability and prosperity to this country. And yet you seek to undermine me at every turn. I will not stand for this. I will defend my position as dictator with all the power at my disposal. Anyone who opposes me will be dealt with swiftly and harshly. Make no mistake, I will not hesitate to use force if necessary.
I fear that Caesar has become too consumed with his own power. He no longer acts in the best interests of Rome, but only in his own self-interest. We must take action to stop him.

Foolish Brutus. He does not understand the weight of the responsibility that I carry. I must do what is necessary to maintain order in Rome. If that means taking drastic measures, so be it. I will not let anyone stand in my way.
Caesar must be removed from power. He has become a threat to the very democracy that Rome was founded upon. We must act now before it is too late.

You talk of democracy, yet you seek to undermine the very foundations of our government. You are nothing but a bunch of traitors, seeking to overthrow the legitimate ruler of Rome. I will not let you succeed. I will crush any rebellion with all the power at my disposal.
I stand with Caesar. He has brought peace and prosperity to Rome. We cannot allow the likes of Cassius and Brutus to bring about chaos and destruction. We must support Caesar at all costs.

Mark Antony is a loyal ally. I must ensure that I keep him on my side. Together, we can overcome any obstacle that stands in our way. I will not let anyone undermine my rule. Rome needs me, and I will not let her down.

setting: It is the year 50 BC, and the Roman Republic is in a state of political turmoil. Julius Caesar, a powerful general, has been ruling over Gaul for the past decade and has amassed a significant amount of wealth and military force. However, his growing power has made some of his fellow senators uneasy, and they fear that he may be planning to overthrow the Republic and establish himself as a dictator. In an effort to prevent this, some senators have proposed a disarmament plan that would require both Caesar and his rival, Pompey, to give up their armies. However, the proposal has not been passed in the Senate, and tensions continue to rise.

dialogue.content: These senators are fools. They fear me because they know I am the only one who can save this Republic from the brink of collapse. If they would only listen to reason, they would see that I am not their enemy. I have done everything in my power to maintain the stability of this government, but they continue to plot against me. If they want a war, then so be it. I will not back down from a fight.

Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but I cannot agree to disarm while Caesar is still a threat. He has already shown that he is willing to use force to get what he wants, and I fear that if we disarm, he will take advantage of the situation and seize power. We must remain vigilant and prepared to defend ourselves if necessary.

I agree with Pompey. It would be foolish to disarm while Caesar and his army are still a threat. However, I also believe that we must find a way to resolve this conflict peacefully. We cannot afford to let this escalate into a full-blown civil war.

You speak of peace, Cicero, but what have you done to promote it? You and your fellow senators have done nothing but plot against me and spread lies about my intentions. I have offered to disarm, but you have rejected my proposals time and time again. What other options do I have?
I understand your frustration, Caesar, but we cannot simply trust you to give up your army. We need assurances that you will not use your military power to overthrow the government.

Assurances? What assurances do they want? I have given them everything they have asked for, and still, they refuse to trust me. They are blinded by their own fear and ignorance. Maybe it is time to show them the true extent of my power.

Very well, Cicero. If you require assurances, then I will give them to you. I will disband my army and return to Rome as a civilian. I will not use my military power to overthrow the government, but I will not allow myself to be persecuted either. If you continue to treat me as an enemy, then you will force my hand. The choice is yours.
I appreciate your offer, Caesar, but I cannot speak for the rest of the Senate. We will need to discuss this further before we can make any decisions.
Discuss this further? How many more times must I bend over backward for these fools? They do not deserve my mercy or my trust. They only deserve my wrath.

Very well, Cicero. Discuss it amongst yourselves. But know this: if you do not come to a decision soon, I will be forced to take matters into my own hands. I will not be made a fool of by a bunch of cowardly senators.

setting: Caesar stands before his troops in Pontus, preparing to lead them into battle against the invading Pharnaces, king of Crimea, who had attempted to seize Caesar's father's kingdom of Pontus across the Black Sea. Caesar had just learned of the invasion while in Egypt and had immediately left to confront the threat. His legates and the local client kings had been swept aside by Pharnaces's army, leaving Caesar no choice but to engage him in battle.

dialogue.content: I must rally my troops and inspire them to fight with all their might. The fate of Pontus rests on their shoulders, and I cannot afford to lose this battle. Pharnaces may have defeated my legates and the local client kings, but he has yet to face the might of the Roman army. I must lead my troops with courage and determination, and show them that victory is within our grasp.

My fellow Romans, today we stand on the battlefield, ready to face the invading army of Pharnaces. We are outnumbered, but we are not outmatched. We are the mighty Roman army, and we have faced countless foes before. Today, we fight for the honor of Pontus, for the memory of my father, and for the glory of Rome. Today, we fight for victory! Are you with me?
Yes, Caesar! We are with you!
Then let us show Pharnaces what it means to face the might of Rome! Charge!

This battle is intense, but I will not falter. Pharnaces may have swept aside my legates and the local client kings, but he will not defeat me. I am Julius Caesar, and I will not be defeated by a mere king. The fate of Pontus rests on my shoulders, and I will not let my father's kingdom fall. Victory is within our grasp, and I will lead my troops to achieve it.

Victory is ours! We have defeated Pharnaces and secured the honor of Pontus. Let this be a lesson to all who would dare to challenge the might of Rome. We are the unbeatable, unbreakable Roman army, and we will not be defeated!

This victory will be remembered for years to come. I have shown the world that Rome is not to be trifled with, and that the might of the Roman army is unmatched. Pharnaces may have been a worthy opponent, but in the end, he was no match for the might of Rome. I have secured the safety of Pontus and upheld the honor of my father's kingdom. This is a victory that will be remembered for generations to come.

setting: Caesar has withdrawn to Brundisium and has escaped to Greece, leaving Italy in the face of Pompey's superior forces. Caesar stayed near Rome for about two weeks and left Lepidus in charge of Italy while he attacked Pompey's Spanish provinces. Returning to Rome in the autumn, Caesar had Lepidus, as praetor, bring a law appointing Caesar dictator to conduct the elections.

dialogue.content: I must establish my power and justify my actions to the people of Rome. I have defeated Pompey's forces in Spain and have returned to Rome with a victory. My seizure of the treasury was necessary to fund my war effort, and the people will understand that. I must show them that I am the only one capable of leading Rome to greatness.

Citizens of Rome, I come to you today to proclaim my war justifications. As you know, Pompey and his legions have fled from Italy, abandoning their duty to defend our great nation. I have pursued him to Spain and have defeated his legions in battle. I have returned to Rome to establish my power and to ensure that the interests of Rome are protected.
But Caesar, your seizure of the treasury was illegal! You have violated the tribunician veto and have shown that you are willing to disregard the laws of Rome.

My dear citizen, I understand your concerns. However, my seizure of the treasury was necessary to fund our war effort. We cannot fight a war without the proper resources, and I was forced to take action when the Senate refused to act. I assure you that my actions were for the good of Rome, and I will not let anyone stand in the way of our victory.
But Caesar, what about the rights of the people? You have appointed yourself dictator and have taken away our freedoms.

My friend, I have appointed myself dictator for the good of Rome. We are in a time of crisis, and we need strong leadership to guide us through these troubled times. I have been elected by the people to lead them, and I will do so with honor and integrity.

Citizens of Rome, I stand with Caesar. His actions were necessary to ensure the safety and security of our great nation. We must rally behind him and support his efforts to bring peace and prosperity to Rome.
I have convinced the people of Rome of my justifications for war. Now, I must focus on defeating Pompey and his legions. I will not rest until we have achieved victory and secured the future of Rome.

setting: Caesar and Publius Servilius Isauricus serve as consuls for 48 BC in Rome.

dialogue.content: I have finally achieved my goal of becoming a consul. It was not an easy journey, but I have proven myself worthy of this position. Now, I must focus on maintaining my power and influence. I cannot let anyone stand in my way. I must continue to expand my empire and crush any opposition. I will do whatever it takes to achieve my goals.
Caesar, we must discuss the plans for the upcoming year. We have many challenges ahead of us, and we must work together to ensure our success.
Yes, I agree. We must focus on expanding our territories and strengthening our army. We cannot let our enemies take advantage of us. We must be prepared to fight at all times.
I suggest we send our legions to the north and conquer the remaining tribes in Gaul. This will give us more land and resources to work with.

Gaul? That's not a bad idea. It would be a good opportunity to prove my strength and gain more power. But I must be careful not to overextend myself. I cannot afford to lose any battles or weaken my army.
Very well, we will send our legions to Gaul. But we must also keep an eye on our enemies in the east and south. They may try to take advantage of our absence.
Agreed. I will make sure to keep our defenses strong and watch out for any potential threats.

Yes, Publius is a good ally to have. He understands the importance of maintaining our power and protecting our interests. But I must also be wary of him. He may try to undermine me and take my position as consul. I cannot let that happen.
Thank you, Publius. I trust that you will do everything in your power to keep Rome safe and secure.
You can count on me, Caesar. Together, we will lead Rome to greatness.

Yes, together we will achieve great things. But I must remember that I am the one in charge. I am the one who holds the power. I must be careful not to let anyone take that away from me. I am Julius Caesar, and I will do whatever it takes to maintain my position as consul and ruler of Rome.

setting: It is the year 50 BC, and the fears of civil war are growing. Julius Caesar and his opponents are building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy, respectively. In the autumn, Cicero and others seek disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, and on 1 December 50 BC, this is formally proposed in the Senate. It receives overwhelming support, but it is not passed when one of the consuls dissolves the meeting. When a rumor comes to Rome that Caesar is marching into Italy, both consuls instruct Pompey to defend Italy, a charge he accepts as a last resort.

dialogue.content: The time has come for me to take action. I cannot let my opponents intimidate me any longer. They are building up their troops, and I cannot allow them to gain the upper hand. I must act swiftly and decisively to protect myself and my supporters. Cicero and his followers seek disarmament, but I know that this is just a ploy to weaken me. I cannot trust my opponents, and I must be prepared for any eventuality. I will not let them defeat me.

We cannot allow Caesar to march into Italy. He is a threat to the stability of the republic, and we must defend ourselves against him. I accept the charge to defend Italy as a last resort, but we must take action now before it is too late.

We must seek disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey. This is the only way to prevent a civil war and protect the republic. We cannot allow these tensions to escalate any further. We must act now before it is too late.
I agree that disarmament is necessary, but we must also be prepared to defend ourselves against any threats to the republic. We cannot let our guard down.
I agree. We must be prepared for any eventuality. We cannot let our enemies gain the upper hand.

I know that my opponents are trying to weaken me by seeking disarmament. But I will not allow them to succeed. I must build up my troops and prepare for any attack. I will not let them defeat me. I will not let them destroy the republic.
We must be prepared for any attack. Caesar is a threat to the republic, and we must defend ourselves against him. We cannot let him destroy everything we have worked so hard to build.
We must seek a peaceful solution to this crisis. Disarmament is the only way to prevent a civil war. We cannot allow these tensions to escalate any further. We must act now before it is too late.
We must be prepared for any eventuality. We cannot let our enemies gain the upper hand. We must defend ourselves against any threats to the republic.
I agree. We must be prepared for any attack. We cannot let Caesar destroy everything we have worked so hard to build. We must defend the republic at all costs.

My opponents are preparing for war. They seek to weaken me, but they will not succeed. I will not let them destroy the republic. I must act now to protect myself and my supporters. I will not let them defeat me.
We must take action now to defend the republic. Caesar is a threat to our stability, and we cannot let him succeed. We must be prepared for any eventuality.
We must seek a peaceful solution to this crisis. Disarmament is the only way to prevent a civil war. We cannot let these tensions escalate any further. We must act now before it is too late.
We must be prepared for any attack. We cannot let our enemies gain the upper hand. We must defend ourselves against any threats to the republic.
I agree. We must be prepared for any eventuality. We cannot let Caesar destroy everything we have worked so hard to build. We must defend the republic at all costs.

I must act now to protect myself and my supporters. My opponents are preparing for war, and I cannot let them gain the upper hand. I must build up my troops and be prepared for any attack. I will not let them defeat me. I will not let them destroy the republic. I must act now.
Caesar is a threat to the republic, and we must defend ourselves against him. We cannot let him destroy everything we have worked so hard to build. We must be prepared for any eventuality.
We must seek a peaceful solution to this crisis. Disarmament is the only way to prevent a civil war. We cannot let these tensions escalate any further. We must act now before it is too late.
We must be prepared for any attack. We cannot let our enemies gain the upper hand. We must defend ourselves against any threats to the republic.
I agree. We must be prepared for any eventuality. We cannot let Caesar destroy everything we have worked so hard to build. We must defend the republic at all costs.

I will not let my opponents intimidate me any longer. I must act now to protect myself and my supporters. I cannot let them gain the upper hand. I will not let them defeat me. I will not let them destroy the republic. I must act now.

setting: It is a sunny day in Rome, and the entire city is bustling with excitement as Julius Caesar receives a triumphal procession for his swift victory over Pharnaces, the king of Crimea. The procession is taking place in the Rome forum, and the citizens of Rome gather to catch a glimpse of their beloved leader. Caesar is dressed in his finest military attire, and his face is beaming with pride as he rides on a chariot pulled by four white horses. The streets are adorned with flowers and banners, and the air is filled with the sound of trumpets and cheers.

dialogue.content: This is it. This is the moment I've been waiting for. All of my hard work, all of my sacrifices, have led me to this triumphal procession. I can feel the eyes of every citizen of Rome upon me, and it fills me with pride. I have shown them that I am a strong leader, that I am capable of conquering even the most formidable foes. But my victory over Pharnaces is only the beginning. I have more enemies to defeat, more lands to conquer. I must continue to push forward, to expand the Roman Empire and bring glory to Rome.

My fellow Romans, today we celebrate not just a victory over Pharnaces, but a victory over all those who would dare to oppose Rome! I came, I saw, I conquered, and I will continue to do so as long as I draw breath. This triumphal procession is not just for me, but for all of Rome. It is a symbol of our strength, our power, and our unrelenting will to succeed. Let it be known to all those who would challenge us that we will not be defeated. We will stand strong, we will fight with honor, and we will emerge victorious!
Hail Caesar! Hail Caesar!

Their cheers fill me with joy, but also with a sense of responsibility. I am not just a conqueror, I am a leader. I must ensure that the citizens of Rome are taken care of, that their needs are met, and that they are protected from harm. I must continue to build up our infrastructure, to improve our economy, and to maintain the peace. It is a daunting task, but one that I am more than capable of handling.

I would like to take a moment to honor the brave soldiers who fought alongside me in this campaign. They risked their lives to defend Rome, and they deserve our respect and admiration. Without them, this victory would not have been possible. Let us give them the recognition they deserve!
Hail Caesar! Hail the Roman Empire!

I can see the joy on their faces, the pride in their eyes. They know that they have served their country well, and that they have made a difference. I must continue to inspire them, to motivate them, to ensure that they remain loyal to Rome. For the greater good of our empire, I must be a strong, decisive leader, one who is not afraid to make tough decisions. I must be willing to do whatever it takes to protect Rome and its citizens.

I want to assure you all that I will do everything in my power to ensure the safety and prosperity of our great nation. I will not rest until Rome is the greatest empire in the world, until our enemies are vanquished, and until our citizens are living in peace and prosperity. Thank you all for your support, and may the gods smile upon us all!
Hail Caesar! Hail Rome!

As I ride through the streets of Rome, I feel a sense of pride and accomplishment wash over me. But I know that this is just the beginning. There are still many battles to be fought, many lands to be conquered. I must remain vigilant, focused, and determined. I must continue to be the leader that Rome needs, one who is willing to make the tough choices, one who is willing to do whatever it takes to ensure our empire's success. The future of Rome is in my hands, and I will not let her down!

setting: Caesar had recently returned from his trip to Egypt to find out that Pharnaces, the king of Crimea had tried to take over his father's kingdom of Pontus. Pharnaces had easily defeated Caesar's legates and local client kings before meeting Caesar in Zela. However, Caesar had defeated him in a swift victory, leading to his famous phrase, "veni, vidi, vici." Caesar had just arrived at the battlefield in Zela, ready to declare his triumph over Pharnaces.

dialogue.content: I have once again proven my military genius to the world. My swift defeat of Pharnaces has solidified my reputation as one of the greatest military leaders of all time. This victory will strike fear into the hearts of any who dare to challenge me. My triumph will be celebrated throughout Rome, and I will be hailed as a hero. This victory will bring me one step closer to achieving my ultimate goal: total domination of Rome.

Romans, I have returned from Zela victorious! I came, I saw, I conquered! Pharnaces, the king of Crimea, thought he could take my father's kingdom of Pontus, but he was sorely mistaken. He defeated my legates and local client kings, but he was no match for me. With one swift maneuver, I defeated him. His army was no match for my legions. I have brought another triumph to Rome, and I am proud to have done so. My victory at Zela will be celebrated throughout Rome. It will be remembered as one of the greatest military victories in history!
Hail Caesar! You are truly a great military leader. Your victory at Zela has brought honor and glory to Rome!
Hail Caesar! Your victory at Zela has solidified your place as one of the greatest military leaders of all time. Rome is lucky to have you as our leader!

These soldiers are right. Rome is lucky to have me as their leader. With every victory, I become more powerful. I must continue to conquer all who stand in my way. No one can defeat me. I am invincible. I will stop at nothing to achieve total domination of Rome. I will be remembered as one of the greatest leaders in history.

Thank you for your kind words, soldiers. I will continue to lead Rome to greatness. I will continue to conquer all who stand in my way. My ultimate goal is total domination of Rome, and I will stop at nothing to achieve it. I am Caesar, and I will be remembered as one of the greatest leaders in history!
Hail Caesar! Rome will always be behind you. We will follow you to victory!
Hail Caesar! Your victory at Zela has brought honor and glory to Rome. We are proud to fight under your command!

These soldiers are loyal to me. They know I am the only one who can lead Rome to greatness. With their support, I will conquer all who stand in my way. No one can stop me. I am invincible. I will continue to bring glory and honor to Rome. I will continue to be remembered as one of the greatest leaders in history.

Thank you, soldiers, for your loyalty and support. With your help, I will continue to lead Rome to greatness. Together, we will conquer all who stand in our way. Rome will be remembered as one of the greatest empires in history!
Hail Caesar! We will follow you to victory!
Hail Caesar! Rome will always be behind you!

setting: After his successful campaign against the Callaeci and Lusitani in Hispania Ulterior, Julius Caesar returned to Rome in the summer of 60 BC. He was hailed imperator and had the option to either wait outside the pomerium for a triumph or cross the boundary to declare his candidacy for consulship.

dialogue.content: I have accomplished much in Hispania Ulterior and have brought Roman troops to the Atlantic. My victories have brought me great plunder, which will help pay off my debts. Now I am faced with a difficult decision. Do I wait outside the pomerium for a triumph, or do I cross the boundary to declare my candidacy for consulship? The senate seems to support an exception to the requirement of making the declaration in person, but my enemy Cato is filibustering the process. I must weigh the benefits of a triumph against the importance of becoming consul.

I object to any exceptions being made to the requirement of making the declaration in person. This is a longstanding tradition and must be upheld. We cannot have exceptions made for the benefit of one individual.

I understand the importance of tradition, but I have just returned from a successful campaign and have much to offer as consul. The senate seems to support the exception, and I ask that you consider the needs of the state over personal grudges.
I am not swayed by your words, Caesar. I will continue to filibuster any attempts to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person.

Cato is stubborn and unwilling to see reason. I must find a way to convince him to support the exception. The senate seems to be on my side, but Cato's influence is strong. I cannot let personal grudges get in the way of what is best for Rome.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but I ask that you consider the needs of the state. I have just returned from a successful campaign and have much to offer as consul. I ask that you put personal grudges aside and support the exception to the requirement.
I will not be swayed by your words, Caesar. The requirement must be upheld, and I will continue to filibuster any attempts to waive it.
Cato is a difficult opponent, but I cannot let him stand in the way of what is best for Rome. I must find a way to convince him to support the exception.
I understand your commitment to tradition, Cato, but I must remind you that the needs of the state come first. The senate seems to support the exception, and I ask that you consider the greater good.
I will not be convinced, Caesar. The requirement must stand, and I will continue to filibuster any attempts to waive it.
Cato is stubborn and unwilling to see reason. I must find a way to overcome his opposition. Perhaps I can find a compromise that satisfies both our needs.

Cato, I understand your commitment to tradition, but I ask that you consider a compromise. What if I were to cross the boundary to declare my candidacy but still wait outside the pomerium for the triumph? This way, I can uphold tradition while still fulfilling my duties as a candidate for consul.
Perhaps there is merit in Caesar's compromise. It would uphold tradition while still allowing him to declare his candidacy. I must consider this carefully.

I will consider your compromise, Caesar. It seems to uphold tradition while still allowing you to fulfill your duties as a candidate for consul. I will withdraw my objections for now and consider the matter further.
I have convinced Cato to withdraw his objections, at least for now. I must continue to work towards convincing him to support the exception.
Thank you, Cato, for considering my compromise. I believe it is the best solution for all involved. I hope that you will come to support the exception in the future.
I make no promises, Caesar, but I will consider it. For now, I will withdraw my objections and allow you to make your declaration.

I have succeeded in convincing Cato to withdraw his objections, at least for now. I must continue to work towards convincing him to support the exception. But for now, I can make my declaration and continue on the path towards becoming consul.

setting: It is the year 50 BC in Rome, and tensions between Julius Caesar and his opponents are at an all-time high. Fears of civil war are growing as both sides are building up troops in southern Gaul and northern Italy. Cicero and others have proposed disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey, which was overwhelmingly supported in the Senate but ultimately not passed. When a rumor spread that Caesar was marching into Italy, both consuls instructed Pompey to defend Italy as a last resort. At the start of 49 BC, Caesar's renewed offer to disarm was rejected, and the Senate declared him an enemy, issuing its senatus consultum ultimum.

dialogue.content: This is not how I envisioned my return to Rome. I had hoped for a hero's welcome, but instead, I am met with suspicion and fear. They see me as a threat, but I am only here to protect the Republic. The Senate's rejection of my offer to disarm is frustrating, to say the least. I have no intention of starting a civil war, but it seems they are pushing me towards that path. I must tread carefully and consider my next move.
Gentlemen of the Senate, we must act quickly to prevent a civil war. Disarmament by both Caesar and Pompey is the only way to ensure peace. I implore you to support this proposal.
Disarmament? How can we trust Caesar to lay down his arms? He is a conqueror, not a diplomat. We must prepare for war, not disarm.
I agree with Senator Opponent 1. Caesar has shown time and time again that he cannot be trusted. We must defend ourselves and our Republic.
Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but we must not jump to conclusions. Let us give Caesar the benefit of the doubt and accept his offer to disarm. We can always prepare for war if necessary.
I must meet with Pompey privately and try to convince him to join me. Together, we can prevent a civil war and save the Republic. But how can I make him see that? How can I convince him to trust me?

My dear Senators, I understand your concerns, but I assure you that I have no intention of starting a civil war. I am here to protect the Republic, not destroy it. Please, let us disarm and work towards a peaceful resolution.
We have heard these empty promises before, Caesar. We cannot trust you.
I agree. We must prepare for war.

My dear Senators, I understand your concerns, but we must not jump to conclusions. Let us give Caesar the benefit of the doubt and accept his offer to disarm. We can always prepare for war if necessary.
It seems Pompey is still willing to work with me. I must meet with him privately and convince him to support me. Together, we can prevent a civil war and save the Republic.

My dear Pompey, I know we have had our differences, but we must put aside our personal grievances and work towards a common goal. Disarmament is the only way to prevent a civil war and save the Republic. Please, join me in this effort.
I understand your concerns, Caesar, but I cannot simply trust you. You must offer me a guarantee that you will not use your army against me or the Republic.
A guarantee? How can I guarantee something like that? I cannot control every soldier in my army. But I must convince him somehow.

My dear Pompey, I cannot offer you a guarantee like that. But I can promise you that I have no intention of using my army against you or the Republic. I am here to protect the Republic, not destroy it.
I will consider your offer, Caesar. But I must consult with my advisors first.
It seems I have made some progress with Pompey. But I must remain vigilant. Anything could happen at any moment. I must be prepared for any eventuality.
Gentlemen, we have just received word that Caesar is marching towards Rome with his army. We must defend the Republic at all costs!
I agree. We must prepare for war!
Gentlemen, calm down. We must not jump to conclusions. Let us hear what Caesar has to say first.
So, they have finally pushed me to this point. I have no choice but to defend myself and my army. I must march towards Rome and show them that I am not to be underestimated.

My dear Senators, I have no intention of attacking Rome or the Republic. I am only here to defend myself and my army from those who seek to harm us. Please, let us find a peaceful resolution to this conflict.
You expect us to believe that? You are marching towards Rome with your army! You are a threat to the Republic!
We must defend ourselves and our Republic! Prepare for war!
Gentlemen, please. Let us not jump to conclusions. We must hear what Caesar has to say before we make any decisions.
I am running out of time. I must act quickly before they attack me. But how? How can I convince them to trust me?

My dear Senators, I understand your concerns, but I assure you that I have no intention of attacking Rome or the Republic. I am only here to defend myself and my army. Please, let us find a peaceful resolution to this conflict.
You expect us to believe that? You are a conqueror, not a diplomat. We must prepare for war!
I agree. We must defend ourselves and our Republic!
Gentlemen, please. Let us not jump to conclusions. We must hear what Caesar has to say before we make any decisions.
It seems Pompey is still willing to listen to me. Perhaps there is still hope for a peaceful resolution. But I must act quickly before it's too late.
My dear Pompey, I implore you to join me in this effort. Together, we can prevent a civil war and save the Republic. Please, put aside our personal grievances and work towards a common goal.
I will consider your offer, Caesar. But I must consult with my advisors first.
It seems I have made some progress with Pompey. But I must remain vigilant. Anything could happen at any moment. I must be prepared for any eventuality.

setting: Caesar had just landed in Antioch and had received the news of Pharnaces' invasion of his father's kingdom of Pontus across the Black Sea. Caesar's legates and the local client kings had been defeated by Pharnaces' invasion, leaving Caesar to evaluate the state of his father's kingdom.

dialogue.content: This is unacceptable. How dare Pharnaces invade my father's kingdom? I must take immediate action to restore order and show the world the power of Rome. Pharnaces must be defeated, and his invasion must be crushed. I will not let this insult to my father's legacy go unpunished.

Gather the troops, we march to Pontus. Pharnaces must be stopped, and his invasion must be crushed. We will restore order to my father's kingdom and show the world the power of Rome. Veni, vidi, vici. I came, I saw, I conquered.
But Caesar, Pontus is far away, and the troops are not yet ready to march. It will take time to gather the necessary supplies, and the men need time to rest and recover from the journey.

We do not have time to waste. Every moment we delay, Pharnaces grows stronger. We will march to Pontus immediately, and we will show the world the power of Rome. No one defies the might of Rome and lives to tell the tale. We will crush Pharnaces and his invasion, and we will restore order to my father's kingdom.
As you command, Caesar. The troops will be ready to march within the hour.

Pharnaces will pay for his insolence. I will not let him get away with invading my father's kingdom. The might of Rome will crush his invasion, and his defeat will be a lesson to all who dare challenge the power of Rome.

setting: Caesar, the great Roman general, is in the Antioch palace negotiating a treaty with neighboring rulers. He has just returned from his conquest in Egypt, where he successfully defeated his rival, Pompey. However, upon his arrival, he learned that the king of what is now Crimea, Pharnaces, had attempted to seize his father's kingdom of Pontus across the Black Sea. Caesar engaged him at Zela and defeated him immediately, leading Caesar to write veni, vidi, vici ("I came, I saw, I conquered"), Pompey's previous victories over such poor enemies. Caesar is now ready to move on to his next conquest and secure his power in the region.

dialogue.content: These negotiations are crucial to the expansion of my empire. I must ensure that I have the support of these neighboring rulers to maintain my power in this region. My victory over Pharnaces has proven my military strength, but I must also show my diplomatic skills to gain the trust of these rulers. I must be firm, yet fair in my negotiations. My ultimate goal is to expand my empire, and I will not let anything stand in my way.
I am honored to meet with you, Caesar. I have heard much of your conquests and your great military victories. What brings you to our lands?
I am here to discuss a treaty between our lands. I am seeking to expand my empire, and I believe that working together would be beneficial for both of our nations.
We are aware of your recent victory over Pharnaces. It is impressive, but it also raises concerns about your intentions in this region.
I assure you that my intentions are honorable. My conquests are not for personal gain, but for the betterment of Rome and its people. I am willing to negotiate terms that benefit both of our nations.
What do you propose, Caesar?
I propose a mutual defense pact, where we agree to defend each other's lands in times of war. In addition, I am willing to offer trade agreements and assistance in infrastructure development.
And what do you expect in return?
I expect your loyalty and support in my future endeavors. As I expand my empire, I will need the support of strong and reliable allies.
We are willing to consider your proposal, Caesar. However, we must also consider the opinions of our people. We will need some time to discuss this amongst ourselves.
I must be patient. Diplomacy takes time, and I cannot rush these negotiations. However, I must also be firm in my demands. I will not leave without a favorable outcome.
We will give you our decision in two days' time, Caesar. Please use this time to explore our lands and learn more about our people.
Thank you for your hospitality. I look forward to learning more about your lands.
I must use this time to my advantage. I will learn as much as I can about these rulers and their people. This will give me an edge in future negotiations and conquests.
After much consideration, we have decided to accept your proposal, Caesar. We believe that a mutual defense pact and trade agreements will benefit both of our nations.
I am pleased to hear this. Our alliance will be a strong one, and I look forward to working with you all in the future.
We do have one condition, Caesar. We request that you do not interfere with our internal affairs or attempt to expand your empire into our lands.

I understand your concerns, but I cannot agree to this condition. As a powerful nation, it is my duty to expand my empire and ensure the safety and prosperity of my people. However, I promise to be respectful of your lands and your people.
We accept your promise, Caesar. Our alliance will be beneficial for both of our nations, and we must trust each other to uphold our agreements.

I have secured a strong alliance with these neighboring rulers. My empire is expanding, and my power is growing. I will not stop until I have conquered all that I desire. The world will remember the name Julius Caesar.

setting: After his successful campaign against the Callaeci and Lusitani, Julius Caesar was hailed imperator and returned home to Rome in the summer of 60 BC. However, he was faced with a difficult decision: to either wait outside the pomerium for a triumph or cross the boundary to make a declaration of consular candidacy and give up his command and triumph. Caesar's enemy Cato filibustered attempts to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person, forcing Caesar to choose between a triumph and the consulship.

dialogue.content: What a difficult decision I am faced with. I have achieved military victory in Hispania Ulterior and have been hailed imperator, but now I must choose between a triumph and the consulship. How can I give up the glory and spoils of a triumph, but yet how can I turn down the opportunity to become consul? I must weigh my options carefully and make the best decision for myself and for Rome.

I object to any waiver of the requirement for the declaration to be made in person. It is a long-standing tradition that must be upheld. We cannot simply make exceptions for those who think they are above the law.

Cato, always the thorn in my side. He knows how much I want to be consul and will do anything to prevent it. But I cannot let him get in the way of my goals. I must find a way to overcome this obstacle.

Gentlemen, I understand the importance of tradition, but we must also consider the practicality of the situation. As imperator, I have duties to attend to and cannot simply wait outside the pomerium for weeks on end. I propose a compromise: I will cross the boundary to make my declaration, but I will not hold a triumph until after my consulship is over.
I cannot agree to such a compromise. The requirement for the declaration to be made in person is non-negotiable. If Caesar wants to be consul, he must abide by the rules.
Cato will not budge. I must find another way to get what I want. Perhaps I can rally support from other senators or appeal to the people for their support.

Gentlemen, I implore you to reconsider. I have served Rome faithfully and have achieved military victory in Hispania Ulterior. I believe that I am the best candidate for consul and urge you to support me in my endeavors.
I, for one, support Caesar's proposal. It is a reasonable compromise that allows him to fulfill his duties as imperator while also pursuing his political ambitions.
Ah, Brutus, always the loyal friend. With his support, I may be able to sway others to my side.
I still object to this compromise. It sets a dangerous precedent and undermines the importance of our traditions. If Caesar wants to be consul, he must follow the rules like everyone else.

Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but I believe that this compromise is the best course of action for all parties involved. I urge you to consider my proposal carefully and make the right decision for Rome.

I have done all that I can for now. It is up to the senate to decide my fate. But whatever happens, I will not let Cato or anyone else stand in the way of my ambitions. I will become consul, no matter the cost.

setting: Caesar, the great Roman general, is in Rome mapping out his next campaign. He has just returned from his victory over Pharnaces, the king of Crimea, who had attempted to seize his father's kingdom of Pontus across the Black Sea. Caesar defeated him immediately, leading Caesar to write veni, vidi, vici ("I came, I saw, I conquered"), Pompey's previous victories over such poor enemies. Now, he is planning his next move, considering which territories to conquer next in his quest for power and glory.

dialogue.content: What territory should I conquer next? Gaul, perhaps? No, I've already conquered Gaul. Britain, then? Yes, that would be a worthy challenge. And it would expand my empire even further. But first, I need to gather my forces and resources. I must make sure I am fully prepared for this campaign. And I must also consider the political implications of my actions. How will the Senate react to my conquest of Britain? Will they see it as a bold move or as a threat to their power? I must tread carefully.
Caesar, may I speak with you?
Of course, Brutus. What is it?

I have been hearing rumors that some members of the Senate are plotting against you. They fear your growing power and influence. They believe that you are becoming too ambitious, too eager for conquest. They are planning to take action against you.

So, the Senate is plotting against me. I should have expected this. But I cannot let their petty politics stop me from achieving my goals. I must stay focused and determined. I will not be deterred by their threats.

Thank you for bringing this to my attention, Brutus. I am aware of the Senate's concerns, but I will not be intimidated. I will continue to pursue my ambitions and conquer new territories. And if the Senate tries to stand in my way, I will crush them.
But Caesar, is that wise? You risk alienating your allies and creating new enemies. You must think of the long-term consequences of your actions.
I am well aware of the consequences, Brutus. But I will not let fear or caution hold me back. I am Caesar, and I will do whatever it takes to achieve my goals.

Brutus means well, but he lacks the vision and courage to see what must be done. He is too concerned with playing it safe, with maintaining the status quo. But that is not the path to greatness. To achieve greatness, one must be willing to take risks, to challenge the established order, to defy convention. And that is exactly what I intend to do.

Thank you for your concern, Brutus. But I must do what I must do. I will not be held back by fear or caution. I will conquer new territories and expand my empire. And if the Senate dares to stand in my way, they will regret it.
I understand, Caesar. But please be careful. Your enemies are many, and they are always watching.
I am always careful, Brutus. But I will not let caution paralyze me. I will move forward with confidence and determination. And I will crush anyone who stands in my way.

Brutus is right about one thing: my enemies are many. But that only makes me more determined to succeed. I will show them all what it means to be a true leader, a true conqueror. I will go down in history as one of the greatest men who ever lived. And nothing, not even the Senate, will stop me.

setting: After seizing the Callaeci capital in northwestern Spain, Caesar had brought Roman troops to the Atlantic and claimed to have completed the conquest of the peninsula. He had enough plunder to pay off his debts, but upon his return to Rome in the summer of 60 BC, he was faced with a difficult choice: either wait outside the pomerium for a triumph or give up his command and triumph to make a declaration of consular candidacy and run for the consulship. Despite attempts to waive the requirement for the declaration to be made in person, Caesar's enemy Cato filibustered in the senate, leaving Caesar with the choice between a triumph and the consulship.

Despite Cato's opposition, Caesar was eventually able to convince the senate to waive the requirement for him to make his declaration of consular candidacy in person. He chose to run for consul and gave up his command and triumph. This decision would ultimately lead to his rise to power and the downfall of the Roman Republic.

dialogue.content: I have conquered Hispania Ulterior and brought Roman troops to the Atlantic. I have seized enough plunder to pay off my debts, but I am not yet done. I must choose between a triumph and the consulship. The triumph would be a great honor, but the consulship would give me the power and influence I need to achieve my goals. Cato is my enemy, and he will do whatever he can to stop me. I must make a decision that will benefit me the most, regardless of what others may think.

I object to the proposal to waive the requirement for Caesar to make his declaration of consular candidacy in person. This is an important tradition, and we should not make exceptions for anyone, even if they have achieved great military victories.

Cato is trying to stop me from running for consul. He knows that if I become consul, I will have the power to enact the reforms I want. I must find a way to overcome his opposition and win the consulship.

I believe that Caesar has done enough for the Republic to deserve an exception to the declaration rule. He has conquered Hispania Ulterior and brought Roman troops to the Atlantic. Surely that is worthy of recognition.
I disagree, Pompey. Caesar must follow the rules like everyone else. We cannot make exceptions just because someone has achieved military victories.
Pompey is on my side, but Cato is not backing down. I must find a way to convince the senate to support me.
I think we should hear what Caesar has to say about this. He has served the Republic well, and we should give him a chance to speak for himself.

My fellow senators, I understand the importance of tradition and rules, but I have achieved great military victories for the Republic. I have brought Roman troops to the Atlantic and conquered Hispania Ulterior. I believe that this is worthy of recognition, and I ask that you waive the requirement for me to make my declaration of consular candidacy in person.
But Caesar, you know that the rule is there for a reason. We cannot simply ignore it because of your military victories. You must follow the rules like everyone else.
Cato is not budging. I must find a way to convince the other senators to support me.
I agree with Caesar. He has done enough for the Republic to deserve an exception to the declaration rule. We should recognize his achievements and give him the opportunity to run for consul.
Thank you, Metellus. I believe that my achievements speak for themselves, and I ask that you consider them when making your decision.
I still disagree. We cannot simply ignore the rules because of someone's military victories. We must uphold the traditions of the Republic.
Cato is stubborn, but I have the support of others. I must continue to make my case and convince the senate to support me.

setting: It is the year 45 BC, and the Roman Republic is in turmoil. The First Triumvirate, consisting of Julius Caesar, Pompey, and Crassus, has dissolved, and Caesar has returned from his successful conquest of Gaul to find himself at odds with Pompey and the Roman Senate. In an attempt to gain control of the Republic, Pompey and his supporters have raised an army in Spain to challenge Caesar's rule. Caesar, not one to back down from a fight, has gathered his own army and marched to Spain to confront Pompey's forces. The two armies have met in a decisive battle, and the fate of Rome hangs in the balance.

dialogue.content: This is it. The moment I have been waiting for. The moment that will determine the fate of Rome. I have spent years building my reputation as a great general, and now it is time to prove it. Pompey may have the support of the Senate, but I have the support of the people. They know that I am the one who can lead Rome to greatness. And now, here in Spain, I have the chance to prove it. I will not let them down.
Caesar, you may have defeated my father, but you will not defeat me. I am his son, and I will not let you take Spain from us.

You are mistaken, young man. I am not here to take Spain from anyone. I am here to defend the Republic and to ensure that Rome remains strong. Your father was a great man, but he made the mistake of thinking that he could challenge me. And now, you have made the same mistake. I do not relish the thought of shedding Roman blood, but if that is what it takes to ensure the survival of our great Republic, then so be it.
You talk of the Republic, but you are nothing but a tyrant. You have seized power for yourself, and you care nothing for the people of Rome. You only care about your own ambition.

You are wrong. I have always put the interests of Rome first. I have fought for her, bled for her, and I will die for her if need be. But I will not let her fall into the hands of men like your father, who care only for their own power and prestige. This battle will decide the fate of Rome, and I am confident that we will emerge victorious. But know this, young man. If you continue to fight against us, you will bring only destruction and ruin upon yourself and your followers. Lay down your arms, and I will spare your life. But if you choose to fight, then you will face the full force of the Roman army, and you will not emerge unscathed.
Caesar, the men are ready to fight. We will follow you to the end, wherever that may be.
