dialogue.content: I cannot believe Sulla would try to force me to abandon my wife and disregard our marriage. It is a matter of principle to me, and I will not let him take that away from me. I know what I have to do.
Caesar, I demand that you comply with my orders and abdicate your position as flamen Dialis and divorce Cornelia. Your defiance will not be tolerated.
Sulla, you have no right to interfere with our marriage. Caesar is my husband, and I will stand by him no matter what.
I will not abandon my wife and my beliefs just because you demand it, Sulla. I will not comply with your unjust orders.
Then you leave me no choice, Caesar. You will be put on the proscription lists, and you will face the consequences of your actions.
I knew this was a possibility, but I will not back down. I must go into hiding and hope that my relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins can intercede on my behalf.
I will do everything in my power to protect my husband. You will not break us apart.
I am grateful for Cornelia's support, but I cannot risk her safety. I must leave her behind and seek refuge elsewhere.
Caesar, we have successfully interceded on your behalf. Sulla has agreed to a compromise where you will resign your priesthood but keep your wife and chattels.
I am relieved to hear this news. Thank you for your assistance. I will comply with Sulla's compromise.
I see in Caesar many Mariuses. He will be a thorn in my side for years to come.
I may have to be cautious and bide my time, but I will not forget Sulla's actions towards me. I will seek revenge and make him pay for his injustice.

setting: Caesar arrived in Rome in October after his victory at the bloody battle of Munda. He celebrated an unseemly triumph over fellow Romans and started preparations for war on the Parthians to avenge Crassus' death at Carrhae in 53 BC. The war was set to start on 18 March 44 BC.

dialogue.content: I have finally returned to Rome, and my victory at Munda has solidified my power. The people of Rome will see that I am their rightful leader, and my triumph will prove it. But my work is not done yet. I must avenge Crassus' death and show the Parthians that Rome will not be defeated. The war will be difficult, but I am determined to succeed.
Caesar, it's good to see you back in Rome. Your triumph was impressive, but some of the senators are concerned about your growing power.

I understand their concerns, Brutus, but I have done nothing to warrant suspicion. I am simply trying to protect Rome and avenge our fallen soldiers. The Parthians must be held accountable for their actions.
Caesar, we support your desire for vengeance, but we must also consider the cost of war. The people of Rome are tired of conflict, and our resources are stretched thin.
I understand your concerns, Cassius, but we cannot let the Parthians get away with what they did to Crassus. I have already made preparations for the war, and I will not back down now.
Caesar, I have some news that may interest you. The Senate has voted to grant you the title of dictator for life.
This is exactly what I needed. With this title, I will have the power to lead Rome to greatness and ensure that my enemies are crushed. The Parthians will regret crossing me.
Thank you, Mark Antony. This is a great honor and I will use this power wisely. The Parthians will soon learn that Rome will not be defeated.

setting: The Roman Senate is in session, with senators debating Caesar's future role and powers within the government. Some are calling for his overthrow, while others argue for his continued leadership. The tension in the room is palpable, as both sides present their arguments with fervor and conviction. Caesar sits stoically in his seat, listening intently to the arguments being made.

dialogue.content: I knew this day would come. My rise to power has made me many enemies, and I have always known that there would be those who would seek to undermine me. But I will not go quietly into the night. I am Julius Caesar, and I will fight tooth and nail to maintain my position of power. These senators may think they can bring me down, but they underestimate me at their peril.
Caesar's actions have been nothing short of tyrannical. He has amassed too much power and influence, and it is time for us to take action to restore the balance of power in the Republic.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but I assure you that I have no intention of becoming a tyrant. My only desire is to see Rome prosper and thrive under my leadership. I have brought many victories to this great nation, and I intend to continue doing so. If you have evidence of any wrongdoing on my part, I urge you to present it now.

Caesar, we do not need evidence of wrongdoing to see that you have exceeded your bounds as a leader. Your actions have been increasingly authoritarian, and we fear for the future of the Republic if you are allowed to continue unchecked.

Cicero... I had hoped he would be on my side. He is a brilliant orator, and his support would have been invaluable. But it seems he has turned against me. No matter. I will not be swayed by his words. I must stand firm and defend my position.

Friends, I understand that there are concerns about Caesar's power, but we must remember all that he has done for Rome. He has brought us victory after victory, and his leadership has been instrumental in securing our place as a world power. We cannot simply cast him aside like yesterday's news.

I thank you for your support, Antony. You have always been a loyal friend to me, and I appreciate your words. But we must remember that this is not about me as an individual. This is about the future of Rome. I am willing to work with the Senate to find a solution that satisfies everyone, but I will not simply step down and allow chaos to reign.

Caesar, I have always respected you as a leader, but I fear that your ambition has clouded your judgment. We cannot allow one man to hold all the power in Rome. It is our duty as senators to ensure that the Republic remains strong and stable.

I understand your concerns, Brutus, and I respect your opinion. But I must remind you that I hold the support of the people. They have seen what I can do, and they believe in me. I will not simply abandon them because a few senators are unhappy with my leadership.

These senators are like wolves, circling around me, waiting for the right moment to strike. But I will not be brought down by their petty bickering. I will continue to fight for what I believe in, no matter the cost. Rome needs a strong leader, and I am the only one capable of filling that role.

setting: Caesar and his generals are gathered in his tent in Illyricum, planning their next military action against their enemies in the region around the Adriatic. The atmosphere is tense as they discuss their strategies, each man weighing in with his own ideas and opinions. Caesar sits at the head of the table, his gaze intense as he listens to his advisors. Around him are some of his most trusted generals, including Mark Antony and Decimus Brutus.

dialogue.content: As he listens to his generals' suggestions, Caesar can feel the weight of his responsibilities bearing down on him. He knows that the decisions he makes in this tent could mean the difference between victory and defeat, between life and death for his men. He takes a deep breath, trying to steady his nerves, and reminds himself that he is Julius Caesar, conqueror of Gaul, and that he has faced greater challenges than this.

My lord, I believe that our best course of action would be to launch a surprise attack on the enemy's stronghold. We know that they have been stockpiling weapons and supplies, and if we move quickly, we can catch them off guard and deal them a decisive blow.

With all due respect, Mark Antony, I must disagree. Our scouts have reported that the enemy has fortified their position, and an attack would be suicidal. I suggest we try to draw them out into the open, where we can engage them on more even ground.

Both of your suggestions have merit, my friends. However, I think we need to consider the long-term implications of our actions. We are not just fighting a battle here, but a war. We need to think about how our actions will affect our ability to maintain control of this region in the months and years to come.

Of course, my lord. But I think that a surprise attack would give us a significant advantage, both in terms of morale and strategy. If we can take out their leader and destroy their weapons, they will be forced to retreat or surrender.
I still believe that a more cautious approach is warranted. We should wait for reinforcements and try to wear down the enemy's resolve before engaging them in battle.

As he listens to his advisors bickering, Caesar can feel a headache coming on. He knows that he needs to make a decision soon, but he can't shake the feeling that there is no easy solution to this problem. He takes another deep breath and looks around the table, hoping for some inspiration.
Gentlemen, I appreciate your input, but I fear we are getting bogged down in details. We need to take a step back and look at the bigger picture. What is our ultimate goal here?
To defeat our enemies, my lord, and secure our position in this region.
To protect our men and ensure that we do not suffer any unnecessary losses.

Exactly. And how do we achieve those goals? We need to be strategic, but we also need to be flexible. We cannot afford to be too cautious, but we cannot be reckless either. We need to strike a balance between our short-term and long-term objectives.

He can see that his generals are starting to get restless, and he knows that he needs to wrap up this meeting soon. But he also knows that he cannot make a hasty decision. He needs to consider all the factors at play and come up with a plan that will ensure their victory.

I think we need to take some time to think about this, gentlemen. We will reconvene tomorrow and continue our discussion. In the meantime, I want each of you to come up with a proposal for our next move. We will review them all and make a decision based on the best course of action.
As you command, my lord.
Very well, Caesar. We will prepare our proposals and present them to you tomorrow.

As his generals file out of the tent, Caesar can feel the weight of the world on his shoulders. He knows that the decisions he makes in the coming days will have far-reaching consequences, not just for his own career, but for the future of Rome itself. He takes a deep breath and reminds himself that he is up to the challenge. After all, he is Julius Caesar, conqueror of Gaul, and there is nothing he cannot achieve if he sets his mind to it.

setting: The Roman Senate is gathered to discuss the recall of Julius Caesar from Gaul. The conservatives, led by Cato and Bibulus, seek to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return without honours or a second consulship. Caesar's victory against Vercingetorix in 52 BC led to his provincia in Gaul, but he continued to fight the Bellovaci in the following year, leading to the proposal to recall him. The Senate is divided between those who support Caesar's continued command and those who believe he must return to Rome.

dialogue.content: As I sit here in the Senate, I can feel the tension rising. The conservatives have been trying to undermine my position for years, and now they have the support of Pompey. It's clear that they want me gone, and I know they'll stop at nothing to achieve their goal. But I won't go quietly. I've worked too hard to establish my position in Gaul, and I won't let them take it away from me. I need to find a way to outmaneuver them, to turn the tables on them before it's too late.

Senators, we must act now before it's too late. Caesar's continued command in Gaul is a threat to the stability of the Republic. We have already seen how he has abused his power, declaring himself dictator and refusing to step down. We cannot allow this to continue. Pompey, I implore you to join us in calling for his recall. It is the only way to restore order and protect the interests of the people.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but we must be cautious. Caesar has many supporters in the Senate and among the people. If we move too quickly, we risk a backlash that could undermine our own position. Perhaps we should consider a compromise, a way to bring Caesar back to Rome without causing a confrontation.

With all due respect, Pompey, I think you're being too cautious. We can't afford to let Caesar continue to flout the laws of the Republic. If we don't act now, who knows what he'll do next? He's already demonstrated that he has no respect for the Senate or the people. We need to show him that we won't tolerate this kind of behavior.

Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but I must remind you that I am still the governor of Gaul, appointed by the Senate itself. I have done nothing to warrant a recall, and I will not submit to your demands. If you want to remove me from office, you will have to do so by force. But be warned, I have the loyalty of my legions and the support of the people. You will not succeed without a fight.

Caesar, we do not seek a fight. We only want what is best for the Republic. If you truly care about Rome, you will come back and submit to the will of the Senate. We are not your enemies, but we cannot allow you to continue to act outside the law.

This is a delicate situation. On the one hand, I understand the concerns of my fellow Senators. Caesar has amassed a great deal of power and influence, and there are legitimate fears that he could use it to seize control of the Republic. On the other hand, I know that many people support him, and any move against him could cause a backlash that could threaten our own position. I need to find a way to navigate these competing interests and come up with a solution that everyone can live with.

Caesar, let's be clear. We're not asking you to step down from your position in Gaul. We're merely asking you to return to Rome and resume your duties as a private citizen. We're not trying to take away your power or influence. We just want to ensure that the Republic is governed according to the law, not the whims of any one individual.

These men are fools. They think they can bully me into submission, but they don't understand the power that I wield. If they want a fight, I'll give them one. I'll show them what it means to cross me. But first, I need to bide my time, to wait for the right moment to strike. I won't let them take me down without a fight.

setting: The scene takes place in the Roman Forum during the period of civil war. Julius Caesar, a prominent political figure, is addressing the people of Rome about the need for political stability and the importance of strong leadership. The trust between Caesar and Pompey has disintegrated, and the conservatives around Cato in the Senate seek to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honors or a second consulship. Cato, Bibulus, and their allies were successful in winning Pompey over to take a hard line against Caesar's continued command.

dialogue.content: As I stand here before the people of Rome, I feel a great responsibility towards them. The trust between Pompey and me has been broken, and the conservatives around Cato are trying to force me to return from Gaul without honors or a second consulship. They underestimate my abilities and my loyalty towards Rome. I must convince the people of Rome that I am the only one who can provide the stability and leadership needed in these times of turmoil. I must show them that I am willing to put Rome's interests above everything else.
What are your plans, Caesar? How do you intend to bring stability to Rome?

My dear citizens of Rome, I understand your concerns, and I assure you that I have a plan to bring stability to our great city. First and foremost, we must put an end to this civil war. The bloodshed and chaos must stop. We must come together and find a way to reconcile our differences. I am willing to negotiate with Pompey and his allies to find a peaceful solution to this conflict. But make no mistake; I will not compromise on the safety and security of Rome.
But Caesar, how can we trust you after what happened with Pompey? How can we be sure that you will not betray us?

I understand your concerns, my friend, and I can only ask you to look at my record of service to Rome. I have always put Rome's interests above everything else. I have fought for Rome in Gaul and brought wealth and prosperity to our city. I have always been loyal to Rome, and I will continue to be so. Trust is not something that can be given; it must be earned. And I intend to earn your trust through my actions.
But Caesar, how can we trust you when you have defied the Senate's authority? You have taken matters into your own hands and acted without our consent.

My dear senator, I have acted in the best interests of Rome. The Senate's authority is important, but it must not come at the cost of Rome's safety and security. The enemy is at our gates, and we must act swiftly and decisively to protect our city. I have not acted without reason, and I am willing to explain my actions to the Senate. But make no mistake; I will not hesitate to do what is necessary to protect Rome.
What about Pompey, Caesar? How do you intend to deal with him?

Pompey is a great general and a worthy opponent. But he is also a Roman, and I believe that we can find a way to reconcile our differences. I am willing to negotiate with him and find a peaceful solution to this conflict. But make no mistake; I will not compromise on Rome's safety and security. I will do what is necessary to protect our city and our people.

As I finish my speech, I feel a sense of relief. The people of Rome seem to be on my side. But I know that the road ahead will not be easy. I must be prepared to do what is necessary to protect Rome and its people. I must be willing to make sacrifices and take risks. But I am ready for the challenge. I am Julius Caesar, and I will do whatever it takes to ensure the safety and security of Rome.

setting: It is the start of 53 BC, and Julius Caesar is in Gaul suppressing insurgencies. In the previous winter, there was an ambush and destruction of a legion and five cohorts in Gaul, which produced substantial concern in Rome about Caesar's command and competence. The death of Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife Julia in childbirth c. late August 54 did not create a rift between Caesar and Pompey. At the start of 53 BC, Caesar sought and received reinforcements by recruitment and a private deal with Pompey before two years of largely unsuccessful campaigning against Gallic insurgents.

dialogue.content: I need more soldiers to suppress the insurgencies in Gaul. The ambush and destruction of the legion and five cohorts in the previous winter have weakened my army, and I cannot afford any more losses. I must seek reinforcements through recruitment and a private deal with Pompey. I know that Pompey has been appointed as the sole consul to restore order to the city, but he owes me a favor for supporting him during his consulship. I must use this to my advantage and get the reinforcements I need.
Caesar, what brings you to my doorstep today?

Greetings, Pompey. I have come to seek your assistance in getting reinforcements for my army in Gaul. As you know, we have been facing insurgencies, and I have had to deal with the loss of a legion and five cohorts in the previous winter. I need more soldiers to suppress these insurgencies and bring peace to the region.
I am aware of the situation in Gaul, Caesar. And I am willing to help you. But what do I get in return?
I understand your concerns, Pompey. And I am willing to offer you a private deal. I can help you with anything you need in the future, and you can count on my support.

Hmm, I see. Well, I am willing to provide you with the reinforcements you need. But I must warn you, Caesar, that the situation in Rome is becoming increasingly unstable. I have been appointed as the sole consul to restore order to the city, and I cannot afford any distractions.

I know that the situation in Rome is unstable, but I cannot let that distract me from my mission in Gaul. I must get the reinforcements I need to suppress the insurgencies and bring peace to the region.

I understand your concerns, Pompey. And I assure you that I will not let anything distract me from my mission in Gaul. I need the reinforcements to ensure the safety of my army and bring peace to the region. I am grateful for your help, and I will make sure that you get what you need in the future.
Very well, Caesar. I will provide you with the reinforcements you need. But remember, our deal is private, and no one else must know about it. The stability of Rome depends on it.
I understand, Pompey. Our deal is private, and no one else will know about it. Thank you for your assistance, and I will make sure to keep my end of the bargain.

I am relieved that I have secured the reinforcements I need. With Pompey's help, I can now focus on suppressing the insurgencies in Gaul and bringing peace to the region. I know that the situation in Rome is unstable, but I must not let that distract me from my mission. I will make sure that I keep my end of the bargain with Pompey, and our deal remains private.

setting: It is 63 BC and the location is the Roman Forum. The scene is a debate on issues of state religion. The participants are Julius Caesar, Quintus Lutatius Catulus, and Publius Servilius Isauricus. Caesar is standing for the praetorship and for the post of pontifex maximus, the highest ranking state religious official. He is facing two influential senators, Catulus and Isauricus.

dialogue.content: I can feel the tension in the air as I stand here in the Forum. This is a crucial moment for me, as I stand for the praetorship and the post of pontifex maximus. I know that I am facing tough competition in the form of Catulus and Isauricus, but I am confident that I can win this. I have prepared well, and I have the support of Pompey, who opposes Catulus' candidacy. I need to make my case convincingly and win over the people.

My fellow Romans, I stand before you today as a candidate for the praetorship and for the post of pontifex maximus. I am honored to have the opportunity to serve my country in these important roles. As you all know, the position of pontifex maximus is the highest ranking state religious official, and it is a position that requires great responsibility and dedication. I believe that I am the best candidate for this job, and I will work tirelessly to uphold the traditions and values of our great Republic.

I must object to Caesar's candidacy for the position of pontifex maximus. He is a man known for his ambition and his lack of respect for our traditions. We cannot allow someone like him to hold such an important position in our state religion. I urge you all to consider my candidacy instead, as I have a long record of service to our Republic and a deep respect for our traditions.

I agree with Catulus. Caesar may be a skilled politician, but he does not have the experience or the temperament to hold the position of pontifex maximus. We need someone who is deeply committed to our religious traditions and who will uphold them with honor and dignity. I believe that I am the best candidate for this job, and I ask for your support.

I understand your concerns, my esteemed colleagues, but I believe that you are mistaken. I have the utmost respect for our religious traditions, and I am committed to upholding them with honor and dignity. As for my ambition, I believe that it is a good thing for someone in my position to be ambitious. It shows that I am dedicated to serving our Republic and that I am willing to work hard to achieve my goals. I ask that you consider my qualifications and my dedication to our Republic, and vote for me in the upcoming election.
I cannot in good conscience support Caesar's candidacy for pontifex maximus. I believe that he is not the right person for the job, and I will be voting for myself in the upcoming election.
I agree with Catulus. I cannot support Caesar's candidacy either. I will be voting for myself in the upcoming election.

It seems that Catulus and Isauricus are not convinced by my arguments. I need to find a way to win them over or to convince the people to support me. Perhaps I need to offer them something in return for their support. Or perhaps I need to find a way to discredit them in the eyes of the people. Whatever I do, I need to act quickly and decisively if I want to win this election.

I understand that you may have concerns about my candidacy, but I urge you to consider the bigger picture. We are facing challenging times, and we need strong and capable leaders to guide us through these troubled waters. I believe that I am that leader, and I ask for your support in the upcoming election. Together, we can build a better future for our Republic.
I cannot support Caesar's candidacy, but I wish him luck in the upcoming election.
I too cannot support Caesar's candidacy, but I wish him luck in the upcoming election.

It seems that I have not been able to win over Catulus and Isauricus, but I still have a chance to win the election if I can win over the people. I need to find a way to appeal to their emotions and to convince them that I am the best candidate for the job. I must work harder and find a way to make my case more convincing.

My fellow Romans, I stand before you today as a candidate for the praetorship and for the post of pontifex maximus. I know that there are those who doubt my qualifications and my dedication to our religious traditions, but I assure you that I am deeply committed to serving our Republic and upholding our values. I ask that you consider my qualifications and my dedication to our Republic, and vote for me in the upcoming election. Together, we can build a better future for our Republic.

setting: Caesar's absence from Italy put Mark Antony, as magister equitum, in charge. His rule was unpopular; Publius Cornelius Dolabella, serving as plebeian tribune in 47 BC, agitated for debt relief and after that agitation got out of hand the senate moved for Antony to restore order. Delayed by a mutiny in southern Italy, he returned and suppressed the riots by force, along with his popularity. Cato had marched to Africa and there Metellus Scipio was in charge of the remaining republicans; they allied with Juba of Numidia; what used to be Pompey's fleet also raided the central Mediterranean islands. Caesar's governor in Spain, moreover, was sufficiently unpopular that the province revolted and switched to the republican side.

dialogue.content: I have returned to Rome to find it in chaos. Mark Antony has failed to maintain order, and the people are calling for debt relief. Meanwhile, Cato has gone to Africa, and the republicans there have allied with Juba of Numidia. And to make matters worse, my governor in Spain has lost control of the province, and it has switched to the republican side. This is a dire situation, and I must act quickly to restore order and secure my position as the leader of Rome.

Gentlemen of the Senate, I have returned to Rome to find it in a state of unrest. The people are calling for debt relief, and there are rebels in Spain and Africa. However, I believe that we can resolve these issues peacefully. I propose that we grant amnesty to the rebels in Italy and work together to find a solution to the debt crisis.
But Caesar, granting amnesty to rebels sends the message that we are weak and cannot control our own territory. We cannot allow rebels to act with impunity.

I understand your concerns, but we must consider the bigger picture. If we continue to fight these rebels, it will only lead to more bloodshed and instability. We must show mercy and work towards a peaceful resolution. I believe that by doing so, we can win the hearts and minds of the people and restore order to Rome.
But what about the debt crisis? How do we address the concerns of the people?

I propose that we create a commission to investigate the debt crisis and find a solution that is fair to all parties involved. We must address the root causes of the problem and work together to find a sustainable solution. By doing so, we can show the people that we are committed to their well-being and the stability of Rome.
But what about the rebels in Africa and Spain? We cannot simply ignore them.

I understand your concerns, but we must approach these issues with caution. We cannot risk further conflict and instability. I propose that we send envoys to negotiate with the rebels and work towards a peaceful resolution. We must be willing to compromise and find common ground if we hope to restore order to Rome.

I have managed to convince the Senate to grant amnesty to the rebels in Italy and create a commission to investigate the debt crisis. However, I still face challenges in Africa and Spain. I must find a way to negotiate with the rebels and secure my position as the leader of Rome. This will not be an easy task, but I am confident that I can find a way forward.

Gentlemen, I thank you for your time and consideration. Let us work together to restore order and stability to Rome. We must show the people that we are committed to their well-being and the future of our great empire.

setting: It is 60 BC in Rome. Julius Caesar, Crassus, and Pompey have formed the First Triumvirate and hold significant power in the Roman Republic. Caesar has passed a bill to redistribute land to veterans, angering many in the Senate. He has also gained allies in the plebeian tribunes and has successfully passed bills to forgive tax debts and assign him control of provinces. However, fear of Gallic invasion has grown and the Senate is wary of Caesar's military power.

dialogue.content: These fools in the Senate underestimate me. They fear my power and seek to limit me, but they do not see the greater good I am working towards. My agrarian bill will provide land for my veterans and strengthen the Republic. The tax forgiveness and control of provinces will bring stability to our economy and protect us from foreign threats. And yet they cling to their old ways, refusing to see the need for change. But I will not be held back by their narrow-mindedness. I will continue to push forward, for the good of Rome.
My dear Caesar, I must say I am impressed with your recent successes in the Senate. The forgiveness of tax debts and control of provinces will greatly benefit us both.
Thank you, Crassus. Your support has been invaluable.
I agree with Crassus. Your leadership has been remarkable, Caesar. And I am pleased to announce that my daughter Julia and your son have been wed, solidifying our alliance.
That is wonderful news, Pompey. Our alliance is a strong one, and together we will accomplish great things.
I move the lex Vatinia, assigning the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years.
This is outrageous! Caesar cannot be allowed to control so much territory. We must stop this bill!

Bibulus is a fool. He cannot see the benefits of my control of these provinces. He only seeks to undermine me. But I will not be deterred. I have the support of the Triumvirate and the plebeian tribunes. I will see this bill passed.
Gentlemen, there is no need for debate. This bill is necessary for the protection and prosperity of Rome. I urge you to consider the greater good and pass this bill.
Another victory for me. The Senate may resist, but they cannot stop me. I will continue to push forward, for the good of Rome.

setting: Julius Caesar, a well-accepted member of the aristocracy, was co-opted into the pontifices in place of his deceased relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta. He was absent from Rome during this time. On his return, he was elected one of the military tribunes for 71 BC. There is no evidence that Caesar served in war during his term. He agitated for the removal of the Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for those who supported Lepidus' revolt to be pardoned. These advocacies were common and uncontroversial. The next year, 70 BC, Pompey and Crassus were consuls and brought legislation restoring the plebeian tribunate's rights. One of the tribunes, with Caesar supporting, then brought legislation pardoning the Lepidan exiles.

dialogue.content: It's time for me to make a move. My political career needs to advance, and I need to make a name for myself. I can't keep playing it safe forever. I need to show the people what I'm capable of. It's time to take some risks.

I propose that we go beyond pardoning the Lepidan exiles. We need to show the people that we are a just and merciful government. We need to bring them back into the fold and make them feel like they are part of our society once again. We need to give them a chance to contribute to Rome's greatness.
But Caesar, these are people who rebelled against the state. They committed treason.

I understand that, but we need to move forward. We can't keep punishing people for their past mistakes. We need to show them that we can be forgiving. If we don't, we risk alienating a large portion of our population. We need to be just, but we also need to be merciful.
But what about the message we send to other potential rebels? Won't they think they can get away with anything?

We need to trust that our justice system will prevent that from happening. We can't let fear control us. We need to show the people that we trust them and that we are willing to work with them. We need to show them that we are a government of the people, not just a government that rules over them.
I think Caesar has a point. We should consider pardoning the Lepidan exiles. It's time to move forward and start healing the divisions in our society.
I have them on my side. Now, I just need to make sure this legislation passes. I need to use all my skills to convince the other senators to vote for it. This is my chance to prove myself.
I'm glad we're all in agreement. We need to make sure this legislation passes. I'll do everything in my power to make sure it does. With your help, we can make this a reality.
I'm not convinced. I think we need to send a message to potential rebels. We can't let them think they can get away with anything.

I understand your concerns, but we can't let fear control us. We need to trust that our justice system will prevent future rebellions. We need to show the people that we are a just and merciful government. If we don't, we risk alienating a large portion of our population.
I agree with Caesar. We need to be just, but we also need to be merciful. It's time to move forward and start healing the divisions in our society.
I've convinced them. The legislation has passed. This is just the beginning. I'm ready for whatever comes next.

setting: Caesar was travelling through the Mediterranean Sea when he was intercepted and taken captive by pirates. The pirates demanded a ransom of fifty talents for his release, and Caesar paid it. After his release, Caesar returned with a fleet to capture and execute the pirates.

dialogue.content: What a humiliating experience to be taken captive by pirates. My reputation has been tarnished, and I cannot let this stand. I must return with a fleet and show them the consequences of crossing Julius Caesar.
You are a rich man, Caesar. We demand a ransom of fifty talents for your release.
I will pay your ransom, but mark my words, I will return with a fleet to capture and execute you and your men.
Hah! You are in no position to make threats. We have you at our mercy.
I must bide my time and wait for the opportune moment to strike. These pirates will regret ever crossing me.
I will pay your ransom, but I will not forget this humiliation. You will pay for it with your lives.
Very well. We will release you once we have received the ransom.
I will pay their ransom and bide my time until I can exact my revenge. No one crosses Julius Caesar and gets away with it.
Release me now, and I will leave in peace. But remember, I will return.
You are free to go. But remember this, Caesar, we are not afraid of you.
They should be afraid. Soon, they will regret ever crossing me.

setting: Julius Caesar sat behind his desk in his office, deep in conversation with Cicero. The two men were discussing Caesar's plans for political reform, which had been met with resistance from many members of the Senate. Caesar had risen to power through a string of military victories in the Gallic Wars, which had greatly extended Roman territory. His achievements, along with the support of his veteran army, had threatened to eclipse the standing of Pompey, who had realigned himself with the Senate after the death of Crassus in 53 BC. With the Gallic Wars concluded, the Senate had ordered Caesar to step down from his military command and return to Rome. In 49 BC, Caesar had openly defied the Senate's authority by crossing the Rubicon and marching towards Rome at the head of an army. This had begun Caesar's civil war, which he had won, leaving him in a position of near-unchallenged power and influence in 45 BC.

dialogue.content: I must convince Cicero of the necessity of my reforms. He is a man of great intelligence, and his support would be invaluable in overcoming the opposition in the Senate. But I must also be wary of his ambitions. Cicero may be a friend now, but his loyalties are fickle. I must tread carefully and not reveal too much of my plans.

Cicero, I appreciate your support in this matter. You are a man of great intellect, and your opinion carries much weight in the Senate. However, I sense that you have reservations about my plans. Please, speak freely. I value your honest opinion.

Julius, I fear that your reforms may be too radical. The Senate is already suspicious of your intentions, and I fear that you may be playing into their hands. The people may support you now, but they can be fickle. Once they turn against you, there will be no turning back.

I understand your concerns, Cicero, but I cannot sit idly by while the Republic crumbles around us. The Senate is corrupt and ineffective. It is time for a change. My reforms will bring about a new era of prosperity and stability for Rome.

I do not doubt your intentions, Julius. But I fear that your methods may be too extreme. You must remember that the Senate still holds much power. If you alienate them, you may find yourself in a precarious position.

Cicero is right to be cautious. The Senate is a powerful institution, and I cannot afford to underestimate their influence. But I am confident in my abilities. I have faced many challenges in my life, and I have always emerged victorious. I will not let the Senate stand in the way of progress.

I appreciate your concern, Cicero, but I must press on. The people of Rome have entrusted me with their future, and I cannot let them down. I will do what is necessary to bring about the changes that are needed.
Very well, Julius. I respect your determination, but I urge you to be careful. The road ahead will not be easy.
I understand the risks, Cicero. But I am willing to face them. Together, we can bring about a new era of greatness for Rome.

setting: Caesar sits at the head of a long table in his war council tent, surrounded by his closest generals. Maps and battle plans are scattered across the table, as the men discuss their strategy for the upcoming civil war. The tension in the tent is palpable, as the fate of the Roman Republic hangs in the balance.

dialogue.content: I have come too far to turn back now. The Senate has ordered me to disband my army and return to Rome, but I cannot let them strip me of my power. I have spent years conquering Gaul and building a loyal army, and I will not let it all go to waste. The time has come to cross the Rubicon and march on Rome. It will be a risky move, but I have faith in my men and in myself.

Caesar, we have discussed this plan at length, but I must advise caution. The Senate has many supporters, and we cannot be sure of the loyalty of all our troops. Once we cross the Rubicon, there is no turning back.

Decimus, I appreciate your concern, but we have no other choice. If we do not act now, the Senate will crush us and all we stand for. I have faith in the loyalty of my men, and I know that they will follow me to the end. We will cross the Rubicon and march on Rome, and we will emerge victorious.
Caesar, I have no doubt that your plan will succeed, but what of the people of Rome? They will not take kindly to a civil war, and it could damage our reputation among the citizens.

Mark Antony, I understand your concerns, but we cannot let the people of Rome stand in our way. We must do what is necessary to secure our power and protect our interests. The people will come to see the wisdom of our actions in time. We march on Rome at dawn.

setting: In Rome, after Sulla's victory in the civil war, Cinna's acta were annulled. Caesar was named as flamen Dialis during Cinna's dominance which led to his marriage to Cinna's daughter, Cornelia. Caesar's father did not seek a consulship during the domination of Lucius Cornelius Cinna and instead chose retirement. Caesar's father died suddenly in early 84 BC. Sulla consequently ordered Caesar to abdicate and divorce Cinna's daughter. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment. Caesar then went into hiding before his relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins were able to intercede on his behalf. They then reached a compromise where Caesar would resign his priesthood but keep his wife and chattels.

dialogue.content: Sulla thinks he can just take away everything I have worked for, including my marriage to Cornelia, just because he won a war? No, I cannot let him do that. I know the religious taboos of the priesthood would have forced me to forego a political career, but I cannot just give up everything that I have worked for. I will not let Sulla take away my marriage and my position as a flamen Dialis so easily. I need to find a way to negotiate with him and keep what is rightfully mine.

Caesar, you must understand that I cannot allow you to keep your priesthood and your marriage to Cornelia. Your father chose to retire during Cinna's dominance, and you were named as flamen Dialis during that time. You must resign from your priesthood and divorce Cornelia if you want to avoid being put on the proscription lists.

I understand your position, but I cannot just give up everything that I have worked for. The religious taboos of the priesthood would have forced me to forego a political career, but I have already made significant achievements. I cannot just abandon them. Is there no way we can come to a compromise?
I am willing to listen to your proposal, but you must understand that I am not going to make any concessions that go against the interests of the state.

I need to come up with a proposal that will satisfy Sulla and allow me to keep my marriage to Cornelia and my position as a flamen Dialis. I cannot lose everything I have worked for. But what can I offer him that he would be willing to accept?

I propose that I will resign from my priesthood, as you have demanded. However, I would like to keep my marriage to Cornelia and my chattels. In exchange, I am willing to offer my services to the state. I am a skilled military leader and can be of great use to you in your future campaigns.

This is an interesting proposal. Caesar is a talented military leader, and his services could be of great use to me. However, I cannot allow him to keep his marriage to Cornelia. It would set a bad precedent for other members of the aristocracy.
I am willing to accept your proposal, but you must understand that I cannot allow you to keep your marriage to Cornelia. I will allow you to keep your chattels, but you must divorce her.
I understand your position, but I cannot just abandon my wife. Is there no way we can come to a compromise on this issue as well?
I cannot allow Caesar to keep his marriage to Cornelia. However, I do not want to push him too far. He is a talented military leader, and I need him on my side.

I will allow you to keep your marriage to Cornelia, but you must resign from your priesthood and give up your right to run for political office. You can continue to serve the state in a military capacity, but you must give up your political ambitions.

This is not the perfect compromise that I was hoping for, but it is better than losing everything. I can continue to serve the state in a military capacity and keep my marriage to Cornelia. It is a small victory, but it is a victory nonetheless.

Thank you, Sulla. I accept your compromise. I will resign from my priesthood and give up my right to run for political office. I will continue to serve the state in a military capacity, and I will keep my marriage to Cornelia.
Very well, Caesar. I am glad that we were able to come to a compromise. I will expect great things from you in the future.

I have managed to keep my marriage to Cornelia and my position as a flamen Dialis. It is not the perfect compromise, but it is better than losing everything. I will continue to serve the state in a military capacity and make sure that my talents are recognized. I will not let Sulla or anyone else take away what is rightfully mine.

setting: Caesar and his generals were gathered in his tent to discuss the strategy for the upcoming campaign against Mithridates. The atmosphere was tense, and everyone was focused on the task at hand. Caesar sat at the head of the table, his brow furrowed in concentration, while his generals sat around him, silently waiting for his instructions.

dialogue.content: This campaign against Mithridates is crucial for my political career. If I can emerge victorious, it will cement my position as one of Rome's greatest generals and pave the way for my eventual rise to power. But I must be careful. The other generals are experienced and skilled, but they are also ambitious and may try to undermine me. I must assert my dominance and make it clear that I am in charge.
Caesar, we have scouted the enemy's position and believe that we have identified a weakness in their defenses. If we attack from the north, we can catch them off guard and take them by surprise.
Interesting. But what about their cavalry? Won't they be able to flank us if we attack from that direction?
We have devised a plan to deal with their cavalry. We will station our own cavalry on the flanks and use them to keep the enemy's cavalry at bay.

These men are competent, but they lack the vision and boldness that I possess. If I want to win this campaign, I must take risks and make bold moves. But I must also be careful not to overstep my bounds and risk alienating my allies.
Caesar, what are your thoughts on the supply situation? We will need to ensure that our troops are well-fed and equipped if we are to make any headway against the enemy.

I have already taken care of the supply situation. I have arranged for a steady stream of provisions to be sent to our camp from the nearby cities. We will have more than enough to sustain us throughout the campaign.
I must keep a close eye on these men. They are loyal for now, but they are also ambitious and may turn on me if they sense weakness. I must be strong and decisive if I am to lead them to victory.
Caesar, what about the terrain? We will be marching through some difficult terrain, and the weather is unpredictable at this time of year.

We will march at night and use the cover of darkness to conceal our movements. As for the weather, we will simply have to make do with what we have. We are Romans, after all. We are used to hardship and adversity.

These men are competent, but they lack the vision and boldness that I possess. If I want to win this campaign, I must take risks and make bold moves. But I must also be careful not to overstep my bounds and risk alienating my allies.
Caesar, what about the enemy's fortifications? They have had months to prepare their defenses, and we will be hard-pressed to breach them.

We will attack their weakest point. I have studied their fortifications carefully and believe that there is a vulnerability that we can exploit. We will concentrate our forces at that point and use our superior training and discipline to overwhelm their defenders.

These men are skilled, but they lack the vision and strategic thinking that I possess. If I want to win this campaign, I must take bold risks and make unconventional moves. But I must also be careful not to alienate my allies or make any fatal mistakes.
Very well, gentlemen. We have a plan. Let us put it into action and show the world what the might of Rome is capable of.

setting: Caesar is in his house with his closest allies, discussing strategy and planning their next move against their opponents. The time is mid-March, and Caesar's consulship has just ended. The political opposition led by Bibulus and Cato has caused serious difficulties for Caesar and his allies, despite the common depiction of triumviral political supremacy.

dialogue.content: These political defeats are unacceptable. I cannot let Bibulus and Cato get in the way of my plans for Rome. I need to come up with a new strategy to outmaneuver them. I must show them that I am still in control, despite their attempts to undermine me.
Caesar, what do you propose we do about the opposition? They seem to be gaining traction with their tactics.

We need to show them that we are not weakened by their attacks. We must continue to push forward with our plans and not let them disrupt our progress. We will need to come up with new ways to gain support and outmaneuver them.
But how do we do that, Caesar? They have been successful in building revulsion against us.

We need to change the narrative. We must paint ourselves as the victims of their attacks and show the people that we are fighting for their interests. We need a new strategy to gain support and show them that we are still in control.
Caesar, what about the praetors who challenged your legislation? Should we address that issue?
No, let it go. It's better to focus our efforts on gaining support and outmaneuvering our opponents. We can deal with those issues later, once we have secured our power.
But what about Bibulus and Cato's attempts to cancel all the days on which we can hold votes? That could severely limit our power.
We will need to find a way around that. We cannot let them limit our power in Rome. I will consult with my advisors and come up with a plan to work around their edicts.
What about the people, Caesar? They seem to be turning against us.

We need to show them that we are still fighting for their interests. We need to come up with new policies and initiatives that will win them over. We cannot let our opponents paint us as the enemy of the people.

I need to show the people that I am still on their side. I must come up with new policies and initiatives that will win them over. Perhaps a new public works project or a tax cut for the lower classes. I cannot let Bibulus and Cato turn the people against me.
Caesar, what about the Senate? They seem to be stalling on your legislation.

We will deal with the Senate in due time. For now, we need to focus on gaining support and outmaneuvering our opponents. Once we have secured our power, we can deal with the Senate and any other opposition.
But how do we gain support, Caesar? What can we do to win over the people?

We need to show them that we are still fighting for their interests. We need to come up with new policies and initiatives that will benefit them directly. We must also paint ourselves as the victims of our opponents' attacks. We cannot let them paint us as the enemy of the people.

I need to come up with a new policy initiative that will win over the people. Something big that will show them that I am still on their side. Perhaps a new public works project or a tax cut for the lower classes. I must also find a way to turn the narrative against our opponents and show the people that we are the ones fighting for their interests.
Caesar, what about the military? They have been a strong source of support for us in the past.

We must not forget about the military. They have been a strong source of support for us in the past. We must continue to show them that we are fighting for their interests and that we will support them in return. We also need to make sure that our opponents do not gain any support from within the military.

The military is important. I must make sure that they remain loyal to me and do not defect to our opponents. I must show them that we are fighting for their interests and that we will support them in return.
Caesar, what about the other factions in Rome? Should we try to gain their support as well?

Yes, we must not forget about the other factions in Rome. We need to reach out to them and show them that we are willing to work with them. We cannot let our opponents gain any support from within these factions.
I must reach out to the other factions in Rome and show them that we are willing to work with them. We cannot let our opponents gain any support from within these factions.
Caesar, what about Bibulus and Cato? Should we try to negotiate with them?

No, negotiations are pointless. They have shown that they are our enemies and will stop at nothing to undermine us. We must continue to outmaneuver them and show the people that we are the ones fighting for their interests.

Negotiations are pointless. Bibulus and Cato have shown that they are our enemies and will stop at nothing to undermine us. We must continue to outmaneuver them and show the people that we are the ones fighting for their interests.

setting: It is a beautiful day in early March, and Julius Caesar is gathered with his family and close political allies at his luxurious villa. He is seeking advice and support for his ongoing political endeavors, which have faced opposition and setbacks in recent months. Among those present are his wife Calpurnia, his close friend and ally Mark Antony, and several other trusted advisors.

dialogue.content: As I look around this room, I am reminded of how much I have to be grateful for. These people have stood by me through thick and thin, and I know they will continue to do so as I fight for the future of Rome. But I cannot deny that the recent political defeats have taken a toll on me. I need their support and guidance now more than ever.
My dear Julius, you look so tired. Have you been sleeping well?
I cannot deny that the recent political battles have taken their toll. But I am not one to give up easily. I have come too far to turn back now.
Indeed, my friend. We have faced setbacks before, and we have always emerged victorious in the end. What is our next move?

Mark is right. We have faced tough times before, and we have always found a way to come out on top. But this time feels different. The opposition is strong, and their tactics are becoming more creative. I need to find a way to turn the tide in my favor.
I believe we need to focus on building support among the people. If we can win over the public, then the opposition's tactics will be less effective.
I agree. But how do we win over the people? The opposition has been spreading lies and propaganda about me for months now.
I believe we need to go on the offensive. We need to launch a media campaign that shows the people who you really are and what you stand for.
Yes, a media campaign could be just what we need. But it will take resources and manpower that we may not have. I need to think carefully about how to proceed.
Julius, have you considered reaching out to our allies in the Senate? Perhaps we can rally support among our fellow politicians.
I have considered it, but many of our allies are afraid to speak out publicly. The opposition has been using intimidation tactics to silence those who oppose them.
Then we will have to be even more strategic. We need to find ways to support our allies without putting them in danger.

Mark is right. We need to be careful not to put our allies in harm's way. But we also cannot afford to sit back and do nothing. We need to find a way to fight back against the opposition's tactics and win over the people.
I have an idea. What if we organize a series of public rallies and speeches? We can use these events to showcase your platform and rally support among the people.
That could work. But we need to be careful not to violate any laws or provoke a violent response from the opposition.
I agree. We need to be strategic and careful. But we also cannot afford to be too cautious. We need to take bold action if we want to win this fight.
Yes, bold action is what we need. But we also need to be smart and strategic. We cannot afford to make any mistakes or missteps. The stakes are too high.

setting: It is 70 BC and Rome is under the consulship of Pompey and Crassus. Julius Caesar, a well-accepted member of the aristocracy with great future prospects in his political career, is back in Rome after being co-opted into the pontifices in place of his deceased relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta. He was also elected one of the military tribunes for 71 BC, but there is no evidence that he served in war during his term. However, he did advocate for the removal of the Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for those who supported Lepidus' revolt to be pardoned. These advocacies were common and uncontroversial.

dialogue.content: I must make a move in this political game. Pompey and Crassus are powerful men, but I am not afraid. I have a long and illustrious career ahead of me, and I will not let anyone stand in my way. I must find a way to gain more power, to make myself indispensable to the people of Rome. Perhaps I can use my position as a military tribune to my advantage. I must find a way to make my voice heard and to make a difference.

Crassus, my dear friend, have you heard about Caesar's latest advocacy? He wants to remove the Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate. This is quite a bold move for a young man like him, don't you think?
Yes, I have heard about it. But I don't think it's anything to worry about. It's a common advocacy, and it won't gain him any real power. We have nothing to fear from Caesar.

They underestimate me. They think I am a young and inexperienced man, but they will soon see that I am a force to be reckoned with. I must find a way to make myself indispensable to them, to make them see that I am a valuable asset to their cause.
Gentlemen, I have a proposal. I believe that we should work together to restore the plebeian tribunate's rights. This will show the people that we are united in our efforts to improve their lives.
I agree with you, Caesar. This is a noble cause, and I believe that it will gain us some support among the plebeians.
I don't see the harm in it. But we must be careful not to anger the patricians. They will not take kindly to our efforts to restore the plebeian tribunate's rights.
I have gained their support, but I must be careful not to make any missteps. I must be tactful and strategic in my actions, or I may find myself on the wrong side of Rome's powerful elite.
Gentlemen, I also believe that we should pardon the Lepidan exiles. This will show the people that we are merciful and just, and it will gain us more support.
I don't see why not. It's a small matter, and it will make us look good in the eyes of the people.
I agree. We should always strive to be merciful and just in our actions. It will help us to gain the people's trust.

I have succeeded in gaining their support. They see me as a valuable ally, and they trust me to make the right decisions. But I must continue to be careful, to tread lightly in these dangerous political waters.
I thank you both for your support. I believe that we can accomplish great things together if we work as a team.
Indeed, we can. We must always remember that our goal is to improve the lives of the people of Rome.
And we must always remember that we are stronger together than we are alone. Let us work together to make Rome a better place for all.

I have gained their trust and their support. Now I must use this to my advantage, to gain more power and influence in Rome's political landscape. I am a force to be reckoned with, and I will not be stopped.

setting: Julius Caesar is in the Rome Senate, where he is facing objections from Catulus regarding his plan to restore his family's public monuments. Caesar served as curule aedile and staged lavish games that won him further attention and popular support. He also restored the trophies won by Marius, and taken down by Sulla, over Jugurtha and the Cimbri. According to Plutarch's narrative, the trophies were restored overnight to the applause and tears of joy of the onlookers. These actions were broadly supported by the senate, but Catulus is still objecting to Caesar's plan.

dialogue.content: Catulus is such a stubborn man. He can't see the importance of restoring our family's public monuments. It is not just a matter of family pride, but it is also about respecting our ancestors and keeping their legacy alive. These monuments are a testament to the greatness of our family, and they should be restored to their former glory. I can't let Catulus stand in my way. I need to convince him and the rest of the Senate that my plan is the right one.

Julius Caesar, I object to your plan. These monuments have been lying in ruins for years, and there is no need to restore them now. It is a waste of resources and time. We have more pressing matters to attend to.

I understand your concerns, Catulus, but I respectfully disagree. These monuments are not just a symbol of my family's greatness, but they are also a symbol of Rome's power and glory. We must restore them to show the world that Rome is still a great empire. The cost of restoration is minimal compared to the benefits we will reap. I urge you to reconsider your objections.
I will not change my mind, Caesar. Your plan is unnecessary and a waste of resources. I will not support it.

I can see that Catulus is not going to budge. I need to find a way to win the support of the other senators. I can't let one man stand in the way of progress. I will need to make a compelling argument to sway their opinions.

My fellow senators, I implore you to consider the importance of restoring these monuments. They are not just a symbol of my family's greatness, but they are also a symbol of Rome's power and glory. By restoring them, we show the world that Rome is still a great empire. These monuments are a testament to the greatness of our ancestors, and they should be treated with the respect they deserve. I urge you to support my plan and help me restore these monuments to their former glory.
I agree with Caesar. These monuments are an important part of our history, and they should be restored. It is a small price to pay for the benefits we will receive.
I also agree with Caesar. These monuments are a symbol of our power and glory. We must restore them to show the world that we are still a great empire.
I was initially skeptical, but after hearing Caesar's argument, I am convinced. We should restore these monuments and show the world that we are still a great empire.

I can see that my plan is gaining support. I am glad that the other senators can see the importance of restoring these monuments. It is not just a matter of family pride, but it is also about respecting our ancestors and keeping their legacy alive. I will make sure that these monuments are restored to their former glory.
I am pleased to see that my plan has gained support. I will make sure that these monuments are restored to their former glory. Thank you for your support.

setting: The scene is set in the Roman Senate, where Julius Caesar is addressing the senators. The political situation in Rome is turbulent, with violent street clashes between Clodius and two tribunes who were friends of Cicero, now supporting the allies. Caesar sends news of his victories in Gaul, claiming total victory and pacification. The senate, at Cicero's motion, has voted Caesar an unprecedented fifteen days of thanksgiving. His success is evident when the senate votes state funds for some of Caesar's legions, which until this time Caesar paid for personally.

dialogue.content: The time has come for me to address the Senate and secure my position in Gaul. The political situation in Rome is unstable, and I must ensure that my command in Transalpine Gaul is not reassigned. The lex Vatinia guarantees my position in Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum until 54 BC, but I must consolidate my power and influence in Rome. The news of my victories in Gaul will help me achieve this goal. I must convince the Senate of my success and pacification of Gaul, even if some senators are opposed to me.

Honorable Senators, I bring news of my victories in Gaul. The campaign has been long and arduous, but we have achieved total victory and pacification of the region. The Gauls have been subdued, and the Roman Empire has expanded its borders. These victories have been possible due to the bravery and discipline of my legions and the unwavering support of the Roman people. I ask for your continued support and recognition of my achievements in Gaul.

Honorable Senators, I fully endorse Julius Caesar's achievements in Gaul. His victories have ensured the safety and security of the Roman Empire, and his leadership has been exemplary. I propose that the Senate award Caesar an unprecedented fifteen days of thanksgiving. This is a small token of our gratitude for his service to Rome.

Honorable Senators, I do not dispute Caesar's victories in Gaul, but I must remind the Senate that his command in Transalpine Gaul is temporary. The lex Vatinia guarantees his position in Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum until 54 BC, but we must ensure that his power does not become absolute. I propose that the Senate discuss the reassignment of his command in Transalpine Gaul and appoint a new commander to oversee the region.

Pompey is my greatest rival in Rome, and he will do anything to undermine my power. I must counter his proposal and ensure that the Senate does not reassign my command in Gaul. I have the support of Cicero and some senators, but I must convince the others of my loyalty to Rome and my achievements in Gaul.

Honorable Senators, I assure you that my command in Gaul is temporary and that I have no ambition beyond serving Rome and expanding its borders. The victories in Gaul have not only ensured the safety and security of the Roman Empire but have also enriched it with new territories and resources. The state funds for my legions are a small token of recognition for their service to Rome. I ask the Senate to continue its support for my command in Gaul and help me consolidate the region's peace and prosperity.

Honorable Senators, I must remind you that Caesar's victories in Gaul have come at a great cost to the Roman people. The resources and manpower used in the campaign could have been better utilized in addressing the pressing needs of our citizens. We must also not forget that Caesar's command in Gaul is temporary, and we cannot allow him to become too powerful. I propose that the Senate appoint a commission to investigate the costs and benefits of Caesar's victories in Gaul and the reassignment of his command in Transalpine Gaul.

Clodius is a thorn in my side, and he will stop at nothing to undermine my achievements. I must counter his proposal and ensure that the Senate recognizes the benefits of my victories in Gaul. I have the support of some senators, but I must convince the others of the importance of expanding the Roman Empire and consolidating its power.

Honorable Senators, I understand your concerns about the costs and benefits of my victories in Gaul, but I must remind you that the expansion of the Roman Empire is essential to its survival and prosperity. The Gauls were a threat to Rome, and their subjugation has ensured the safety and security of our citizens. The resources and manpower used in the campaign have enriched Rome with new territories and resources, and the state funds for my legions are a small token of recognition for their service to Rome. I ask the Senate to continue its support for my command in Gaul and help me consolidate the region's peace and prosperity.

Honorable Senators, we recognize Julius Caesar's achievements in Gaul and his service to Rome. We award him an unprecedented fifteen days of thanksgiving and state funds for his legions. We also endorse his command in Gaul and recognize the importance of expanding the Roman Empire. We ask him to continue his service to Rome and ensure the safety and security of our citizens.

I have achieved my goal of securing my position in Gaul and consolidating my power in Rome. The Senate has recognized my achievements and endorsed my command in Gaul. I must continue to expand the Roman Empire and ensure its prosperity and power. The road ahead will be challenging, but I am confident that I can overcome any obstacle with my legions and the support of the Roman people.

setting: It is after Sulla's victory in the civil war (82 BC), and Cinna's acta are annulled. Caesar's father has died suddenly, and Caesar has been named as flamen Dialis (a priest of Jupiter), leading to his marriage to Cinna's daughter, Cornelia. In early 84 BC, Caesar's father died suddenly. Sulla consequently ordered Caesar to abdicate and divorce Cinna's daughter. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment. Sulla may have put Caesar on the proscription lists, though scholars are mixed. Caesar then went into hiding before his relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins were able to intercede on his behalf. They then reached a compromise where Caesar would resign his priesthood but keep his wife and chattels; Sulla's alleged remark he saw "in [Caesar] many Mariuses" is apocryphal.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe that Sulla would dare to annul Cinna's acta. This is a blatant disregard for the law and the people of Rome. I was named as flamen Dialis, and it was one of the highest non-political honors. The appointment was an indication that there were few expectations of a major career for me. The religious taboos of the priesthood would have forced me to forego a political career. But now Sulla has taken away even that. He has ordered me to abdicate and divorce Cornelia, my wife. I cannot let him get away with it. I must find a way to challenge his decision and prove that my marriage is legitimate.
Julius, what are we going to do? Sulla has ordered you to divorce me, and we cannot ignore his decree.

Cornelia, I will not divorce you. Our marriage is legitimate, and I will fight for it. I have already gone into hiding, and I am seeking the help of our relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins. I will not let Sulla's decree destroy our love.
Julius, I am afraid. What if Sulla puts you on the proscription lists?
I will not let him catch me. I will stay in hiding until we can find a way to challenge his decree. I will not abandon you, Cornelia. We will face this together.
Julius, we have good news. We have reached a compromise with Sulla. You can keep your wife and chattels, but you must resign your priesthood.

Resigning my priesthood is a small price to pay for keeping Cornelia. I am glad that the Vestal Virgins were able to intercede on my behalf. But I must be careful. Sulla sees "many Mariuses" in me, and I cannot let him have a reason to put me on the proscription lists.
Thank you, Vestal Virgin. I accept your compromise. I will resign my priesthood, but I will keep my wife and chattels. I hope that Sulla will accept this decision and not cause any further trouble.
Julius Caesar has resigned his priesthood, but I will keep an eye on him. He is a dangerous man, and I see "many Mariuses" in him. I will not let him challenge my authority.

I must be careful. Sulla may be watching me, but I will not give him a reason to suspect me. I will bide my time and wait for the right moment to strike. I will prove to him that I am not a threat to his authority.
Julius, I am glad that we can be together. But I am still afraid. What if Sulla changes his mind?
We cannot live in fear, Cornelia. We must be strong and face whatever comes our way. I will protect you, and we will overcome any challenges together. Our love is stronger than any decree or law.

setting: Julius Caesar is addressing a crowd in the Forum, as he prepares to leave Italy and head to Spain. In his absence, Mark Antony is left in charge as magister equitum. However, his rule has been unpopular, with Publius Cornelius Dolabella agitating for debt relief and causing riots in the city. Meanwhile, Cato has marched to Africa, where Metellus Scipio is in charge of the remaining republicans. They have allied with Juba of Numidia, and what used to be Pompey's fleet has been raiding the central Mediterranean islands. Additionally, Caesar's governor in Spain is unpopular, and the province has revolted and switched to the republican side.

dialogue.content: I must leave Italy to take care of matters in Spain, but I cannot leave the city in chaos. Mark Antony has not been able to keep order, and the riots are getting out of hand. I must reassure the people that everything will be under control in my absence. I know that many are unhappy with my recent actions, but I must convince them that I have their best interests at heart. It is imperative that I gain their trust and support, or my plans for the future may be in danger.

Citizens of Rome, I stand before you today to ask for your trust and support. As many of you know, I must leave the city to resolve matters in Spain. In my absence, Mark Antony will be in charge, but I assure you that everything will be under control. The recent riots in the city have caused much unrest, and I understand your concerns. However, I ask that you have faith in me and my decisions. I have always had your best interests at heart, and I will do everything in my power to ensure that Rome remains stable and prosperous.
But what about the debt relief we have been asking for? The people are suffering, and we need help now. Will you not listen to our pleas?

I understand your concerns, Dolabella, but we cannot simply forgive all debts. We must find a way to balance the needs of the people with the needs of the state. I promise you that I will work to find a solution that benefits all parties involved.
And what of Africa? Cato has joined forces with Juba of Numidia, and our army is vastly outnumbered. We need your help, Caesar.

I am aware of the situation in Africa, Scipio. Rest assured that I will do everything in my power to ensure that our troops are well equipped and prepared for battle. We must stand strong against our enemies and defend the Republic at all costs.
And what of me, Caesar? Am I not capable of maintaining order in your absence?

Of course, Antony. I have faith in your abilities, but you must also gain the trust and support of the people. I ask that you work closely with the Senate and the other magistrates to ensure that the city remains peaceful and prosperous. Together, we can overcome any obstacle that comes our way.

I must be careful with my words and actions. The people are restless, and any misstep on my part could have disastrous consequences. I must reassure them that I have their best interests at heart, while also maintaining my own power and authority. It is a delicate balance, but I am confident that I can achieve my goals. For the good of Rome, I must succeed.

setting: Caesar is in his camp in Gaul, receiving orders from Rome to suppress insurgencies. The date is uncertain, but it is likely sometime in the early 50s BC. Caesar has been engaged in a long and difficult campaign to subdue the Gauls, and his success has been mixed. He is under pressure from the Roman Senate to bring the situation under control, and he is facing criticism for his handling of the situation. Nonetheless, Caesar is a skilled general and a charismatic leader, and he is determined to see the campaign through to a successful conclusion.

dialogue.content: The orders have arrived from Rome. It's time to suppress these insurgencies once and for all. I've been fighting these Gauls for years now, and it's been a long, hard slog. But I'm not going to give up now. I've got to be careful, though. The Senate is watching me closely, and they're looking for any excuse to recall me to Rome. I can't afford any mistakes.

Gentlemen, the orders have arrived from Rome. We're to suppress the insurgencies and bring stability to this region. I know it's been a long and difficult campaign, but we can't give up now. We've made progress, and we can't let that progress go to waste. We need to be careful, though. The Senate is watching us closely, and they're looking for any excuse to recall me to Rome. We need to be precise and efficient in our operations. We can't afford any mistakes.
Understood, sir. We'll do everything in our power to carry out your orders.

I need to be careful with these officers. They're loyal, but they're also ambitious. They're looking for opportunities to advance their careers, and they'll do whatever it takes to do so. I need to keep them in check. But I also need to inspire them. They need to believe in our cause, and they need to be willing to fight for it.

Gentlemen, I know this is a difficult task, but I have faith in your abilities. We've been through a lot together, and I know that you're up to the challenge. We need to work together, and we need to be smart. We can't just charge into battle blindly. We need to be strategic, and we need to use our resources wisely. But I know that we can do this. We can bring stability to this region, and we can make a difference in the lives of the people who live here.
Sir, what about the Gauls who have already surrendered? What will happen to them?
That's a good question. I need to be careful with how I handle the Gauls who have surrendered. I don't want to be seen as too harsh, but I also can't let them go free. I need to find a balance.

We'll treat the Gauls who have surrendered fairly. We won't mistreat them or harm them in any way. But we also can't let them go free. We'll need to detain them and make sure that they're not a threat. But I want to emphasize that we're not here to be cruel or oppressive. We're here to bring stability and security to this region. And we'll do that by treating the people here with respect and kindness.
What about supplies, sir? We're running low on food and water. Should we request a resupply from Rome?
Supplies are always a concern. We're far from Rome, and it's not easy to get what we need. But we can't let that stop us. We need to be resourceful and find a way to make do with what we have.

That's a good point. We are running low on supplies. But we can't request a resupply from Rome. It would take too long, and we can't afford to wait. We need to find a way to make do with what we have. We'll need to ration our food and water carefully, and we'll need to be creative in how we get our supplies. But I know that we can do it. We've faced challenges before, and we've always found a way to overcome them.
Sir, what about the local population? How will we interact with them?
The local population is always an issue. We need their support, but we also need to be careful not to alienate them. We need to show them that we're here to help, not to harm.
