Caesar, your words are persuasive, but they do not excuse your actions. You have defied the Senate's authority and threatened the very foundations of our Republic. We cannot allow one man to hold so much power, for it will only lead to tyranny and oppression. We must uphold the principles of our Republic and limit the power of any one individual, no matter how capable he may be.

These senators cannot see the bigger picture. They are blinded by their own desire for power and their fear of what I might do with mine. But I know what is best for Rome, and I will do whatever it takes to protect her. If that means defying the Senate and marching on Rome with my army, so be it. I will not let the Republic fall to ruin because of their shortsightedness.

setting: It is 63 BC, and the location is the Roman Forum. Julius Caesar is standing for the praetorship and the post of pontifex maximus, the highest-ranking state religious official. In the pontifical election before the tribes, Caesar faces two influential senators, Quintus Lutatius Catulus and Publius Servilius Isauricus. The debate today is about economic policies, and Caesar and his rivals are about to present their arguments to the people of Rome.

dialogue.content: I need to make a strong impression on the people of Rome today. My opponents are powerful men, and they will try to discredit me at every opportunity. But I know that I am the best candidate for the job. I have the charisma, the intelligence, and the vision to lead Rome into a new era of prosperity. I just need to convince the people of that.

Caesar, you talk a good game, but where is the substance? You promise the people wealth and prosperity, but how do you plan to achieve it? Your rhetoric is empty, and your promises are hollow. I urge the people of Rome to vote for me, a man with a proven track record of success.

Senator Catulus, you may have a record of success, but it is a record of success for yourself and your fellow elites. What about the common people of Rome? What have you done for them? I have a plan to reduce taxes for small business owners, to increase funding for public works projects, and to create new jobs for the people of Rome. These are not empty promises; they are concrete actions that I will take if I am elected.

But Caesar, your promises are unrealistic. You cannot simply wave a magic wand and create wealth out of thin air. The economy is a complex system, and it requires careful management by experienced leaders. Senator Catulus and I have that experience, and we know how to make Rome prosper.

Senator Isauricus, you are right that the economy is a complex system. But it is also a system that has been rigged in favor of the wealthy for too long. I want to level the playing field and give the common people of Rome a fair shot at success. I believe that with the right policies and leadership, we can create a more just and prosperous society for all.

Caesar, your talk of justice and fairness is just empty rhetoric. You are a demagogue who seeks only to advance your own interests. You have no real solutions to the problems facing Rome, only grandiose promises that you cannot keep.

These men are formidable opponents, and they will do everything in their power to undermine me. But I will not be deterred. I believe in myself, and I believe in the people of Rome. I will fight for them, and I will win this election.

setting: Caesar sits in his law offices, surrounded by his political advisors. They discuss his candidacy for the praetorship and the post of pontifex maximus, as well as how best to handle his opponents in the race. Two influential senators, Quintus Lutatius Catulus and Publius Servilius Isauricus, are also running for the position. Caesar's victory in the pontifical election before the tribes has caused astonishment among many scholars, who question how seriously his candidacy was taken. However, historical precedent suggests that bribery alone is insufficient to explain his victory. Caesar's advisors consider the possibility that Pompey, whom Caesar supports and who opposes Catulus' candidacy, may have underwritten any bribes or other monies needed for Caesar's victory.

dialogue.content: How can I secure my victory in both the praetorship and the post of pontifex maximus? I must ensure that my opponents, especially Catulus, do not gain any advantage over me. I cannot let anyone stand in the way of my political ambitions. I must find a way to eliminate any threats to my power.

Caesar, we must be cautious. We cannot afford any mistakes or missteps in this election. Our opponents are powerful and influential, and they will stop at nothing to defeat us. We must have a solid strategy in place to ensure your victory.

I agree. We need to consider all possible scenarios and plan accordingly. We cannot rely solely on bribery or underhanded tactics. We must also win the support of the people and show them that you are the best candidate for the job.

I understand your concerns, but we must also be realistic. This is a political race, and we cannot afford to be naive or idealistic. We must do whatever it takes to win, even if it means resorting to less than honorable tactics.

Caesar, I understand your point of view, but we must also consider the long-term consequences of our actions. If we engage in unethical behavior, it could backfire and damage your reputation. It could also harm our political relationships with other influential figures.

I appreciate your input, but I am the one who will be held responsible for the outcome of this election. I am willing to take risks and make difficult decisions to ensure my victory. We must find a way to eliminate our opponents and secure the support of the people. I will not let anyone stand in the way of my political ambitions.
Understood. We will work together to come up with a plan that will ensure your victory. We will leave no stone unturned and spare no expense to make sure that you emerge victorious in this election.
We will also focus on your strengths and emphasize your accomplishments. We will show the people that you are the best candidate for the job and that you have their best interests at heart.

I agree. We must also be strategic in our messaging and outreach efforts. We need to target specific demographics and tailor our message to their interests and concerns. If we can win over key voting blocks, we will have a better chance of winning this election.

My advisors are right. We must be strategic and calculated in our approach. We cannot rely solely on bribery or underhanded tactics. We must also win the support of the people and show them that I am the best candidate for the job. I will do whatever it takes to ensure my victory in this election.

setting: The scene takes place in the Roman Senate, with Julius Caesar discussing his plans for the future of Gaul and the Roman Empire. It is the period between 52 to 49 BC, and trust between Caesar and Pompey has disintegrated. The consul Marcellus proposed recalling Caesar in 51 BC, arguing that his task in Gaul was complete. However, the proposal was vetoed, and it seemed that the conservatives around Cato in the Senate would seek to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honours or a second consulship. Cato, Bibulus, and their allies were successful in winning Pompey over to take a hard line against Caesar's continued command.

dialogue.content: These men in the Senate are fools. They do not understand the grand vision I have for the Roman Empire. They seek to limit my power, to prevent me from achieving greatness. But I will not be stopped. I have built a loyal following among my legions and have the support of the people. If these Senators wish to challenge me, they will fail. I will continue to lead my troops and expand the power of Rome.
Caesar, we have concerns about your continued command in Gaul. It is time for you to return to Rome and take up your duties as a consul.

I am aware of your concerns, Cato. But I have unfinished business in Gaul. The people there require my leadership, and I will not abandon them. As for my duties as a consul, I have fulfilled them to the best of my abilities. It is time for new leadership to take up the mantle.
But Caesar, you have exceeded your term in Gaul. It is time for you to return to Rome and relinquish your command.

I understand your concerns, Bibulus, but I cannot abandon my post. The people of Gaul need my leadership, and I will not leave them to fend for themselves. As for my term, I have done more for Rome than any consul in recent memory. I have expanded our territories and brought wealth and glory to the Empire.

Caesar, I must say that I agree with Cato and Bibulus. Your continued command in Gaul is a threat to the stability of Rome. It is time for you to return to Rome and face the consequences of your actions.

Pompey, I am disappointed that you would take the side of these Senators. You and I have fought side by side, and I had hoped that you would see the value in my leadership. But if you wish to challenge me, then I am ready. I will not be cowed by those who seek to limit my power.
Caesar, we are not seeking to limit your power. We are simply concerned about the stability of Rome. Your continued command in Gaul is a threat to that stability.

These men are fools. They do not understand the grand vision I have for the Roman Empire. They seek to limit my power, to prevent me from achieving greatness. But I will not be stopped. I have built a loyal following among my legions and have the support of the people. If these Senators wish to challenge me, they will fail. I will continue to lead my troops and expand the power of Rome.
Caesar, we implore you to return to Rome and relinquish your command. The people there need you, and Rome needs stability.

I understand your concerns, Bibulus, but they are misplaced. The people of Gaul need my leadership, and I will not abandon them. As for Rome, I have done more for the Empire than any consul in recent memory. I have expanded our territories and brought wealth and glory to our people. I will continue to do so, with or without the support of the Senate.
Caesar, I urge you to reconsider. Your actions threaten the stability of Rome, and we cannot allow that to continue. Please, return to Rome and relinquish your command.

Pompey, I am disappointed in you. You and I have fought side by side, and I had hoped that you would see the value in my leadership. But if you wish to challenge me, then I am ready. I will not be cowed by those who seek to limit my power. I will continue to lead my troops and expand the power of Rome, with or without your support.
Caesar, we do not wish to challenge you. We simply seek to ensure the stability of Rome. Your continued command in Gaul threatens that stability.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but they are misplaced. The people of Gaul need my leadership, and I will not abandon them. As for Rome, I have done more for the Empire than any consul in recent memory. I have expanded our territories and brought wealth and glory to our people. I will continue to do so, with or without the support of the Senate.

setting: The Senate House was filled with the sound of hushed voices as the Senators waited for Julius Caesar to arrive. The air was thick with tension, for everyone knew that the issue at hand was a contentious one. Caesar had called this meeting to discuss the calendar reform that he had been proposing for months. Some of the Senators were in favor of the reform, while others were vehemently opposed to it. All eyes were on the entrance as Caesar finally entered the room, his imposing figure silencing all murmurs.

dialogue.content: As I walk into the Senate House, I can feel the weight of their expectations on my shoulders. I know that this may be one of my most important speeches yet, and I must convince the Senators of the need for this calendar reform. It is a challenging task, but I have never shied away from a challenge. I take a deep breath and prepare to address the room.

Honorable Senators, I thank you for joining me today to discuss this important matter. As you know, I have been advocating for a reform of the calendar for some time now. The current system is flawed and outdated, causing confusion and inconvenience for many of our citizens. We must modernize our calendar if we wish to remain the great empire that we are. I implore you to consider the benefits of this reform and to set aside any personal biases or political agendas that may cloud your judgment.
But Caesar, why must we change what has worked for us for so long? The calendar has served us well for generations. Is it really worth the disruption to our way of life?
I expected this question, and I have prepared a response. I must stay calm and rational in my delivery, or I risk losing the attention of the room.

Senator, I understand your concerns, but we must not be blinded by tradition. Our current calendar is based on the lunar cycle, which is not accurate and leaves us with an inconsistent number of days in each month. This causes confusion and makes it difficult for our citizens to plan ahead. The new calendar I propose will be based on the solar cycle, with 365 days in each year and 12 months of varying lengths. This will ensure consistency and make it easier for our citizens to plan for the future.
But what about the religious implications? Our current calendar is tied to the lunar phases, which are important for many religious festivals and events. How will the new calendar account for this?
Another anticipated question. I must reassure the Senators that their religious beliefs will not be compromised.

Senator, I assure you that the new calendar will still account for the lunar phases and religious events. In fact, it will be more accurate than our current system in predicting these events. The months will be named after the gods and goddesses that are important to our religion, and the festivals and celebrations will still be observed on the appropriate days. We will not be sacrificing tradition or religion in this reform.
But Caesar, what about the cost? This reform will require significant resources to implement, and we are already dealing with economic struggles. How can we justify this expense to our citizens?
This is a valid concern, and I cannot deny the cost of this reform. I must appeal to their sense of duty and responsibility to the empire.

Senator, I understand your concern for our finances, but we must not forget our duty to our citizens. This reform will benefit them in the long run, and we cannot let short-term costs deter us from doing what is right for our empire. The cost of the reform will be offset by the increased efficiency and productivity that it will bring. We must have faith in our vision for the future and invest in it now.

setting: It is March 17, 45 BC, and a bloody battle is raging in Munda between Julius Caesar's army and his enemies. The battle is fierce and chaotic, with no clear winner in sight. Labienus, one of Caesar's opponents, dies on the field, and Pompey's son, Sextus, manages to escape. Despite the odds, Caesar narrowly emerges victorious, and his enemies are treated as rebels and massacred. With the war effectively over, Caesar remains in the province until June before setting out for Rome. He arrives in Rome in October of the same year and celebrates an unseemly triumph over fellow Romans. By this point, he has started preparations for war on the Parthians to avenge Crassus' death at Carrhae in 53 BC with wide-ranging objectives that would take him into Dacia for three or more years; it is set to start on 18 March 44 BC.

dialogue.content: As I stand here, victorious in battle, my thoughts turn to the future. I have many enemies who seek to bring me down, but I will not be defeated. I must continue to expand my empire and prove to the world that I am the greatest of all rulers. The Parthians will pay for their crimes against Crassus, and I will emerge triumphant once again. But first, I must deal with Sextus Pompey. He may have escaped me today, but he will not escape me forever. I will hunt him down and make an example of him, showing all who oppose me that they will meet a similar fate.

I have narrowly escaped death today, but I know that I am not safe. Caesar will not rest until he has captured or killed me, and I must remain vigilant. I will rally my forces and continue to fight against his tyranny. We must not let him win.

My victory today was hard-won, but it is just the beginning. I will not rest until all my enemies are brought to justice. Sextus Pompey may have escaped me today, but he will not be so lucky next time. I will make an example of him, and all those who oppose me will tremble at my feet.

I have fought for what I believe in, but it seems that fate has decided against me. I die today, but my legacy will live on. My fellow rebels will continue to fight against Caesar's tyranny, and they will be victorious in the end. I die with honor, knowing that I have done all that I can to defend my beliefs.

I have won this battle, but at what cost? The bloodshed and loss of life weigh heavily on my conscience, but I must push these thoughts aside. I am a conqueror, and I must continue to conquer. The Parthians will fall, and I will emerge victorious once again. My legacy will be one of triumph and greatness, and all will remember my name for centuries to come.

I may have escaped today, but I know that my days are numbered. Caesar will come for me, and I must be ready. I will rally my forces and continue to fight against him, no matter the cost. We must not let him win.

I will not rest until all my enemies are brought to justice. Sextus Pompey may have escaped me today, but he will not be so lucky next time. I will make an example of him, and all those who oppose me will tremble at my feet.

I have fought for what I believe in, but it seems that fate has decided against me. I die today, but my legacy will live on. My fellow rebels will continue to fight against Caesar's tyranny, and they will be victorious in the end. I die with honor, knowing that I have done all that I can to defend my beliefs.

I have won this battle, but at what cost? The bloodshed and loss of life weigh heavily on my conscience, but I must push these thoughts aside. I am a conqueror, and I must continue to conquer. The Parthians will fall, and I will emerge victorious once again. My legacy will be one of triumph and greatness, and all will remember my name for centuries to come.

I may have escaped today, but I know that my days are numbered. Caesar will come for me, and I must be ready. I will rally my forces and continue to fight against him, no matter the cost. We must not let him win.

I will not stop until I have avenged Crassus' death and conquered the Parthians. This is only the beginning of my great conquest, and all those who oppose me will fall. My legacy will be one of triumph and greatness, and all will remember my name for centuries to come.

setting: Julius Caesar, the newly elected consul of Rome, arrived at the Treasury seeking funds to support the tax farmers in Asia. He had reconciled two political foes, Pompey and Crassus, forming an alliance known as the "First Triumvirate." Caesar's aim was to gain allies for his consulship, and the alliance was finalised only around the start of his term. The trio joined forces to pursue their respective goals, with Pompey seeking land grants for his veterans, and Crassus aiming to bail out tax farmers in Asia, many of whom were his clients.

dialogue.content: I must secure these funds to maintain the loyalty of my allies and ensure my position of power in Rome. The support of Pompey and Crassus is essential to my success, and I must show them that I can deliver on my promises. The tax farmers in Asia are a vital source of revenue for the Republic, and their financial troubles must be resolved. I cannot let them fail, nor can I risk losing the support of my allies. I must convince the Treasury to provide the necessary funds.
Greetings, Consul Caesar. How may I assist you today?

I require funds to support the tax farmers in Asia. Their financial troubles threaten the stability of the Republic, and I cannot allow them to fail. I request that the Treasury provide the necessary funds to bail them out.

I understand your concerns, Consul. However, the Treasury is already stretched thin, and we cannot simply provide funds at your behest. We require proper justification and evidence of their financial troubles before we can release any funds.
This official is obstructing my plans. I must find a way to convince them to release the funds without arousing suspicion. Perhaps I can offer them something in return.

I understand your concerns, and I appreciate the need for proper justification. However, I can assure you that the tax farmers in Asia are in dire need of assistance. Their failure would not only harm the Republic's finances but also risk the lives of our soldiers stationed in the East. If you release the necessary funds, I promise to ensure that the Treasury receives a significant return on its investment.
I see. And what sort of return do you propose, Consul?

I propose that the tax farmers repay the Treasury with interest on their loans. In addition, I can offer you a share of the profits from their future harvests. With such a lucrative deal, the Treasury stands to benefit greatly from this investment.

This is a tempting offer. If the tax farmers can indeed repay their loans with interest, the Treasury could profit greatly. However, the risk of default is high, and the Treasury cannot afford to lose such a significant sum.

I will consider your proposal, Consul. However, I must remind you that the Treasury cannot simply provide funds without proper justification and assurance of repayment. If you can provide such evidence, we may be willing to release the necessary funds.

I understand your concerns, and I will ensure that the tax farmers provide the necessary evidence. I assure you that this investment will benefit the Republic greatly, and I will take full responsibility for its success.

I have secured the Treasury's cooperation, for now. I must ensure that the tax farmers provide the necessary evidence and repay their loans with interest. If I can pull this off, I will have gained a significant victory for myself and my allies. The First Triumvirate will be one step closer to achieving our goals and securing our power in Rome.

setting: Julius Caesar and Marcus Licinius Crassus were both present in the Roman Forum, engaged in a heated debate about the economy and taxation. The sun was high in the sky, casting a bright light on the marble columns surrounding the Forum. Citizens of Rome had gathered around to listen to the two powerful men exchange arguments and rebuttals. Caesar looked confident and composed, his toga draped elegantly over his shoulders. Crassus, on the other hand, looked tense and agitated, his face twisted into a scowl.

dialogue.content: This debate is crucial for my political career. I must display my knowledge and expertise on the subject of taxation to win over the people of Rome. Crassus is a formidable opponent, but I am confident in my abilities to outsmart him. I must remain calm and collected, using my charisma and eloquence to sway the audience in my favor.

Caesar, you speak of taxation as if it is a necessary evil. But I believe that taxation is a burden on the people of Rome. They work hard to earn their money, and it is not fair for the government to take a large portion of their earnings. We must reduce taxes to alleviate the financial strain on our citizens.

Crassus, you are mistaken. Taxes are essential for the functioning of our government and the maintenance of our infrastructure. Without taxes, we would not be able to fund our military campaigns, build roads and aqueducts, and provide public services. It is true that taxes can be a burden on the people, but we must ensure that they are distributed fairly and used for the greater good of our society.

Fairly distributed? How can you say that when the wealthy elite are exempt from most taxes, while the common people bear the brunt of the burden? This is not fair, Caesar. We must reform our tax system to ensure that everyone pays their fair share.

Crassus, you are making baseless accusations. The wealthy elite contribute a significant portion of their wealth to the state through other means, such as funding public works and investing in the economy. We cannot punish the wealthy for their success, as it is their contributions that drive the growth of our society. Instead, we must focus on improving the lives of the less fortunate through social programs and education.

Improving the lives of the less fortunate? That is just empty rhetoric, Caesar. You have no real plan to address the poverty and inequality that plagues our society. We need concrete action, not just words.
Crassus is getting under my skin with his accusations. But I must remain composed and stick to my argument. I cannot let him sway the audience with his emotional appeals.

Crassus, I have a plan to address poverty and inequality in our society. We must invest in education and vocational training, so that our citizens can acquire the skills they need to succeed in the workforce. We must also provide financial assistance to those in need, so that they can afford basic necessities such as food and shelter. But we cannot do this without the revenue generated by taxes. We must strike a balance between providing for the needs of our citizens and maintaining the stability of our government.

Your plan is nothing new, Caesar. It is the same tired rhetoric that we have heard from politicians for centuries. I propose a radical solution: abolish all taxes and let the people keep their hard-earned money. This will stimulate economic growth and create a society where everyone has the opportunity to succeed.

Abolish all taxes? That is a reckless and irresponsible proposal, Crassus. Without taxes, we would have no means of funding our government and providing for the common good. It would lead to chaos and anarchy. We must find a way to reduce the burden of taxes on the people, while still maintaining the stability of our society. Your proposal is nothing more than a pipe dream.

You call it a pipe dream, Caesar. But I call it a vision for the future. A future where every citizen of Rome can live without fear of financial ruin or government oppression. You may have the support of the wealthy elite, but I have the support of the common people. And in the end, it is the voice of the people that will decide who leads this great empire.

Crassus is playing to the emotions of the crowd, using his populist rhetoric to win their favor. But I cannot let him undermine my authority and credibility. I must find a way to refute his arguments and win back the support of the people.

Crassus, you speak of the voice of the people. But the people of Rome are not so easily swayed by your empty promises. They know that taxes are necessary for the functioning of our government and the stability of our society. They know that we must work together to find solutions to the problems that face us. And they know that I am the leader who can guide us to a prosperous and just future. So I say to you, Crassus, do not underestimate the intelligence and wisdom of the people. They will see through your lies and choose the path of reason and progress.

setting: Julius Caesar, the great Roman general and statesman, addresses the people of a Spanish town. Caesar is there to convince the people to switch sides and support his cause. The year is 47 BC, and Caesar's absence from Italy has left Mark Antony in charge. Antony's rule was unpopular, and the senate had to intervene to restore order. Cato has marched to Africa, where Metellus Scipio is in charge of the remaining republicans. They have allied with Juba of Numidia, and Pompey's fleet has raided the central Mediterranean islands. Caesar's governor in Spain is unpopular, and the province has revolted and switched to the republican side. Caesar must convince the people of this Spanish town to support him and join his cause.

dialogue.content: I must win the support of these people if I am to defeat the republicans. I must make them see that I am the only one who can save Rome from destruction. They must understand that the republicans are a threat to their way of life, and that they must join me in this fight. But how can I convince them? What can I say to make them see the truth?

People of this town, hear me! I come to you today as a friend and ally. I come to you to ask for your support in my fight against the republicans. They seek to destroy Rome and all that it stands for. They seek to take away your freedom and your way of life. But I am here to stop them. I am here to fight for you and for all of Rome. Will you join me in this fight?
But why should we trust you, Caesar? You are a conqueror, a man who has taken what he wants by force. How do we know that you will not turn on us once you have what you want?

I understand your concerns, my friend. But let me tell you this. I have fought for Rome my entire life. I have spilled my blood on her behalf, and I will do so again in this fight. I am not here to conquer, but to save. I am here to save Rome from the republicans, to save your way of life, and to bring prosperity to this land. Will you join me in this fight?
But what about our governor, Caesar? He has switched sides and joined the republicans. How can we trust you when your own man has betrayed you?

I understand your concerns, my friend. But let me tell you this. The governor was a weak man, a man who could not see the truth. But I am not like him. I am a strong man, a man who understands what must be done to save Rome. I will not abandon you, and I will not let the republicans take this land from us. Trust me, my friends, and join me in this fight. Together, we will save Rome and all that it stands for.
What about the others who have switched sides, Caesar? What about Cato and his allies in Africa? What about Pompey's fleet? How can we hope to win against such odds?

My friends, do not be discouraged by the odds. Yes, we face powerful enemies, but we have something that they do not. We have the courage and the will to fight for what we believe in. We have the strength to overcome any obstacle, and we have the intelligence to outsmart our enemies. We will not be defeated, my friends. We will fight until the republicans are defeated, and Rome is saved. Will you join me in this fight?
But what about the cost of this war, Caesar? What about the lives that will be lost? Is it worth it?

My friend, I understand your concerns. War is never easy, and it always comes at a cost. But let me ask you this. What is the cost of not fighting? What is the cost of letting the republicans destroy Rome and all that it stands for? The cost is too high, my friend. We must fight, and we must win. The lives that will be lost are a sacrifice that we must make for the greater good. Join me, my friends, and let us save Rome from destruction.

setting: After narrowly winning the battle at Munda on 17 March 45 BC, Caesar treated his enemies as rebels and had them massacred. Labienus died on the field and one of Pompey's sons, Sextus, escaped but the war was effectively over. He remained in the province until June before setting out for Rome. He arrived in Rome in October of the same year and celebrated an unseemly triumph over fellow Romans. By this point, he had started preparations for war on the Parthians to avenge Crassus' death at Carrhae in 53 BC with wide-ranging objectives that would take him into Dacia for three or more years; it was set to start on 18 March 44 BC.

dialogue.content: The time has finally come to avenge the death of Crassus and restore the pride of Rome. The Parthians must pay for their treachery and I must prove to the world that Rome is not to be trifled with. This will be a long and arduous campaign, but I am ready for it. My army is well-trained and battle-hardened, and I have no doubt that we will emerge victorious. The glory of Rome demands it.

Gentlemen, the time has come to take revenge on the Parthians. They have insulted us for far too long, and it is time for us to teach them a lesson. Our campaign will be long and difficult, but I have no doubt that we will emerge victorious. We will march into their lands, take their cities and plunder their riches. The glory of Rome demands it, and we shall not rest until it is achieved.

But Caesar, our troops are tired and battle-weary. They have just fought a long and grueling war in Spain, and many of them are in need of rest and recuperation. Is it wise to embark on another campaign so soon?

I understand your concerns, General, but the threat of the Parthians cannot be ignored. We cannot allow them to continue their provocations against Rome. Our troops will be given ample time to rest and recover before we set out. And I have every confidence that they will rise to the challenge once again.

But Caesar, the Parthians are a formidable foe. They have a reputation for being expert horsemen and archers, and their tactics are unlike anything we have faced before. Are we truly prepared for such a campaign?

I am well aware of the Parthians' reputation, Advisor. But Rome has faced many formidable foes in the past, and we have emerged victorious every time. We have the finest soldiers in the world, and I have no doubt that they will adapt to the Parthians' tactics and emerge victorious. We must have faith in our abilities and in the righteousness of our cause.
But Caesar, what about our families? Many of us have not seen our loved ones in years. We cannot simply abandon them and march off to war once again.

I understand your concerns, my dear soldier. But we are soldiers of Rome, and our duty is to the Republic. Our families will be taken care of in our absence, and we will return to them victorious and proud. We are not fighting for ourselves, but for the glory of Rome and the honor of our ancestors. And that is a cause worth fighting for.

My soldiers are understandably apprehensive about embarking on another campaign so soon after the war in Spain. But their loyalty to Rome is unwavering, and I have no doubt that they will once again rise to the occasion. This will be a long and difficult campaign, but the glory of Rome demands it. And I will not rest until that glory is restored.

setting: Julius Caesar stands in the Senate House, his eyes scanning the room as he prepares to deliver his speech. The time is the late 70s BC, and Caesar is one of Pompey's supporters. He has joined forces with Pompey, and has thrown his support behind efforts to restore tribunician rights. Currently, Caesar is advocating for the law recalling the Lepidan exiles, a move that may be related to the same tribune's bill to grant lands to Pompey's veterans. Caesar also supported the lex Gabinia in 67 BC granting Pompey an extraordinary command against piracy in the Mediterranean and the lex Manilia in 66 BC to reassign the Third Mithridatic War from its then-commander Lucullus to Pompey.

dialogue.content: Julius Caesar took a deep breath as he prepared to address the Senate. He knew that his words would carry weight, and that many of the senators present would be swayed by his arguments. He was determined to see the law recalling the Lepidan exiles passed, and he knew that he had to make a compelling case if he wanted to win over his fellow lawmakers.

Honorable senators, I come before you today to speak in favor of the law recalling the Lepidan exiles. As you all know, this law is of great importance to the people of Rome, and it is our duty as lawmakers to ensure that justice is served.
But Caesar, what of the crimes that these exiles have committed? Should they not be held accountable for their actions?

I understand your concerns, my dear colleague, but we must also consider the fact that many of these exiles were forced to flee Rome due to circumstances beyond their control. They deserve a chance to return home and rebuild their lives.
But what of the victims of their crimes? Will they not be left without justice if these exiles are allowed to return?
We must also consider the possibility that some of these exiles were unfairly accused or convicted. It is our duty to ensure that justice is served for all, not just for the privileged few.

As he spoke, Caesar could feel the weight of the room shifting in his favor. He knew that he had made a strong case for the law recalling the Lepidan exiles, and he could sense that many of the senators were beginning to see things his way.

Furthermore, let us not forget the sacrifices that many of these exiles have made for the good of Rome. Many of them served in our armies, fighting to defend our great city from its enemies. Is it not our duty to show them the same loyalty and honor that they showed us?
But what of the precedent that this law would set? If we allow these exiles to return, will we not be opening the floodgates for others to do the same?

I understand your concerns, my dear colleague, but we must also consider the unique circumstances of each case. We cannot allow fear to dictate our actions, but must instead be guided by reason and justice. I urge you all to consider these factors carefully before making your decision.

As he finished speaking, Caesar could feel a sense of satisfaction washing over him. He knew that he had made a strong case for the law recalling the Lepidan exiles, and he was confident that many of the senators would be swayed by his arguments. He had done his duty as a Roman lawmaker, and he could rest easy knowing that he had fought for what he believed in.

setting: It is the year 47 BC, and Julius Caesar is absent from Italy, leaving Mark Antony in charge as magister equitum. The rule of Mark Antony is not well received, and there is unrest in Italy. Publius Cornelius Dolabella, plebeian tribune, demands debt relief and the agitation turns into riots. The Senate orders Antony to restore order, and after a mutiny in southern Italy, he returns to suppress the riots by force. Meanwhile, Cato has marched to Africa, where Metellus Scipio and Juba of Numidia lead the remaining republicans. Pompey's fleet also raids the central Mediterranean islands. In Spain, Caesar's governor is unpopular, and the province revolts and switches to the republican side.

dialogue.content: The situation in Italy is dire. The unrest caused by Dolabella has only added to the problems that Antony has had to deal with. I should have been there to prevent this. But I cannot be in two places at once. I trust Antony to handle the situation, but I must keep a close eye on what is happening. The news from Africa is troubling. Cato and Scipio are formidable opponents, and Juba's support makes them even more dangerous. I need to find a way to turn the tide in my favor. As for Spain, I will have to deal with the governor's betrayal. I cannot let any province slip away from me.

My fellow Romans, I understand that many of you are unhappy with my rule. I assure you that I am doing everything in my power to restore order to Italy. The riots that occurred were regrettable, but necessary to prevent further chaos. I ask for your patience and cooperation in these difficult times. Together, we can overcome these challenges and emerge stronger than before.

Mark Antony's rule has been a disaster for the people of Italy. He cares only for his own power and wealth, and has no regard for the suffering of the common folk. We demand debt relief and fair treatment, and we will not stop until our voices are heard!

Fellow republicans, we must not lose heart. Our cause is just, and the people of Africa are with us. With Metellus Scipio and Juba by our side, we can defeat Caesar's forces and restore the republic. We will not be intimidated by his tyranny.

Indeed, Cato is right. We have the support of the people, and we have the military might to defeat Caesar's legions. We must strike quickly and decisively, before he can reinforce his troops. Victory is within our grasp!

I stand with my fellow Africans and the republicans. Caesar's greed and ambition have no place in our lands. We will fight until our last breath to preserve our freedom and independence. Let us show him the strength of our resolve!

I cannot let Cato and Scipio gain the upper hand in Africa. I need to send reinforcements, but I cannot spare too many troops from Italy. Perhaps I can persuade some of Juba's allies to switch sides and join me. I will also need to find a way to disrupt their supply lines and weaken their morale. As for Spain, I need to act swiftly and decisively. The governor's betrayal cannot go unpunished. I will send a loyal general to put down the rebellion and restore order. And I must also find a way to address the root causes of the discontent in Italy. Dolabella's demands may be legitimate, but I cannot afford to give in to them completely. I will need to find a compromise that satisfies both sides.

setting: Caesar learns about the privileges associated with the civic crown in Rome after his victory at the Siege of Mytilene. He is eager to gain more honours and recognition.

dialogue.content: Finally, I have received the recognition I deserve. The civic crown is a great honour, and I will wear it with pride. It is my first step towards the ultimate goal – the consulship. I must continue to work hard and prove my worth to the Senate and the people of Rome. The privileges that come with the crown are tempting – the right to wear it at public occasions and the respect of the Senate. I must use these privileges to my advantage and gain more power and influence in Rome. It is time for me to start planning my next move.
Caesar, my dear friend, I am glad you could stay with me for a while. I hope you found our hospitality to your liking.
Thank you, Nicomedes. Your hospitality has been more than generous. I enjoyed my stay here in Bithynia and the opportunity to collect naval reinforcements for Rome.
It was my pleasure to assist Rome in any way I can. I hope our alliance will continue to strengthen in the future.

Nicomedes may be a useful ally in the future. His naval reinforcements will be valuable to Rome, and his friendship could help me gain more influence in the Senate. But I must be careful not to be associated with the rumors of our supposed homosexual relationship. It could damage my reputation and hinder my political ambitions.
Caesar, I am honored to have you on my staff. Your military expertise and leadership skills are valuable assets to our mission in Cilicia.
Thank you, Servilius. It is an honor to serve under your command. I will do my best to ensure our mission is successful.

This mission in Cilicia is a great opportunity for me to gain more military experience and prove my worth to the Senate. I must continue to impress my superiors and gain their trust. It is a stepping stone towards my ultimate goal – the consulship.
Caesar, I heard you wanted to join my revolt against Sulla. I could use someone like you on my side.
I apologize, Lepidus, but I have no intention of joining your revolt. I am a loyal servant of Rome and will not participate in any treasonous activities.

My loyalty to Rome is unwavering. I will not risk my reputation and political future by joining a doomed revolt. But perhaps I can use this opportunity to gain more information about Lepidus and his plans. It could be useful in the future.

setting: At a bloody battle at Munda on 17 March 45 BC, Caesar narrowly found victory; his enemies were treated as rebels and he had them massacred. Labienus died on the field and one of Pompey's sons, Sextus, escaped but the war was effectively over. He remained in the province until June before setting out for Rome. He arrived in Rome in October of the same year and celebrated an unseemly triumph over fellow Romans. By this point, he had started preparations for war on the Parthians to avenge Crassus' death at Carrhae in 53 BC with wide-ranging objectives that would take him into Dacia for three or more years; it was set to start on 18 March 44 BC.

dialogue.content: The victory at Munda was a close call, but I emerged victorious nonetheless. My enemies thought they could stand against me and they paid the price for their foolishness. I must maintain my power and control over Rome, and this massacre was necessary to ensure that. But now, my attention turns to the Parthians. They must pay for their role in Crassus' death, and I will make sure they regret ever crossing me.
I cannot believe what has happened. My father and our allies, all massacred by Caesar. This is not justice, this is butchery.
Sextus, your father and his allies were nothing but rebels. They threatened the stability of Rome and I could not let that stand. You are lucky to have escaped with your life.
Lucky? My father is dead, our allies are dead, and for what? Your thirst for power and control? You are no better than a tyrant.

Sextus is a fool to speak to me in such a manner. He does not realize the power I hold over him. But he is Pompey's son, and I must tread carefully with him. I cannot let him become a threat to my rule.
Sextus, you are free to go. But know this, if you ever raise arms against Rome, I will not hesitate to have you executed.
I will never forget what you have done here today, Caesar. Your actions will not go unpunished.

Sextus may be a threat in the future, but for now, he is of no consequence. My attention must turn to the Parthian campaign. I will show the world the power and might of Rome, and I will make sure that our enemies fear us.

My fellow Romans, I have returned victorious from the battle at Munda. Our enemies have been defeated and Rome has emerged stronger because of it. But our work is not done. The Parthians must pay for their role in Crassus' death, and I will make sure they regret ever crossing us. We will show the world the power and might of Rome. Ave Caesar!

setting: It is 77 BC, and Julius Caesar is in Rome. After an unsuccessful attempt to prosecute Gnaeus Cornelius Dolabella, Caesar goes after Gaius Antonius Hybrida for profiteering from the proscriptions. Caesar's oratorical attempts are successful, but a tribune intercedes on Antonius' behalf, forestalling Caesar's prosecution. Caesar decides to leave Rome for Rhodes to seek the tutelage of the rhetorician Apollonius Molon.

dialogue.content: Finally, I have decided to leave Rome. I am tired of these unsuccessful attempts to prosecute the corrupt aristocracy. I need to improve my oratory skills, and who better to learn from than Apollonius Molon? I have heard that he is the best rhetorician in the world. I can't wait to learn from him and return to Rome as a better orator.

I need to travel to Rhodes to seek the tutelage of the rhetorician Apollonius Molon. I have heard that he is the best rhetorician in the world, and I need to improve my oratory skills. I will return to Rome as a better orator.
Are you sure this is a good idea, Caesar? Leaving Rome and going to Rhodes is a big step. What if something happens to you?
I have made up my mind. I need to improve my skills, and Apollonius Molon is the best. I will be fine. Don't worry.
These pirates think they can hold me for ransom? They have no idea who they are dealing with. I will pay the ransom for now, but I will return and make them pay for their actions.
I will pay the ransom, but mark my words, I will return and capture and execute you all for your actions.
Ha! You think you can capture us? You are just one man.
I am not just any man. I am Julius Caesar, and I always keep my word.

Finally, I am learning from Apollonius Molon. He is a great teacher, and I am improving my oratory skills. I will be able to use my newfound skills to prosecute the corrupt aristocracy and make a difference in Rome.
Thank you, Apollonius Molon. I am learning so much from you. I can't wait to return to Rome and put my new skills to use.
You are a quick learner, Julius. I have no doubt that you will become one of the best speakers in Rome.
I have learned so much from Apollonius Molon. I can't wait to return to Rome and put my new skills to use. The corrupt aristocracy won't know what hit them.

The Third Mithridatic War has broken out, and I need to do my part. I will go around collecting troops in the province at the locals' expense and lead them successfully against Mithridates' forces. I will show Rome what I am capable of.
I need to go around collecting troops in the province at the locals' expense. We need to lead them successfully against Mithridates' forces. I will do everything in my power to ensure victory.
We can't afford to pay for your troops, Caesar. We are already struggling as it is.
If you want to win this war, you will need to pay. It's as simple as that. I will ensure victory, but I need your support.
I have proven myself as a military leader. My soldiers respect and admire me, and I have shown Rome what I am capable of. I will use my newfound reputation to make a difference in Rome.
Victory is ours! We have defeated Mithridates' forces, and Rome is safer because of it. I will continue to fight for Rome and make a difference in this great city.

setting: Julius Caesar has arrived at Pompey's Villa to persuade Pompey to join his political party. The purpose of the meeting is to form an alliance where Pompey and Caesar will work together to achieve their respective goals. Pompey and Crassus are political foes who have been reconciled by Caesar and are now working together in pursuit of their goals. Caesar wants to find allies for his consulship and Pompey and Crassus have joined him in pursuit of their respective goals. Pompey and Crassus want to ratify Pompey's eastern conquests and bail out tax farmers in Asia. They all seek the extended patronage of land grants, with Pompey especially seeking the promised land grants for his veterans.

dialogue.content: I need to persuade Pompey to join my political party. We have different goals, but we can work together to achieve them. I am confident that I can convince him to join me. I need to be persuasive and show him that we can achieve more together than we can alone.
Julius, what brings you to my villa today?
Pompey, I have come to talk to you about forming an alliance. I believe that we can achieve great things together if we work towards a common goal.
What goal would that be?
I want to find allies for my consulship, and I believe that you and I can work together to achieve that goal. You have your own goals as well, and I am willing to help you achieve them.

I am skeptical of working with Caesar. He has his own agenda, and I do not want to be used for his benefit. However, if we work together, we can achieve more than we can alone. I need to hear him out and see what he has to offer.
Julius is right, Pompey. We can achieve more together than we can alone. We have our own goals, but we can support each other and work towards a common goal.
Fine, I will hear you out. What do you propose?

I propose that we form an alliance to achieve our respective goals. We can support each other and work towards a common goal. I can help you with the land grants for your veterans, and you can help me find allies for my consulship.
This alliance could benefit me, but I need to be careful. I do not want to be used by Caesar, and I need to make sure that I am not giving up too much for too little.
We can also help each other with our other goals. I have some clients who need to be bailed out in Asia, and I believe that we can work together to make that happen.
This alliance could benefit me in the short term, but I need to think about the long term as well. I need to make sure that I am not giving up too much for too little.
I believe that this alliance can benefit all of us. We can achieve great things together, and we can support each other in our respective goals.
I am willing to consider your proposal, but I need to think about it first. I will let you know my decision soon.

I have made my proposal, and now I need to wait for Pompey's decision. I am confident that I can persuade him to join my political party, and I am willing to work with him to achieve our respective goals.

setting: Caesar sits at a large wooden table in his tent, surrounded by his top generals. Maps of the surrounding areas and battle plans are spread out in front of them. The atmosphere is tense as they discuss military strategies before setting out for battle.

dialogue.content: I must ensure that my army is prepared for this battle. The Gauls are a fierce opponent, and I cannot afford to make any mistakes. I must listen to the advice of my generals and make calculated decisions. The fate of Rome rests on this campaign.
Caesar, we believe that it would be best to divide our forces into three groups and attack the Gauls from different directions. This will catch them off guard and give us a strategic advantage.

I see your point, Brutus. However, I worry that our forces may become too spread out and vulnerable to attacks. We must also consider the terrain and weather conditions. I suggest we focus our attack on the hills to the east. This will allow us to maintain a strong defensive position and prevent the Gauls from surrounding us.
But Caesar, the hills to the east are heavily fortified. It will be difficult to break through their defenses.

I understand your concerns, Cassius. However, we must take risks in order to achieve victory. I will personally lead the charge and inspire our troops to push through their defenses. We will catch them off guard and show them the might of Rome.
Caesar, I believe in your plan. We will follow you to the end and fight with all our might.

I am confident in my plan, but I cannot let my guard down. The Gauls are known for their cunning tactics, and I must be prepared for any surprises. I will lead my troops with honor and bravery, and together we will emerge victorious.

setting: It is May and Julius Caesar has extended his agrarian bill to Campania. This is a significant move as it is an expansion of his previous bill and shows his determination to redistribute land to the people. The senate has also assigned him the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul for five years, and Transalpine Gaul subject to annual renewal. Caesar's alliance with Pompey has been strengthened with the marriage of his daughter Julia to Pompey. The senate has also passed bills to write down tax farmers' arrears for Crassus and ratify Pompey's eastern settlements. Caesar is determined to pursue his political agenda and consolidate his power, despite opposition from his rivals.

dialogue.content: I have extended my agrarian bill to Campania, and with the support of my allies, I can push for even more reforms. The people need land, and I can provide it for them. The senate may try to resist, but I have the people on my side. I must consolidate my power and ensure that my rivals cannot challenge me. The assignment of provinces to me is a step in the right direction, but I must be careful not to overstep my bounds. Pompey's alliance is also crucial to my success, and I must maintain it at all costs. I must continue to push for reforms and ensure that my enemies do not gain the upper hand.
Caesar, I am grateful for your support in the senate. The write-down of tax farmers' arrears will greatly benefit me and my business interests. I am glad we are on the same side.
Caesar, the marriage of our children has strengthened our alliance. I hope we can continue to work together to achieve our goals.
Caesar, I have moved the lex Vatinia assigning the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to you for five years. I believe you will use these provinces wisely and for the benefit of Rome.

Caesar's agrarian bill is a threat to the stability of the republic. We must resist his attempts to consolidate power and redistribute land to the people. I will do everything in my power to oppose him.

I will not be deterred by the opposition of my enemies. The people need land, and I will provide it for them. The assignment of provinces to me is a sign that the senate recognizes my abilities and trusts me to use them for the benefit of Rome. I will continue to push for reforms and ensure that my enemies cannot challenge me. The republic needs strong leadership, and I am prepared to provide it.

setting: The Senate House was filled with tension as Caesar and Cato debated the merits of the lex Gabinia, which granted Pompey an extraordinary command against piracy in the Mediterranean. Caesar, a supporter of Pompey, argued that the measure was necessary to protect Roman commerce and trade routes. Cato, a staunch opponent of the measure, believed that it gave too much power to Pompey and threatened the integrity of the Roman Republic. The two men stood facing each other, their arguments echoing off the marble walls of the chamber.

dialogue.content: This debate is crucial to my future political ambitions. I must convince the Senate of the necessity of the lex Gabinia and demonstrate my loyalty to Pompey. If I can sway the Senate to my side, I will gain favor with Pompey and secure his support for my own future endeavors. But I must be careful not to anger Cato and his supporters, or I risk alienating a powerful faction in the Senate.

Caesar, you speak of protecting Roman commerce, but at what cost? This measure grants Pompey unprecedented power and sets a dangerous precedent for future military commands. We must uphold the principles of the Republic and not give in to the whims of a single man.

Cato, you underestimate the threat of piracy in the Mediterranean. Roman merchants are losing their livelihoods to these bandits, and our trade routes are being disrupted. We need a strong leader like Pompey to put an end to this menace and restore order to the seas.

But at what cost, Caesar? This measure gives Pompey command over a vast fleet and army, answerable only to himself. Who will hold him accountable for his actions? Who will ensure that he does not abuse this power?
Cato makes a valid point, but I must counter with a stronger argument. I will appeal to the Senate's sense of duty and responsibility to the Republic.

Cato, I understand your concerns, but we cannot let our fear of tyranny paralyze us. It is our duty as senators to act in the best interests of the Republic, and that includes protecting our citizens from harm. Pompey has proven himself a capable commander, and I have no doubt that he will use this power wisely and responsibly.
But what if he doesn't, Caesar? What then? Will you stand by and watch as the Republic crumbles under the weight of a single man's ambition?
Cato's words are powerful, and I must tread carefully. I cannot afford to appear weak or indecisive in front of the Senate.

Cato, I share your concerns for the Republic, but we must also trust in the wisdom and judgment of our fellow senators. This measure has been debated and discussed at length, and it is now up to us to make a decision. I urge you to consider the greater good and vote in favor of the lex Gabinia.
But what of the precedent it sets, Caesar? If we allow Pompey to wield such power, who knows what other ambitious men may seek to follow in his footsteps?
Cato's arguments are persuasive, but I cannot let him sway the Senate. I must appeal to their sense of pragmatism and remind them of the practical benefits of this measure.

Cato, I understand your concerns, but we cannot let our fear of the unknown prevent us from taking action. Pompey has a proven track record of success, and I have every confidence that he will use this power to protect Roman interests. We must put aside our personal biases and act in the best interests of our Republic.
But at what cost, Caesar? At what cost?
Cato's words echo in my mind, but I cannot let my resolve waver. I must stand firm in my convictions and convince the Senate to support the lex Gabinia.

Cato, the cost of inaction is far greater than the cost of action. We cannot let our fear of the unknown prevent us from protecting our citizens and our economy. This measure is necessary, and I urge you to reconsider your position.
I cannot, Caesar. My conscience will not allow me to support such a measure.
Cato's refusal is a setback, but I cannot let it deter me. There are still others in the Senate who may be swayed by my arguments.

Very well, Cato. I respect your position, but I urge the rest of the Senate to vote in favor of the lex Gabinia. Let us not allow our fear of the unknown to prevent us from taking action to protect our Republic.

setting: Julius Caesar, the famous Roman statesman, author, and military commander, stands in the center of a large tent within a Roman camp, surrounded by a group of Gaulish tribal leaders. They have come to discuss their integration into the Roman Empire. The atmosphere is tense, with each side wary of the other's intentions.

dialogue.content: I must handle this situation carefully. These Gaulish tribes are proud and fierce, and they have a long history of resistance against Roman rule. But if I can convince them to join our empire, it could bring great benefits to Rome. More territory, more resources, and more soldiers to strengthen our armies. But I must tread carefully. I cannot afford to offend these proud warriors.

Gentlemen, I am honored to meet with you today. I understand that there may be some concerns and reservations about joining the Roman Empire, but I assure you that we come in peace. We only seek to bring stability and prosperity to this region.
We have heard rumors of Roman brutality and oppression. We have our own way of life, our own traditions and customs. Why should we give that up to become subjects of Rome?

I understand your concerns, but I must emphasize that Rome is not here to destroy your way of life. On the contrary, we seek to preserve and protect it, to bring the benefits of Roman law and civilization to your people. And as for the rumors of brutality, I can only say that they are greatly exaggerated. Rome is a fair and just empire, and we always seek to avoid unnecessary conflict and bloodshed.
But what about our independence? Our freedom to govern ourselves?

I understand your desire for independence, but let us not forget the realities of the world we live in. This region is surrounded by powerful enemies, such as the Germanic tribes to the north and the Mediterranean powers to the south. By joining Rome, you will gain the protection and support of the greatest military power in the world. And as for governance, I can assure you that you will have a great deal of autonomy under Roman rule. Your customs and traditions will be respected, and you will have a voice in the decisions that affect your people.
And what about our warriors? Will they have a place in your army?

Of course. We value the skills and bravery of your warriors, and we would be honored to have them fight alongside us. Your warriors will be given the same pay and benefits as Roman soldiers, and they will have the opportunity to rise through the ranks and gain glory and honor.
And what about our religion? Will we be forced to abandon our gods and worship Roman ones?

Absolutely not. Rome is a tolerant and pluralistic empire, and we respect the religious beliefs of all our subjects. You will be free to worship your gods as you see fit, and we will not interfere with your religious practices.
I can see that I am making progress. These tribal leaders are beginning to see the benefits of joining Rome. But I must be careful not to push too hard. I need to be patient and build trust.

Gentlemen, I understand that this is a difficult decision. But I urge you to consider the benefits of joining Rome. Together, we can build a better future for all our people. Think about it carefully, and let me know your decision.
We will discuss this among ourselves and give you our answer in a few days.
Very well. I look forward to hearing from you. And I hope that we can continue to work together in peace and cooperation, whether or not you choose to join the Roman Empire.
I have done what I can for now. The rest is up to them. But I am confident that they will see the wisdom of joining Rome. And if they do, it will be a great victory for the Roman Empire.

setting: Julius Caesar stood at the center of the Roman Forum, surrounded by a crowd of people eagerly listening to his words. He was there to advocate for the lex Manilia, a law that would reassign the Third Mithridatic War from its then-commander Lucullus to Pompey. Caesar was a well-known figure in the Forum, having served as an aedile and gained popularity among the people. He was now using his influence to support Pompey, one of his political allies. As he began to speak, the crowd grew silent, waiting to hear what he had to say.

dialogue.content: I must convince the people of the importance of this law. The Third Mithridatic War has been dragging on for too long, and Lucullus has proven to be an ineffective commander. Pompey, on the other hand, has shown his military prowess time and time again. If we want to win this war, we need to put our faith in him. But the people are hesitant. They fear giving too much power to one man. I need to address their concerns and show them that this is the best course of action.

People of Rome, I stand before you today to advocate for the lex Manilia. This law would reassign the Third Mithridatic War to Pompey, a man who has proven himself time and time again on the battlefield. Some of you may be hesitant to give so much power to one man, and I understand your concerns. But let me ask you this: who else is capable of leading us to victory in this war? Lucullus has proven himself to be an ineffective commander, and we cannot afford to lose any more lives on the battlefield. We need a leader who can get the job done, and that leader is Pompey.
But what about the power he would have? Would he not become too powerful?

I understand your concerns, my friend, but we must remember that this is not a time for politics. This is a time for war. If we want to win this war, we need to put our faith in the best leader available. And that leader is Pompey. He has the experience, the skill, and the determination to see this through to the end. We must trust in him and give him the power he needs to get the job done.
But what if he becomes a tyrant? What if he turns on us?

My dear friend, Pompey is a man of honor. He has dedicated his life to serving Rome and has never shown any desire for personal gain. I assure you that he will use his power only for the good of Rome. We must have faith in him and trust that he will lead us to victory.

I can see that some of the people are still hesitant, but I must continue to persuade them. I need to remind them of the importance of this war and the sacrifices that have already been made. I need to show them that there is no other choice but to support Pompey.

My fellow Romans, I know that this war has been long and difficult. Many of you have lost loved ones on the battlefield, and I share your grief. But we cannot let their sacrifices be in vain. We must see this war through to the end and emerge victorious. And the only way to do that is to support Pompey. He has the skills and the experience to lead us to victory, and we cannot afford to let this opportunity slip away. I urge you to support the lex Manilia and give Pompey the power he needs to win this war.
But what about Caesar? What about his ambitions?

My dear friend, I have no personal ambitions beyond serving Rome. I have dedicated my life to the betterment of this great city, and I will continue to do so. I support Pompey because I believe he is the best man for the job, and I urge you to do the same. Together, we can win this war and secure a brighter future for Rome. Thank you.

I can see that my words have had an impact on the people. They are still hesitant, but I have planted the seed of doubt in their minds. They will think about what I have said and, hopefully, come to the right decision. Pompey needs their support, and I will do everything in my power to make sure he gets it. Roma victor!

setting: Caesar's absence from Italy left Mark Antony in charge as magister equitum. His rule was unpopular and riots broke out in Italy. Publius Cornelius Dolabella agitated for debt relief, and the senate asked Antony to restore order. Delayed by a mutiny in southern Italy, Antony returned and suppressed the riots by force. Meanwhile, Cato had marched to Africa and there Metellus Scipio was in charge of the remaining republicans. They allied with Juba of Numidia, and what used to be Pompey's fleet raided the central Mediterranean islands. Caesar's governor in Spain was unpopular, and the province revolted, switching to the republican side.

dialogue.content: The news of the rebellion in Spain was a blow to me. I had entrusted the governorship to a man I thought was capable, but it seems I was wrong. The province switching to the republican side meant that I had lost a valuable asset. Spain was a crucial source of resources for me, and its loss would severely weaken my position. I needed to act fast to regain control.

Send a message to my legate Quintus Fabius Maximus. Tell him to gather all the loyal troops in Spain and march towards the rebellious province. I want him to take swift action and crush the rebellion. We cannot afford to lose Spain to the republicans.
As you command, Caesar. I will send the message at once.

I need to make an example out of the governor who betrayed me. His actions have cost me dearly, and I cannot let him get away with it. I will make sure that he faces the consequences of his treachery.
Bring the governor of Spain to me. I want to speak with him.
At once, Caesar.
Greetings, Caesar. I am at your service.

I trusted you to govern Spain in my absence, but you have betrayed me. Your actions have caused the province to revolt, and we have lost a valuable asset. You will face the consequences of your treachery.
Please, Caesar, I had no choice. The people were unhappy with your rule, and they demanded change. I had to appease them, or they would have turned against me.
You should have known better than to defy my orders. Your actions have cost me dearly, and I cannot let you get away with it. You will be punished for your treachery.
As you wish, Caesar. I am ready to face the consequences of my actions.

The rebellion in Spain had to be crushed, or it would spread to other provinces. I needed to act fast and send a message to the other governors that disobedience would not be tolerated. The punishment for treachery had to be severe.
Send a message to all the governors under my command. Tell them that any disobedience or treachery will not be tolerated. The punishment for such actions will be severe.
As you command, Caesar. I will send the message at once.

The rebellion in Spain was a setback, but I would not let it defeat me. I would crush the rebellion and reassert my authority over the province. The republicans would soon learn that they could not defeat me.
Prepare the troops. We march for Spain at once.

setting: At a bloody battle at Munda on 17 March 45 BC, Caesar narrowly found victory; his enemies were treated as rebels and he had them massacred. Labienus died on the field and one of Pompey's sons, Sextus, escaped but the war as effectively over. He remained in the province until June before setting out for Rome. He arrived in Rome in October of the same year and celebrated an unseemly triumph over fellow Romans. By this point he had started preparations for war on the Parthians to avenge Crassus' death at Carrhae in 53 BC with wide-ranging objectives that would take him into Dacia for three or more years; it was set to start on 18 March 44 BC.

dialogue.content: The victory at Munda was a close one, but I emerged victorious. My enemies were nothing but rebels, and I had to deal with them accordingly. The death of Labienus was unfortunate, but it was necessary to show the rest of them what happens when they fight against me. Sextus may have escaped, but he is no threat to me anymore. The war is over now, and it's time to move on to bigger things. The Parthians have to pay for what they did to Crassus, and I am the man to make them pay. This war will be long and difficult, but I am ready for it. Nothing can stop me now.
Caesar, congratulations on your victory at Munda. The people of Rome are proud of you.
Thank you, Lucius. It was a difficult battle, but we emerged victorious in the end. The people of Rome should be proud of their army.
Caesar, what are your plans now? Are you going to stay in Spain or return to Rome?
I will stay in Spain for a while longer before returning to Rome. There are still some matters that need my attention here. But rest assured, I will be back in Rome soon enough.
Caesar, I heard that you're planning a war against the Parthians. Is that true?
Yes, Brutus, it's true. The Parthians have to pay for what they did to Crassus. I will avenge his death and restore Rome's honor.
Caesar, are you sure about this? The Parthians are a powerful enemy, and we don't have the resources to fight them.
I am sure, Cassius. Rome's honor is at stake, and I will not rest until it is restored. We will find a way to defeat the Parthians, no matter what it takes.

The Parthian War will not be easy, but it is necessary. I will not let the Parthians get away with what they did to Crassus. I will show them the might of Rome, and they will regret ever crossing me. This war will be my legacy, and I will be remembered as the greatest general Rome has ever known.
Caesar, I have some news from Rome. There are rumors of a conspiracy against you.
A conspiracy? Who is behind it?
I don't know for sure, but there are whispers of Brutus and Cassius being involved.
Brutus and Cassius? I trusted them both. But if they are plotting against me, then they must be dealt with. I cannot allow anyone to threaten my rule.
Thank you for bringing this to my attention, Octavian. I will deal with Brutus and Cassius accordingly.

The conspiracy against me is a grave threat, but I will not let it succeed. I will crush any who oppose me, no matter who they are. Rome belongs to me, and I will not let anyone take it away from me. The Parthian War will have to wait until this matter is dealt with. But once it's over, nothing will stop me from achieving my goals.

setting: Julius Caesar stands before the Roman Senate, his eyes fixed on the assembled senators. He is dressed in full military regalia, a symbol of his triumphs on the battlefield. The senators, many of whom are wary of Caesar's growing power, sit in silence, waiting to hear what he has to say. Caesar clears his throat and begins to speak, his voice ringing out through the chamber. His words are persuasive, his arguments compelling. With every passing moment, it becomes clear that Caesar is a master orator, able to sway even the most stubborn of minds.

dialogue.content: I must convince the Senate to declare war against Gaul. The conquest of Gaul will bring great glory to Rome and cement my place in history. But I must be careful. There are those in the Senate who are wary of my growing power. I must persuade them that this war is necessary for the good of Rome.

Senators of Rome, I stand before you today to speak of a matter of the utmost importance. The barbarians of Gaul threaten our very way of life. They are a constant threat to our borders, and their savagery knows no bounds. If we do not act now, we risk losing everything we hold dear. It is time for us to take up arms and march against these barbarians. We must show them that Rome is not to be trifled with.
But Caesar, is war truly necessary? Can we not negotiate with the Gauls and come to a peaceful resolution?

I understand your concerns, Senator. But we have tried negotiating with the Gauls before, and they have proven time and again that they cannot be trusted. They are a barbaric people who understand only the language of force. If we do not act now, they will continue to raid our borders and threaten our very existence.
But what of the cost of this war? We cannot simply march into Gaul without considering the toll it will take on our resources and our people.

I understand your concerns, Senator. But I assure you, the cost of this war will be far outweighed by the benefits. The conquest of Gaul will bring great wealth and resources to Rome. And think of the glory we will earn! The conquest of Gaul will be remembered for centuries to come. Do not let our fear of the unknown hold us back from achieving greatness.
But what of the lives of our soldiers? Are we to send them to die on foreign soil for the sake of glory?

I understand your concerns, Senator. But our soldiers are the finest in the world. They are brave and disciplined, and they will be victorious. And think of the legacy they will leave behind. They will be remembered as heroes, as champions of Rome. Is that not a worthy cause?
They are beginning to come around. My words have stirred something within them, a desire for greatness. I must press on.

Senators of Rome, I implore you to consider the greater good. The conquest of Gaul will bring wealth, glory, and security to our great nation. It is time to put aside our petty squabbles and unite for the good of Rome. Will you stand with me?

setting: The Roman Forum is crowded with people as Julius Caesar and Cicero engage in a heated debate. The topic of discussion is a proposed law that would limit Caesar's powers as dictator. Caesar is known for his military conquests and political prowess, while Cicero is an accomplished orator and statesman. Other senators and citizens gather around to witness the debate and express their opinions.

dialogue.content: I cannot let this law pass. My power is necessary to maintain order and stability in Rome. Cicero and his allies seek to weaken me, but I will not allow it. I must convince the people that this law is unnecessary and harmful to the state.

Julius Caesar, I understand your concerns, but this law is necessary to prevent tyranny and ensure the freedom of the Roman people. We cannot allow one man to hold all the power without any checks and balances. It goes against the principles of our democracy.

Cicero, you are mistaken. I have only taken power to restore order and protect Rome from its enemies. I have no desire to become a tyrant. This law would only serve to weaken our defenses and make us vulnerable to our enemies. Rome needs a strong leader like me to guide it through these troubled times.
But Caesar, what if you become corrupted by power? What if you turn against the people and become a tyrant? We need to have safeguards in place to protect us from such a possibility.

I have no intention of becoming a tyrant, my fellow citizen. I have only ever acted in the best interests of Rome. I have fought for this city and its people, and I will continue to do so. But I cannot do it alone. I need the power to make the tough decisions and take the necessary actions to protect our great city.

Caesar, you speak of protecting Rome, but what about protecting its democracy? What about protecting the rights of its citizens? We cannot sacrifice our freedoms for the sake of security. It is a slippery slope that will lead to our downfall.
