Once I am free, I will make sure these pirates never harm anyone again. They will regret ever crossing me.
You have made a grave mistake by kidnapping me. I will not rest until you are brought to justice for your crimes.
We were just trying to make a living. We didn't mean to cause you any harm.
These pirates are nothing but cowards. They are trying to make excuses for their criminal behavior. They will pay for what they have done to me.
You will pay for your crimes. You have no right to kidnap innocent people and demand ransom for their release.
We will do anything to make it up to you. Please spare our lives.
These pirates are begging for mercy now, but it is too late for that. They will be punished for their crimes.
I will spare your lives, but you will be sold into slavery. You will never harm anyone again.
Please have mercy on us. We promise we will never harm anyone again.
I have no mercy for these pirates. They will pay for what they have done to me.
Take them away. I have no use for them anymore.

setting: Julius Caesar's father chose retirement during the reign of Lucius Cornelius Cinna and did not seek a consulship. Caesar was named as a priest of Jupiter, flamen Dialis, and married Cinna's daughter, Cornelia. Due to the religious taboos of the priesthood, it was unlikely that Caesar would have a significant political career. However, after his father's sudden death in 84 BC, Caesar's political fate took a turn for the worse. After Sulla's victory in the civil war, he ordered Caesar to divorce Cornelia. Caesar refused, leading to questions about the legitimacy of Sulla's actions. Scholars are divided on whether Sulla put Caesar on the proscription lists, but Caesar ultimately had to resign his priesthood to keep his wife and possessions.

dialogue.content: Sulla's victory has turned my life upside down. I was content with my position as a priest, but now I am in danger of losing everything. My father's death has made things worse, and I fear for my safety. I cannot believe Sulla would ask me to divorce Cornelia. What right does he have to interfere in my personal life? I refuse to let him control me.
My love, I fear for your safety. Sulla is a powerful man, and he will not take kindly to your disobedience. Please, consider his offer. We can rebuild our lives together.
No, Cornelia. I will not abandon you. Sulla has no right to interfere in our personal lives. I will not let him control me. I must find a way to protect us both.
Julius Caesar, we have interceded on your behalf, and we have reached a compromise with Sulla. You must resign your priesthood, but you can keep your wife and possessions.

I cannot believe this is happening to me. I never wanted to be involved in politics, but Sulla has forced my hand. I will resign my priesthood, but I will not forget this injustice. I will find a way to make things right.
My love, please be careful. I fear for your safety. Sulla is not to be trifled with.
Cornelia is right. Sulla is a dangerous man, and I must be careful. But I cannot let him get away with this. I will find a way to make him pay for what he has done.

setting: Caesar had just crossed the Rubicon, igniting the civil war. He was seeking to capture Pompey and force a conference. In the midst of this conflict, Caesar arrived in Alexandria and met Cleopatra, forming an alliance with her and taking her side in the Egyptian conflict.

dialogue.content: This alliance with Cleopatra may be the key to securing my position. With her by my side, I will have access to the riches of Egypt, and the support of her army. It is a risky move, considering the political climate, but I have never been one to shy away from risk. I must tread carefully, however, and ensure that this alliance does not backfire on me.
Welcome to Alexandria, Caesar. I am honored to have you here as my guest.
Thank you, Cleopatra. I am pleased to be here. I have heard much about your beauty and intelligence, and I must say that the rumors do not do you justice.
You flatter me, Caesar. But I am not without my own sources of information. I know of your military prowess and your political cunning. You are a formidable opponent, but also a valuable ally.
I am glad that we see eye to eye, Cleopatra. I believe that we can be of great benefit to each other. But first, let us discuss the matter at hand. I understand that you are in need of my assistance.
Yes, Caesar. My brother, Ptolemy, has seized control of the throne and is attempting to eliminate me. I need your support in order to regain my rightful place as ruler of Egypt.

This is a delicate situation. If I support Cleopatra openly, it may anger the Roman Senate and damage my reputation. But if I refuse her, I risk losing her support and the benefits that come with it. I must tread carefully.

I understand your predicament, Cleopatra. Rest assured that I am willing to assist you in any way that I can. However, we must be cautious in our approach. I cannot openly declare my support for you, as it may cause problems for me back in Rome. But I will do everything in my power to help you regain your rightful place.
Thank you, Caesar. Your support means everything to me. I promise that you will not regret this decision.

I hope that I am making the right decision. This alliance with Cleopatra has the potential to bring me great success, but it also carries significant risks. I must stay vigilant and ensure that I am not caught off guard.
Let us begin our preparations, Cleopatra. We have much work to do if we are to succeed in this endeavor.

setting: It is the year 51 BC and Julius Caesar is addressing the people of Rome in the Roman Forum. The consul Marcellus has proposed recalling Caesar from his task in Gaul, arguing that it is complete. However, Caesar is still fighting the Bellovaci and the proposal is vetoed. The conservative faction in the Senate, led by Cato, is seeking to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honours or a second consulship. Cato, Bibulus, and their allies have successfully won Pompey over to take a hard line against Caesar's continued command.

dialogue.content: Citizens of Rome, I stand before you today as a victorious general. My recent victory against Vercingetorix in Gaul has secured the safety and prosperity of our great nation. But it seems that some in the Senate are not content with my success. They seek to recall me from my task in Gaul, claiming that it is complete. I assure you, my fellow Romans, that this is not the case. The Bellovaci still resist, and it is my duty to bring them under our rule.

My fellow Romans, I have listened carefully to the arguments of both sides in this matter. While I have great respect for my esteemed colleague Caesar, I must also consider the best interests of our republic. It is my belief that Caesar's continued command in Gaul poses a threat to the stability of our government and the balance of power in the Senate. Therefore, I must support the proposal to recall him without honours or a second consulship.

Fellow senators, we must not allow Caesar to defy the will of the Senate and the laws of our republic. His continued command in Gaul is a violation of our traditions and an insult to the authority of this august body. We must unite behind Pompey's proposal and show Caesar that he cannot act with impunity.

I agree with my esteemed colleague Cato. Caesar's actions in Gaul are a threat to our republic and its institutions. We must recall him without honours or a second consulship, and remind him that he is a servant of the people, not their master.

setting: It is the year 84 BC in Rome, and Lucius Cornelius Cinna is in power. Julius Caesar's father has chosen to retire instead of seeking a consulship during this time of political hopelessness. Caesar himself has been named flamen Dialis, a high priest of Jupiter, which means he cannot pursue a political career due to the religious taboos of his priesthood. While his appointment is one of the highest non-political honors, it indicates that there are few expectations of a major career for him. In 82 BC, after Sulla's victory in the civil war, Cinna's acta were annulled, and Sulla ordered Caesar to abdicate and divorce Cinna's daughter. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment. It is unclear if Sulla put Caesar on the proscription lists, but Caesar went into hiding before his relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins were able to intercede on his behalf. They then reached a compromise where Caesar would resign his priesthood but keep his wife and chattels.

dialogue.content: What a mess. My father chose to retire during this time of political hopelessness, and now I am unable to pursue a political career due to my appointment as flamen Dialis. But I refuse to divorce Cornelia, no matter what Sulla says. The man has no right to annul my marriage and force me to give up my wife. I will not stand for it. I must find a way to protect my family and my honor while also navigating this treacherous political landscape.
Julius, I am so scared. Sulla's men have been asking about you, and I fear they will come for you soon.
Do not worry, my love. I will not let anything happen to us. I have a plan.
What plan?
I will go into hiding, and I have contacts among the Vestal Virgins who can intercede on my behalf. We will find a way to protect ourselves, I promise.
Julius Caesar, I hear you have been defying my orders.
I have not defied anything. I simply refuse to give up my wife and my honor.
You are a fool, Caesar. You do not understand the power I hold. You will regret crossing me.
This man is dangerous. I must tread carefully and make sure I have enough support to protect myself and my loved ones. But I will not back down. I will fight for what is right, no matter the cost.

setting: Julius Caesar and his supporters have gathered in the Roman Forum to discuss the growing hostility towards his continued command in Gaul. The trust between Caesar and his former ally, Pompey, has disintegrated, and the conservatives around Cato in the Senate seek to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honours or a second consulship. Caesar's provincia in Gaul, due to his victory against Vercingetorix in 52 BC, was argued to be complete, but Caesar was still fighting the Bellovaci in 51 BC. The proposal to recall Caesar was vetoed, and it is clear that the political tensions between Caesar and his opponents are escalating.

dialogue.content: I cannot let them force me to return to Rome without honours or a second consulship. My conquest in Gaul is not complete, and I have much work to do. I must find a way to win over Pompey and turn the tide of this political battle in my favour. Perhaps I can appeal to his sense of loyalty or remind him of our past alliances. But I must also prepare for the worst-case scenario and ensure that I have the support of my army. This civil war could turn ugly, and I must be ready for anything.

Caesar, the Senate has grown increasingly wary of your continued command in Gaul. They fear that you have become too powerful and may use your army against the state. I have tried to reason with them, but they are not willing to compromise. You must return to Rome without honours or a second consulship.

Pompey, I understand your concerns, but my conquest in Gaul is not complete. I have much work to do, and I cannot simply abandon my army and leave Gaul vulnerable to attack. I urge you to reconsider your position and remember our past alliances. We have fought side by side in the past, and I hope that we can continue to do so in the future.

Caesar, your loyalty to Rome is in question. You have defied the Senate and continued to command your army in Gaul without their permission. You have become too powerful, and we fear that you may use your army against the state. You must return to Rome and answer for your actions.

Cato, I have always been loyal to Rome and have only acted in its best interests. My conquest in Gaul has benefited Rome greatly, and I have no intention of using my army against the state. I urge you to consider the consequences of forcing me to return without honours or a second consulship. It will only lead to civil war and further instability in Rome.
Caesar, your time in Gaul is up. You have completed your task, and it is time for you to return to Rome. We cannot allow one man to hold so much power. It goes against the principles of our Republic.

Bibulus, my task in Gaul is not complete. I am still fighting the Bellovaci, and there is much work to be done. I understand your concerns about one man holding too much power, but I have no intention of using my army against the state. I urge you to reconsider your position and work with me to find a solution that benefits Rome.

I am torn between my loyalty to Caesar and my duty to Rome. Caesar has been a valuable ally in the past, but I cannot ignore the concerns of the Senate. If I side with Caesar, I risk being seen as a traitor to Rome. If I side with the Senate, I risk losing Caesar's support and potentially starting a civil war. This decision will have far-reaching consequences, and I must choose wisely.

Caesar, your actions have shown that you have no respect for the Senate or the Republic. Your continued command in Gaul is a threat to the stability of Rome, and we cannot allow it to continue. You must return to Rome without honours or a second consulship.

Cato, I understand your concerns, but I cannot simply abandon my army and leave Gaul vulnerable to attack. I have no intention of using my army against the state, and I urge you to reconsider your position. We must find a way to work together for the good of Rome.
Caesar, the Senate has spoken. Your time in Gaul is up, and it is time for you to return to Rome. We cannot allow one man to hold so much power. It goes against the principles of our Republic.

Bibulus, I understand the position of the Senate, but my task in Gaul is not complete. I am still fighting the Bellovaci, and there is much work to be done. I urge you to consider the consequences of forcing me to return without honours or a second consulship. It will only lead to civil war and further instability in Rome.

Gentlemen, I believe that we must find a way to compromise. Caesar, you must return to Rome, but you will be allowed to keep your army and receive the honours you deserve. The Senate will agree to this if you promise not to use your army against the state.

This is not the outcome I had hoped for, but it may be the best I can get. I must accept Pompey's compromise and hope that it will be enough to appease the Senate. I will keep my army and receive the honours I deserve, but I must also promise not to use my army against the state. It is a small price to pay for the continuation of my conquest in Gaul and the preservation of Rome's stability.

Pompey, I accept your compromise. I will return to Rome and receive the honours I deserve, but I promise not to use my army against the state. I hope that this will be enough to appease the Senate and preserve the stability of Rome.

setting: It is a grand day for Julius Caesar. He leads a Roman triumphal procession through the streets of Rome, celebrating his victories and achievements in Gaul and other campaigns. The streets are packed with cheering crowds as Caesar rides in a chariot, his soldiers marching behind him in full battle dress. Captive enemies, treasures, and triumphal arches are all displayed to impress the crowds and show the might of the Roman Empire. Caesar is dressed in his finest military uniform, his chest adorned with medals and his head crowned with a laurel wreath. He looks proud and confident, basking in the adulation of the people.

dialogue.content: Today is a day I will never forget. The people of Rome have come out in their thousands to celebrate my victories, to honor me as their leader. I have triumphed over the Gauls, conquered their lands, and brought them under the rule of Rome. I have shown the world the power and might of the Roman Empire. Today, I stand before my people as a true conqueror, a hero of Rome. But this is only the beginning. I have more campaigns planned, more lands to conquer, more glory to achieve. I will not rest until the whole world is under the rule of Rome.

My fellow Romans! Today we celebrate not just the victories of Caesar, but the might of Rome itself! Look around you, at the riches and treasures we have brought back from our campaigns. Look at the captive enemies, defeated and humbled before us. They are a testament to the power of Rome, to the strength of our armies and the courage of our soldiers. But this is not just a celebration of the past. This is a promise of the future. I have more campaigns planned, more lands to conquer, more peoples to bring under the rule of Rome. And I promise you this, my fellow Romans: I will not rest until the whole world is under our dominion!

Caesar, the people of Rome celebrate your victories, but some of us are concerned about the cost of your campaigns. The treasury is nearly empty, and the people are overtaxed. How do you plan to pay for your future campaigns?

Fear not, Senator. The wealth of Gaul is vast, and I have brought much of it back to Rome. I will use this wealth to finance our future campaigns. And as for the people, they know that the glory of Rome comes at a price. They are willing to bear the burden, knowing that their sacrifices will bring them honor and prestige. Trust me, Senator, I have a plan. Rome will never falter, never fail, as long as I am at the helm.

That Senator is a fool. He does not understand the true cost of war, the true value of conquest. But I will not let his doubts and fears hold me back. I will continue to conquer, to expand the glory of Rome, no matter what the cost. I am Caesar, and Rome is mine to command.

setting: The Roman Senate is in session and a heated debate is ongoing. The topic of discussion is Caesar's extended stay in Gaul, and the senators are divided on whether he should return or not. The conservatives, led by Cato and Bibulus, are pushing for Caesar's return without honors or a second consulship. On the other hand, Caesar is arguing for his right to continue his command in Gaul.

dialogue.content: These senators don't understand the importance of my mission in Gaul. They are blinded by their own selfish interests and are unable to see the bigger picture. If I were to return to Rome without completing my task, all my efforts would be for nothing. I cannot let that happen. I must convince them of the necessity of my continued command.
Caesar, your provincia in Gaul is completed. It is time for you to return to Rome and step down from your command.

Senator Cato, with all due respect, I must disagree with you. My province in Gaul is far from complete. I am still fighting the Bellovaci, and there is much work to be done. If I were to return to Rome now, all that I have achieved would be lost. You must understand that my mission in Gaul is of great importance to the Republic.

Caesar, we understand the importance of your mission in Gaul, but it is time for you to return to Rome. The Senate has spoken, and we cannot allow you to continue your command indefinitely. It is not good for the Republic.

These senators are not listening to reason. They are only interested in their own power and influence. They cannot see that my mission in Gaul is crucial to the security of the Republic. I must find a way to convince them of the necessity of my continued command.

Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but we must not forget the great service that Caesar has done for the Republic. He has defeated our enemies in Gaul and secured our borders. We cannot simply cast him aside like a used piece of armor. We must find a way to accommodate his request.
But Pompey, allowing Caesar to continue his command is against the law. The Senate has already spoken. We cannot allow one man to defy the will of the people.

Senator Cato, I am not defying the will of the people. I am simply asking for the opportunity to complete my mission in Gaul. I have spent years fighting for the Republic, and I believe that my efforts should not be in vain. I am not asking for special treatment, only for the chance to finish what I have started.
But Caesar, how long will you continue your command? When will it be enough? We cannot allow you to rule over Gaul indefinitely.

Senator Bibulus, I understand your concerns, but I assure you that I have no desire to rule over Gaul indefinitely. My mission is to secure the borders of the Republic and to bring peace to the region. As soon as I have completed that task, I will return to Rome and step down from my command.

Gentlemen, I believe that we can come to a compromise. Caesar, I propose that you be allowed to continue your command in Gaul for one more year. After that, you must return to Rome and step down from your command. This way, we can ensure the security of the Republic while also respecting the law.

Pompey is a wise man. He understands the importance of my mission in Gaul and is willing to work with me to find a solution. I must accept his proposal and continue my command for one more year. After that, I will return to Rome and step down from my command, as promised.

Senator Pompey, I accept your proposal. I will continue my command in Gaul for one more year, after which I will return to Rome and step down from my command. I thank you for your wisdom and your willingness to work with me to find a solution.
Very well, Caesar. We will allow you to continue your command for one more year. But remember, you are not above the law. You must return to Rome when your time is up.
I understand, Senator Cato. I am not above the law, and I will return to Rome when my time is up. But until then, I must continue my mission in Gaul. The security of the Republic depends on it.

setting: Mark Antony is in charge of Italy while Caesar is away. Dolabella, as a plebeian tribune, agitates for debt relief which leads to riots in Rome. Meanwhile, Cato marches to Africa where Metellus Scipio and Juba of Numidia lead the remaining republicans. Pompey's fleet also raids the central Mediterranean islands. In Spain, Caesar's governor is unpopular and the province revolts, switching to the republican side.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe the chaos that has erupted in my absence. Mark Antony has proven to be an ineffective leader. The people are rioting and causing destruction in the streets. I must find a way to restore order and stability to Rome. The situation in Africa is also concerning. Cato and his allies must be stopped before they gain more power. In Spain, I have lost control of the province. I must act quickly to prevent further rebellion.
People of Rome, we have suffered enough under the weight of our debts. It is time for us to rise up and demand relief from our oppressors! We will not be silenced any longer!
Debt relief! Debt relief!
Enough! These riots have gone on for too long. I will restore order, even if it means using force. Return to your homes now or face the consequences.
We must continue our fight against Caesar and his tyranny. The people of Rome deserve better than a dictator who seeks to rule with an iron fist.
I agree, Metellus Scipio. We must unite and fight for our freedom. We will not be oppressed any longer.
We will continue to raid the central Mediterranean islands and disrupt Caesar's supply lines. He will soon regret underestimating our strength.
I will not stand for this rebellion in Spain. Those who have defected to the republican side will face the full force of my army. I will not tolerate any more insubordination.

I must act swiftly to put an end to these rebellions. I cannot allow dissent to spread any further. The people must understand that I am the only one capable of leading Rome to greatness. I will not let anyone stand in my way.

setting: It is the year 84 BC in Rome. Julius Caesar's father has just died suddenly, leaving him with no clear path forward. During the dominance of Lucius Cornelius Cinna, Caesar was appointed as Flamen Dialis, a prestigious religious position that would have prevented him from pursuing a political career. However, after Cinna's reign was annulled by Sulla's victory in the civil war, Caesar found himself in a difficult position as Sulla ordered him to abdicate and divorce Cinna's daughter.

dialogue.content: What am I to do now? My father has just passed away, leaving me with no clear direction in life. And now with Sulla's orders to divorce Cornelia, I am left with even less certainty. How can I simply abandon the woman I love and the life I have built for myself? But going against Sulla's wishes could mean my death. I must find a way to navigate this treacherous situation.
Julius, what are we to do? Sulla's orders are clear, but I cannot bear the thought of being separated from you.

Cornelia, my love, I will not abandon you. We must find a way to appease Sulla while also maintaining our life together. I will speak to my contacts among the Vestal Virgins and see if they can intercede on our behalf.
Julius, we have spoken with Sulla and reached a compromise. You must resign your priesthood, but you may keep your wife and possessions.

A compromise. It's not ideal, but it's better than the alternative. I can resign my priesthood and still maintain my love for Cornelia. And perhaps there is still a path forward for me in politics. I must tread carefully, but this compromise has given me hope.

setting: Caesar and Cicero were dining at Caesar's villa discussing politics. Caesar was one of Pompey's supporters, and for much of this period, he had joined with Pompey to support the restoration of tribunician rights. Caesar had supported several laws and bills that were beneficial to Pompey, including the lex Gabinia and the lex Manilia. The conversation between Caesar and Cicero was intense, and they were both passionate about their political beliefs. The villa was decorated with intricate frescos and was lit with candles that casted a warm glow over the room.

dialogue.content: I need to convince Cicero that I am the right man for the job. I know he has his doubts about me, but I can't let that stop me. If I want to be elected as Pontifex Maximus, I need Cicero's support. He is a powerful man, and his endorsement could sway many others to my side. I need to be careful with my words and present myself in the best possible light.

Julius, you know I respect you as a politician, but I have my doubts about your loyalty. You have supported Pompey at every turn, and I fear you may be more interested in his success than that of the Republic.

I assure you, Cicero, my loyalty is to the Republic first and foremost. I support Pompey because I believe he is the best man for the job. He has proven himself time and time again, and I am proud to stand by his side. But make no mistake, I would never put his interests above those of the Republic.
I understand your reasoning, but I can't help but feel uneasy. You have a lot of power and influence, and I worry that you may use it for your own gain.

I can see that Cicero is still skeptical. I need to convince him that I am trustworthy and that I have the Republic's best interests at heart. Perhaps if I appeal to his sense of duty and honor, he will see things my way.

Cicero, I understand your concerns, but I assure you that I am a man of honor. I have dedicated my life to serving the Republic, and I would never do anything to harm it. I am not interested in personal gain or power. My only goal is to ensure that the Republic remains strong and prosperous for generations to come.
I appreciate your words, Julius, but words are not enough. I need to see action. I need to see that you are willing to put the Republic's interests above your own.
Cicero is a tough negotiator, but I need his support. I need to find a way to prove to him that I am a man of action.

Cicero, I understand your position, and I am willing to do whatever it takes to earn your trust. Perhaps if I were to take on a more significant role in the Senate, you would see that I am serious about my commitment to the Republic.
What role are you suggesting?
This is it. This is my chance to convince Cicero that I am the right man for the job. I need to choose my words carefully.
I have been considering running for Aedileship. It would be an excellent opportunity for me to prove my dedication to the Republic and demonstrate my leadership skills. What do you think, Cicero?
This could be a good opportunity for Caesar. It would give him a chance to prove himself and show his commitment to the Republic. But I still have my doubts.

I think it's a good start, Julius. But you need to do more than just run for Aedileship. You need to show that you are willing to work with all factions in the Senate and put the Republic's interests above your own. If you can do that, then I will consider supporting you for the Pontifex Maximus position.

I have a lot of work to do, but I am up for the challenge. I will do whatever it takes to prove myself to Cicero and the rest of the Senate. I am determined to become Pontifex Maximus and lead the Republic into a new era of prosperity.

setting: It is a time of power shift in Rome, and Julius Caesar is at the forefront of it. Through alliances with Pompey and the passing of bills in the senate, Caesar's power is growing stronger, and the balance of power in Rome is shifting. The bills passed include a one-third write-down of tax farmers' arrears for Crassus and ratification of Pompey's eastern settlements. Caesar also moved to lift the extend his agrarian bill to Campania, and his ally, plebeian tribune Publius Vatinius, moved the lex Vatinia assigning the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years. The senate assigned to Caesar the Transalpine Gaul as well, subject to annual renewal, likely to control his ability to make war on the far side of the Alps.

dialogue.content: I am the most powerful man in Rome, and I will not let anyone stand in my way. With each passing day, my power grows stronger, and my enemies weaker. The senate may try to resist me, but they cannot deny the will of the people. Through my alliances with Pompey and Crassus, I have secured the support of the most powerful men in Rome, and no one can stand against us. I will continue to pass bills and expand my power, and soon, Rome will be mine to command.
My dear Caesar, I am pleased to hear that your daughter Julia has agreed to marry me. This alliance will strengthen our bonds and secure our power in Rome. Together, we will be unstoppable.
Caesar, the passing of the one-third write-down of tax farmers' arrears has secured my support for you. I am grateful for your assistance, and I will do anything to help you maintain your power.
The lex Vatinia assigning the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years has passed. This will give Caesar much-needed resources to expand his power and control the region.
I must withdraw to my house. Caesar's power grows stronger every day, and I fear for my safety. He must be stopped before it is too late.

These fools cannot stop me. I am the rightful ruler of Rome, and I will not let anyone stand in my way. The passing of these bills has secured my power, and soon, all of Rome will bow down to me. I will continue to expand my power and crush my enemies until I am the undisputed ruler of Rome.

setting: It was a tumultuous time in Rome. Caesar had just ended his consulship and faced opposition from Bibulus, who had issued edicts to cancel voting days for religious reasons. Cato also attempted to undermine Caesar's power, successfully building revulsion to Caesar and his allies. Despite the common depiction of triumviral political supremacy, Caesar faced serious political difficulties.

dialogue.content: As I stand here in the Roman Forum, I can feel the eyes of my supporters upon me. They look to me for strength and leadership, and I will not disappoint them. The opposition may think they have won, but they underestimate my determination to secure victories for the Roman people. I will not let Bibulus and Cato stand in the way of progress.

My fellow Romans, I stand before you today to address the challenges we face as a nation. The opposition may seek to undermine our progress, but we will not be deterred. We will fight with all our might to secure victories for the Roman people. We will not let Bibulus and Cato stand in the way of our success. We will show them that the power of the people is stronger than any individual's ambitions. Together, we will build a better future for Rome, and for all who call it home.
Caesar, we stand with you! We will fight to the end to ensure our voice is heard.
The opposition cannot stop us! We will overcome any obstacle in our path.

I can feel the energy in the crowd, the passion and determination to succeed. They believe in me, and I must not let them down. My mind races with plans and strategies to overcome the opposition's tactics. I will not rest until we secure victories for the Roman people.

My fellow Romans, I ask you to stand with me in this fight. Together, we can overcome any obstacle and achieve greatness for our nation. The road ahead may be difficult, but we will not falter. We will not let the opposition's tactics divide us. We must remain united and strong in the face of adversity. Rome deserves nothing less than our unwavering commitment to its success.
Caesar, we believe in you! Your leadership will guide us to victory.
The opposition may try to stop us, but they cannot defeat us. We will emerge victorious!

I am filled with a sense of purpose and determination. The opposition may think they have won, but they have not seen the full extent of my power. I will not let them stand in the way of progress. Rome deserves nothing less than my absolute commitment to its success.

My fellow Romans, I leave you with this message: we will not falter, we will not be defeated. We will emerge victorious, stronger than ever before. The opposition may try to stop us, but they will not succeed. Together, we will build a brighter future for Rome, and for all who call it home. Thank you.

setting: Caesar faces off against fierce opposition from the senators, attempting to push through legislation that would benefit the common people. After suffering political defeats, Bibulus withdrew to his house to issue edicts in absentia purporting to cancel all days on which Caesar or his allies could hold votes for religious reasons. Cato too attempted symbolic gestures against it, allowing him and his allies to feign victimization. These tactics were successful in building revulsion to Caesar and his allies through the year. This opposition caused serious political difficulties to Caesar and his allies, belying the common depiction of triumviral political supremacy. When his consulship ended, Caesar's legislation was challenged by two of the new praetors but discussion in the senate stalled and was regardless dropped. He stayed near the city until some time around mid-March.

dialogue.content: This is outrageous. How can they cancel the voting days just because they fear that I might win? This is not how democracy works. I must find a way to convince the senators that my legislation is in the best interest of the people. I cannot let them derail my plans.

Caesar, your actions are a threat to the Republic. You seek to undermine the authority of the Senate by pushing through legislation that benefits only your allies and supporters. The people will not stand for this.

Cato, I understand your concerns, but my legislation benefits all the people, not just my allies. You and your allies are only interested in preserving the status quo, even if it means keeping the poor in poverty. I seek to bring real change to Rome.

Caesar, your words are empty promises. Your actions speak louder than your words. You seek to manipulate the people by promising them the world, but in reality, you only seek to consolidate power for yourself. You are a danger to the Republic.

Bibulus, I am not seeking to consolidate power for myself. I am seeking to give power to the people. The people of Rome are tired of being oppressed by the wealthy elites. They want change, and I am here to deliver it. My legislation will benefit all the people, not just the wealthy few.
Caesar, your legislation is unconstitutional. It violates the principles of the Roman Republic. We cannot allow you to subvert the rule of law.

Praetor, my legislation is not unconstitutional. It is in line with the principles of the Roman Republic. The people have a right to be heard, and my legislation gives them that right. I urge you to reconsider your position and support my legislation.
Caesar, I cannot support your legislation. It goes against everything that I believe in. I cannot in good conscience vote for it.

Praetor, I understand your concerns, but please consider the consequences of your actions. If you vote against my legislation, you will be voting against the people of Rome. You will be denying them their right to representation. Is that the kind of legacy you want to leave behind?
Caesar, your rhetoric is baseless. You seek to manipulate the people with your empty promises. You are a snake oil salesman, nothing more.

Bibulus, your insults do not bother me. I am here to do what is right for the people of Rome, not to win popularity contests. You and your allies may try to stop me, but you will not succeed. The people of Rome are with me, and I will not let them down.

setting: Julius Caesar, the Roman politician and general, is discussing the payment for the restoration work with architects and restorers at his workplace. The time is around 65 BC, four years after his aunt Julia's funeral, and Caesar is serving as curule aedile. He has staged lavish games that won him further attention and popular support. Caesar is now restoring the trophies won by Marius, and taken down by Sulla, over Jugurtha and the Cimbri. The restoration work is not sudden and secret as architects, restorers, and other workmen have been hired and paid for. Caesar is facing objections from Catulus, but these actions were broadly supported by the senate.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe Catulus is still objecting to me restoring these trophies. These are my family's public monuments, and it is my duty to restore them. I am merely being consistent with standard aristocratic practice and the virtue of pietas. The people of Rome will appreciate my efforts, and it will only increase my popularity. However, I need to carefully consider the payment for the restoration work with the architects and restorers. I cannot afford to overspend, and I need to ensure that the work is of high quality.
Caesar, we have estimated the cost for the restoration work, and it will come to around 5000 denarii.
5000 denarii? That seems a bit steep. Can you break down the cost for me?
Of course, Caesar. The cost includes the materials for the restoration work, the wages for the workers, and our fee for supervising the work.
5000 denarii is a lot of money, but I cannot compromise on the quality of the work. I need to ensure that the restoration is done correctly, and the monuments are restored to their former glory.
Caesar, we will need to use the finest materials for the restoration work. We cannot compromise on the quality.
I understand, but we need to keep the costs down. Is there any way we can use cheaper materials without compromising on the quality of the work?
I am afraid not, Caesar. The trophies are made of marble, and we need to use the same material for the restoration work. We can use slightly lower quality marble, but it will still be expensive.

It seems like I have no choice but to go ahead with the expensive materials. I cannot compromise on the quality of the work, and I need to keep the people of Rome happy. I will have to find a way to cover the costs.
Very well, let's go ahead with the expensive materials. We need to ensure that the work is of high quality, and we cannot compromise on that.
Understood, Caesar. We will ensure that the work is done to the highest standards.
I need to find a way to cover the costs of the restoration work. Perhaps I can increase taxes or find other sources of revenue. I cannot let the expense of the restoration work affect my popularity.
Thank you for your work. Please ensure that the work is done as quickly as possible, and the quality is not compromised.
Understood, Caesar. We will ensure that the work is done to the highest standards.

The restoration work will be expensive, but it will be worth it in the end. The people of Rome will appreciate my efforts, and it will increase my popularity. I need to find a way to cover the costs and ensure that the work is done to the highest standards.

setting: The Roman Senate is in session, with senators debating the outcome of the civil war. Some are calling for Caesar's exile. The setting is tense, with emotions running high and the future of Rome hanging in the balance. Caesar, the main character, is present and listening to the debates.

dialogue.content: These senators dare to challenge my authority? After all I have done for Rome? The nerve of them! They should be grateful for the peace and prosperity I have brought to this once divided republic. But no, they are blinded by their jealousy and fear. They cannot see that I am the only one capable of leading Rome into a new era of greatness. I will not stand for their insolence. I will not be exiled like some common criminal. I am Julius Caesar, and I will not be humiliated in front of these fools.

Julius Caesar, you have violated the laws of the Roman Republic by crossing the Rubicon and leading your army against Rome. You have shown contempt for the Senate and the people, and brought nothing but chaos and destruction to our once great city. I call upon my fellow senators to vote for your exile and restore order to our beloved Rome.

Order, Cato? You speak of order when the Senate is divided and the people are starving? When the barbarians are at our gates and the very foundations of our republic are threatened? You dare to accuse me of violating the laws of Rome when you and your cronies have done nothing but obstruct progress and cling to your own power? I did what was necessary to protect Rome and ensure its future. And now you would cast me out like some common criminal? No, I will not be exiled. I will not be silenced. I am the only hope for this republic, and I will not rest until it is restored to its former glory.

Caesar, I understand your passion and your desire to lead Rome, but you must understand that your actions have consequences. You have defied the Senate and the people, and that cannot go unpunished. I urge you to accept exile and spare Rome from further bloodshed and turmoil.

Pompey, always the coward. He thinks he can sway the Senate with his honeyed words and empty promises. But I know his true intentions. He wants me out of the way so he can take control of Rome for himself. He is blinded by his own ambition, and he cannot see that I am the only one who can save Rome from destruction. I will not let him or anyone else stand in my way.

Pompey, you speak of consequences, but what about the consequences of inaction? What about the consequences of letting Rome fall into chaos and darkness? You would have me accept exile and abandon my duty to Rome? No, I will not do it. I will not let the cowardice of others dictate the fate of our republic. I will fight for Rome until my dying breath, and I will not rest until it is restored to its rightful place as the greatest empire in the world.

Caesar, I understand your passion and your sense of duty, but you must understand that the Senate cannot condone your actions. We are a republic, not a monarchy. We cannot let one man hold all the power and rule over us like a tyrant. You must accept the consequences of your actions and submit to the will of the Senate.

Cicero, always the pragmatist. He thinks he can reason with me and persuade me to accept exile. But he is wrong. I am not a man who will back down from a fight. I am not a man who will let others dictate my fate. I am Julius Caesar, and I will do whatever it takes to protect Rome and ensure its future.

Cicero, you speak of the will of the Senate, but what about the will of the people? What about the will of those who have suffered under the corruption and incompetence of the old regime? They look to me for leadership and guidance, not to a bunch of petty politicians who care only for their own power and prestige. I will not submit to the will of the Senate, Cicero. I will submit only to the will of the people and the gods themselves. And they have spoken. They have spoken through my victories and my triumphs. They have spoken through the loyalty and devotion of my soldiers. They have spoken through the very blood and sweat that I have shed for Rome. I will not be silenced, Cicero. I will not be exiled. I will not rest until Rome is restored to its former glory.

setting: The Roman Senate is in session, with Senators debating the legality of Caesar's extended command in Gaul. It is the year 51 BC, and the trust between Caesar and Pompey has begun to disintegrate. The consul Marcellus has proposed recalling Caesar, arguing that his task in Gaul is complete, but the proposal was vetoed. The conservatives around Cato in the Senate are seeking to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honours or a second consulship. Cato, Bibulus, and their allies are successful in winning Pompey over to take a hard line against Caesar's continued command.

dialogue.content: These senators have no idea what it takes to conquer Gaul and expand the Roman Empire. They sit here in their comfortable chairs, debating my authority, while I am out there fighting for Rome. I have sacrificed so much for this city, and yet they still question my loyalty. But I will not back down. I will not let them take away my command and my honour. I will fight to keep my position and prove to them that I am the best general Rome has ever seen.
Caesar, your command in Gaul was only supposed to last five years. It has now been over seven. Do you not think it is time to return to Rome and let someone else take charge?

Cato, you know as well as I do that Gaul is still a threat to Rome. The Belgae and the Germans are still a danger to our nation, and I will not leave until they are defeated. My task is not complete, and I will not abandon it just because some senators want me to.
But Caesar, the Senate has the final say in matters of war and peace. Your command has been extended for too long, and it is time for you to return to Rome and face the consequences of your actions.

Pompey was once my ally, but now he has turned against me. He is nothing more than a puppet of the Senate, and I will not let him or anyone else dictate my actions. I must find a way to convince him to support me once again.

Pompey, I understand your concerns, but I cannot simply abandon my troops and leave Gaul vulnerable to attack. If the Senate wants to remove me from my command, they must do so legally and with honour. I will not be forced out by political manoeuvring.
Caesar, the Senate has already voted to recall you from Gaul. You are defying the will of the people and risking civil war. Is that what you want?

I do not want civil war, Bibulus, but I will not let the Senate strip me of my command unjustly. If they want to recall me, they must do so through legal means. Until then, I will continue to fight for Rome and defend our nation against its enemies.
Caesar, you are putting your own ambitions above the needs of Rome. You are risking the stability of our government and the safety of our people. Is that what a true Roman does?

Cato is a hypocrite. He claims to be a defender of Rome, but all he cares about is his own power. He is using this situation to undermine me and further his own agenda. But I will not let him succeed.

Cato, you are the one who is putting your own ambitions above the needs of Rome. You are using this situation to gain more power and influence, and you are willing to risk the lives of our soldiers and the safety of our nation to do it. I will not let you undermine me or the work I have done in Gaul. I will fight for what is right, and I will defend Rome at all costs.

setting: Caesar has just been appointed as consul and he has proposed a land reform bill to purchase land from willing sellers to be distributed among Pompey's veterans and the urban poor. The bill would be administered by a board of twenty and financed by Pompey's plunder and territorial gains. Caesar referred the bill to the senate in hopes that it would take up the matter to show its beneficence for the people. However, there is opposition to the bill and any indication of radicalism.

dialogue.content: I cannot let them stop me now. This land reform bill is necessary for the people and I will not let the selfish interests of the senate get in the way. I must find a way to get this bill passed, even if it means going against their wishes.
We cannot allow this bill to pass. It goes against the principles of our republic and undermines the power of the senate. We must stand firm against this radical proposal.
I agree with Cato. This bill is a threat to our very way of life. We must use any means necessary to stop it, even if it means using the veto.
Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but this bill is for the greater good of the people. We must not let our own self-interest get in the way of progress.
But at what cost? This bill will set a dangerous precedent and lead us down a path of tyranny. We cannot allow it to pass.
I must use my veto power to stop this bill. It is the only way to protect the interests of the senate and the people.

They are obstructing my efforts to help the people. I must find a way to get this bill passed, even if it means going against the senate's wishes. I will not let their selfish interests get in the way of progress.
Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but I will not let the veto stop this bill from passing. I will take it to the people and let them decide.
You cannot do that! It is against the auspices and violates the sovereignty of the senate. You will face consequences for your actions.
I must be careful, Bibulus is a threat to my plans. I cannot let him stop me now.
I will not be threatened by your veto, Bibulus. I will take this bill to the people and let them decide. They have the right to know what is best for them.
You are making a grave mistake, Caesar. The senate will not stand for this.
I cannot let the senate stop me now. I must find a way to get this bill passed, even if it means using force.
I am not afraid of the senate's threats. I will use any means necessary to get this bill passed, even if it means using force.
We support Caesar! We demand the land reform bill be passed!
The people are with me. I must use their support to get this bill passed.
I hear your voices, my fellow Romans. I will not let the senate's selfish interests get in the way of progress. We will pass this bill and help those in need.
Long live Caesar! Long live the land reform bill!

I have done it. The land reform bill has passed and the people are on my side. This is just the beginning. I will continue to fight for the greater good of Rome, even if it means going against the senate's wishes.

setting: It is a busy day in the public square of Rome, with citizens bustling about their daily business. There is a sense of anticipation in the air as Julius Caesar, the great military commander and statesman, steps onto a raised platform to address the people of Rome. The sun is high in the sky, casting a warm glow on the scene, and the sounds of chatter and laughter fill the air. A hush falls over the crowd as Caesar raises his hand to signal for silence, and all eyes turn to him. His demeanor is calm and collected, but there is a hint of triumph in his expression as he prepares to make a momentous announcement.

dialogue.content: My fellow Romans, today is a day of great rejoicing. I stand before you as your victorious leader, having emerged triumphant from a long and arduous civil war. The struggle has been long and difficult, but we have emerged stronger and more united than ever before. Our great Republic has been preserved, and our enemies have been vanquished. The forces of chaos and disorder have been defeated, and Rome stands once again as a shining example of order and civilization. I have come before you today to declare the end of the civil war and the restoration of peace and stability to our beloved nation.
Hail Caesar! Long live the Republic!
Caesar, you are a true hero! You have saved us from destruction and brought us back from the brink of disaster!

It is a moment of triumph for me, but I must be careful not to let my success go to my head. The people of Rome are fickle, and they will turn on me if I appear too arrogant or overbearing. I must be gracious in victory, and show them that I am a leader who cares about their welfare and prosperity.
But what of Pompey, Caesar? What will become of him?

Pompey is no longer a threat to the Republic. He has fled to Egypt, where he will no doubt try to seek refuge. But his fate is no longer my concern. The civil war is over, and I have no desire to shed any more blood. Let us look to the future, and work together to build a better Rome for all its citizens.
Hail Caesar! You are the savior of Rome!

I must be careful not to become too complacent, however. There are still many challenges that lie ahead, and I must be prepared to face them with all my strength and cunning. Rome is a city of great power and influence, but it is also a city of danger and intrigue. I must be vigilant at all times, and never let down my guard.

My fellow Romans, let us raise our voices in celebration of this great victory! Let us rejoice in the knowledge that our Republic has been saved, and that we stand together as one people, united in our love for Rome and our dedication to its future. Long live the Republic! Long live Rome!

setting: It is a night in ancient Rome, in the year 44 BC. Julius Caesar, the great general who expanded the Roman Empire, is dead. His assassination is reenacted in a play performed in Pompey's theater, where Caesar was previously granted a triumph. The audience is packed with people of all social classes, from senators to commoners. The play is a popular entertainment, and the audience is excited to see the dramatic depiction of Caesar's death. The stage is set as the Roman Senate, where Caesar was assassinated. The actors are dressed in the traditional Roman togas and are ready to begin the play. The atmosphere is tense, and there is a feeling of anticipation in the air.

dialogue.content: I can't believe they're doing this. How dare they mock me and my death? I am Julius Caesar, the great conqueror of Rome. I deserve respect, not ridicule. They think they can erase my legacy by turning my death into a play, but they are wrong. My name will live on forever. They can try to assassinate me, but they can never assassinate my legacy.
Et tu, Brute?" - Caesar
Then fall, Caesar!" - Brutus

I remember this moment all too well. The moment when my trusted friend, Brutus, stabbed me in the back. I never thought he would betray me, but he did. And now, here he is, reenacting my death on stage. I wonder if he feels any remorse for what he did. Does he regret his decision? Or does he still believe that he did the right thing? I will never know.
Romans, countrymen, and lovers! Hear me for my cause, and be silent that you may hear." - Mark Antony

Ah, Mark Antony. He was a loyal friend to me, and he spoke those words at my funeral. He was the one who turned the people against my assassins and secured my legacy. But here he is, on stage, speaking those same words once again. It's as if he's trying to bring me back to life, to undo what has been done. I wish I could hear his words one more time, to see if he still speaks of me with such passion and conviction.
I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him." - Brutus

Bury me? They may have buried my body, but they will never bury my spirit. I am Julius Caesar, the greatest general in Roman history. My name will be remembered long after these actors are forgotten. They can try to bury me, but they will never succeed. I am immortal.
Good friends, sweet friends, let me not stir you up to such a sudden flood of mutiny." - Mark Antony

Mark Antony is trying to calm the crowd, to prevent them from rioting. He knows how passionate the people are about me, and he doesn't want anyone to get hurt. He was always a wise man, and I'm glad he's here to keep the peace. If only he had been there on the Ides of March, to prevent my assassination. But what's done is done. I can only watch as my legacy is played out on stage, for all the world to see.
Let each man render me his bloody hand." - Mark Antony

Mark Antony is asking the people to show him their hands, to see if they have blood on them. He wants to know who was involved in my assassination, so that he can bring them to justice. It's a noble cause, but I doubt he will succeed. The conspirators were too careful, too cunning. They covered their tracks well. But I appreciate his efforts. It shows that he still cares about me, even in death.
This was the noblest Roman of them all." - Mark Antony

Those words. They bring tears to my eyes. Mark Antony is speaking of me, calling me the noblest Roman of them all. It's a great honor, and I am grateful for it. But it's also bittersweet. I wish I could hear those words spoken in real life, not just on a stage. I wish I could see the people's faces as they hear those words, to know that I made a difference in their lives. But I can't. All I can do is watch, and remember, and hope that my legacy will live on.

setting: The scene takes place inside the Senate House, where a senate session is ongoing. Julius Caesar passed two bills with little or no debate in the senate, one-third write-down of tax farmers' arrears for Crassus and ratification of Pompey's eastern settlements. Caesar then moved to lift the extend his agrarian bill to Campania some time in May; this may be when Bibulus withdrew to his house. Pompey, shortly thereafter, also wed Caesar's daughter Julia to seal their alliance. An ally of Caesar's, plebeian tribune Publius Vatinius, moved the lex Vatinia assigning the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years. Suetonius' claim that the senate had assigned to Caesar the silvae callesque (woods and tracks) is likely an exaggeration; fear of Gallic invasion had grown in 60 BC and it is more likely that the consuls had been assigned to Italy and that Caesarian partisans dismissed this defensive posture as "mere 'forest tracks'". The senate was also persuaded to assign to Caesar the Transalpine Gaul as well, subject to annual renewal, likely to control his ability to make war on the far side of the Alps.

dialogue.content: As I sit here in the Senate House, I can't help but feel a sense of satisfaction. It's clear that my political power is growing, and the other senators are starting to recognize it. Passing those two bills was effortless, and I'm certain that my agrarian bill will be just as easy. I need to keep pushing forward, no matter what obstacles come my way. The key to success is to remain focused and determined, and I won't let anyone stand in my way.
Julius, I must say, I'm impressed with your political maneuvering. You seem to have a way of getting what you want without any pushback from the other senators.

Thank you, Crassus. I've spent years building relationships with the other senators, and it's finally starting to pay off. But I can't take all the credit. I have some allies who are just as passionate about my vision for Rome as I am.
Speaking of allies, I have some news that may interest you, Julius. I've decided to wed your daughter, Julia. It's time that we solidify our alliance once and for all.
That's excellent news, Pompey. I've been looking for ways to strengthen our bond, and this is the perfect way to do it. I'm honored that you would choose my daughter as your wife.
I must object to this. Caesar, your grasp on power is growing too strong, and I fear that you will use your alliance with Pompey to further your own ambitions.
Bibulus, I understand your concerns, but I assure you that my intentions are pure. I only want what's best for Rome, and I believe that working with Pompey is the best way to achieve that.
I, too, have news that may interest you, Julius. I have moved the lex Vatinia, which assigns the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to you for five years.
That's excellent news, Vatinius. With these provinces under my control, I'll be able to make significant progress in expanding Rome's territory. I'm grateful for your support.

setting: Julius Caesar stood at the Forum Romanum, surrounded by a sea of people. He was giving a speech to the masses, urging them to support his vision for the future of Rome. It was a passionate plea, filled with emotion and conviction. The year had been a difficult one for Caesar, with political opposition from Bibulus and Cato causing serious difficulties for him and his allies. But he was determined to push forward and make the changes he believed were necessary for the benefit of the people.

dialogue.content: As I stand here before you today, I am filled with a deep sense of purpose and conviction. The road to this moment has been a difficult one, with many obstacles thrown in my path. But I have persevered, and now I stand before you as your leader, ready to guide Rome into a new era of prosperity and greatness. I know that there are those who oppose me, who seek to undermine my efforts and sow discord among the people. But I will not be deterred. I will continue to fight for what is right, for what is just, and for what is best for Rome.
But Caesar, what of the rumors we have heard about your intentions? We have heard that you wish to make yourself king, and that you seek to rule over us with an iron fist. Is this true?

I understand your concerns, my friend. But let me assure you, these rumors are nothing more than baseless lies spread by my enemies. I have no desire to be king. My only desire is to serve the people, and to make Rome the greatest city in the world. I do not seek power for its own sake, but rather, I seek to use my power to benefit all of you. Trust in me, my friends, and together, we will create a brighter future for Rome.
But Caesar, what of the opposition you have faced from Bibulus and Cato? How can we trust that you will be able to overcome them and achieve your goals?

I will not lie to you, my friend. The road ahead will be difficult. There are those who seek to undermine our efforts at every turn, who seek to sow discord and division among the people. But we must not let them win. We must stand together, united in our vision for the future of Rome. We must be strong in the face of adversity, and we must never lose sight of our goals. I believe in you, my friends. I believe that together, we can overcome any obstacle, and achieve greatness for ourselves and for our beloved Rome.

As I look out over the sea of faces before me, I am filled with a sense of hope and determination. I know that the road ahead will be difficult, but I also know that with the support of the people, we can achieve anything. I am grateful for the opportunity to serve as your leader, and I promise you that I will do everything in my power to make Rome the greatest city in the world.

setting: Julius Caesar, a prominent member of the aristocracy with great future prospects in his political career, returned to Rome in 71 BC and was elected as one of the military tribunes. Although the war on Spartacus was on-going during his term, there is no evidence that Caesar served in any war. Instead, he agitated for the removal of Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for those who supported Lepidus' revolt to be pardoned. These advocacies were common and uncontroversial. The next year, 70 BC, Pompey and Crassus were consuls and brought legislation restoring the plebeian tribunate's rights, one of the tribunes, with Caesar supporting, then brought legislation pardoning the Lepidan exiles.

dialogue.content: As I sit here in the Senate, I can't help but feel a sense of frustration. My colleagues seem content with the status quo, unwilling to take bold action to move our great Republic forward. It's clear that we need to make some changes, but the question is, how? I've been thinking a lot about the recent legislation restoring the plebeian tribunate's rights and the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles. These were important steps in the right direction, but they don't go far enough. We need to do more, to push harder, to make the changes that are necessary to ensure a brighter future for our Republic.
Julius, my friend, what's on your mind? You seem lost in thought.
Oh, nothing of consequence, Cicero," I reply, trying to hide my frustration. "Just thinking about the future of our Republic.
Well, I couldn't agree more. It's a difficult time for us all, and we must work together to find a way forward. Perhaps we could discuss some ideas over dinner tonight?
Thank you for the offer, Cicero, but I fear that I have other pressing matters to attend to tonight. Perhaps another time.
Julius, my boy, how are you? It's good to see you back in Rome.
Thank you, Crassus. It's good to be back.
I hear you've been causing quite a stir in the Senate. Some are saying that you're becoming quite the troublemaker.

I suppose that depends on one's point of view," I reply, trying to keep the frustration out of my voice. "I simply believe that we need to do more to move our Republic forward, to ensure that it remains strong and prosperous for generations to come.
Well, I couldn't agree more, my boy. But you must be careful not to alienate your colleagues. We need allies, not enemies, if we're going to make any progress.

As I walk away from Crassus, I can't help but feel a sense of disgust. He's a coward, a man who's more interested in his own self-preservation than in the good of the Republic. I need to find others who are willing to stand up to the powers that be, who are willing to fight for what's right no matter the cost. It won't be easy, but I'm determined to see it through.
Caesar, I hear you're proposing some rather radical changes to the way things are done around here.
I'm simply proposing what's necessary to ensure the future of our Republic, Metellus. If that's radical, then so be it.
Well, I think you're going about it all wrong. We need stability, not chaos. We need to maintain the status quo, not upset the applecart.

Maintain the status quo? Are you serious, Metellus? The status quo is what got us into this mess in the first place. We need to be bold, to take risks, to push the boundaries of what's possible. That's the only way we're going to make any real progress.
You're a fool, Caesar. A dangerous fool. I fear for the future of our Republic if people like you are allowed to run rampant.

As I watch Metellus storm out of the Senate, I can't help but feel a sense of satisfaction. He's a relic of the past, a man who's more interested in maintaining his own power than in doing what's right. I need to find others who share my vision, who are willing to stand up to the old guard and fight for what's right. It won't be easy, but I'm ready for the challenge.

setting: Caesar and his generals are gathered in his camp in Transalpine Gaul to discuss and plan their next campaign against the Gauls. They are seated around a large table, poring over maps and other military documents. The atmosphere is tense, as they know that this campaign will be crucial in securing their hold over the region.

dialogue.content: I must be careful in my approach to this next campaign. The Gauls are fierce warriors, and I cannot afford to underestimate them. But I also need to maintain my grip on the region and show the senate back in Rome that I am capable of bringing this land under Roman control. I will need to rely on my generals and their expertise to make this campaign a success.
Caesar, we have received reports that the Gauls have been gathering their forces in the north. They seem to be preparing for a large-scale attack on our positions.

Thank you, Decimus. I had suspected as much. We cannot let them catch us off guard. I want all of our troops to be on high alert, and I want our scouts to be monitoring their movements closely. We need to know when and where they plan to strike.
Caesar, may I suggest that we launch a preemptive strike? If we can catch them off guard, we can deal a significant blow to their forces and weaken their resolve.

Lucius makes a good point. A preemptive strike could give us the upper hand in this campaign. But it could also backfire if the Gauls are more prepared than we think. I need to weigh the risks carefully before making a decision.

Lucius, your suggestion has merit. But we need to be cautious. I want to gather more intelligence on their movements before we make any decisions. In the meantime, let us prepare our troops and make sure they are ready for battle.
Caesar, what about our supply lines? We will need to make sure that we have enough food and other provisions to sustain our troops during the campaign.

Excellent point, Titus. We cannot afford to let our supply lines falter. I want our logistics teams to start stockpiling food and other resources, and I want our engineers to fortify our supply routes. We cannot let the Gauls disrupt our supply lines.
Caesar, what about our allies? Do we have their support for this campaign?

Our allies have been loyal to us thus far, but we cannot take their support for granted. I want our diplomatic envoy to meet with them and ensure that they will stand with us in the coming battle. We need all the support we can get.

This campaign will be a challenge, but I am confident in our abilities. If we can strike hard and fast, we can crush the Gauls and cement our hold on Transalpine Gaul. But I must also be mindful of the political situation back in Rome. I cannot afford to let my enemies use this campaign against me.
Thank you, gentlemen, for your insights. Let us continue to prepare for the coming campaign. We have much work to do.

setting: The scene is set in the Roman Senate during the period of civil war from 52 to 49 BC. Caesar and the senators are discussing the economic and political ramifications of the war. There is a lack of trust between Caesar and Pompey, and the conservatives around Cato in the Senate seek to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honours or a second consulship. Cato, Bibulus, and their allies are successful in winning Pompey over to take a hard line against Caesar's continued command.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe that Pompey has turned against me. We were once friends and allies, but now he has joined forces with my enemies. They want to strip me of my power and my accomplishments, to take away everything I have worked so hard to achieve. But I will not back down. I will not let them defeat me. I will fight with everything I have to protect my legacy and my people. And if that means going to war, so be it. I will not let them win.
Caesar, you have overstepped your bounds. Your command in Gaul has gone on for too long, and it is time for you to return to Rome and face the consequences of your actions.

I have done nothing wrong. My conquests in Gaul have brought great wealth and prosperity to Rome. I have expanded our borders and secured our safety. Why should I be punished for doing what is best for our people?
You have become too powerful, Caesar. You have amassed too much wealth and influence, and we fear you will use it to seize control of Rome for yourself.

I have no desire to rule Rome. I am a loyal servant of the Republic, and I will do whatever is necessary to protect it. But I will not be bullied into submission by those who seek to undermine my authority. I have earned my position through hard work and dedication, and I will not let anyone take it away from me.

I agree with Cato and Bibulus. Caesar, you have become a threat to the stability of Rome. Your actions have caused division and unrest, and it is time for you to step down and let others take the reins of power.
I will not step down. I will not abandon my troops and my people. I will fight for what is right, and I will not let you take away everything I have worked so hard to achieve.
Then it seems we have no choice but to declare war on you, Caesar. We will not let you destroy the Republic with your ambition and greed.

So it has come to this. War. I had hoped to avoid it, but it seems my enemies have left me no choice. I must prepare my armies and my people for battle, to protect them from those who seek to harm them. I will not let Rome fall into chaos and despair. I will fight with all my strength and all my heart, for the Republic and for the people of Rome.

setting: It is a sunny day in the Roman marketplace. Julius Caesar has gathered a group of farmers and landowners to discuss agricultural policies and the distribution of land. The time is mid-morning, and the air is filled with the sounds of merchants haggling and the smell of fresh produce. Caesar is dressed in his finest toga, and his entourage of advisors and guards stand a few paces behind him. The farmers and landowners are a mix of young and old, some dressed in simple tunics, while others wear more ornate robes. They stand in a semi-circle around Caesar, waiting for him to address them.

dialogue.content: As I stand here, surrounded by the people I aim to serve, I feel a sense of pride and responsibility. These farmers and landowners are the backbone of Rome, and it is my duty to ensure their prosperity. I know that many of them are struggling, and it is up to me to find a solution. I cannot let them down.
Caesar, we are honored to be in your presence. We have heard of your plans to distribute land more fairly. Can you tell us more about it?

My fellow Romans, I understand the struggles that many of you are facing. The current distribution of land is unjust, and it is my goal to fix that. I plan to redistribute the land so that every citizen has an equal opportunity to prosper. This will not happen overnight, but I assure you that I am working tirelessly to make it a reality.
But Caesar, what about those of us who have worked hard to acquire our land? Will we be forced to give it up?

I understand your concerns, but I assure you that I am not here to take away what is rightfully yours. My plan is to take back land that has been unfairly acquired and redistribute it to those who need it. I believe that this is the only way to ensure a fair and just distribution of land.
But Caesar, what about those who do not have the skills or knowledge to farm the land? How will they benefit?

I am glad you asked that question, my friend. My plan includes providing education and training to those who need it. We will work together to ensure that every citizen has the skills and knowledge they need to succeed. We cannot leave anyone behind.
But Caesar, what about the cost? Who will pay for all of this?

I understand that this will not be an easy task, but it is one that we must undertake. We will work together to find a solution that benefits everyone. It is my hope that we can come to an agreement that is fair and just for all.

setting: It is the year 84 BC in Rome, during the dominance of Lucius Cornelius Cinna. Julius Caesar's father has just passed away suddenly, leaving Caesar to face a world of political uncertainty. Caesar has been named as Flamen Dialis, a high priest of Jupiter, which would have forced him to forego a political career. However, his marriage to Cinna's daughter, Cornelia, may have been used as a political tool to calm the tense political environment. After Sulla's victory in the civil war in 82 BC, Caesar's acta were annulled, and Sulla ordered Caesar to abdicate and divorce Cornelia. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment, and went into hiding before his relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins were able to intercede on his behalf. They then reached a compromise where Caesar would resign his priesthood but keep his wife and chattels.

dialogue.content: The audacity of Sulla to annul my acta and demand that I divorce Cornelia! Does he not understand that my marriage to her may be used as a political tool to bring stability to this city? I cannot simply comply with his demands and abandon my wife. But if I refuse, I risk being put on the proscription lists and losing everything. I must tread carefully and find a way to protect myself and my family.
Julius, what are we going to do? Sulla has ordered us to separate, and I fear for our safety.
Do not worry, my dear. I have a plan. We will go into hiding until I can figure out a way to protect us.
But how will we survive? We have no money or resources.
I have some friends and contacts who can help us. We will have to live modestly and keep a low profile until the situation improves.

I must find a way to protect my family and my reputation. Sulla may have won the civil war, but he does not have the support of the people. If I can rally enough support, I may be able to challenge his authority and reclaim my place in society. But I must be careful not to provoke him or his supporters.
Caesar, you have been ordered to abdicate your priesthood and divorce Cornelia. You have three days to comply, or you will be put on the proscription lists.
I refuse to comply with Sulla's demands. My marriage to Cornelia is legitimate, and I will not abandon her.
You leave us no choice. You are now on the proscription lists, and a bounty has been placed on your head. You and your family must leave Rome immediately.
This is worse than I feared. I must protect my family and find a way to fight back against Sulla's tyranny. I cannot let him get away with this.
Julius, what are we going to do now?
We must leave Rome and go into hiding. I have some friends who can help us. But we must be careful not to draw attention to ourselves.

I must find a way to rally support and challenge Sulla's authority. I cannot let him get away with this. But for now, I must focus on protecting my family and staying alive. The road ahead will be difficult, but I must remain strong and determined.

setting: It is the year 59 BC, and we are in Rome. The current setting is in the Senate, where Julius Caesar has successfully passed two bills - a one-third write-down of tax farmers' arrears for Crassus and ratification of Pompey's eastern settlements. Caesar then moves to extend his agrarian bill to Campania, and this may be when Bibulus withdrew to his house. Following this, Pompey wed Caesar's daughter Julia to seal their alliance. Plebeian tribune Publius Vatinius would move the lex Vatinia assigning the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years. The senate was also persuaded to assign to Caesar the Transalpine Gaul as well, subject to annual renewal, likely to control his ability to make war on the far side of the Alps.

dialogue.content: I have been able to pass two bills in the Senate with little to no debate.
