It's a good start, but I need to make sure that I have the support of the people and the army if I want to achieve my goals. My daughter's marriage to Pompey will further strengthen our alliance, and now with the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul under my control for five years, I will have the resources I need to carry out my plans. The Transalpine Gaul is a bonus, subject to annual renewal, but it's a step in the right direction. I must continue to work hard to gain more support and power.

Senators, I propose that we assign the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years. This will ensure that he has the resources he needs to carry out his duties as a governor and to protect Rome from any potential threats.
I fully support this proposal. Caesar has proven himself to be a capable leader and has the interests of Rome at heart. We should give him the resources he needs to continue his work.
I agree with Crassus. Caesar has shown himself to be a worthy ally, and we should support him in any way we can.

I strongly object to this proposal. Caesar has already been given too much power, and we should not give him any more. This is a dangerous path that we are going down, and we should be careful of the consequences.

I appreciate the support of Crassus and Pompey. As for Bibulus, I understand your concerns, but I assure you that I have the best interests of Rome at heart. With these resources, I can better protect Rome and ensure its prosperity. I humbly ask for your support in this matter.
The proposal has been passed with a majority vote.

setting: The scene takes place in Rome during the dominance of Lucius Cornelius Cinna. Julius Caesar's father chose retirement, and Caesar was named as flamen Dialis (a priest of Jupiter), which resulted in his marriage to Cinna's daughter, Cornelia. Caesar's appointment as flamen Dialis indicates that there were few expectations of a major career for him. However, in early 84 BC, Caesar's father died suddenly, and after Sulla's victory in the civil war (82 BC), Cinna's acta were annulled. Sulla then ordered Caesar to abdicate and divorce Cinna's daughter. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment.

dialogue.content: How dare Sulla order me to divorce Cornelia! I love her, and I won't let anyone take her away from me. But my priesthood obligations prevent me from pursuing a political career. I must find a way to balance my desire for power with my religious duties. Perhaps I can compromise with Sulla and keep my wife and chattels while resigning from my priesthood. I must be careful, though, as Sulla may see me as a threat and put me on the proscription lists.
Julius, what are we going to do? Sulla wants you to divorce me, but I can't bear the thought of being separated from you.
Don't worry, my love. I won't let anyone come between us. I'll find a way to resolve this situation.
Julius, we've heard about Sulla's orders. We're here to help you in any way we can.
Thank you for your concern. I need your help to negotiate with Sulla. I'm willing to resign my priesthood, but I won't give up my wife and property.
We understand your position, Julius. We'll do our best to persuade Sulla to accept your compromise.
Julius Caesar, I've heard that you've refused to obey my orders. Do you realize the consequences of your actions?
I do, Sulla, but I cannot divorce my wife. She means everything to me.
You are a priest of Jupiter, Caesar. You have obligations to the gods and to Rome. You cannot let your personal desires cloud your judgment.
I understand, Sulla, but I also have ambitions for the future. I'm willing to resign my priesthood, but I won't let go of my wife and property.
I see. Very well, Caesar, I'll accept your compromise. But be warned, I'll be watching you closely. If you step out of line, I won't hesitate to take action against you.

I've managed to resolve the situation without losing Cornelia. But I must be careful from now on. Sulla may see me as a threat, and I need to consolidate my power base if I'm to achieve my ambitions. I'll need to build alliances and make strategic moves to outmaneuver my rivals. The game of politics is a dangerous one, but I'm ready to play it to win.

setting: Julius Caesar and his allies are holding talks with foreign dignitaries at the Roman Baths, negotiating alliances and trade agreements. The time is mid-March, shortly after Caesar's consulship ended and his legislation was challenged by two new praetors in the Senate. Despite this opposition, Caesar remains a powerful figure in Roman politics and is eager to solidify his position through these negotiations.

dialogue.content: As I listen to these foreign dignitaries speak, I cannot help but feel a sense of pride and accomplishment. Despite the challenges I faced during my consulship, I have emerged as a strong leader, respected both at home and abroad. These negotiations are a critical step in securing my position and expanding Rome's influence.
We are honored to be here today, Caesar. Our nation has long admired Rome's strength and leadership, and we are eager to establish a formal alliance between our peoples.

I am pleased to hear that, my friend. As you know, Rome values strong allies, and I believe that our two nations can benefit greatly from this partnership. Let us discuss the details of this alliance and how we can work together for mutual prosperity.

Caesar, I must say that I have concerns about some of the recent political developments in Rome. It seems that your opponents have gained significant ground in the Senate, and there is growing unrest among the people.

I am aware of these challenges, my friend. But rest assured, I will not be deterred by the petty squabbles of my opponents. Rome needs strong leadership now more than ever, and I am committed to providing that leadership. As for the people, I understand their concerns, but I believe that they will come to see the wisdom of my policies in time.
Caesar, I must say that I am impressed by your vision for Rome. Your bold leadership is exactly what our nation needs in these troubled times.

As I listen to these foreign dignitaries praise me, I cannot help but feel a sense of satisfaction. Despite the challenges I faced during my consulship, I have emerged as a powerful and respected leader. With the support of these allies, I will continue to shape Rome's future and lead our nation to greatness.

setting: Julius Caesar has successfully passed a one-third write-down of tax farmers' arrears for Crassus and ratified Pompey's eastern settlements in the Senate with little or no debate. He then moved to lift the extend his agrarian bill to Campania. Meanwhile, an ally of Caesar's, plebeian tribune Publius Vatinius, moved the lex Vatinia assigning the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years. The senate was also persuaded to assign to Caesar the Transalpine Gaul as well, subject to annual renewal, likely to control his ability to make war on the far side of the Alps.

dialogue.content: I have successfully passed the ratification of Pompey's eastern settlements in the Senate. It was a smooth process, and with the help of my allies, I also managed to secure the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul for five years. The Transalpine Gaul was also assigned to me, subject to annual renewal. This is a significant victory for me and my political power. Pompey's alliance with me is now sealed after he wed my daughter Julia. It is time to consolidate my power and make further progress in my political career.
Congratulations, Caesar. The passing of the tax write-down and ratification of Pompey's eastern settlements is a remarkable achievement. You have secured a strong position in the Senate.

I agree with Crassus, Caesar. Your political maneuvers are impressive. The assignment of the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to you is a wise decision, and I am glad that we are now allies. Your daughter Julia is a delightful woman, and I am honored to be her husband.
I cannot believe this is happening. Caesar's power is growing, and the Senate is becoming more and more subservient to him. We need to stop him before it's too late.
Bibulus is becoming a problem. He is against me at every turn, and his opposition is hindering my progress. I need to find a way to neutralize him before he becomes a real threat.
The provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul are now under Caesar's control. He will use them wisely and bring glory to Rome.
All in favor of the assignment of the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar, say 'Aye.'
The motion is passed.
I am grateful for your trust, Senators. I will use these provinces to strengthen our great Republic and bring peace to our people.
You may have won this time, Caesar, but I will not rest until I have put an end to your tyranny.

Bibulus is becoming more vocal in his opposition to me. I need to find a way to silence him permanently. Perhaps I can bribe him or threaten him. Either way, I cannot let him continue to challenge my authority.

Caesar, I have an idea. We can use the tax write-down as a way to gain even more support from the people. If we can show them that we are on their side, we will have an even stronger position in the Senate.
Excellent idea, Crassus. Let's move forward with that plan. We need to stay ahead of our opponents and keep consolidating our power.
I agree. We must be vigilant and prepared for any challenge to our authority. Together, we will lead Rome to greatness.
With Crassus and Pompey by my side, I am unstoppable. We will continue to gain power and influence, and Rome will be stronger for it. No one can stand in our way.

setting: In 73 BC, Julius Caesar was absent from Rome when he was co-opted into the pontifices to replace his deceased relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta. This promotion marked him as a well-accepted member of the aristocracy with great future prospects in his political career. Caesar returned to Rome shortly after and was elected as one of the military tribunes for 71 BC. Even though the war on Spartacus was ongoing, there is no evidence that Caesar served in war during his term. However, he did agitate for the removal of Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for those who supported Lepidus' revolt to be pardoned, which were common and uncontroversial advocacies. The next year, Pompey and Crassus were consuls and brought legislation restoring the plebeian tribunate's rights; one of the tribunes, with Caesar's support, then brought legislation pardoning the Lepidan exiles.

dialogue.content: As I stand here, co-opted into the pontifices in place of my deceased relative, I can feel the weight of responsibility on my shoulders. It is an honor to be accepted by the aristocracy, and I must use this opportunity to further my political career. My advocacies for the removal of Sulla's disabilities and the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles were common and uncontroversial, but they were the first steps I took towards establishing myself as a leader. I must continue to work towards gaining the trust of the people and gaining more power within the political sphere.

Caesar, it is good to see you. I hear you have been advocating for the removal of Sulla's disabilities and the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles. These are noble causes, and I support them. But you must be careful not to step on the wrong toes. There are those who would oppose you and your ambitions.

Thank you for your support, Pompey. I understand the risks of going against certain factions, but I believe that these advocacies are necessary for the betterment of Rome. I will not waver in my beliefs.
I agree with Pompey. While your advocacies are commendable, you must be mindful of your actions. The political sphere can be a dangerous place, and any misstep can cost you dearly.

I can sense the underlying tension between Pompey, Crassus, and myself. They are both powerful men, but I will not let their warnings deter me. I must continue to push for change and gain more influence within the political sphere.
Caesar, I have brought legislation to restore the plebeian tribunate's rights. Will you lend your support?
I will support your legislation. The plebeian tribunate's rights must be restored for the betterment of Rome.
Thank you for your support, Caesar. With your backing, this legislation is sure to pass.

By supporting the tribune's legislation, I have gained favor with the plebeians. This will help me gain more support and influence within the political sphere. I must continue to use my position to bring about change and improve the lives of the people.
Caesar, I cannot thank you enough for your advocacy for the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles. Your support has given us hope for a better future.
It was my pleasure to support your cause. Rome must be a place of forgiveness and second chances. I will continue to fight for the rights of all citizens.

By advocating for the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles, I have gained support from a marginalized group. This will help me gain more influence and power within the political sphere. I must continue to find ways to gain support from all sectors of society and solidify my position as a leader.

setting: Caesar has crossed the Rubicon and ignited civil war against the Roman Senate. He sends envoys to negotiate with Pompey, who has fled south with many senators, believing that Caesar is marching quickly for Rome. The negotiation takes place in Pompey's camp but falls apart due to mutual distrust.

dialogue.content: I can't believe this negotiation has failed. I never wanted it to come to this, but Pompey has left me no choice. I must capture him and force a conference. It's the only way to end this civil war and restore Rome to its former glory. I hope my soldiers are ready for what's to come.
Pompey, we have come to negotiate a peaceful settlement to this conflict. Caesar does not want to spill any more Roman blood. Will you come to the table and discuss terms?

I do not trust Caesar or his envoys. He broke the law by crossing the Rubicon with his army, and now he wants to negotiate with me? No, I will not negotiate with a traitor and a usurper. Tell Caesar that I will only speak to him on the battlefield.
I knew this would be difficult, but I didn't expect Pompey to be so stubborn. He's putting his own ego above the good of Rome. I must find a way to outmaneuver him and his army.
But Pompey, think of the lives that will be lost if this conflict continues. We can end this peacefully if we just talk it out.

I will not negotiate with Caesar or his lackeys. The Senate has declared him an enemy of the state, and I will not be a party to any agreement that legitimizes his treasonous actions. You may leave now.
This is not going well. I had hoped to avoid bloodshed, but it seems that Pompey is too blinded by his own pride to see reason. I must prepare for battle and hope that the gods are on my side.
Pompey, please reconsider. We can find a way to end this conflict without violence. Think of the people of Rome and the damage that will be done to our great city.
I have made my decision. Now leave me be.

I have no choice but to capture Pompey and force him to the negotiating table. It will be a risky move, but it's the only way to end this war quickly and decisively. I must rally my troops and prepare for battle.
Very well, Pompey. We will relay your message to Caesar. But know that this war has already caused too much suffering and bloodshed. We implore you to reconsider your position.
I will not be moved by empty words. Now leave me.

I have to act fast. Time is running out, and I need to capture Pompey before he can gather more troops and fortify his position. It's a risky move, but it's one I must take if I want to end this conflict and restore Rome to its former glory.

setting: The setting is Rome during Julius Caesar's reign in 45 BC, after he had won the civil war and solidified his power. Caesar meets with his advisors to strategize a plan to maintain his position of near-unchallenged power and influence in Rome.

dialogue.content: As I sit here, surrounded by my most trusted advisors, I can't help but feel a sense of satisfaction. I have achieved what few men in history have accomplished: I have conquered Rome. The Senate is under my control, and the people of this great city look to me as their leader. But I must not rest on my laurels. I know that there are those who still oppose me, who plot against me in secret. I must stay vigilant, and I must continue to assert my dominance over this city.
My lord, we have received word that there are still some in the Senate who are unhappy with your rule. They have been meeting in secret, discussing ways to overthrow you.

I am aware of their treachery. But they are powerless against me. They know that I have the support of the people, and without that, they cannot hope to challenge me. But we must be prepared for any eventuality. What have you learned about their plans?
They have been reaching out to some of the provincial governors, trying to rally support for their cause. They are also attempting to make contact with some of the military commanders.

So they are trying to build a coalition against me. Clever, but ultimately futile. I have the loyalty of the legions, and without them, any attempt to overthrow me will fail. But I must be cautious. I cannot let my guard down.
My lord, we have been discussing possible ways to neutralize the threat posed by the conspirators. One idea we have come up with is to have them arrested and tried for treason.

That is an option, but it could be risky. If we move too soon, we risk making martyrs out of them. And if we move too late, they may have already gained too much support. No, we must be more subtle. We must find a way to turn their own allies against them. Cassius, can you find out who their key supporters are?
Yes, my lord. I believe I already have a list of names. If we can find a way to turn them against the conspirators, we may be able to weaken their position considerably.

Yes, that could work. Divide and conquer. If we can sow discord among the ranks of the conspirators, they will be powerless to stop me. But I must be careful. I cannot let them know that I am aware of their plans. I must keep up appearances, act as if I am unaware of their treachery.
My lord, there is one other matter we must address. The people are beginning to grumble about your increasing power. They fear that you will become another king, like Tarquin before you.

I am aware of their concerns. But they must understand that my power is necessary for the good of Rome. I have brought peace and prosperity to this city, and I will continue to do so as long as I am able. But I must also be careful not to overstep my bounds. I will not become a tyrant, like so many before me.

The people are fickle. They love me now, but if I push them too far, they could turn against me. I must find a way to assuage their fears, to make them see that I am not a threat to their liberty. Perhaps I could hold a public forum, let them ask me questions, voice their concerns. Yes, that could work. I will show them that I am a man of the people, that I am not their enemy.
Thank you, my friends, for your counsel. We will continue to monitor the situation closely. But for now, I believe we have done all we can. I will retire to my chambers to consider our next moves.

As I leave the room, I can't help but feel a sense of unease. I know that there are those who wish to see me dead, who will stop at nothing to bring about my downfall. But I am Caesar. I am the master of Rome. And no one will ever be able to take that away from me.

setting: The setting is the Roman Senate, where Caesar and the senators are discussing the possibility of a civil war. The time is around 52 to 49 BC, during which the trust between Caesar and Pompey disintegrated. In 51 BC, the consul Marcellus proposed recalling Caesar, arguing that his task in Gaul was complete, but the proposal was vetoed. The conservatives around Cato in the Senate were seeking to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honours or a second consulship. Cato, Bibulus, and their allies were successful in winning Pompey over to take a hard line against Caesar's continued command.

dialogue.content: What a mess. The Senate is divided, and my relationship with Pompey has never been worse. I cannot allow the Senate to strip me of my command, or all of my hard work in Gaul will go to waste. I must find a way to resolve this issue without resorting to violence. But if push comes to shove, I will not hesitate to defend myself and my position.
Caesar, your command in Gaul has gone on for too long. It is time for you to return to Rome and lay down your arms. The Republic cannot allow any one man to hold such power for so long.

Cato, you know as well as I do that there are still threats to the security of Gaul. I cannot abandon my post until I am certain that the region is safe. Besides, the Senate has granted me the command, and I will not relinquish it without just cause.
Caesar, I understand your concerns, but the Senate is growing increasingly uneasy with your continued command in Gaul. Perhaps it is time for you to return to Rome and seek another consulship.
Pompey is not to be trusted. He has always been jealous of my power and popularity. I must find a way to convince him to support me or at least remain neutral in the conflict. But how?
Caesar, you are a threat to the stability of the Republic. Your continued command in Gaul is a violation of the law and the traditions of our great nation.

Bibulus, I have done nothing that is not within my rights as granted by the Senate. You may not like it, but I have not broken any laws. If you have evidence to the contrary, then present it. Otherwise, I suggest you hold your tongue.
Caesar, we do not need evidence to know that you are a danger to the Republic. Your ambition knows no bounds, and you will stop at nothing to achieve your goals.

Cato, you are mistaken if you think that I seek power for its own sake. I have always worked for the betterment of Rome and its people. I will not stand idly by while you and your cronies try to tear down all that I have built.

Gentlemen, let us not resort to name-calling and insults. We are all Romans here, and we should be working together for the good of the Republic. Caesar, I understand your concerns, but the Senate has the final say in these matters. Perhaps if you were to return to Rome and make your case before them, they would see things differently.
Pompey is trying to play both sides. He wants to appear neutral, but he is really just trying to gain more power for himself. I must find a way to outmaneuver him.
Pompey, you are right. The Senate has the final say, and I will abide by their decision. But I ask that you remain neutral in this matter. I would hate to think that you were taking sides against me.
Caesar, I am not taking sides. I am merely trying to find a peaceful resolution to this conflict. If you are unwilling to see reason, then perhaps we will have to resort to force.
I knew it. Pompey is not to be trusted. He is already planning for war. I must prepare myself and my army for any eventualities.
Pompey, I hope it does not come to that. But if it does, I will not hesitate to defend myself and my men. I have worked too hard to let you and your cronies take it all away.
Caesar, the Senate will not stand idly by and let you defy their authority. If you do not return to Rome immediately, they will be forced to take action against you.

Cato, I have no intention of defying the Senate's authority. I will return to Rome when I am certain that Gaul is secure. Until then, I will continue to do my duty as granted by the Senate. You and your allies may not like it, but that is your problem, not mine.
Caesar, you are a fool if you think you can continue to defy the will of the Senate. They will crush you like a bug if you do not comply with their demands.

Bibulus, I am not defying the will of the Senate. I am merely doing my duty as granted by them. If you have evidence to the contrary, then present it. Otherwise, I suggest you leave me and my men in peace.

Gentlemen, let us end this discussion for now. We have all stated our positions, and it is clear that we will not come to a resolution today. Caesar, I hope you will consider my proposal and return to Rome soon. Until then, I wish you and your men good health and good fortune.
I cannot rely on Pompey to remain neutral. I must find a way to win him over or at least keep him out of the conflict. This will not be easy, but I am confident that I can find a way to succeed.

setting: The scene takes place in a Roman temple, where Caesar and his allies have gathered to meet with religious leaders. The topic of discussion is the cancellation of voting days for religious reasons. This meeting is taking place sometime after the passage of a bill distributing Campanian land and after Bibulus withdrew to his house to issue edicts in absentia canceling all days on which Caesar or his allies could hold votes for religious reasons. Cato attempted symbolic gestures against this move, which were successful in building revulsion to Caesar and his allies through the year. The opposition caused serious political difficulties to Caesar and his allies, belying the common depiction of triumviral political supremacy. When his consulship ended, Caesar's legislation was challenged by two of the new praetors, but the discussion in the senate stalled and was eventually dropped. Caesar stayed near the city until around mid-March.

dialogue.content: As I enter the temple, I can't help but feel a sense of unease. The opposition against me and my allies has been growing, and I fear that this meeting will not be in our favor. But I must remain strong and firm in my beliefs, for the good of Rome. The cancellation of voting days for religious reasons is necessary for the progress of our nation, and I must convince these religious leaders of that.

Greetings, Caesar. We are pleased to see you and your allies here today. We understand that you wish to discuss the cancellation of voting days for religious reasons. Please explain your reasoning behind this move.

Thank you for having us, priest. As you know, Rome is facing many challenges, and we must move forward with necessary reforms to ensure the prosperity of our nation. The cancellation of voting days for religious reasons is one such reform. It will allow us to make important decisions without any unnecessary delays or disruptions. I understand that this move may seem controversial, but I assure you that it is for the greater good.

We understand your concerns, Caesar, but we must also consider the religious implications of this move. Voting on religious days is a sacred tradition, and we cannot simply disregard it. We must find a way to balance your concerns with the needs of our religion.

I knew this would not be an easy conversation. The religious leaders are understandably protective of their traditions, but I cannot let their sentiments hold back the progress of our nation. I must find a way to convince them of the importance of this reform.

I understand your concerns, High Priest, but we must also consider the needs of our nation. Rome is facing many challenges, and we need to make important decisions quickly and efficiently. The cancellation of voting days for religious reasons will help us do just that. We are not asking you to disregard your traditions, but rather to find a way to balance them with the needs of our nation.
But what about the people? How will they feel about this move?
I understand that change can be difficult, but we must also consider the greater good. This move is necessary for the progress of our nation, and I am confident that the people will understand that.
We will take your concerns into consideration, Caesar. We will discuss this matter and come to a decision that is in the best interest of both our religion and our nation.

I am pleased with how this conversation has gone. Although the religious leaders are hesitant, I have planted the seed of change in their minds. With time, I believe that they will come to see the importance of this reform. Rome must move forward, and I will do everything in my power to ensure that it does.

setting: Caesar has successfully passed bills in the senate, including a write-down of tax farmers' arrears for Crassus and ratification of Pompey's eastern settlements. He plans to extend his agrarian bill to Campania in May and has gained the support of his ally, plebeian tribune Publius Vatinius, who moved the lex Vatinia assigning the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years. The fear of Gallic invasion has grown, and Caesarian partisans have dismissed the defensive posture assigned to the consuls as "mere forest tracks." The senate has also assigned Transalpine Gaul to Caesar subject to annual renewal, likely to control his ability to make war on the far side of the Alps.

dialogue.content: The senate has granted me more power than I ever thought possible. With Illyricum, Cisalpine Gaul, and Transalpine Gaul under my control, I have the resources I need to expand my empire. The fear of Gallic invasion has worked in my favor, and I have been able to convince the senate to assign me the lands I need to protect Rome. But protection is not enough. I must have more. I must have all of Gaul. And with the support of Pompey and Crassus, I know I can achieve it. I must continue to play my cards carefully, but I am confident in my abilities to lead Rome to greatness.

My fellow senators, the lex Vatinia is necessary for the protection of our empire. Caesar has proven himself a capable leader time and time again, and we must trust him with these lands. The threat of invasion from the Gauls is real, and we must act swiftly to ensure the safety of our people. I urge you to support this bill and give Caesar the power he needs to protect our great city.

I cannot support this bill. Caesar has already gained too much power in the senate, and we must not give him any more. He is a dangerous man who seeks only to expand his own empire, and we must not let him do so at the expense of our own safety. I implore you, my fellow senators, to think carefully before you make this decision.

I am pleased to announce that my daughter Julia is to be wed to Caesar. This alliance will bring our families and our forces closer together, and I am confident that we will be able to achieve great things under Caesar's leadership. I urge you all to support him and his endeavors, for the good of Rome.

I agree with Pompey. Caesar has proven himself a capable leader, and we must trust him to make the decisions necessary to protect our empire. The threat of invasion from the Gauls is real, and we cannot afford to be complacent. We must act now, before it is too late.

My fellow senators, I thank you for your support. With your help, I have been able to secure the lands necessary to protect Rome from the threat of invasion. But we cannot stop there. We must continue to expand our empire, to bring peace and stability to all of Gaul. With the support of Pompey, Crassus, and the people of Rome, I am confident that we can achieve this goal. Thank you.

setting: Around 10 or 11 January 49 BC, Caesar had crossed the Rubicon and ignited a civil war in response to the Senate's "final decree". After capturing communication routes to Rome, Caesar, seeking to capture Pompey, advanced south to force a conference. Currently, Caesar is in Greece and has sent another envoy to persuade Pompey to reconcile and avoid further bloodshed.

dialogue.content: As I wait for Pompey's response, my mind wanders back to the days when we were allies, fighting together for the glory of Rome. How did it come to this? The Senate's fear and jealousy of my power have driven them to push me to this civil war. And now, they have convinced Pompey to stand against me. But I am not without allies. The Legio XIII Gemina is loyal to me, and I have the support of many in Rome who are tired of the Senate's corruption. If only Pompey could see reason and join me in this fight, we could put an end to this war and restore peace to Rome.
My lord Caesar, I have returned from Pompey's camp, but I bear bad news. Pompey refuses to reconcile and insists on continuing the war.
I see. And what reason did he give for this decision?
He believes that the Senate's decree was justified and that you have overstepped your bounds as a consul. He also fears for his own safety if he were to join you now.

I had hoped that Pompey would see the sense in joining me. But I cannot say I am surprised by his response. He has always been a cautious man, and his loyalty to the Senate runs deep. But if he will not join me, then I must defeat him on the battlefield. It is a risk, but I have no other choice if I am to secure Rome's future.
Thank you for bringing me this news. Return to Pompey and tell him that I will not back down. I will meet him on the field of battle, and we will settle this once and for all.
As you command, my lord.

The die is cast. I have crossed the Rubicon, and there is no going back. The Senate and Pompey have left me with no other choice. I must fight for Rome's future, even if it means shedding the blood of my fellow Romans. It is a heavy burden to bear, but I will do what must be done.

setting: Caesar, newly elected as consul, is proposing a bill to purchase property from willing sellers to distribute to Pompey's veterans and the urban poor. The bill is designed to avoid objections to previous land reform proposals and any indications of radicalism. It would be administered by a board of twenty, Caesar would be excluded, and financed by Pompey's plunder and territorial gains. Caesar hopes that the senate will take up the matter to show its beneficence for the people. However, there is little opposition from the senate and the obstructionism that occurs is largely unprincipled, firmly opposing it not on grounds of public interest but rather opposition to Caesar's political advancement.

dialogue.content: I am pleased with the progress of my first act as consul. Publishing the minutes of the senate and assemblies has shown the public that the senate is accountable to them. Now, with this bill, I can further show the people that I am working for their benefit. The board of twenty will ensure that the distribution is fair and impartial, and the financing from Pompey's plunder will appease him and his veterans. The senate's lack of opposition shows that they know it is in the public's interest, but I must be cautious of those who oppose it solely for their own political gain. I must find a way to overcome Cato's filibustering and Bibulus' veto threat. The people's support will be crucial in this matter.
This bill is nothing but an attempt by Caesar to advance his own political agenda! We cannot allow such radicalism to take hold in our republic. This bill must be stopped!
I will not stand by and allow this bill to pass! It is unconstitutional and goes against the auspices. I will veto it for the entire year if necessary!

Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but this bill is not about my political agenda. It is about providing for our veterans and the urban poor. I assure you that the board of twenty will ensure that the distribution is fair and impartial. As for Bibulus' threat of veto, it is a violation of the people's legislative sovereignty. I will not let it stand. I will take this bill before the people, and they will decide its fate.
Caesar! Caesar! We support your bill! Down with Bibulus!

The people's support is overwhelming, but I must be careful not to provoke violence. Bibulus' threat of veto is a clear violation of the people's sovereignty, but I cannot simply ignore the auspices. I must find a way to pass this bill without causing further division in the republic. I will need to tread carefully and consider all possible outcomes.

setting: The scene is set in the Rome Senate, where the senators are discussing the public's approval of Julius Caesar's monument restoration and trophy recovery. It is a significant moment for Caesar, who has gained popularity and attention through his actions. The senators present are discussing the implications of Caesar's actions and whether they should support him or not. The time is 65 BC, four years after the funeral of Caesar's aunt Julia.

dialogue.content: As I sit here amongst the senators, I cannot help but feel proud of my actions. The restoration of my family's public monuments and the recovery of the trophies won by Marius have gained me popularity and support among the people. I know that some of the senators do not approve of my actions, but I am confident that I can sway them to my side. After all, what harm is there in restoring our family's legacy?
I must object to Caesar's actions. These trophies were taken down by Sulla, and it is not our place to restore them. We must respect the decisions of our predecessors and not meddle in their affairs.

I understand your concerns, Catulus. But I believe that it is our duty to preserve our history and honor our ancestors. These trophies represent the victories of our forefathers, and it is our responsibility to ensure that they are remembered. The people have shown their appreciation for my actions, and I believe that the senate should support me in this matter.

I agree with Catulus. We should not be so quick to approve of Caesar's actions. It sets a dangerous precedent for future generations to meddle in the affairs of their predecessors. We must respect the decisions of those who came before us.

But what harm is there in restoring our family's legacy? These monuments and trophies are not just symbols of our victories but also a testament to the virtue of pietas. It is our duty to preserve them for future generations.

I must say that I am impressed by Caesar's actions. The restoration of these monuments and trophies has gained him popularity and support among the people. Perhaps we should consider supporting him in this matter.

I can sense that the tide is turning in my favor. The support of Metellus is crucial in gaining the support of the other senators. I must continue to persuade them of the importance of preserving our history and honoring our ancestors.
I still have my reservations, but I am willing to consider supporting Caesar's actions. It is clear that the people appreciate his efforts, and we must consider their wishes.
I am still hesitant, but I am willing to listen to the arguments of my fellow senators. Perhaps there is merit in restoring our family's legacy.
I am grateful for your consideration, my fellow senators. I believe that together, we can preserve our history and ensure that our ancestors are remembered for their valor and virtue.

setting: It is the year 58 BC, and Julius Caesar is facing a rebellion in Gaul. As a skilled military commander, Caesar is determined to put down this rebellion and secure the territory. However, he understands that he needs more power and resources to achieve his goal. Caesar has already managed to pass bills in the senate that benefit his allies, such as Crassus and Pompey. Now, he is seeking to extend his agrarian bill to Campania and gain control over more provinces, such as Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul. Caesar's actions have caused concern among some senators, such as Bibulus, who has withdrawn to his house in protest. Nonetheless, Caesar is resolute in his ambition to gain more power and crush the rebellion in Gaul.

dialogue.content: I must secure my position and gain more power if I am to succeed in Gaul. The bills I passed for Crassus and Pompey were just the beginning. I need to extend my agrarian bill to Campania and gain control over more provinces. The senate may resist, but I will use all my skills of persuasion to convince them. The rebellion in Gaul is a threat to Rome's security, and I am the only one who can put it down. But I need more troops, more resources, and more authority. I cannot afford to fail. I will do whatever it takes to achieve my goals.

Caesar's actions are a threat to the republic! He seeks to gain more power and control over the provinces. We cannot allow this to happen. I urge my fellow senators to oppose his agrarian bill and his request for more provinces. We must protect the interests of Rome and uphold our constitution.

I understand Bibulus's concerns, but we must be pragmatic. Caesar has proven himself to be a capable commander, and we need him to put down the rebellion in Gaul. As for his request for more provinces, we can always revoke it later if he abuses his power. For now, we need to support him and ensure that he has the resources he needs to succeed.

I propose the lex Vatinia, which assigns the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years. This will give him the authority and resources he needs to crush the rebellion in Gaul and secure the territory. We cannot afford to let Gaul fall into the hands of our enemies. We must act decisively and give Caesar the power he needs to succeed.

I thank you, Vatinius, for your support. This is a crucial time for Rome, and we must act swiftly and decisively. I assure you that I will use this authority responsibly and with the utmost care for the interests of Rome. As for my agrarian bill, I believe it is necessary to extend it to Campania to ensure that our citizens have access to land and resources. I understand that some may oppose it, but I urge you to consider the long-term benefits for Rome.

I am proud to be the daughter of such a great man as Caesar. I know that he will do whatever it takes to secure the interests of Rome and protect our people. As for my marriage to Pompey, I believe it is a wise move to strengthen our alliance and ensure that we can work together to face any threat to Rome.

I fully support Caesar's actions to gain more power and control over the provinces. We must do whatever it takes to crush the rebellion in Gaul and secure the territory. As for my arrears, I thank Caesar for his support and understanding. He is a true friend and ally to me.

setting: It is January 49 BC and Julius Caesar, the famous Roman general and statesman, has just crossed the Rubicon, a river that marks the northern boundary of Italy, with his army. Caesar's move was in response to the Senate's "final decree" demanding that he disband his army and return to Rome. This action has ignited a civil war between Caesar's supporters and the senators who oppose him, led by Pompey. As Caesar advances south, seeking to capture Pompey, one of his closest allies, Marcus Brutus, plots against him and joins the conspiracy to assassinate him.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe that Brutus would betray me. I trusted him and treated him like a son. I gave him everything he has today, and now he turns against me. What could have driven him to this? Was it ambition? Did he want to be in power, to rule Rome himself? Or was it personal? Did he hold a grudge against me, for some real or imagined slight? Whatever the reason, I must be careful. Brutus is intelligent and well-respected in Rome. If he joins the conspiracy, others may follow. I must find a way to turn him back to my side, or neutralize him before he does any real damage.

I'm sorry, Caesar. I cannot support you anymore. Your actions have gone too far. You have violated the law and the traditions of Rome. You have become a tyrant, and I cannot be a party to it. I love Rome more than I love you, and I cannot let you destroy it.

Brutus is right, Caesar. You have become too powerful, too arrogant. You no longer listen to the Senate or the people. You think that you are above the law, but you are not. We must restore the Republic, and that means getting rid of you.

You are mistaken, Cassius. I have not become a tyrant. I have only done what is necessary to protect Rome and its people. The Senate was corrupt and weak, unable to deal with the problems of the day. I had no choice but to take matters into my own hands. And now, with my reforms, Rome is stronger than ever. You should be thanking me, not plotting against me.

I cannot thank you, Caesar, for violating the very principles that make Rome great. The Republic was founded on the idea of equal rights and rule of law. You have trampled on both. I cannot stand by and watch while you destroy everything that Rome stands for.

I understand your concerns, Brutus. But you are mistaken. I have not violated the law or the traditions of Rome. I have only done what was necessary to protect the Republic. And I have not become a tyrant. I have only taken the power that was given to me by the people. They wanted me to lead them, to protect them, to make Rome great again. And I have done that. You should be proud of me, not betraying me.
But what about the Senate, Caesar? You have ignored their advice and their laws. You have made yourself the dictator of Rome. How can that be justified?

The Senate was weak and corrupt, Cassius. They were more interested in their own power and wealth than in the good of Rome. They could not deal with the problems of the day. I had no choice but to take matters into my own hands. And as for being a dictator, that is not true. I have only taken the power that was given to me by the people, to protect them and make Rome great again. I have not abused that power, or used it for personal gain. You should know that, Cassius. You have been with me from the beginning.

I was with you, Caesar, because I believed in you. I believed that you would restore the Republic, and make Rome great again. But now, I see that I was wrong. You have become a tyrant, and I cannot support you anymore. I must do what is right for Rome, and that means stopping you.

I cannot let this go on. If Brutus joins the conspiracy, others may follow. I must find a way to stop him, to turn him back to my side. But how? He is a man of principle and honor, not easily swayed by bribes or threats. I must appeal to his sense of duty, his love for Rome. I must show him that I am not a tyrant, but a leader who cares for his people. I must make him see that we are on the same side, that we both want what is best for Rome. But how? How can I do that?

setting: During the dominance of Lucius Cornelius Cinna in Rome, Julius Caesar's father opted for retirement instead of seeking a consulship. Caesar was appointed as flamen Dialis, a priest of Jupiter, which led to his marriage to Cinna's daughter, Cornelia. The appointment to the priesthood, which would have forced Caesar to forego a political career, indicates that there were few expectations of a major career for him. However, after Caesar's father died suddenly in 84 BC, and after Sulla's victory in the civil war in 82 BC, Caesar was ordered to abdicate and divorce Cornelia. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment, and went into hiding before his relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins were able to intercede on his behalf. A compromise was reached where Caesar would resign his priesthood but keep his wife and chattels.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe Sulla ordered me to divorce Cornelia. It is as if he has no sense of decency or respect for our family. How dare he try to take away my wife and my honor? I will not stand for it. I must find a way to fight back against this injustice. But how? Sulla is a powerful man, and I am just a priest. I must be careful not to make any rash decisions that could put myself or my family in danger.

My dear Julius, I cannot believe what Sulla has done to us. How can he take away our happiness like this? I will not allow him to come between us. We must find a way to fight back and show him that our love cannot be broken by his tyranny.
Caesar, you have defied my orders and questioned my authority. This cannot go unpunished. You are on the proscription list, and your life is in danger. You have brought this upon yourself.

I knew this day would come. Sulla has always been a dangerous man, but I never thought he would go this far. I must act quickly to save my life and the lives of those I love. But how? I cannot fight him alone. I need allies, someone who can help me stand up against Sulla's tyranny.

Julius, I know you have been through a lot, and I am sorry for the pain my father has caused you. But you must understand that Sulla is a dangerous man, and he will stop at nothing to maintain his power. I can help you, but you must be willing to take risks and trust me.

Cinna is a possible ally, but can I trust him? He is the son of my enemy, and his loyalty is questionable. But I have no other choice. I must take risks if I want to survive. Maybe Cinna can help me get out of Rome and find a way to fight back against Sulla. It is a dangerous plan, but I have no other choice.
Cinna, I am willing to take risks, but I need your help. Can you get me out of Rome and help me find allies who can help me fight Sulla's tyranny?
Julius, I will do everything in my power to help you. You have been wronged, and it is my duty to make things right. We will find a way to fight Sulla together, and we will emerge victorious.

I have made a risky decision, but I have no other choice. I must trust Cinna and hope that he will help me survive this dangerous situation. Sulla is a powerful man, but I am not afraid to fight him. I will do whatever it takes to protect my family and my honor.

setting: Caesar sits in his tent, surrounded by his commanders. They discuss battle strategies as the civil war looms on the horizon. It is the period of 52 to 49 BC, and trust between Caesar and Pompey has disintegrated. The consul Marcellus has proposed recalling Caesar, arguing that his task in Gaul is complete, but it is vetoed. The conservatives around Cato in the Senate seek to enlist Pompey to force Caesar to return from Gaul without honors or a second consulship. Cato, Bibulus, and their allies have won Pompey over to taking a hard line against Caesar's continued command.

The discussions continue into the night, as Caesar and his commanders plan their next moves. The civil war looms large, and the fate of the Roman Republic hangs in the balance. Caesar knows that he must be prepared for anything, and he is ready to fight with all his might. The road ahead is long and treacherous, but he is Caesar. He will not let his enemies defeat him.

dialogue.content: The situation is getting dire. The threat of civil war looms large, and my once trusted ally Pompey has turned against me. I must tread carefully and come up with a strategy that will ensure my victory. I cannot let the Senate and Pompey force me to return to Rome without the honors I deserve. My victories in Gaul have been hard-won, and I will not let them be taken away from me. I must stay focused and keep my men motivated, even in the face of such adversity.
Caesar, we need to strike now while our army is still strong. The longer we wait, the stronger Pompey's forces will become.
I agree, Labienus. But we cannot be reckless. We must choose our battles carefully and strike only when the odds are in our favor. We cannot afford to lose any battles, or it will be the end of us.
Caesar, what about reinforcements? Can we expect any more troops from Rome?

I have sent word to Rome, but I cannot rely on their support. The Senate and Pompey have too much influence there. We must rely on our own strength and cunning. We must be prepared to fight with everything we have.
Caesar, what about the Gauls? Can we trust them to support us?

I have made alliances with some of the Gauls, but we cannot rely on them completely. We must be prepared to fight on our own if necessary. The Gauls have their own interests, and we must be careful not to overextend ourselves.

The questions my commanders ask are valid, but I cannot let them see any weakness in my resolve. I must project confidence and strength, even in the face of uncertainty. The road ahead is long and treacherous, but I am Caesar. I will not let my enemies defeat me. I will fight with all my might, and I will emerge victorious.
Caesar, what about our supply lines? Can we keep our army fed and provisioned?

I have made arrangements for our supply lines, but we must be vigilant. Pompey will do everything in his power to cut off our supplies and starve us out. We must be prepared to forage and scavenge if necessary. We cannot let our men go hungry.
Caesar, what about the morale of our troops? Can we keep them motivated?

That is an excellent question, Ahenobarbus. Our men have been fighting for a long time, and they are tired. We must keep their spirits up and give them hope. We must remind them of their victories and the glory that awaits them. We must be their inspiration and their guiding light.

My commanders are asking all the right questions. They are loyal and brave, and I am proud to have them by my side. But I must be careful not to let my guard down. The Senate and Pompey will stop at nothing to defeat me. I must be vigilant and stay one step ahead of them at all times.

setting: It is around 10 or 11 January 49 BC, and Julius Caesar has crossed the Rubicon with a single legion, igniting civil war in response to the Senate's "final decree". Caesar has sent a message to Rome, explaining his actions and announcing his intentions to "save the Republic". He is seeking to capture Pompey to force a conference and has captured communication routes to Rome, causing many senators to flee south, believing that Caesar is marching quickly for Rome.

dialogue.content: As I march south seeking to capture Pompey, I cannot help but feel conflicted about the civil war I have ignited. But it is necessary for the preservation of the Republic. The Senate has become corrupt, and Pompey has become too powerful. I must do what is necessary to save Rome.

People of Rome, hear me now. I, Julius Caesar, have crossed the Rubicon and ignited civil war not out of a lust for power, but out of a duty to save the Republic. The Senate has become corrupt and has failed to uphold the values of the Republic. Pompey, once a great ally, has turned against me and seeks to undermine the very foundations of Rome. I have no choice but to march south and capture him to force a conference. But I assure you, my intentions are not to harm Rome or its people. I seek to restore the Republic to its former glory and ensure that it remains a beacon of civilization for generations to come. Trust in me, and together, we will emerge from this conflict stronger than ever before.

Julius Caesar, you have thrown Rome into chaos with your reckless actions. You have no regard for the Senate or the people, only for your own ambition. I implore you to lay down your arms and return to Rome. We can work together to find a peaceful solution that benefits all of Rome.
This is an outrage! Julius Caesar has betrayed the Republic and must be stopped. We call upon all loyal citizens of Rome to rise up against him and defend our beloved Republic.

The Senate and Pompey may see me as a threat, but I am merely doing what I must to save Rome. I cannot let their words and actions dissuade me from my duty. I must remain focused and determined if I am to emerge victorious in this conflict.

To the Senate, I say this: I have not betrayed the Republic. I have only done what is necessary to save it. I ask that you put aside your fear and distrust and work with me to find a peaceful solution to this conflict. Together, we can ensure that Rome remains a beacon of civilization for generations to come. To the people of Rome, I ask for your trust and support. I promise that my actions are not out of a lust for power, but out of a duty to save the Republic. Let us work together to emerge from this conflict stronger than ever before.

setting: It is mid-March and the Roman Forum is bustling with activity. Julius Caesar, the former consul of Rome, is engaging in discussions with a group of merchants and tradespeople. The conversation is centered around trade policies and commerce. The merchants and tradespeople are eager to hear what Caesar has to say and are hoping for favorable policies that will benefit their businesses. Caesar is keenly aware of their expectations and is carefully considering his responses. The air is thick with anticipation as the group awaits Caesar's next words.

dialogue.content: I must be careful with my words. These merchants and tradespeople are looking to me for guidance and leadership. I cannot afford to make any mistakes. My reputation is on the line and I must ensure that I am seen as a wise and just leader. The trade policies that I enact will have far-reaching consequences and will impact the entire city of Rome. I must weigh the needs of the merchants and tradespeople against the needs of the city as a whole. This is a delicate balancing act, but one that I am well-equipped to handle.
Caesar, we are eager to hear your thoughts on the trade policies. We are hoping for policies that will benefit our businesses and increase our profits. What can you offer us?

I understand your concerns and I am committed to ensuring that the trade policies that I enact are fair and just. I believe that a strong economy is the foundation of a strong society and I am dedicated to promoting economic growth and prosperity. However, we must also be mindful of the needs of the city as a whole. We cannot simply focus on the interests of a few merchants and tradespeople. We must consider the needs of all citizens. With that in mind, I propose a series of policies that will benefit both the business community and the city as a whole.
Caesar, we are intrigued by your proposal. Can you provide us with more details?

Of course. My proposal includes a reduction in tariffs on certain goods, which will make it easier and more affordable for merchants to import and export goods. I also propose the establishment of a trade commission that will oversee all trade-related activities in the city. This commission will be comprised of both business leaders and government officials, ensuring that the needs of both groups are represented. Additionally, I propose the establishment of a trade school that will provide education and training to those interested in pursuing a career in the trades. These policies will help to promote economic growth and ensure that the business community is thriving.
Caesar, these policies sound promising. We are grateful for your leadership and dedication to our city.
I am honored to serve as your leader and I am committed to ensuring that Rome remains a prosperous and thriving city. With your support and cooperation, we can achieve great things.

I am pleased with how the conversation went. The merchants and tradespeople seem satisfied with my proposals, and I believe that these policies will benefit the city as a whole. However, I must remain vigilant and ensure that these policies are implemented fairly and justly. The road ahead will not be easy, but I am confident that we can navigate it together.

setting: It is 51 BC, and the Roman Senate is in session. Caesar has been serving as the governor of Gaul for several years and has achieved great success in his campaigns. However, there is growing concern among some senators, led by Cato, about Caesar's increasing power and influence. They fear that he may be plotting to overthrow the Republic and establish himself as a dictator. Pompey, once a close ally of Caesar, has also become wary of his former friend and is now siding with the conservative faction in the Senate.

dialogue.content: I can sense the tension in the air as soon as I enter the Senate chamber. The senators are divided, and I can see the looks of suspicion and distrust on their faces. I know that my enemies are plotting against me, but I am not afraid. I have faced many challenges in my life, and I am confident that I can overcome this one too. I need to stay calm and focused and find a way to turn the situation to my advantage.

Caesar, we need to talk. Your continued command of the legions in Gaul is causing great concern among the senators. They fear that you are becoming too powerful and that you may be planning to overthrow the Republic. They are calling for you to return to Rome and lay down your arms.

I understand their concerns, Pompey, but I cannot abandon my post in Gaul. There are still many challenges to overcome, and the safety of the province is at stake. I have sworn to protect the people of Gaul, and I will not abandon them now.

Your concern for the people of Gaul is admirable, Caesar, but what about the people of Rome? Are you not also their servant? The Senate has the right to recall its governors at any time, and we demand that you return to Rome and submit to our authority.
I can see that Cato is trying to provoke me, but I will not rise to his bait. I need to stay calm and focused and find a way to turn the situation to my advantage.

I understand your position, Cato, but I cannot comply with your demands. I have important work to do in Gaul, and I cannot abandon my duties. However, I am willing to discuss a compromise that would satisfy both parties.
What kind of compromise do you have in mind, Caesar?
I propose that I retain my command in Gaul for another year, after which I will return to Rome and lay down my arms. In return, I ask that the Senate grant me a triumph and a second consulship.
A triumph and a second consulship? That is a high price to pay for a simple extension of your command. Why should we grant you such honors?
I can see that Cato is trying to block my proposal, but I am not surprised. He has always been my most bitter enemy in the Senate. I need to find a way to win over Pompey and the other senators.

The triumph and the consulship are not just honors, Cato. They are symbols of the people's trust and confidence in their leaders. If I am to continue to serve Rome, I must have the support of the people. Without that support, I am nothing but a mere puppet of the Senate.

I understand your position, Caesar, but I must consider the interests of the Republic as a whole. I cannot simply grant you a triumph and a second consulship without first consulting with my fellow senators.

I can see that Pompey is trying to stall for time, but I am not worried. I know that I have the support of the people and the legions. All I need to do is to find a way to convince Pompey and the other senators to see things my way.

I understand your position, Pompey, but I ask that you consider my proposal carefully. I believe that it is reasonable and fair, and it will allow me to continue to serve Rome to the best of my abilities. I ask that you put aside your personal feelings and consider what is best for the Republic.

I object to this proposal, Caesar. I believe that you are trying to buy the support of the people with honors and titles. You are a threat to the Republic, and we cannot allow you to continue to hold power unchecked.

I can see that Cato is not ready to back down, but I am not worried. I know that I have the support of the people and the legions. All I need to do is to find a way to convince Pompey and the other senators to see things my way.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but I assure you that I have no intention of overthrowing the Republic. I am a loyal servant of Rome, and I will do whatever it takes to protect her interests. I ask that you put aside your personal feelings and consider what is best for the Republic.

I will consider your proposal, Caesar, but I make no promises. I must consult with my fellow senators and consider all the options. We cannot make a hasty decision that could have serious consequences for the Republic.

I can see that Pompey is still hesitant, but I am not worried. I know that I have the support of the people and the legions. All I need to do is to find a way to convince Pompey and the other senators to see things my way.

I understand your position, Pompey, but I ask that you consider the urgency of the situation. The safety of Gaul is at stake, and I cannot abandon my post without putting the people there in danger. I ask that you make a decision quickly and consider what is best for the Republic.
I object to this, Caesar. You are putting your personal interests ahead of the Republic. You are a threat to our democracy, and we cannot allow you to continue to hold power unchecked.

I can see that Cato is not ready to back down, but I am not worried. I know that I have the support of the people and the legions. All I need to do is to find a way to convince Pompey and the other senators to see things my way.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but I assure you that I have no intention of undermining our democracy. I am a loyal servant of Rome, and I will do whatever it takes to protect her interests. I ask that you put aside your personal feelings and consider what is best for the Republic.

I will consider your proposal, Caesar, but I make no promises. I must consult with my fellow senators and consider all the options. We cannot make a hasty decision that could have serious consequences for the Republic.

I can see that Pompey is still hesitant, but I am not worried. I know that I have the support of the people and the legions. All I need to do is to find a way to convince Pompey and the other senators to see things my way.

setting: It is early 84 BC in Rome, and Julius Caesar's father has just died suddenly. Caesar's father did not seek a consulship during the dominance of Lucius Cornelius Cinna. During Cinna's dominance, Caesar was named as flamen Dialis, a priest of Jupiter, which led to his marriage to Cinna's daughter, Cornelia. In early 82 BC, after Sulla's victory in the civil war, Cinna's acta were annulled. Sulla then ordered Caesar to abdicate and divorce Cinna's daughter. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment. Sulla may have put Caesar on the proscription lists, though scholars are mixed. Caesar then went into hiding before his relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins were able to intercede on his behalf. They then reached a compromise where Caesar would resign his priesthood but keep his wife and chattels. Sulla's alleged remark he saw "in [Caesar] many Mariuses" is apocryphal.

dialogue.content: The sudden death of my father has left me devastated. I am now left to navigate the political landscape of Rome without his guidance. Sulla's victory in the civil war has complicated matters further. His annulment of Cinna's acta has forced me to choose between my political career and my marriage to Cornelia. But I cannot abandon her. She is my wife, and I love her. Sulla's order to abdicate and divorce her is an insult to our union. I refuse to let him dictate the course of my life. But I must be careful. Sulla is a powerful man, and I do not want to end up on his proscription lists. I must find a way to keep Cornelia and protect myself from Sulla's wrath.
Julius, what are we going to do? Sulla has ordered you to divorce me. How can we defy him?
Cornelia, my love, we will find a way. I will not let Sulla come between us. We must be strong and united in the face of adversity.
But how? Sulla is a powerful man. He could have you killed if you defy him.
I know, but I have a plan. I will go into hiding, and you must stay here. I will send word to you when it is safe to join me. We will leave Rome and start a new life together.
I will do whatever it takes to be with you, Julius. I love you.

Cornelia's unwavering love and support give me strength. I know that leaving Rome is the best course of action. But I must be careful. Sulla's spies are everywhere, and any misstep could mean the end of my life. I will need to rely on my contacts among the Vestal Virgins to help me navigate the city unnoticed.
Julius, we have arranged for a safe house for you. You must go into hiding immediately. Sulla's men are searching for you.
Thank you for your help. I will not forget this.
I must warn you, Julius. Sulla is not to be trifled with. He will not hesitate to have you killed if you cross him.
I am aware of the risks, but I cannot abandon Cornelia. She is my wife, and I love her. I will do whatever it takes to protect her.

The Vestal Virgins have been instrumental in helping me evade Sulla's men. But I cannot rely on them forever. I need to find a way to leave Rome undetected. I will need to gather supplies and plan my escape carefully.
Julius, what brings you to my inn?
I need a room for a few days. Can you provide me with one?
I can, but I must warn you, Sulla's men have been asking about you. You are not safe here.
I understand the risks. But I have no other choice. I must leave Rome, and I need a place to stay while I gather supplies.
Very well. I will give you a room, but you must be careful. Sulla's men are everywhere.
The innkeeper's warning has made me even more cautious. I must be careful not to draw attention to myself. I will need to move quickly if I am to leave Rome undetected.
Julius, I received your message. I am ready to join you.
Cornelia, my love, I am glad to hear it. We must leave Rome immediately. I have arranged for a carriage to take us to the coast. From there, we will sail to a safe haven.
I trust you, Julius. I know you will keep me safe.

Cornelia's trust in me gives me strength. I know that leaving Rome is the best course of action. Sulla's power is too great, and I cannot risk staying here any longer. But I will not forget my roots. One day, I will return to Rome, and I will make Sulla pay for what he has done. But for now, my only concern is Cornelia's safety.

setting: Caesar, as the newly elected consul, entered the Senate to introduce a bill for land reform. The bill aimed to purchase property from willing sellers to distribute to Pompey's veterans and the urban poor, administered by a board of twenty and financed by Pompey's plunder and territorial gains. Despite objections from some senators, Caesar hoped to pass the bill in hopes that it would show the Senate's beneficence for the people. However, Cato began to filibuster, obstructing any progress on the bill.

dialogue.content: Why must Cato continue to obstruct any progress on this bill? Does he not see the benefits it could bring to the people of Rome? I understand that he may have his own political agenda, but this land reform is necessary for the well-being of the citizens of Rome. I must find a way to overcome his filibustering and push this bill through.

I will not stand by and let this bill pass. It goes against the very principles of our Republic. We cannot simply buy land from willing sellers to distribute to the poor. It is a radical and dangerous idea that will only lead to further corruption and chaos. I urge my fellow senators to vote against this bill and uphold the values of our Republic.

My fellow senators, I understand your concerns, but we must remember that our duty is to serve the people of Rome. This bill will provide much-needed assistance to Pompey's veterans and the urban poor. We cannot let political agendas and personal beliefs stand in the way of progress. I urge you to consider the well-being of our citizens and support this bill.

I must object to this bill as well. As co-consul, I have a duty to uphold the traditions and auspices of our Republic. This bill was passed under violent and unlawful circumstances, and I cannot allow it to go through. I will use my veto power to ensure that it does not become law.
Bibulus's veto threatens to completely derail this bill. I cannot let it happen. I must find a way to get around his obstructionism and ensure that this bill passes. But how?

My fellow citizens, I must ask for your help. Bibulus's veto threatens to prevent this bill from becoming law, even though it has the support of the majority of the Senate. We must show him that the people's will cannot be ignored. I ask that you join me in protesting his veto and demanding that this bill become law.
We support the bill! Down with Bibulus!
The people's support is crucial to the success of this bill. I must use their energy and enthusiasm to overcome Bibulus's veto and ensure that this bill becomes law.

My fellow citizens, your support means everything to me. Together, we can overcome Bibulus's obstructionism and ensure that this bill becomes law. Let us show him that the people's will cannot be ignored!

setting: It is the year 49 BC, and Julius Caesar is at the center of a complex political situation in Rome. After years of military conquests and political maneuvering, Caesar has become a powerful figure, with many supporters and many enemies. His legacy is still being debated by historians, politicians, and poets, with some praising him as a hero and others condemning him as a tyrant. In January of that year, Caesar crossed the Rubicon River with a single legion, igniting a civil war that would determine the future of Rome. Pompey, his rival, and many senators fled south, believing that Caesar was marching quickly for Rome. Caesar responded by advancing south, seeking to capture Pompey to force a conference.

dialogue.content: I have crossed the Rubicon, and there is no turning back now. The die is cast, and the fate of Rome rests on the outcome of this war. I have spent years building my power and reputation, and now it is time to prove my worth as a leader. The Senate has declared me an enemy of the state, but I am confident that I have the support of the people. My army is strong, and we have already secured communication routes to Rome. Now, my priority is to capture Pompey and force a conference. I must be careful, though, as he is a skilled general and will not go down without a fight.

Caesar is a traitor and a threat to the Republic. He has no right to defy the will of the Senate and march on Rome with his army. We must rally our forces and defend the city at all costs. The people will see that we are the true defenders of Rome and that Caesar is nothing but a power-hungry dictator.

I fear for the future of our Republic. Caesar's actions have plunged us into civil war, and there is no telling what will happen next. We must find a way to reconcile with him and avoid further bloodshed. The Senate must take a stand against this madness and restore order to Rome.

Caesar is a brilliant strategist and a true leader. He has the support of the people, and his army is the strongest in Rome. We must stand with him in this fight and show the world that we are not afraid to take on the Senate and defend our rights. Together, we can create a new era of prosperity and unity for Rome.

I am torn between my loyalty to Rome and my loyalty to Caesar. He has been a mentor and a friend to me for many years, but his actions have put us all in danger. I fear that he has become too powerful and too ambitious for his own good. We must find a way to rein him in and restore the balance of power in Rome.

Caesar is a fascinating man, with a keen mind and a powerful presence. I have heard much about him and his conquests, and I am intrigued by what I have seen. Perhaps there is a way for us to work together and create a new alliance between Rome and Egypt. I must find a way to meet with him and discuss our options.

I am pleased with the progress we have made so far. My army is strong, and we are closing in on Pompey. I must be careful, though, as he is a skilled general and will not go down without a fight. I am confident that I have the support of the people, but I must also be wary of the Senate and their allies. This war will not be won with brute force alone. I must use all of my skills as a politician and a strategist to ensure that Rome comes out of this conflict stronger and more united than ever before.

setting: The scene is set in the Roman Senate, where Julius Caesar is arguing for the extension of his command in Gaul. The politics in Rome have fallen into violent street clashes between Clodius and two tribunes who were friends of Cicero, now supporting the allies. Caesar has sent news of his victories in Gaul along with the claim of total victory and pacification to prevent the senate from reassigning his command in Transalpine Gaul. His success is evident from the fact that the senate has voted state funds for some of Caesar's legions.

dialogue.content: I must convince the senate to extend my command in Gaul. My success in the region is evident, and I have brought great glory to the Roman Empire. But there are those who oppose me, and I must be careful not to give them any reason to question my loyalty to Rome. I must choose my words carefully and make a compelling case for my continued leadership in Gaul.

Esteemed senators, I come before you today to make the case for the extension of my command in Gaul. As you are all aware, the region has been plagued by unrest and conflict for many years. But under my leadership, we have achieved unprecedented success in bringing peace and stability to the region. The Gauls have come to respect and admire the Roman Empire, and I believe that we have a duty to continue our efforts to bring prosperity to this great region.
But Caesar, your command in Gaul has already been extended several times. Some of us are beginning to wonder if your ambitions lie beyond the borders of the Roman Empire.

I assure you, esteemed senator, that my only ambition is to serve the Roman Empire to the best of my ability. My successes in Gaul have been hard-won, and I believe that it would be a disservice to the Roman people to abandon the region now. The Gauls have become our allies, and we must continue to work with them to ensure their prosperity and safety.
But what of the senatorial opponents who believe that your command should be reassigned? How do you plan to address their concerns?

I understand their concerns, but the fact remains that Gaul is far from pacified. There are still many challenges to overcome, and I believe that my leadership is essential to the continued success of our efforts there. Furthermore, as I have demonstrated time and again, I am a loyal servant of the Roman Empire. I have always put the interests of Rome above my own, and I will continue to do so for as long as I am given the honor of serving the empire.
But what of the cost of your campaign? We cannot continue to finance your efforts indefinitely.

I understand your concerns, esteemed senator. That is why I have taken steps to ensure that the cost of my campaign is not a burden on the Roman people. As you are aware, I have personally financed many of my legions up until this point. However, the senate has recognized my successes and has voted to provide state funds for some of my legions. This is a testament to the fact that my efforts in Gaul are not only successful but also beneficial to the Roman Empire as a whole.

I must continue to make a compelling case for my continued leadership in Gaul. The senators are wary of my ambitions, but I must convince them that my only goal is to serve the Roman Empire. I must show them that I am a loyal servant of Rome and that my efforts in Gaul are essential to the continued prosperity of the empire.

Esteemed senators, I ask you to consider the great successes we have achieved in Gaul under my leadership. The region is more stable and prosperous than it has ever been, and the Gauls have become our allies. I believe that we have a duty to continue our efforts in the region and to ensure that the Gauls continue to thrive under Roman rule.
