I move that we assign the provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul to Caesar for five years. This will give him the resources he needs to maintain stability in these regions and protect the Republic from external threats.

I thank my ally Vatinius for his support. The provinces of Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul are crucial for the Republic's defense, and I will use them wisely. But we must not forget the threat of the Transalpine Gaul. We cannot allow the Gauls to threaten our borders, and I must have the means to defend the Republic. I urge the senate to assign me the Transalpine Gaul as well, subject to annual renewal.
This is outrageous! Caesar is asking for more power, and we cannot allow it. The Republic is at stake, and we must stop him before it's too late.

I understand your concerns, Cato, but we cannot ignore the reality of the situation. The Republic faces external threats, and we must be prepared to defend it. I assure you that I have no intention of becoming a tyrant, but I must have the means to protect the Republic.

setting: Caesar and his advisors are seated in his tent, discussing the logistics and benefits of conquering the Germanic tribes beyond the Rhine. Maps and scrolls are spread out on a large table in the center of the tent, and the group appears to be deep in discussion. Despite the seriousness of the topic, Caesar is calm and collected, his eyes scanning over the maps with a focused intensity. His advisors, however, appear more hesitant, exchanging worried glances as they weigh the risks of such an undertaking.

dialogue.content: I cannot let the Germanic tribes beyond the Rhine continue to be a threat to Rome. If we can conquer them, we will have secured our borders and expanded our territory. The benefits far outweigh the risks. But my advisors are right to be cautious. The Germanic tribes are fierce warriors, and their terrain is difficult to navigate. We will need a careful plan if we are to succeed.

Caesar, I understand the strategic importance of this campaign, but we must consider the potential consequences. If we fail, we risk losing our army and damaging our reputation. Are these risks worth it?

I understand your concerns, Decimus. But we cannot let fear hold us back. We have the resources and the manpower to conquer these tribes. And the rewards will be great. Imagine the glory of expanding Rome's borders and securing our place in history. We must be bold if we are to succeed.
But what of the terrain, Caesar? The forests and rivers will make it difficult to navigate. And the Germanic tribes are known for their guerrilla tactics. We risk being ambushed at every turn.

True, the terrain will be a challenge. But we have faced difficult terrain before and come out victorious. And as for the guerrilla tactics, we will need to adapt our strategies accordingly. We are Romans, we are trained for this. I have no doubt that we can overcome any obstacle.
But what of the cost, Caesar? We will need to spend a great deal of resources and manpower on this campaign. And what of the soldiers who may die in battle? Is their sacrifice worth it?

The cost is a necessary evil, Gaius. We must spend money to make money, as they say. And as for the soldiers, their sacrifice will not be in vain. They will be fighting for the glory of Rome, for the expansion of our empire. Their names will go down in history as heroes. We cannot let sentimentality cloud our judgment.

I can see that my advisors are still hesitant, but I cannot let their doubts sway me. I must remain confident and resolute if I am to lead my army to victory. The Germanic tribes may be fierce, but we are Romans. We will not be intimidated. I must convince my advisors that this campaign is worth the risk.

My friends, I understand your concerns. But we must be bold if we are to succeed. The Germanic tribes may be fierce, but we are Romans. We have the strength and the skill to defeat them. And the rewards will be great. We will expand our territory, secure our borders, and cement our place in history. I urge you to trust me on this. Together, we will achieve greatness.

setting: Caesar, a politician and military general, is in the Senate and has just published the minutes of the senate and assemblies. This signals the senate’s accountability to the public. He has also brought in a bill to purchase property from willing sellers to distribute to Pompey's veterans and the urban poor. The bill would be administered by a board of twenty, Caesar would be excluded, and financed by Pompey's plunder and territorial gains.

dialogue.content: It is time to take action. The people need help, and it is my job to provide it. The senate is corrupt, and I must do everything in my power to make them accountable to the public. The bill I have crafted will provide land to those who need it most, and I have done everything in my power to make it appeal to the senate. But I know there will be opposition. I must be prepared to face it and do what is right for the people.
“This bill is a travesty! It is nothing but a power grab by Caesar. We cannot allow him to take control of the land and distribute it as he sees fit. This is not democracy! This is tyranny!”
“I agree with Cato. We cannot allow Caesar to take control of this land. It is against the principles of the republic. I will do everything in my power to stop this bill from passing.”

“Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but this bill is for the greater good. We must provide for those who have sacrificed so much for our country. I have crafted this bill to avoid any objections or indications of radicalism. I have excluded myself from the board of twenty, and the bill will be financed by Pompey's plunder and territorial gains. There is no reason to oppose this bill other than political advancement.”
“I refuse to let this bill pass. I will use my veto power to stop it.”
Bibulus is obstructing the progress of this bill. I must find a way to get it passed without his interference. The people need this bill, and I will not let Bibulus stand in the way of progress.
“Gentlemen, I suggest we take this bill to the people. If the senate cannot pass it, then we must allow the people to decide.”
“You cannot do that! This is against the auspices. I will not stand for it.”
Bibulus is getting in the way of democracy. He is standing in the way of progress. I must find a way to get this bill passed, no matter what it takes.
“Gentlemen, I am sorry it has come to this, but I must do what is right for the people. I will take this bill to the people, and they will decide its fate.”
“You cannot do that! You are violating the people's well-established legislative sovereignty.”
Bibulus is wrong. I am doing what is necessary for the people. I will not let him stand in the way of progress.
“I am sorry, Bibulus, but I must do what is right for the people. I will take this bill to the people, and they will decide its fate.”
“Caesar! Caesar! Caesar!”
The people are with me. They know what I am doing is right. I must not let them down. I will fight for them, no matter what it takes.
“Gentlemen, the people have spoken. This bill will pass. We must do what is right for the people, no matter what the cost.”

setting: The Roman Forum is bustling with activity as Julius Caesar, along with other leaders, gather to discuss the rising power of the Parthian Empire in the east. The forum is filled with influential figures from across the Roman Republic, each with their own agenda and political aspirations. The air is filled with tension as the group debates the best course of action to confront this new threat to Roman power and prestige. Caesar stands at the center of the gathering, his imposing presence commanding the attention of all who have assembled before him.

dialogue.content: Caesar casts a critical eye around the forum, taking in the various senators and politicians gathered before him. He is acutely aware of the stakes of this debate, and he knows that the decisions made today will shape the course of Roman history for generations to come. He feels a sense of pride in his own accomplishments, having secured significant victories in Gaul and proven himself as a formidable military leader. But he also knows that the Parthians pose a unique challenge, one that will require careful diplomacy and strategic planning to overcome. Caesar's mind races as he considers his options, weighing the risks and rewards of each potential course of action. He knows that he must convince his fellow leaders to follow his lead if they are to have any hope of success.

We must not underestimate the Parthians," Cato declares, his voice ringing out across the forum. "They are a powerful and cunning enemy, and we must be prepared to face them with all the strength and resolve that Rome can muster.

I agree that we must take the Parthians seriously," Cicero chimes in. "But we must also be careful not to overextend ourselves. We cannot afford to become embroiled in another costly and protracted war, especially when there are so many other threats to our security and stability.

Perhaps we should focus on building alliances with other powers in the region," Brutus suggests. "If we can secure the support of neighboring states, we may be able to contain the Parthians without resorting to military force.

I appreciate your suggestions, my fellow senators," Caesar says, his voice calm and measured. "But I believe that the only way to deal with the Parthians is through strength and determination. We must show them that Rome is not to be trifled with, and that we will defend our interests and our honor at all costs.
I agree with Caesar," Pompey adds, his voice echoing across the forum. "We cannot allow the Parthians to threaten our interests in the east, and we must be prepared to use force if necessary.

Caesar nods in agreement with Pompey's words, recognizing the value of having such a powerful ally on his side. He knows that Pompey's support will be crucial in swaying the other senators to his side, and he feels a sense of gratitude towards his old friend and ally.
But how do we plan to pay for this war?" Crassus interjects, his voice tinged with concern. "We cannot afford to stretch our resources too thin, especially with so many other demands on our treasury.

I have already secured funding for some of my legions," Caesar replies, his voice confident and assured. "And I believe that we can secure additional resources through our conquests in the east. We must be willing to take risks if we are to achieve greatness.
But at what cost?" Cato asks, his voice rising in anger. "Are we willing to sacrifice our principles and our values in pursuit of conquest and glory?

Caesar feels a twinge of annoyance at Cato's words, knowing that the senator's opposition is rooted in political posturing rather than genuine concern for the welfare of the Republic. He knows that he must tread carefully, however, if he is to win over the other senators and secure their support for his plans.

I understand your concerns, Cato," Caesar says, his voice calm and measured. "But we cannot allow fear and hesitation to paralyze us. We must be willing to take bold action if we are to secure our future and protect the interests of Rome.

setting: Julius Caesar is negotiating with the survivors of the Jugurthine War to recover the trophies won by Marius. The negotiation is taking place at the survivors' residence. The time is not specified, but it is likely during Caesar's term as curule aedile in 65 BC. The survivors are likely from the Numidian tribe, which Jugurtha belonged to.

dialogue.content: I must recover the trophies won by Marius for the glory of Rome and my family's honor. It is a matter of pietas, the virtue of loyalty to one's family and ancestors. These trophies have been taken down and neglected for too long. It is time to restore them to their rightful place. I must convince these survivors to give them back to me.
Why do you want these trophies so badly, Caesar? They are just symbols of our defeat at the hands of Rome. They are nothing but reminders of our shame and humiliation.

I understand your feelings, but these trophies are not just symbols of your defeat. They are also symbols of our victory over Jugurtha and the Cimbri. They represent the power and glory of Rome. It is important that we remember our triumphs as well as our failures. By returning these trophies to their rightful place, you will be honoring the memory of your fallen warriors and acknowledging the power and greatness of Rome.
But what will you do with these trophies once you have them back? Will you display them in your home as a trophy of your own victory over us?

No, I will not keep them for myself. I will restore them to their original location and display them for all to see. These trophies belong to Rome, not to me. I am merely a servant of the Republic, and it is my duty to preserve and honor its traditions and achievements.
We are not convinced, Caesar. We have suffered too much at the hands of Rome. We cannot simply give you these trophies without some compensation.

These survivors are stubborn and resistant to reason. I must find a way to convince them to give me what I want. Perhaps I can offer them a bribe or a promise of leniency. Or maybe I can appeal to their sense of honor and duty.
I understand your concerns, and I am willing to offer you a fair compensation for these trophies. What do you want in exchange?
We want a guarantee of our safety and autonomy. We want to be free from Roman interference and oppression.
Their demands are reasonable, but I cannot promise them what I cannot deliver. The fate of their people is not in my hands. I must find a way to satisfy them without compromising my own position.

I cannot promise you complete autonomy and independence, but I can promise you that Rome will treat you fairly and justly. I will do everything in my power to protect your rights and interests. As for your safety, I cannot guarantee it, but I can assure you that any harm done to you or your people will be punished severely.
We are not convinced, Caesar. We have heard these promises before, and they have always been broken. How can we trust you?

They are right to be skeptical. The reputation of Rome is not exactly spotless when it comes to dealing with conquered peoples. I must find a way to show them that I am different, that I am a man of my word.

I understand your doubts, but I ask you to trust me. I am not like other Roman officials. I care about justice and fairness, and I am willing to work with you to achieve a mutually beneficial outcome. If you give me these trophies, I promise that I will not abuse my power or betray your trust.
We will consider your offer, Caesar. We will let you know our decision in due time.

I have made some progress, but I still have a long way to go. These survivors are not easily swayed, and they have good reason to be cautious. I must find a way to break through their defenses and win their trust.

I appreciate your consideration, and I hope that we can come to an agreement soon. In the meantime, I would like to offer you a small token of my goodwill. Please accept these gifts as a sign of respect and friendship.
Thank you, Caesar. We will consider your offer and let you know our decision soon.

I have done all I can for now. It is up to them to decide whether to give me what I want. I can only hope that they will see reason and do the right thing. For the glory of Rome and the honor of my family.

setting: Julius Caesar sat in his spacious residence, surrounded by his closest advisors. They were discussing the execution of a secret plan to recover the trophies won by Marius, which Caesar intended to restore to their former glory. The plan had to be executed discreetly, so as not to attract any unwanted attention. Caesar was determined to see it through, and his advisors were equally committed to ensuring its success.

dialogue.content: The restoration of the trophies won by Marius is of utmost importance to me. It is a symbol of my family's legacy and an important part of our history. I will not rest until they are restored to their former glory. This plan must be executed with the utmost discretion, and I will not tolerate any mistakes or missteps.
My lord, we have everything in place for the recovery of the trophies. The workmen are ready, and the necessary materials have been procured. We can begin the restoration process as soon as tonight.

Excellent. I want the restoration to be completed as soon as possible. We must not attract any attention, and the work must be done quickly and efficiently. I trust that you have taken all necessary precautions to ensure that this operation remains a secret.

My lord, we have taken all necessary measures to ensure that the operation is a success. We have hired the most skilled workers, and the restoration process will be completed in record time. We have also taken care to maintain utmost secrecy, and no one outside this room knows of our plans.

I am pleased with the progress we've made so far. The recovery of the trophies must be executed perfectly, and I trust my advisors to ensure that it is. This is an important moment for my family, and I will not let anything stand in the way of its success.
My lord, what if the restoration is discovered? What if someone finds out about our plans?

We cannot afford to be discovered. If anyone finds out, it could spell disaster for us. We must do everything in our power to keep this operation a secret. That means ensuring that only the most trusted individuals are involved and that no one outside this room knows of our plans.

My lord, the restoration process will be complete by tomorrow morning. We have made sure that everything is in place, and the workmen are working around the clock to ensure that the trophies are restored to their former glory.

Excellent. I want to personally oversee the final stages of the restoration process. We must ensure that everything is perfect, and that no one can tell that the trophies were ever removed. This is an important moment for my family, and I want to make sure that it is executed flawlessly.

The recovery of the trophies is an important step in solidifying my family's legacy. It is a symbol of our strength and power, and I will not rest until it is restored to its former glory. My advisors have done an excellent job so far, and I have every confidence that the operation will be a success. This is a momentous occasion, and I am proud to be a part of it.

setting: The scene takes place in Rome during the domination of Lucius Cornelius Cinna and the subsequent victory of Sulla in the civil war. Julius Caesar's father has passed away suddenly, leaving him without a clear path for his future. Caesar was named as flamen Dialis, a priest of Jupiter, which would have forced him to forego a political career due to religious taboos. However, this appointment indicates that there were few expectations of a major career for Caesar. Caesar married Cinna's daughter, Cornelia, but after Sulla's victory, he was ordered to abdicate and divorce her. Caesar refused, implicitly questioning the legitimacy of Sulla's annulment, and went into hiding before his relatives and contacts among the Vestal Virgins were able to intercede on his behalf. They then reached a compromise where Caesar would resign his priesthood but keep his wife and chattels. Sulla's alleged remark that he saw "in [Caesar] many Mariuses" is apocryphal.

dialogue.content: Sulla's words linger in my mind. "In [Caesar] many Mariuses." What does he mean by that? Does he see me as a potential threat, like Marius before me? Or does he see something in me that reminds him of Marius? Either way, it does not bode well for my future in Rome. Sulla has already taken away my priesthood and ordered me to divorce Cornelia. What else does he have in store for me? I must be cautious and strategic in my actions from now on.
Julius, what are we going to do? Sulla has taken away your priesthood and ordered you to divorce me. We cannot stay in Rome anymore.
Cornelia, we cannot leave just yet. We must wait for the right opportunity. I have contacts among the Vestal Virgins who can help us. We must be patient and bide our time.
But Julius, I cannot bear to be away from you. What if something happens to you?
Do not worry, Cornelia. I will find a way to keep us together. We will not be separated.

Cornelia's words weigh heavily on me. I cannot bear the thought of losing her. But I must stay focused and think of a way to protect her and myself. Sulla's power is great, but I have allies who can help me. I must make use of them.
Julius, we have arranged a meeting with Sulla. He has agreed to listen to your grievances.
Thank you for your assistance. I will go to the meeting and plead my case to Sulla.
Ah, Julius Caesar. What brings you here?
General Sulla, I come to plead my case. I have been ordered to abdicate my priesthood and divorce my wife. I have done nothing wrong, and I ask for your mercy.
I see. And why should I grant you mercy, Caesar? You have defied my orders and questioned my authority.
I have only acted according to my conscience, General. I cannot abandon my wife and my duty as a priest. I ask for your understanding.
Hmm, you are a bold one, Caesar. But I see something in you. You have potential. Perhaps I can make use of you in the future.
Sulla's words surprise me. He sees potential in me? Perhaps there is a way for me to turn this situation to my advantage. I must tread carefully and make use of any opportunities that come my way.
Julius, what happened at the meeting? Are we safe?
For now, Cornelia. Sulla has agreed to let us keep our marriage and our property. We must be cautious, but there is hope for us yet.

I breathe a sigh of relief. For now, Cornelia and I are safe. But I cannot let my guard down. Sulla is a powerful man, and he may turn against me at any moment. I must stay vigilant and make use of any opportunities that come my way. Who knows? Perhaps one day I will be the one in power, and Sulla will be at my mercy.

setting: It is a bustling day in the streets of Rome, and Julius Caesar is walking amongst the merchants. He is concerned about the state of the economy and how it affects the citizens of Rome. The merchants are busy selling their wares, but they stop to listen to Caesar's words. They respect him as a powerful politician and hope that he can help them with their struggles.

dialogue.content: Caesar walks among the merchants, observing the state of the market. He is troubled by what he sees. The prices are high, and the goods are scarce. He knows that the people of Rome are suffering, and he wants to help them. He thinks about the praetorship and how it has given him the power to make a difference. He wonders what he can do to improve the economy and make life better for the citizens of Rome.
Caesar, do you have any ideas on how to improve the economy? We are struggling to make ends meet, and the people are suffering.

I understand your concerns, my friend. The economy is indeed in a dire state, but I have some ideas that I believe can help. Firstly, we need to address the issue of scarcity. We must find ways to increase the production of goods and ensure that they are distributed fairly among the people. Secondly, we must reduce the taxes on the merchants to encourage them to invest and grow their businesses. And finally, we must ensure that the people have access to credit so that they can start their own businesses and contribute to the economy.
But Caesar, won't reducing taxes lead to a loss of revenue for the state? How will we fund our projects and initiatives?

I understand your concerns, my friend, but reducing taxes will stimulate the economy and increase revenue in the long run. We can also consider other sources of revenue, such as increasing tariffs on luxury goods and taxing the wealthy more heavily. We must ensure that the burden of taxation is shared fairly among the citizens of Rome.
But Caesar, what about the issue of corruption? We all know that many officials are taking bribes and abusing their power for personal gain. How can we trust that our efforts will not be in vain?

I understand your concerns, my friend. Corruption is indeed a serious problem in our society, but we must not let it discourage us from doing what is right. We must hold those in power accountable and ensure that they are punished for their crimes. We must also work towards creating a more transparent and fair system of governance so that the people can trust their leaders.

As Caesar speaks with the merchants, he feels a sense of purpose and determination. He knows that his ideas can make a difference and that he has the power to implement them. He also knows that it will not be an easy journey. He will face resistance from those who benefit from the current system, and he will need to navigate the complex political landscape of Rome. But he is confident in his abilities and his vision for a better future. He is ready to take on the challenge and lead his people to prosperity.

setting: Julius Caesar sat in his luxurious residence, deep in thought. It had been four years since his aunt Julia's funeral, and he had made significant strides in his political career since then. As curule aedile, he had staged extravagant games that had brought him further attention and popular support. He had also restored the trophies won by Marius, which had been taken down by Sulla. Caesar reflected on these accomplishments with a sense of pride and satisfaction.

dialogue.content: I have achieved so much in these past years. The people love me, and my political power is growing. But there is still so much more to accomplish. I must continue to work hard and make bold moves to secure my position in Rome. These victories are just the beginning.
Caesar, I must protest your actions. The restoration of the trophies won by Marius is unnecessary and a waste of resources.

Catulus, I understand your concerns, but I disagree. These monuments are a part of our history and should be preserved. It is important that we honor those who came before us and remember their accomplishments.
But at what cost, Caesar? The people's money should not be spent on frivolous endeavors. We have more pressing matters to attend to.

I assure you, Catulus, that these restorations were not frivolous. They were done with the utmost care and attention to detail. And the people of Rome appreciate the effort that went into preserving our history.

Catulus may not agree with my actions, but I know that I am doing what is best for Rome. The people may not always understand the decisions of their leaders, but it is my duty to do what is right, regardless of popular opinion.
I have no doubt that my actions as curule aedile will be remembered for years to come. I am proud of what I have accomplished and look forward to continuing to serve the people of Rome.

I am a man of great ambition, and I will stop at nothing to achieve my goals. The road ahead may be difficult, but I am confident in my abilities and know that I have the support of the people. Rome will be mine, and I will do whatever it takes to make it great.

setting: Caesar stands in the Roman Senate, surrounded by senators and political rivals. The atmosphere is tense, with violence erupting in the streets between Clodius and Cicero's allies. Caesar has come to deliver a passionate speech, rallying support for his Gallic campaign and pushing back against his opponents.

dialogue.content: As I stand here before the Senate, I am reminded of the power struggles that define our political landscape. My opponents seek to undermine me at every turn, but I will not be deterred. My victories in Gaul have been hard-won, and I will not let them be taken away from me. I must rally support for my cause and show the Senate that I am the only one capable of leading Rome to greatness.

My fellow senators, I come before you today to share news of my victories in Gaul. For years now, I have fought to pacify the region and bring stability to our borders. And I am proud to say that my efforts have been successful. The Gallic tribes have been subdued, and our control over the region is absolute.

But at what cost, Caesar? Your campaign in Gaul has been nothing but a bloodbath. You have trampled on the rights of the Gallic people and committed countless atrocities in the name of conquest. Is this the kind of leader we want for Rome?

I will not deny that there have been casualties in my campaign. But I assure you, every action I have taken has been for the good of Rome. The Gallic tribes were a constant threat to our borders, and I have done what was necessary to protect our people. And as for the rights of the Gallic people, I have shown them mercy and compassion whenever possible. I have granted them citizenship and treated them with respect. But make no mistake, Rome comes first.

Caesar, I understand your passion for our great city, but we must not forget the rule of law. The Senate has the power to reassign your command, and we must respect that. We cannot allow any individual to have unchecked power. It goes against everything our Republic stands for.

I understand the importance of the rule of law, Cicero. But I also understand the importance of decisive action. The Gallic tribes were threatening our borders, and I could not sit idly by. I took action, and I succeeded. The Senate must recognize that and support my efforts. We cannot afford to let our enemies gain the upper hand.

setting: Julius Caesar stood in the Roman Forum, surrounded by a crowd of people. He was there to defend his leadership against accusations of corruption and abuses of power. The setting was tense, with many people in the crowd angry and shouting at him. Caesar knew that he needed to defend himself convincingly if he was going to maintain his position of power.

dialogue.content: I cannot let these accusations stand. If I am to maintain my position of power, I must prove to the people that I am a strong and capable leader. I will use my charisma and persuasive abilities to turn this situation to my advantage.
Caesar, the people are angry with you. They accuse you of corruption and abuses of power. How do you respond to these accusations?

My dear Brutus, I am a man of the people. I have always acted in their best interests, and I have always put the needs of Rome above my own. These accusations are baseless and unfounded. I have done nothing wrong.
But Caesar, the evidence against you is overwhelming. You have used your position of power to enrich yourself and your allies. You have abused your authority and betrayed the trust of the people.

Cicero, I am disappointed to hear you say that. I have always respected you as a great orator and a wise man. But in this case, I believe you are mistaken. The evidence against me is circumstantial at best. I have always been transparent in my dealings and have nothing to hide.

Caesar is right. He has always acted in the best interests of Rome. These accusations are nothing more than baseless rumors spread by his enemies. We should support him and rally behind him in these trying times.
I can see that Mark Antony is on my side. I need to use his support to my advantage and turn the tide of public opinion in my favor.
Thank you, Mark Antony. Your support means a lot to me. I have always considered you a loyal friend and ally. Together, we can overcome these accusations and emerge stronger than ever.
Caesar! Caesar! Caesar!
I have turned the situation to my advantage. The people are on my side. I must use this momentum to crush my enemies and consolidate my power.
My fellow Romans, I thank you for your support. Together, we will overcome these challenges and emerge stronger than ever. Rome will prevail!

setting: Julius Caesar is negotiating with the survivors of the Cimbri War to recover the trophies won by Marius. The negotiation is taking place at the residence of the survivors.

dialogue.content: I must recover the trophies won by Marius. It is a matter of great importance to me and to the legacy of my family. These trophies belong to us, and I will not rest until they are returned. It is essential that I negotiate with the survivors of the Cimbri War and persuade them to return what rightfully belongs to us. I must be tactful, persuasive, and firm in my negotiations. I cannot afford to fail.
Why do you want these trophies so badly? They are just symbols of your family's past victories. What do they matter to you now?

These trophies are not just symbols. They represent the valor and bravery of my family and the Roman people. They are a testament to the greatness of Rome and the triumphs of our ancestors. It is our duty to preserve and honor them. I implore you to see reason and return them to us.
But these trophies were taken from us fair and square. We earned them in battle, and they are rightfully ours. Why should we give them up?

You are mistaken. Marius won those trophies in battle, but they were taken from him by Sulla. Sulla had no right to take them, and neither do you. I am offering you a fair price for their return, and I promise that you will not regret it.
We are not interested in your money. These trophies are our pride and joy. We cannot simply give them up without a fight.

This negotiation is not going as planned. I must find a way to appeal to their sense of honor and duty. I cannot let them think that I am trying to cheat them. I must be honest and sincere in my intentions.

I understand your attachment to these trophies. They are indeed a great source of pride and joy. But I assure you that I am not trying to cheat you. I am simply asking for what is rightfully mine. I am willing to negotiate a fair deal that will benefit both of us. Please, let us reason together and find a solution that works for everyone.
We will consider your offer. But we must discuss it among ourselves and come to a decision. We will let you know our answer soon.

Thank you for your consideration. I will await your decision eagerly. But please remember that time is of the essence. The longer we wait, the harder it will be to reach a satisfactory agreement. I hope we can come to a fair and just resolution soon.

setting: Caesar and Cicero are sitting in Caesar's villa in Rome, discussing the current political situation and the broader issues facing the Roman Republic. Politics in Rome is falling into violent street clashes between Clodius and two tribunes who were friends of Cicero, now supporting the allies. Caesar has sent to Rome news of his victories in Gaul along with the claim of total victory and pacification. Cicero has been a vocal supporter of Caesar's efforts in Gaul and has been pushing for the Senate to recognize Caesar's successes.

dialogue.content: The situation in Rome is becoming increasingly unstable. The violence between Clodius and Cicero's allies is threatening to tear the Republic apart. But I cannot afford to let this distract me from my goals. My victories in Gaul must be recognized by the Senate, and I must ensure that my position in Transalpine Gaul is not threatened. I must also be careful of my senatorial opponents, who would love nothing more than to see me fall from power. But I am Julius Caesar, and I will not be so easily defeated.

Cicero, I appreciate your support in the Senate. Your voice carries a lot of weight, and I am grateful for your efforts to recognize my victories in Gaul. But I fear that the violence in Rome may distract from the important work that needs to be done. We must ensure that the Republic remains stable, even in the face of these challenges.

I agree, Caesar. The violence in Rome is deeply troubling, but we cannot allow it to distract us from the important work that lies ahead. Your victories in Gaul are a testament to your skill as a general, and the Senate must recognize that. We cannot let your position be threatened by those who seek to undermine your achievements.

Cicero is a valuable ally, but I must be careful not to reveal too much to him. He is a skilled orator and could easily turn the Senate against me if he were to feel threatened by my ambitions. But for now, he is a useful ally, and I must keep him on my side.

I appreciate your support, Cicero. Your words carry great weight in the Senate, and I am grateful for your friendship. But we must remain vigilant. There are those who seek to undermine us, and we must be prepared to face them.
Indeed, Caesar. We must be prepared for whatever challenges lie ahead. But I have faith in our abilities to overcome them. Together, we can ensure that the Republic remains stable and prosperous.

Cicero is a skilled orator, but I cannot let him get too comfortable. He is a potential threat to my ambitions, and I must be careful not to reveal too much to him. But for now, he is a useful ally, and I must keep him on my side.
I am glad to hear that, Cicero. Your faith in our abilities is heartening. But we must remain vigilant. The challenges we face are great, and we cannot afford to be complacent.

setting: It is a sunny day in the Senate House, where Julius Caesar, a Roman politician, general, and author, negotiates with senators over the appointment of a new governor. He is standing in the center of the Senate House, with senators sitting around him. The room is decorated with marble columns and statues of famous Roman figures. The atmosphere is tense, as Caesar is known for his ambitious nature and the senators are cautious of his power.

dialogue.content: I must be careful with my words and actions today. These senators are not my allies, but I need their support to secure my position. I must appear diplomatic and reasonable, but at the same time, I cannot show any weakness. The appointment of the new governor is crucial to my plans, and I cannot afford to lose control of the situation.

Gentlemen, I am grateful for your presence today. As you know, the appointment of the new governor is of great importance to the stability of our province. I have carefully considered the candidates, and I believe that Marcus Aemilius Lepidus is the most suitable for the position. He has proven his loyalty and competence in his previous posts, and I am confident that he will serve our province with distinction.

We appreciate your recommendation, Caesar, but we have reservations about Lepidus's qualifications. He is young and inexperienced, and we fear that he may not be able to handle the challenges of the governorship.

I understand your concerns, but I assure you that Lepidus has the necessary skills and knowledge to fulfill his duties. He has shown great potential in his previous posts, and I have full confidence in his abilities.

Forgive us, Caesar, but we cannot simply take your word for it. We need more information about Lepidus's track record and qualifications. We suggest that a committee be formed to investigate his suitability for the position.

These senators are testing my authority. They are questioning my judgment and trying to undermine my position. I cannot let them gain the upper hand. I need to find a way to convince them to support my choice without appearing weak.

I understand your desire for more information, but time is of the essence. Our province cannot afford to wait for a lengthy investigation. I assure you that Lepidus has been thoroughly vetted, and his qualifications are beyond reproach. I urge you to trust my judgment and support his appointment.

With all due respect, Caesar, we cannot blindly follow your lead. We have a duty to our constituents to ensure that the best candidate is chosen for the job. We propose that a vote be held to determine the most suitable candidate.
A vote? This is a dangerous proposition. If the senators vote against Lepidus, it could jeopardize my plans and weaken my position. I need to find a way to sway the vote in my favor.

I understand your desire for transparency, but a vote would only delay the appointment and cause unnecessary chaos. I propose a compromise. Let us hold a closed-door meeting to discuss Lepidus's qualifications in detail. I will present all the necessary evidence and answer any questions you may have. Afterward, we can hold a vote to determine the most suitable candidate.
That sounds reasonable, Caesar. We agree to your proposal.

Good. The compromise has bought me some time. I need to prepare for the meeting and gather all the evidence I can to convince the senators to support Lepidus's appointment. This is a crucial moment, and I cannot afford to make any mistakes.

setting: Julius Caesar is presenting his plan to restore his family's public monuments at his family residence. The event takes place four years after his aunt Julia's funeral, in 65 BC. Caesar served as curule aedile and staged lavish games that won him further attention and popular support. He also restored the trophies won by Marius, and taken down by Sulla, over Jugurtha and the Cimbri. According to Plutarch's narrative, the trophies were restored overnight to the applause and tears of joy of the onlookers; any sudden and secret restoration of this sort would not have been possible – architects, restorers, and other workmen would have to have been hired and paid for – nor would it have been likely that the work could have been done in a single night. It is more likely that Caesar was merely restoring his family's public monuments – consistent with standard aristocratic practice and the virtue of pietas – and, over objections from Catulus, these actions were broadly supported by the senate.

dialogue.content: This is a moment of great importance. The restoration of my family's public monuments is more than just a display of my wealth and influence. It is a statement of my family's history and legacy. It is a way to honor the memory of those who came before me and to ensure that their achievements are not forgotten. But it is also a political move. By restoring these monuments, I am showing the people that I am a man of the people, that I care about their history and their culture. This will win me their support, and it will help me to achieve my ultimate goal: to become the greatest leader that Rome has ever seen.

Caesar, I must object to this plan. It is a waste of resources and a pointless exercise in vanity. These monuments are nothing but relics of a bygone era. They serve no purpose in the modern world, and they should be left to crumble into dust.

Catulus, I respect your opinion, but I must disagree. These monuments are not relics of a bygone era. They are symbols of our culture and our history. They remind us of the great achievements of our ancestors, and they inspire us to strive for greatness ourselves. And as for the cost, I assure you that I am not foolish enough to waste resources on a pointless exercise in vanity. The restoration of these monuments will be done with great care and attention to detail, and it will be a testament to the skill and dedication of our craftsmen.

But Caesar, there are more important issues facing our city than the restoration of monuments. We have wars to fight, and we have people to feed. We cannot afford to waste resources on such a trivial matter.

I understand your concerns, Catulus, but I must remind you that culture and history are just as important as war and food. Without our culture and our history, we are nothing but savages. We must preserve our heritage if we want to build a better future for ourselves and our children. And I assure you that the cost of this restoration will be minimal compared to the benefits it will bring.
Caesar, we support your plan! We believe that the restoration of these monuments is important, and we thank you for your dedication to our culture and our history!

I can see that the people are with me. They understand the importance of this restoration, and they believe in my vision for the future of Rome. This is just the beginning. With their support, I can achieve anything. I can become the greatest leader that Rome has ever seen, and I can lead our city to a bright and prosperous future.

setting: It is 73 BC in Rome, and Julius Caesar has been co-opted into the pontifices in place of his deceased relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta. He has been absent from Rome but has returned and was elected one of the military tribunes for 71 BC. He has not served in war, but he has agitated for the removal of Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for those who supported Lepidus' revolt to be pardoned. These advocacies were common and uncontroversial.

dialogue.content: I must admit, returning to Rome and being elected as one of the military tribunes is a great honor. It is a sign that the aristocracy has accepted me as one of their own and that I have a promising future in politics. But I cannot rest on my laurels. There is much work to be done, and I must continue to advocate for the rights of the plebeians. Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate must be removed, and those who supported Lepidus' revolt must be pardoned. These are common and uncontroversial advocacies, but they are necessary if I am to make a real difference in Rome.
Julius Caesar, what brings you to the forum today?
I am here to advocate for the removal of Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for the pardon of those who supported Lepidus' revolt.

Ah, I see. Well, I am sympathetic to your cause, but I am not sure that it is the right time to push for such measures. The consuls are currently focused on other matters, and it may be difficult to get them to take up your cause.

I understand your concerns, but I believe that now is the perfect time to push for these measures. There is growing support for the rights of the plebeians, and I believe that we can make a real difference if we work together.
Well, I will certainly consider your proposal. But I cannot make any promises at this time. We will have to see how the consuls react to your advocacy.
I can sense the hesitation in the plebeian tribune's voice, but I will not be deterred. I must continue to push for the rights of the plebeians, no matter how difficult the road ahead may be.

I am here to advocate for the removal of Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for the pardon of those who supported Lepidus' revolt.

I understand your concerns, but I believe that the rights of the plebeians are just as important as the war on Spartacus. We must not forget that all citizens should have a voice in the affairs of the state, regardless of their social status.
I see your point, but I am not sure that the other members of the Senate will see it that way. We must be careful not to upset the delicate balance of power in Rome.
I can sense Crassus' reluctance to take up my cause, but I will not be deterred. I must continue to push for the rights of the plebeians, no matter how difficult the road ahead may be.

Finally, some support! Pompey may be a member of the aristocracy, but he understands the importance of the rights of the plebeians. Perhaps together, we can make a real difference in Rome.
I will speak to Crassus and see if we can get some legislation passed. It may be difficult, but I believe that it is the right thing to do.
Thank you, Pompey. Your support means a great deal to me and to the cause of the plebeians.

I may have faced some resistance today, but I will not be deterred. The fight for the rights of the plebeians is a long and difficult one, but it is a fight that I am willing to undertake. I will continue to advocate for their rights, no matter what obstacles may stand in my way.

setting: It is the time of the Roman Republic, and Julius Caesar has crossed the Rubicon with his Legio XIII Gemina, starting a civil war against the Senate. Caesar has now laid siege to the city of Massilia, which is a strategic port that Pompey's navy uses to control the Mediterranean. Caesar seeks to capture the city and gain control of the port to weaken Pompey's naval power.

dialogue.content: This siege is necessary. Massilia is a key port that Pompey's navy uses to control the Mediterranean. If I can capture it, I will weaken Pompey's naval power and have greater control over the sea. This will give me an advantage in the war. Besides, Massilia has refused to support me, and I cannot allow a city to defy my authority. They must submit to Rome, and to me.

Men of Massilia, you have defied Rome and refused to support me, your rightful leader. You have chosen to side with Pompey, and that is unacceptable. Surrender now, and I will spare your lives and your city. But if you resist, I will show you no mercy. The die has been cast, and your fate is in your hands.

Julius Caesar, we cannot surrender to you. We have always been neutral in your conflict with Pompey, and we will not choose sides now. Besides, we have a treaty with Pompey that we must honor. We cannot betray him.
These Massilians are stubborn. But I cannot allow them to defy me and support my enemy. They must be punished for their disobedience. I must find a way to break their resistance and take their city.

I understand your position, but you must understand mine. I am the leader of Rome, and I cannot allow any city to defy me. You have two choices - surrender or face the consequences. I will give you one more chance to reconsider. Think carefully, for your decision will have grave consequences.
We have made our decision, Julius Caesar. We will not surrender to you, and we will defend our city with all our might. We are prepared to face the consequences of our actions.

So be it. They have made their choice, and they will pay for it. I will show them the power of Rome and the might of my army. This siege will not be easy, but I am confident of victory. I will take Massilia, and Pompey will be weakened. The die has been cast, and I will emerge victorious.

setting: The Roman Senate is in session, with Julius Caesar defending his actions and expenditures during his campaigns in Gaul. Some senators are questioning his methods and motives, while others support him. Caesar is standing before the senate, looking determined and confident, ready to defend his honor and reputation.

dialogue.content: I cannot let these senators question my actions and motives. I have fought hard and sacrificed much for Rome. These campaigns in Gaul have been successful, and I have brought glory to Rome. I must defend myself and prove my worth to the Senate and the people of Rome.
Caesar, you have spent a great deal of money on your campaigns in Gaul. Can you explain why you needed to spend so much?

My campaigns in Gaul were necessary to secure our borders and protect Rome from outside threats. The money spent on these campaigns was well worth it, as we now have a stronger and safer Rome. I have also brought back wealth and treasures from Gaul that will benefit Rome.
But Caesar, some of your methods in Gaul have been questionable. You have taken hostages and forced tribes to submit to Roman rule. Is this the way a Roman general should behave?

I have only acted in the best interests of Rome. Sometimes, tough measures are necessary to ensure our safety and security. The tribes in Gaul were a threat to Rome, and I had to take action to neutralize that threat. The hostages were taken to ensure the compliance of the tribes, and I have treated them well. As for forcing tribes to submit, it was necessary to bring order to the region and prevent further conflict.
But Caesar, some of your victories in Gaul have been exaggerated. We have heard reports that you have downplayed your defeats and exaggerated your successes. Is this true?

I have always been honest in my reports of the campaigns in Gaul. Yes, there have been defeats, but those were necessary to learn from and improve our strategies. As for my victories, they have been hard-won and deserved. I have always given credit to my soldiers and commanders for their bravery and skill in battle.

These senators are trying to discredit me and my achievements. I cannot let them succeed. I must prove that I am a capable and worthy leader of Rome. I will defend my actions and my honor with all my strength.
Caesar, there have been reports of atrocities committed by your soldiers in Gaul. They have killed innocent civilians and destroyed villages. How do you justify these actions?

I do not condone the killing of innocent civilians or the destruction of villages. If any of my soldiers have committed such acts, they will be punished accordingly. However, in times of war, it is impossible to prevent all casualties. Our soldiers have been attacked by the tribes in Gaul, and they have had to defend themselves. As for the destruction of villages, it was necessary to prevent the tribes from using them as bases for their attacks.
But Caesar, you have been away from Rome for a long time. Some are questioning your loyalty to Rome and your ambitions for power. What do you have to say about these accusations?

My loyalty to Rome is unquestionable. I have always acted in the best interests of Rome and its people. As for my ambitions, I have no desire for power beyond what is necessary to serve Rome. I have no intention of becoming a dictator or usurping the authority of the Senate. I am a loyal servant of Rome, and I will continue to serve Rome with all my strength.

These accusations of disloyalty and ambition are baseless and unfounded. I have sacrificed much for Rome, and I will continue to do so. I will prove to these senators that I am a true patriot and a worthy leader of Rome.
Caesar, we have heard reports that you are planning to march on Rome with your army. Is this true?

That is a baseless accusation. I have no intention of marching on Rome with my army. My army is in Gaul, where it belongs. I am here to defend my honor and my reputation, not to threaten the authority of the Senate.

Caesar, we have heard many conflicting reports about your campaigns in Gaul. Some say that you have brought peace and stability to the region, while others say that you have caused more harm than good. Can you give us a clear picture of what has happened in Gaul?

I can assure you that my campaigns in Gaul have been successful. I have brought peace and stability to the region, and I have secured our borders against outside threats. The tribes in Gaul were a danger to Rome, and I had to take action to neutralize that threat. Yes, there have been casualties and losses, but that is the nature of war. Overall, my campaigns have been a great success, and I have brought great glory to Rome.

I have defended myself and my actions to the best of my ability. I hope that the senators will see that I am a capable and worthy leader of Rome. I will continue to serve Rome and its people with all my strength and honor.

setting: Julius Caesar stands in the Roman Marketplace, surrounded by a gathering of citizens. It is a warm, sunny day, and the air is filled with the sounds of bustling commerce and the chatter of the people. Caesar looks out at the crowd with a sense of purpose, his eyes shining with an intensity that hints at the passion and conviction that drive him. He is dressed in his finest robes, his hair and beard immaculately groomed, and his posture is confident and commanding.

dialogue.content: As I stand here today, looking out at the faces of the people I have sworn to serve, I am filled with a sense of pride and purpose. For too long, the forces of division and discord have threatened to tear apart the fabric of our society, leaving us weak and vulnerable to our enemies. But I am here to tell you that we can and will overcome these challenges, as long as we stand together and work towards a common goal. My vision for Rome is one of unity, strength, and prosperity, and I believe that we can achieve it if we are willing to put in the hard work and dedication required.

But how can we trust you, Julius Caesar? You have already shown yourself to be a man of ambition and greed, willing to do whatever it takes to achieve your goals. How can we be sure that you won't use your power to oppress us?

I understand your concerns, my friend, and I do not blame you for your skepticism. But let me ask you this: have I not already proven myself to be a man of honor and integrity? Have I not fought for the rights of the people, even in the face of opposition and adversity? I am not here to oppress you, but to empower you. Together, we can create a Rome that is strong, just, and prosperous for all.
But what about the Senate, Julius Caesar? Are you not betraying their trust by taking power into your own hands?

The Senate has had its chance to lead, my friend. But time and time again, they have failed to act in the best interests of the people. They have become complacent, corrupt, and self-serving, more concerned with maintaining their own power than with serving the greater good. It is time for a new era of leadership, one that is guided by the wisdom and will of the people, not by the whims of a few privileged elites.
But what about your enemies, Julius Caesar? They are powerful and numerous, and they will stop at nothing to bring you down.

My enemies do not scare me, my friend. I have faced many challenges in my life, and I have always emerged victorious. I am a man of action, not words, and I will not be intimidated by those who seek to undermine my authority. But I cannot do this alone. I need the support and loyalty of all those who believe in my vision for Rome, who are willing to stand up and fight for what is right. Together, we can overcome any obstacle, and build a Rome that is strong, just, and prosperous for all.

setting: Julius Caesar was absent from Rome in 73 BC. During his absence, he was co-opted into the pontifices in place of his deceased relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta. Caesar was elected as one of the military tribunes for 71 BC on his return to Rome.

dialogue.content: As I stand here in Rome, I cannot help but feel a sense of pride in my achievements. My promotion to the pontifices has marked me as a well-accepted member of the aristocracy with great future prospects in my political career. I must continue to work hard and ensure that my name is known throughout Rome.
Caesar, my old friend, it is good to see you back in Rome. I hope your absence was fruitful.

Lepidus, it is good to see you too. My absence was indeed fruitful. I have been co-opted into the pontifices in place of my deceased relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta. This marks me as a well-accepted member of the aristocracy. How have things been in Rome in my absence?

Things have been going well. Pompey and Crassus have brought legislation restoring the plebeian tribunate's rights, and we have been working to pardon the Lepidan exiles. I believe you will find Rome to be a much different place than when you left.

It seems that Pompey and Crassus are making moves. I must keep my eyes and ears open and ensure that I am not left behind. The restoration of the plebeian tribunate's rights and the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles are good moves. I must align myself with those who are making progress in Rome.

That is good to hear, Lepidus. I support the restoration of the plebeian tribunate's rights and the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles. I am glad to see that progress is being made in Rome. I look forward to working with you and others to continue this progress.
Caesar, it is good to see you back in Rome. I hear that you have been co-opted into the pontifices. Congratulations on your success.
Thank you, Pompey. It is good to see you too. I am glad to be back in Rome and to see that progress is being made.

Caesar, we have been discussing the restoration of the plebeian tribunate's rights and the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles. We believe that these moves will help to bring about a more united Rome. What are your thoughts?
This is my chance to align myself with Pompey and Crassus. I must show them that I support their moves.

I support the restoration of the plebeian tribunate's rights and the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles. I believe that these moves will help to bring about a more united Rome. I am glad to see that progress is being made, and I look forward to working with you both to continue this progress.
That is good to hear, Caesar. We could use your support. We have many plans for Rome, and we believe that you could be a valuable asset to our cause.
This is exactly what I wanted to hear. I must continue to align myself with Pompey and Crassus and show them that I am a valuable asset to their cause.
I am glad to hear that, Pompey. I believe that I could be a valuable asset to your cause, and I am willing to do whatever it takes to ensure that Rome continues to progress.
That is good to hear, Caesar. We have many plans for Rome, and we believe that you could play a key role in our plans. We will be in touch.
This is it. My chance to make a name for myself in Rome. I must continue to align myself with Pompey and Crassus and show them that I am a valuable asset to their cause.

setting: The Senate of Rome is in session, and Julius Caesar has been appointed as curule aedile. He is discussing his plans with other senators for the upcoming games and restorations he intends to organize. The time is 65 BC, four years after the funeral of Caesar's aunt Julia, and he hopes to gain further attention and support with his lavish displays.

dialogue.content: As I stand here in the Senate, I cannot help but feel a sense of pride and accomplishment at my appointment as curule aedile. This is my chance to prove myself to the people of Rome and show them what I am capable of. I have carefully planned my games and restorations, and I know they will be a great success. But I must also be cautious, for there are those who oppose me, such as Catulus. I must win over the support of the Senate if I am to make my mark on history.
Caesar, I must object to your plans for the restorations of the trophies won by Marius. These monuments were taken down by Sulla for a reason, and I do not believe it is appropriate to restore them.

With all due respect, Catulus, these trophies are not just symbols of victory, but also of our Roman heritage and history. It is our duty to preserve and honor them, and I believe the people of Rome will agree with me.

I can see that my words have swayed the opinions of the other senators, but I must remain vigilant. There are those who would seek to undermine me at every turn, and I cannot afford to make any missteps.
I also plan to host lavish games to honor the gods and entertain the people of Rome. I have spared no expense in their preparation, and I am confident they will be a spectacle to behold.
Yes, this is what I wanted. The support of the Senate and the adoration of the people. With these games and restorations, I will make a name for myself and cement my place in history.
I thank you all for your support. Together, we will make Rome great once more!

As I leave the Senate, I feel a sense of elation and excitement for what is to come. The games and restorations will be a success, I am sure of it. And with the support of the people and the Senate, there is nothing I cannot achieve. Rome will be mine.

setting: The scene takes place in the Forum during Caesar's year as praetor. Caesar announces his intention to deprive his enemy Catulus of the honour of completing the rebuilt Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, accusing him of embezzling funds and threatening to bring legislation to reassign it to Pompey.

dialogue.content: I have had enough of Catulus and his arrogance. He thinks he is above the law and that he can embezzle funds without consequence. But not on my watch. I will show him that no one is above the law, not even the great Catulus. And what better way to do that than to take away the honour of completing the rebuilt Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus? It will be a blow to his ego, and a warning to others who think they can get away with such crimes.

Good citizens of Rome, I come before you today to address a grave matter. It has come to my attention that our esteemed colleague, Catulus, has been embezzling funds meant for the rebuilding of the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus. This is a serious offense, one that cannot be ignored. As praetor of Rome, it is my duty to ensure that justice is served and that the laws of our great republic are upheld. Therefore, I must announce my intention to deprive Catulus of the honour of completing the temple. It is clear that he is not fit to carry out such a task, given his disregard for the law and the people of Rome. I also plan to bring legislation to reassign the task to Pompey, a man who has proven himself time and again to be a loyal and capable servant of Rome.

This is preposterous! I have done no such thing. These are baseless accusations made by a jealous rival who seeks to tarnish my reputation. I demand that you provide evidence to support your claims, Caesar.

Ah, Catulus. Always so quick to defend himself. But he cannot deny the truth forever. I have evidence that he embezzled funds, and I will use it to bring him to justice. But for now, I must play my cards carefully. I cannot reveal my evidence just yet, or he may find a way to escape punishment.

I assure you, Catulus, that I have evidence to support my claims. But I must be careful in how I proceed, for the good of Rome. Rest assured that justice will be served, and that those who seek to undermine our republic will be punished.

I am honored that you would consider me for such a task, Caesar. I would be happy to take on the responsibility of completing the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus. But I must ask, what evidence do you have against Catulus?

Ah, Pompey. Always the loyal servant. He will be a valuable ally in the days to come. As for his question, I cannot reveal my evidence just yet. But I can assure him that it is solid, and that justice will be served.

I appreciate your willingness to take on this task, Pompey. As for the evidence, I cannot reveal it just yet. But I assure you that it is solid, and that justice will be served. For now, I ask that you continue to serve Rome with the same dedication and loyalty that you have always shown.
This is an outrage, Caesar! You cannot simply accuse someone of a crime without providing evidence. This is a mockery of our justice system, and a blow to the very foundations of our republic.

Ah, Cato. Always the voice of reason. But he cannot see the bigger picture. If I reveal my evidence now, it may be used to discredit me and my allies. I must wait for the right moment, and then strike.

I understand your concern, Cato. But I assure you that I have evidence to support my claims. And as for the justice system, it is my duty as praetor to ensure that it is upheld. Rest assured that justice will be served, and that the guilty will be punished.
I support Caesar's proposal. Catulus has shown himself to be a corrupt and unworthy servant of Rome. We need someone like Pompey to complete the temple and restore our faith in the republic.
I agree with Cato. This is a mockery of justice. If you have evidence, present it. Otherwise, you have no right to make such accusations.
The opposition is strong, but I will not be deterred. I have a plan, and I will see it through to the end. But for now, I must bide my time and wait for the right moment.

I understand your concerns, my fellow citizens. But I ask that you trust in me and my judgement. I have a plan, and I will see it through to the end. Justice will be served, and the guilty will be punished. Thank you for your time.

setting: Julius Caesar stands before a large crowd in a public gathering. He has just completed the restoration of the public monuments belonging to his family, including the trophies won by Marius over Jugurtha and the Cimbri. He is expected to make a public announcement about the completion of the restoration work. The atmosphere is charged with excitement and anticipation, and the crowd is eagerly waiting to hear what Caesar has to say.

dialogue.content: I stand before the people of Rome, ready to make my announcement. The restoration work is finally complete, and I can't wait to share the news with everyone. This is an important day for me and my family, and I want to make sure that everyone knows the significance of this moment. I must choose my words carefully and make sure that my message is clear and concise. I can feel the weight of the moment upon me, but I am confident that I can rise to the occasion.

Good citizens of Rome, I stand before you today to share some exciting news. After years of neglect, the public monuments belonging to my family have been restored to their former glory. The trophies won by Marius over Jugurtha and the Cimbri have been returned to their rightful place, and I am proud to say that this restoration work is a testament to the enduring legacy of my family. It was not an easy task, but with the help of skilled architects and restorers, we were able to complete this work in record time. I know that many of you have been eagerly waiting for this moment, and I am pleased to say that you will not be disappointed.

The crowd's cheers are music to my ears. It seems that my words have struck a chord with the people of Rome. This is precisely the kind of support I need if I am to achieve my goals. I must continue to build momentum and win over the hearts and minds of the people. This is just the beginning, and I am determined to see this through to the end.

Julius Caesar, I must object to your actions. The restoration of these trophies is not consistent with our traditions, and I fear that this will set a dangerous precedent for future generations. We must uphold the values of the Republic and not allow individual families to dictate the course of our history.

Respectfully, Senator Catulus, I must disagree. The restoration of these monuments is a matter of family honor and tradition. It is our duty to preserve the legacy of those who came before us and ensure that their accomplishments are not forgotten. I believe that the people of Rome will agree with me when I say that this restoration work is a symbol of our commitment to the principles of pietas and the importance of upholding our family's reputation.

I can sense the tension in the air, but I must stand firm. I cannot allow myself to be swayed by the objections of a single senator. I must continue to stay focused on my goals and do what is necessary to achieve them. The support of the people is crucial, and I must continue to win them over if I am to succeed.

I want to thank all of you for your support and encouragement. This restoration work would not have been possible without the help of many skilled workers and craftsmen, and I am grateful for their contributions. I hope that this moment will serve as a reminder of the rich history and traditions that we all share as Romans. Let us continue to work together to build a brighter future for ourselves and for future generations.

The people of Rome have spoken, and they have made their support clear. This is an important victory for me and my family, and I must continue to build on this momentum. I have much work to do, but I am more determined than ever to see this through to the end. Rome will be mine, and nothing can stop me.

setting: Julius Caesar is standing before the Roman Senate, defending his actions as proconsular governor of Asia. The time is during the first century BC, in Rome. The Julii Caesares were not particularly influential during the middle republic, but Caesar's father had some success in politics and served as proconsular governor of Asia for two years. Caesar's family had recovered politically in the early first century, producing two consuls in 91 and 90 BC. Caesar's homonymous father married Aurelia, a member of the politically influential Aurelii Cottae, producing two daughters along with Caesar. Caesar's aunt married the extremely influential Gaius Marius.

dialogue.content: As I stand before the Senate, I can feel their eyes piercing through me. They are waiting for me to make a mistake, to slip up, to give them a reason to condemn me. But I will not falter. I will defend my actions as proconsular governor of Asia with every fiber of my being. I know that I have done nothing wrong, and I will make sure that everyone in this room knows it.
Caesar, we have received reports of misconduct during your time as proconsular governor of Asia. Can you explain these reports?

Senator, I can assure you that there was no misconduct on my part during my time as governor of Asia. If there were any reports of misconduct, they were most likely fabricated by my enemies in an attempt to discredit me. I have always been a man of honor, and I would never do anything to tarnish the reputation of Rome or the Senate.
Caesar, we have information that suggests otherwise. We have reports that you took bribes from the local governors and allowed them to exploit the people under their rule. How do you explain this?

Senator, I can assure you that these reports are false. I did not take any bribes, nor did I allow anyone else to take bribes under my watch. I made sure that justice was served in every case that came before me, and I did my best to protect the people under my rule.
Caesar, we have also received reports that you engaged in an inappropriate relationship with one of the local women. Is this true?

Senator, I can assure you that these reports are false as well. I did not engage in any inappropriate relationships while I was governor of Asia. I have always been a man of honor, and I would never do anything to compromise my integrity or the integrity of Rome.
Caesar, we have heard enough. It is clear that you are not fit to hold public office, and we will be bringing charges against you. You will be held accountable for your actions.
Senator, I beg of you to reconsider. I have done nothing wrong, and I am confident that I can prove my innocence. Please, do not rush to judgment without giving me a chance to defend myself properly.
Caesar, we have made our decision. You will be held accountable for your actions, and there is nothing you can do to change that.

As I leave the Senate, I can feel the weight of their judgment bearing down on me. I know that I am innocent, but they have already made up their minds. I must find a way to clear my name and restore my honor, no matter what it takes.

setting: Caesar sits in his quarters in Cisalpine Gaul, deep in thought as he converses with his trusted advisor. The room is dimly lit, with only a few candles flickering on the table. Maps of Gaul and other territories adorn the walls, along with various weapons and armor. Caesar appears to be considering a potential shift in strategy in Gaul, his mind focused on the task at hand. His trusted advisor listens intently, awaiting Caesar's instructions.

dialogue.content: The senate may think they have me under their thumb, but they underestimate my power and influence. I have proven myself in Gaul, and they cannot deny my success. But I must remain vigilant, for my enemies are numerous and always seeking to undermine me. I must consider all options and be prepared to act quickly if necessary. Gaul is mine for the taking, and I will not let anyone stand in my way.

My dear advisor, I have been considering a potential shift in strategy in Gaul. Our current tactics have served us well, but I believe it is time to expand our reach and assert our dominance over the entire region. We must strike quickly and decisively, before our enemies have a chance to regroup and counter our moves.
Of course, my lord. What do you suggest we do?

We shall begin by launching a series of surprise attacks against key targets throughout Gaul. We will strike at their supply lines, their farms, and their cities. We will show them that we are not to be trifled with, and that we will stop at nothing to achieve our goals. We will bring the full force of Rome to bear upon them, and they will crumble before us.
But my lord, such actions could be seen as aggressive and could provoke a larger conflict. Are you sure this is wise?

I am more than sure. I am confident in our abilities and our strength. We have the support of the people, and we have the backing of the senate. We will not let anyone stand in our way. Prepare the troops, my friend. We march at dawn.

These are perilous times, and I must be cautious. But I cannot let fear dictate my actions. I have come too far and sacrificed too much to let anyone stop me now. Gaul is mine, and I will do whatever it takes to ensure its submission. The die has been cast, and I am ready to face whatever challenges lie ahead.

setting: In the midst of his praetorship, Julius Caesar attempted to strip Catulus of the honour of completing the rebuilt Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus by accusing him of embezzlement. However, he faced opposition from the people who voiced their disapproval of the proposal at a protest in the Forum. Caesar then supported a move to transfer the command against Catiline from the consul of 63 to Pompey, but this too was met with resistance from some quarters, particularly from the tribunes Cato and Quintus Minucius Thermus. A violent meeting of the comitia tributa ensued, and the senate ultimately passed a decree against tribune Metellus Nepos, who had proposed the transfer of command. Caesar distanced himself from the proposals, as he had other priorities such as securing a provincial command and repairing his relations with the aristocracy. He was also involved in the Bona Dea affair, in which Publius Clodius Pulcher had entered Caesar's house sacrilegiously during a female religious observance, causing Caesar to divorce his wife immediately.

dialogue.content: This opposition is becoming a nuisance. I thought I had made it clear that I will not tolerate any dissent. Catulus is not fit to complete the temple, and it's my duty to ensure that the people have the best representation. But these plebeians are making it difficult for me to achieve my goals. Perhaps it's time I took stronger measures to silence them. I must find a way to assert my authority without creating more enemies.

Fellow citizens, we cannot let Catiline continue to threaten our Republic. The consul of 63 has failed to take decisive action against him, and we need a more capable leader to command our forces. Pompey is the man for the job, and I implore you to support the transfer of command to him.
Nepos, you are a fool to think that Pompey can solve all our problems. We do not need a dictator to save us from ourselves. We need to uphold the values of our Republic and fight for what is right.
Cato is right. We cannot rely on one man to save us. We must work together to root out the corruption and treason that threatens our Republic. Nepos, your proposal is misguided and dangerous.

Gentlemen, please calm down. We are all on the same side here. I understand your concerns, but we must act quickly to prevent Catiline from causing more harm. Pompey has proven himself a capable leader, and I believe he can bring an end to this crisis. Let us put aside our differences and work together for the good of Rome.

These tribunes are becoming a thorn in my side. I must find a way to neutralize them without causing a public outcry. I cannot afford to lose support from the people, but I also cannot allow them to stand in the way of my ambitions. I must tread carefully and think strategically.

My fellow Romans, I come to you today to speak out against the injustice that has been done to me.
