I was wrongly accused of violating the sanctity of the Bona Dea festival, and I demand that my name be cleared. Caesar, you are a man of honor and integrity. Surely you can see that I am innocent and that my accusers are merely trying to besmirch my good name.

Publius, I sympathize with your plight, but I cannot involve myself in this matter. The Bona Dea festival is a sacred event, and any violation of its sanctity must be punished accordingly. I cannot condone such behavior, nor can I allow my reputation to be tarnished by association.

But Caesar, you know me. We have been friends for years. Surely you can vouch for my character and help me clear my name. I am but a victim of political intrigue, and I need your support to fight back.

This is not good. If I support Clodius, I will alienate myself from the aristocracy and lose their support. But if I refuse him, I risk making an enemy of a powerful man. I must find a way to appease him without compromising my own interests.

Publius, I understand your frustration, but I cannot get involved in this matter. It is best that we go our separate ways and let the law take its course. I wish you all the best in your endeavors, but I cannot offer you my support at this time.

I see. I had hoped for more from you, Caesar, but I understand your position. I will not forget this, however. You have made an enemy today, and I will not rest until I have cleared my name and taken revenge on those who have wronged me.

This is not over. I must be careful around Clodius, but I cannot let him undermine my authority. I will need to keep a close eye on him and make sure he does not pose a threat to my plans. Rome is a dangerous place, and I must be prepared for any eventuality.

setting: Julius Caesar has been co-opted into the pontifices in place of his deceased relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta. Then, he was elected one of the military tribunes for 71 BC. During his term, there is no evidence that Caesar served in war, but he did agitate for the removal of the Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for those who supported Lepidus' revolt to be pardoned. The next year, 70 BC, Pompey and Crassus were consuls and brought legislation restoring the plebeian tribunate's rights; one of the tribunes, with Caesar supporting, then brought legislation pardoning the Lepidan exiles.

dialogue.content: The pardoning of the Lepidan exiles was a necessary move. It might seem like a small victory, but it is a step towards a greater goal. The people of Rome must see me as a man of the people, not just another aristocrat. By supporting this legislation, I show that I am willing to stand up for the common people, even if it means going against the wishes of my fellow aristocrats. This move will help me gain more support and power in the future. I must continue to act in the interests of the people and gain their trust.

Senators, I bring before you a proposal for the pardoning of the Lepidan exiles. These are people who have been punished enough for their crimes. It is time to show mercy and grant them a second chance.

I strongly disagree. These exiles committed treason against Rome and they must pay the price for their actions. We cannot simply pardon them and hope that they will change their ways. They must suffer the consequences of their choices.

I understand your concerns, Senator. But we must also consider the impact of our actions on the people of Rome. The Lepidan exiles have already been punished for their crimes, and it is time to move on and focus on rebuilding our society. By pardoning them, we show that we are a merciful and just society, one that values forgiveness and second chances. This is what the people of Rome want and deserve.

I agree with Caesar. We must think of the greater good and the impact of our decisions on the people of Rome. The pardoning of the Lepidan exiles is a necessary step towards a more just and fair society.
I still disagree. But it seems that the majority is in favor of this proposal. I will not stand in the way of progress.

The opposition was expected, but I am pleased with the outcome. The pardoning of the Lepidan exiles is a small victory, but it is a step towards a greater goal. I must continue to think of ways to gain more support and power in the future. The people of Rome must see me as a man of the people, not just another aristocrat.

setting: The marketplace is bustling with activity as Julius Caesar mingles with the common citizens, listening to their needs and concerns. It is a bright, sunny day, and the air is filled with the sounds of people haggling over goods and vendors calling out their wares. Caesar is surrounded by his loyal guards, who keep a watchful eye on the crowd to ensure their leader's safety. As he walks through the market, Caesar greets people with a warm smile and a kind word, eager to hear what they have to say.

dialogue.content: As I walk through this marketplace, I am reminded of why I became a leader. It is not for the glory or the power, but for the people. They are my responsibility, and I must do all that I can to ensure their welfare. These people look up to me, trust me, and rely on me to lead them to a better future. I cannot disappoint them.
Caesar, we need help! Our farms are suffering from a drought, and our crops are dying. We cannot feed our families!
Do not worry, my friend. I will send aid to your village immediately. We will provide you with food and water until the drought passes. Your welfare is my top priority.
Caesar, we need protection! Bandits have been attacking our villages, and we are afraid for our lives!
I understand your concerns, and I promise you that I will send a legion to deal with these bandits. No citizen of Rome should feel unsafe in their own home. You have my word.

Is this the end? Have I failed my people? No, I cannot think like this. I have done all that I can. I have led with honor, courage, and compassion. My legacy will live on, and my people will remember me as a great leader. And perhaps, in some small way, I have made the world a better place.

setting: Caesar has brought in a bill to purchase property from willing sellers to distribute to Pompey's veterans and the urban poor. The bill would be administered by a board of twenty, Caesar would be excluded, and financed by Pompey's plunder and territorial gains. The senate was largely in favor of the bill, but Cato's filibustering prevented its passage. Caesar then moved the bill before the people, and Bibulus threatened a veto for the entire year. In response, a riot broke out, and Bibulus attempted to nullify the bill on grounds it was passed by violence and contrary to the auspices.

dialogue.content: I cannot believe the audacity of Bibulus to threaten a permanent veto of my bill. The people need this land reform, and I will not let Bibulus stand in the way. His actions are a direct violation of the people's legislative sovereignty, and I must find a way to overcome his obstructionism. The riot that broke out shows that the people are on my side, and I must use their support to push this bill through. I cannot let the Senate nullify the bill on false grounds, and I must find a way to combat Bibulus's attempts to undermine my magistracy.
I will not stand by and let this bill pass! It was passed by violence and is contrary to the auspices. The Senate must nullify this bill and uphold the sanctity of our legislative process.
I agree with Bibulus. This bill is nothing but a power grab by Caesar. We must stand firm and prevent him from enacting his radical agenda.
I support this bill and the distribution of land to my veterans and the urban poor. It is a fair and just proposal, and the people deserve this reform.

I will not let Bibulus and Cato stand in the way of progress. The people need this land reform, and I will not let their obstructionism prevent its passage. The Senate's refusal to nullify the bill shows that they support this reform, and I will use that support to push it through. The distribution of land to the veterans and urban poor is a fair and just proposal, and it is my duty as a magistracy to enact it. I will not let Bibulus's threats of veto undermine the people's legislative sovereignty.
I will not back down from my veto threat. This bill is a danger to our republic, and I will do everything in my power to prevent its passage.

Bibulus's stubbornness is a threat to the people's welfare. I must find a way to overcome his veto and ensure that this bill is passed. The people deserve this land reform, and I will not let Bibulus stand in the way of progress.
I urge the Senate to support this bill and the distribution of land to my veterans and the urban poor. It is a fair and just proposal, and it will benefit the people of Rome.
This bill is a threat to our republic. We must stand firm and prevent Caesar from enacting his radical agenda.

The people have spoken, and they demand this land reform. It is my duty as a magistracy to enact their will, and I will not let Bibulus's obstructionism stand in the way. The Senate must uphold the people's legislative sovereignty and pass this bill.
I will not be swayed by Caesar's threats and the people's demands. This bill is a danger to our republic, and I will do everything in my power to prevent its passage.

Bibulus's intransigence is a direct threat to the people's welfare. I must find a way to overcome his obstructionism and ensure that this bill is passed. The people deserve this land reform, and I will not let Bibulus stand in the way of progress.

setting: Julius Caesar, the powerful Roman general and politician, is currently at his villa in Rome, seeking support from several senators who are considered friendly to his cause. The political climate in Rome is tumultuous, with violent street clashes between Clodius and two tribunes who are friends of Cicero, who is supporting the allies. Caesar is aware of the opposition he faces in the senate and needs the support of his allies to prevent them from reassigning his command in Transalpine Gaul.

dialogue.content: Caesar sat at the head of the table, his eyes fixed on the group of senators before him. He knew that the success of his campaigns in Gaul had earned him the respect and admiration of his soldiers. Still, he needed the support of the senate to continue his military campaigns and secure his position in Rome. The thought of losing his command in Gaul filled him with dread. He had worked tirelessly to establish his reputation as a military leader, and he was not prepared to let his enemies take that away from him.
Caesar, we have heard of your recent victories in Gaul. Congratulations are in order!
Thank you, Senator. I appreciate your kind words. But I did not come here for congratulations. I need your support in the upcoming senate votes.
Of course, Caesar. We are your allies, and we will do everything in our power to help you secure your position in Rome.

Caesar smiled inwardly. He knew that these senators were loyal to him, but he needed more than just their support. He needed their influence in the senate, and he needed them to convince other senators to support him. He had faced opposition before, but this time, he knew that his enemies were more determined than ever to see him fall.
Caesar, we have been discussing your situation in the senate, and we believe that we can help you secure your command in Gaul. But we need to know what you plan to do with it.

Gentlemen, I plan to continue my campaigns in Gaul. There is still much work to be done there, and I believe that my soldiers and I can bring peace and prosperity to the region. But I need the support of the senate to do so.
Caesar, we understand your situation, but you must understand ours. The political climate in Rome is volatile, and we cannot be seen to be supporting a military dictator.

Caesar clenched his fists under the table. He knew that these senators were being cautious, but he needed them to take risks if he was to secure his position in Rome. He needed them to trust him and to believe that he was the only one who could bring stability to the region.

Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but I assure you that I have no intention of becoming a dictator. My only goal is to secure peace and prosperity for the people of Gaul and to protect the interests of Rome.
Caesar, we believe you. But we cannot make any promises until we have spoken to our colleagues in the senate. We will do our best to sway them in your favor, but we cannot guarantee anything.
I understand. But I urge you to act quickly. My enemies are watching my every move, and they will not hesitate to use any opportunity to undermine me.
Don't worry, Caesar. We will do everything in our power to help you. We understand the importance of your campaigns in Gaul, and we will not let you down.

Caesar nodded, feeling a sense of relief. He knew that these senators were his best hope for securing his position in Rome. But he also knew that he had to be patient and wait for the right moment to strike. He needed to bide his time and gather his allies, preparing for the inevitable showdown with his enemies. It was a time of great uncertainty and danger, but Caesar was determined to emerge victorious, no matter what it took.

setting: It was January 49 BC when Julius Caesar led his army, the Legio XIII Gemina, to cross the Rubicon, the river that marked the northern boundary of Italy. This was a response to the Senate's final decree, which declared Caesar an enemy of the state. Caesar's decision to cross the Rubicon ignited a civil war, causing panic among the senators and Pompey's supporters. Pompey, along with many senators, fled south, believing that Caesar was marching quickly for Rome. Caesar intercepted an important communication route to Rome, surprising a group of Pompey's soldiers and intercepting messages that showed Pompey's plan to flee to Greece. Caesar paused and opened negotiations, but they fell apart amid mutual distrust. Caesar responded by advancing south, seeking to capture Pompey to force a conference.

dialogue.content: This is it. The moment I have been preparing for. I have always known that the Senate would not let me keep my command of the army and that they would eventually declare me an enemy of the state. But I am not going to go down without a fight. I have the strongest army in Rome, and I will not let anyone take that away from me. I must act quickly to ensure victory.
My lord, we have intercepted a message from Pompey's camp. It appears that he is planning to flee to Greece.
Excellent work. We must act on this information immediately. Send scouts to find out Pompey's exact location and report back to me as soon as possible.
My lord, we have found Pompey's camp. He is planning to leave for Greece in a few days.
Good. We will surprise him before he has a chance to escape. Send word to the army to prepare for an attack. We will take Pompey by surprise and force him to negotiate with me.
My lord, what if Pompey refuses to negotiate?
Then we will destroy his army and capture him. I have no intention of letting him escape to Greece and regroup with his forces. This is a matter of honor, and I will not let him get away.

This is my chance to secure my position as the undisputed leader of Rome. If I can defeat Pompey and his army, I will be able to consolidate my power and ensure that no one challenges me again. But I must be careful not to underestimate him. Pompey is a skilled general, and he will not go down without a fight.
My lord, the army is ready to march.
Good. We will move out at dawn. Make sure that the men are well-rested and well-fed. We have a long march ahead of us, and we cannot afford any mistakes.

setting: In 57 BC, the relations between Pompey, Crassus, and Caesar turned sour when one of Pompey's allies opposed Caesar's land reform bill, and their allies performed poorly in the elections. With Caesar's command and acta at risk in 56 BC due to unfriendly consuls, he needed political support from his allies. Pompey and Crassus also wanted military commands, so they teamed up again, along with Appius Claudius Pulcher and his younger brother Clodius, to run for consulship in 54 BC. Their plan was to secure second consulships for Pompey and Crassus, followed by governorships in 55 BC, and extend Caesar's command for another five years.

dialogue.content: It's time to face the reality that my alliance with Pompey and Crassus has become fragile. The recent election results and the opposition to my land reform bill have weakened our bond. But I cannot afford to lose their support now, especially with the looming threat to my command and acta. I must find a way to persuade them to join forces with me again, even if it means making some concessions.

I think we need to reconsider our stance on Caesar's land reform bill. Yes, it may not be perfect, but we cannot afford to lose his support now. We have a bigger goal to achieve, which is securing our own military commands and extending Caesar's command. Let's put aside our differences and work together again.
I agree with Pompey. We should focus on the bigger picture and not let our personal opinions get in the way. Besides, we all know that Caesar is a valuable ally, and we cannot afford to lose him now.

I concur with my colleagues. We need to form a united front to achieve our goals. I believe that we can work with Caesar to make some compromises on his land reform bill without sacrificing our own interests.
I support my brother's position. We need to think strategically and not let our egos get in the way. Let's work with Caesar and secure our own positions.

I am relieved to see that my allies are willing to work with me again, but I must be cautious. I cannot let them take advantage of me or undermine my authority. I need to find a way to make them see the value of my command and acta, and convince them to support my land reform bill.

So, we have a plan. Let's work together to secure our own consulships and governorships, while extending Caesar's command. We can also make some compromises on his land reform bill to show our support. This is a win-win situation for all of us.
I agree. Let's put our plan into action and show the people of Rome that we are a united force to be reckoned with.
I am with you all the way. Let's make history together.
Let's do it!

I am relieved that my allies are back on my side, but I cannot let my guard down. I need to be vigilant and make sure that they do not betray me or my cause. This is a crucial moment for me and for Rome, and I must do everything in my power to secure my command and acta, and push through my land reform bill. I hope that my allies will stay loyal to me, but I must be prepared for any outcome.

setting: Caesar is in the Senate facing opposition to his political advancement. He has proposed a bill to purchase property from willing sellers to distribute to Pompey's veterans and the urban poor. However, there is little opposition, and the obstructionism that has occurred is largely unprincipled, firmly opposing it not on grounds of public interest but rather opposition to Caesar's political advancement. Unable to overcome Cato's filibustering, he moves the bill before the people, where his co-consul Bibulus threatens a permanent veto for the entire year. This clearly violates the people's well-established legislative sovereignty and triggers a riot in which his fasces are broken, symbolizing popular rejection of his magistracy. The bill is then voted through, but Bibulus attempts to induce the senate to nullify it on grounds it was passed by violence and contrary to the auspices; the senate refused.

dialogue.content: This opposition to my political advancement is becoming tiresome. I have done nothing but work for the betterment of the people, yet they resist me at every turn. But I will not be deterred. I will show them that I am the one who can bring about change and make the lives of the people better. This bill will do just that. I will not let Bibulus or any other obstructionist stand in my way. I will do what is necessary to push this bill through and show the people that I am their champion.

I will not stand for this. This bill is a violation of our traditions and our way of life. We cannot simply take property from willing sellers and give it to the poor. It is not our place to do so. And the violence that occurred during the public meeting is unacceptable. I will use my veto power to ensure that this bill does not pass.

I must agree with Bibulus. This bill is not in the best interest of the Republic. It sets a dangerous precedent and could lead to further abuses of power. We must uphold our traditions and our laws. We cannot simply do whatever Caesar wishes.

You both seem to forget that the people have spoken. They have voted for this bill, and it is our duty to carry out their wishes. You cannot simply ignore the will of the people because you disagree with it. That is not democracy. That is tyranny.

I refuse to be a party to this. I will not let you use the people's will as a shield to cover your own ambitions. This bill is not in the best interest of the Republic, and I will do everything in my power to stop it.
I must agree with Bibulus. We cannot simply ignore our traditions and our laws. We must uphold the principles that have guided us for centuries.

Your principles are nothing more than empty words. You use them to cover your own cowardice and lack of vision. But I will not be held back by your petty concerns. I will push this bill through, and I will show the people that I am the one who can make their lives better. You can stand in my way all you want, but you will not prevail. The people are with me, and I will not let them down.

setting: The Roman Senate is in session, with senators gathered in the Curia Julia. Julius Caesar stands in front of the Senate, defending his decision to cross the Rubicon and risk a civil war against the Republican forces. The Senate is divided over Caesar's actions, with some senators supporting him and others condemning him as a traitor. The tension is palpable as Caesar prepares to make his case before his peers.

dialogue.content: I cannot back down now. The die is cast, and I have crossed the Rubicon with my army to defend Rome against the corrupt Republican forces. I knew this would be a difficult battle, but I did not expect such fierce opposition from my fellow senators. I must convince them that my actions are in the best interests of Rome, and that I am not a traitor.

My fellow senators, I come before you today to defend my actions and the actions of my army. I understand that some of you may view me as a traitor, but I assure you that nothing could be further from the truth. I have crossed the Rubicon to defend Rome against the corrupt forces of the Republic, who seek to undermine our great city and its people.
How can you claim to defend Rome when you have raised an army against its government? Your actions are those of a tyrant, not a defender of the Republic!

These senators are blind to the truth. They do not see the corruption and decay that has infested the Republic. They cling to their power and privilege, even as the people suffer. I must make them understand that I am not a threat to the Republic, but its savior.

I understand your concerns, Senator, but I must remind you that the government you defend has become a shadow of its former self. The Senate has been corrupted by greed and ambition, and the people no longer have a voice in their own government. I have raised an army to defend the people of Rome, to restore their rights and freedoms, and to ensure that the Republic will endure.

But what of the laws and traditions of Rome? You have violated them by crossing the Rubicon and declaring war on your fellow citizens. How can we trust you to lead Rome when you have shown such disregard for its laws and customs?
These senators are grasping at straws. They cannot deny the truth of my words, so they attack me on technicalities. I must show them that my actions are not those of a criminal, but of a patriot.

I understand your concerns, Senator, but I ask you to consider the situation we face. The Republic is in crisis, and the only way to save it is to take bold and decisive action. I did not cross the Rubicon lightly, but out of necessity. I ask you to put aside your prejudices and join me in defending Rome against those who would destroy it.

But what of the consequences of your actions? If you succeed in defeating the Republican forces, what will prevent you from becoming a tyrant yourself? How can we trust you to uphold the ideals of the Republic when you have shown such contempt for its institutions?

These senators are stubborn and blind. They cannot see that the Republic is already dead, and that only a new order can save Rome. I must show them that I am not a threat to their power, but a partner in building a better future.

I understand your concerns, Senator, and I assure you that I have no desire for personal power or glory. I seek only to defend Rome and its people, to restore the greatness of our city, and to build a new order based on justice and freedom. I ask you to join me in this quest, to put aside your fears and prejudices, and to work together for the good of Rome.

setting: In 73 BC, Julius Caesar was co-opted into the pontifices while he was away from Rome. This happened when his relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta passed away. Caesar’s promotion was a clear indication of his bright future in politics, and he was regarded as a well-accepted member of the aristocracy. Eventually, Caesar returned to Rome and was elected one of the military tribunes in 71 BC. During his term, there is no evidence that Caesar served in any war, although the war on Spartacus was ongoing. However, he was known to advocate for the removal of the Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and for pardoning those who supported Lepidus' revolt. These advocacies were common and uncontroversial.

dialogue.content: As I look around me, I can't help but feel like I don't belong here. Sure, I come from a noble family, but I've always felt like an outsider amongst the aristocracy. Maybe it's because I don't share their love for tradition and their aversion to change. But I know that if I'm going to make a name for myself in politics, I need to play the game. And that means advocating for causes that are common and uncontroversial. It's not the most exciting way to make a difference, but it's a start.
Caesar, I can't thank you enough for your support in getting us pardoned. It means everything to me and my family.
It's the least I could do. I know how important it is to have the support of your fellow men, especially in times like these.
Caesar, I've been hearing good things about you. Your advocacy for the plebeian tribunate caught my attention. I believe we could work together to achieve great things.

Pompey is a shrewd politician, and I know that he sees something in me that he can use to his advantage. But I also know that I can use him to further my own goals. Working with him could be a great opportunity to make a real difference in Rome.
I second that, Caesar. I believe that together, we could accomplish great things for the Republic.
I'm honored to have your support, both of you. I believe that by working together, we can truly make a difference for Rome.

This is it. This is my chance to finally make a name for myself in politics. With the support of Pompey and Crassus, I can accomplish anything. But I need to be careful. I know that politics can be a dangerous game, and I can't let my guard down for a second.

setting: The scene unfolds in a grand Roman villa in Gaul, where Julius Caesar is socializing with a group of wealthy and influential Romans who have come to see his victories and establish their own interests in the conquered territories. The sun is setting, casting a warm glow over the patricians as they sip wine and discuss their future plans. Caesar, clad in his military regalia, sits at the head of the table, exuding an air of power and authority. The room is adorned with fine art and intricate mosaics, a testament to the wealth and taste of the host.

dialogue.content: As I sit here surrounded by these powerful men, I can feel their eyes on me, watching my every move. They are impressed by my military prowess, but they are also here to further their own interests. I must be careful not to reveal too much, for they are shrewd and cunning, and I cannot afford to let down my guard. But at the same time, I must keep them satisfied, for their support is crucial to my continued success. It is a delicate balance, one that I have become adept at maintaining over the years.
My dear Julius, I must say, your victories in Gaul have been nothing short of remarkable. It is a testament to your skill as a general and your dedication to Rome.
Thank you, Decimus. Your words are much appreciated. But I cannot take all the credit. My legions have fought bravely, and without their unwavering loyalty, I would not be where I am today.
Speaking of loyalty, Julius, I could not help but notice the vast riches that this land has to offer. Surely, there is enough to go around for all of us.
Are you suggesting that I should share the spoils of war with you, Lucius? I assure you, I have no intention of giving away what my legions have earned through their blood and sweat.
Of course not, my dear Julius. I would never suggest such a thing. But perhaps we could work together to expand our holdings and secure our positions in Rome.
I see what you're getting at, Lucius. And I agree that cooperation is key to our success. But let us not forget that we are all here to serve Rome, not our own selfish desires.

Speaking of cooperation, Julius, I have a proposition that I think you will find intriguing. You see, I have connections in the east, and I believe that together, we could expand our influence far beyond these borders.
Go on, Titus. I'm listening.
I propose that we form an alliance, you and I, and together we will conquer new lands and bring glory to Rome. With your military might and my political savvy, we could accomplish great things.
I must say, Titus, your proposal is tempting. But I must consider all the angles before I make a decision. I will need some time to think it over.

setting: Around 10 or 11 January 49 BC, Julius Caesar stood before his soldiers at the Rubicon River. The Senate had issued a final decree, demanding that Caesar disband his army and return to Rome as a private citizen. Caesar, however, had other plans. He intended to cross the Rubicon, the river marking the boundary of Italy, with a single legion, the Legio XIII Gemina, and ignite a civil war. As he addressed his soldiers, he declared the Senate's decree and his intentions to cross the river, seize Rome, and establish himself as the ruler of the Roman Republic.

dialogue.content: As I stand here before my soldiers, I cannot help but feel a sense of excitement and trepidation. The die has been cast, and there is no turning back now. This moment will go down in history, and I will either be remembered as a great leader or a foolish usurper. But I have no choice. The Senate has left me no other option. I must cross the Rubicon and take control of Rome if I am to secure my place in history and ensure the survival of the Republic. May the gods be with us.

My fellow soldiers, the time has come for us to make a stand. The Senate has issued a final decree, demanding that we disband our army and return to Rome as private citizens. But I ask you, what kind of Republic would Rome be if we were to submit to such tyranny? Are we not the defenders of the people's rights and freedoms? Are we not the ones who have fought and bled for Rome's glory? Yet, the Senate would have us lay down our arms and surrender our hard-won victories. I say to you, this is not the Rome we fought for. This is not the Rome we love. The time has come for us to take a stand, to cross the Rubicon, and seize Rome from those who would see it fall. Are you with me, soldiers of Rome?
We are with you, Caesar! To Rome! To victory!

This is madness, Caesar! You cannot cross the Rubicon and start a civil war. Think of the chaos and bloodshed that will ensue. Think of the innocent lives that will be lost. You must return to Rome and submit to the Senate's decree. It is the only way to prevent a disaster.

I understand your concerns, Pompey. But what choice do I have? The Senate has left me no other option. If I return to Rome, I will be arrested and executed. My army will be disbanded, and all our hard-won victories will be for nothing. Is that what you want, Pompey? To see all our sacrifices go to waste? I cannot submit to such tyranny. I must cross the Rubicon and take control of Rome. If you and the other senators wish to join me, then do so. But if not, then step aside and let us pass.
I cannot support this, Caesar. I must defend the Republic and uphold the laws of the land. I urge you to reconsider your actions and seek a peaceful resolution to this conflict.
I appreciate your concern, Pompey. But the time for talk is over. The die has been cast, and we must see this through to the end. Farewell, my friend. May the gods watch over you.

setting: During his praetorship, Caesar attempted to remove Catulus from completing the rebuilt Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and transfer the command against Catiline from Gaius Antonius Hybrida to Pompey. He supported the attempt by plebeian tribune Metellus Nepos, which led to a violent meeting in the forum where the senate passed a decree against Metellus. Caesar distanced himself from the proposals and focused on repairing relations with the aristocracy.

dialogue.content: I must secure a provincial command to increase my status and power. Supporting Nepos' attempt to transfer the command against Catiline to Pompey was a political move that could have benefitted me, but the violent meeting in the forum and the resulting decree against Nepos and myself has damaged my reputation. I must be careful in my actions and alliances moving forward.

Caesar, your accusations against me are baseless. I have not embezzled any funds and have worked diligently on the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus. I urge the senate to dismiss these claims and allow me to continue my work.

I am honored by Nepos' proposal to transfer the command against Catiline to me, but I must decline. I am currently occupied with my own military campaigns and cannot take on additional responsibilities at this time.
I propose that the command against Catiline be transferred from Gaius Antonius Hybrida to Pompey. He has proven himself as a capable leader and will be able to handle this crisis effectively.

This proposal is outrageous! It is a blatant attempt to consolidate power in the hands of Pompey and undermine the authority of the consul. We must reject this proposal and uphold the laws and traditions of our republic.
I am the consul and I demand that I retain the command against Catiline. It is my duty to protect the republic and I will not allow anyone to interfere with my responsibilities.
I agree with Cato. This proposal is an attack on our democratic values and must be stopped. We cannot allow one man to hold too much power.

I support Nepos' proposal to transfer the command against Catiline to Pompey. It is clear that the current consul is not capable of handling this crisis and we need a strong leader to take charge. Pompey has proven himself in battle and can bring an end to this rebellion quickly.
Some senators nod in agreement with Caesar's words, while others shake their heads in disapproval. The room is filled with tension and uncertainty as they consider the proposal.

I must make a bold move to secure a provincial command. Supporting Nepos' proposal may have been a risk, but it was necessary to show my political power. I will need to repair my relationships with the aristocracy and gain their support if I am to achieve my goals.
I have evidence that Caesar's wife was involved in the Bona Dea scandal. She must be punished for her sacrilege.
My wife has done nothing wrong. I will not allow these baseless accusations to tarnish her reputation. I will divorce her immediately to prove her innocence and uphold the honor of my family.
Some senators whisper in disbelief, while others nod in approval. The scandal has caused a stir in the senate and threatens to damage Caesar's reputation further.

Divorcing my wife was a difficult decision, but it was the right one. I cannot allow this scandal to tarnish my reputation, especially if I am to secure a provincial command. I must be decisive in my actions and show that I am a strong leader who can maintain order in the republic.

setting: Caesar is seated in his villa in Rome, surrounded by his trusted editors. The room is dimly lit, with only a few candles flickering on the table. The air is thick with the smell of ink and parchment. The editors are gathered around Caesar, eagerly waiting for his instructions on the publication and distribution of his Commentaries on his campaigns in Gaul.

dialogue.content: I must ensure that my Commentaries are widely read by the people of Rome. They must understand the importance of my campaigns in Gaul and the victories I have won for the glory of Rome. My reputation is at stake, and I cannot afford any mistakes in the publication and distribution of my work.

Gentlemen, I have called you here today to discuss the publication and distribution of my Commentaries on my campaigns in Gaul. As you know, these writings are of utmost importance to me and to the glory of Rome. I must ensure that they are widely read and appreciated by the people of Rome. Therefore, I need your help in making sure that these writings reach every corner of the city.
Of course, Caesar. We are at your service. How would you like us to proceed?

I want you to make sure that every literate person in Rome has access to my Commentaries. I want them to be translated into every language spoken in the city, so that even those who do not speak Latin can understand the significance of my campaigns. I want them to be distributed in every major library and bookstore in the city, and I want them to be available for purchase at a reasonable price.
Understood, Caesar. We will work tirelessly to ensure that your Commentaries are a success. Is there anything else you would like us to do?

These editors are loyal to me, but I must make sure that they understand the gravity of this task. I must impress upon them the importance of my Commentaries and the consequences if they fail in their duties.

I cannot stress enough the importance of this task. If my Commentaries are not widely read and appreciated, it will reflect poorly on me and on the glory of Rome. I expect nothing but the best from you, and I will hold you accountable if anything goes wrong.
We understand, Caesar. We will not disappoint you.
Rest assured, Caesar. We will do everything in our power to make sure that your Commentaries are a success.

These editors are capable, but I must make sure that they are working efficiently and effectively. I must give them specific instructions and deadlines, so that they understand the urgency of this task.

I want you to start working on the translations immediately. I want them to be completed within the next month. I want you to personally oversee the distribution of the Commentaries to the major libraries and bookstores in the city. I want them to be available for purchase within the next two months. Is that clear?
Absolutely, Caesar. We will get to work immediately.
You can count on us, Caesar. We will make sure that your Commentaries are a success.
I must make sure that these editors are motivated and inspired to do their best. I must give them praise and rewards if they succeed, and punishment if they fail.
Good. I expect nothing but the best from you. If you succeed in this task, you will be rewarded handsomely. But if you fail, there will be consequences. Do not disappoint me.
You can count on us, Caesar. We will not let you down.
We will work tirelessly to ensure that your Commentaries are a success, Caesar.
I have given them specific instructions and deadlines. Now it is up to them to deliver. I must trust that they will do their best and hope for the best outcome. The glory of Rome depends on it.

setting: The scene is set in the Senate where Caesar has brought in a bill to purchase property from willing sellers to distribute to Pompey's veterans and the urban poor, administered by a board of twenty, excluding Caesar and financed by Pompey's plunder and territorial gains. The bill is brought in hopes that the Senate would take up the matter to show its beneficence for the people.

dialogue.content: I am confident that this bill will pass with little opposition. The people deserve to benefit from Pompey's plunder and territorial gains, and it is my duty as a leader to ensure that they do. I cannot let the obstructionism of some senators stand in the way of progress. I must find a way to overcome their objections.
I firmly oppose this bill, not on grounds of public interest, but rather opposition to Caesar's political advancement. We cannot allow him to use this bill to further his own agenda.
I also oppose this bill. It goes against the very foundations of our government. We must not be swayed by populist policies that undermine the authority of the Senate.

Gentlemen, I understand your concerns, but this bill is for the benefit of the people. We must put aside our political differences and work together for the greater good. I urge you to support this bill and show the people that the Senate is accountable to them.
I will not allow this bill to be passed. I will use my veto to stop it from becoming law.
Bibulus's threat of a permanent veto is a clear violation of the people's legislative sovereignty. I cannot let him stand in the way of progress. I must find a way to overcome his obstructionism.

Gentlemen, I understand that there are concerns about this bill, but we cannot let one man stand in the way of progress. The people deserve to benefit from Pompey's plunder and territorial gains, and it is our duty to ensure that they do. I propose that we take this bill to the people and let them decide if it should become law.
That is an unprecedented move, Caesar. We cannot allow the people to override the authority of the Senate.
The people have the right to decide on matters that affect them directly. This bill will benefit them, and they deserve to have a say in whether it becomes law. I urge you to consider this proposal.
I will not allow this bill to become law. I will use every means at my disposal to stop it.
Bibulus's obstructionism is becoming a problem. I must find a way to overcome it and ensure that this bill becomes law.
Gentlemen, the people have spoken. They have voted overwhelmingly in favor of this bill becoming law. I urge you to respect their decision and support this bill.
I refuse to acknowledge the legitimacy of this vote. It was passed by violence and contrary to the auspices. The Senate must nullify it.
Bibulus's attempts to nullify the vote are futile. The people have spoken, and their voice cannot be silenced. I must ensure that this bill becomes law and that the people benefit from it.

Gentlemen, the people have spoken, and their voice cannot be silenced. This bill will become law, and the people will benefit from it. I urge you to accept the will of the people and support this bill.
We accept the will of the people, and we will support this bill becoming law.

I have overcome the obstructionism of some senators, and this bill will become law. The people will benefit from it, and I have shown that I am a leader who is willing to fight for their rights. This is just the beginning of my plans for the people of Rome.

setting: The year is 52 BC, and Julius Caesar has successfully subdued the Gallic tribes after years of bloody warfare. He now stands before a group of Gallic leaders who have surrendered to him and seeks to convince them to submit to Roman rule. Caesar is a tall, imposing figure with sharp features and piercing eyes. He is dressed in his finest armor and carries himself with the confidence of a man who has never known defeat. The Gallic leaders are a mix of young and old, their faces etched with worry and fear. They are dressed in simple tunics and stand huddled together, unsure of what to expect from the conqueror before them. The air is thick with tension as Caesar prepares to address the group.

dialogue.content: These Gallic tribes have caused me no end of trouble over the years. They have fought valiantly and with great ferocity, but in the end, they are no match for the might of Rome. It is time to show them that their best hope for survival lies in submitting to our rule. They must understand that they will be treated fairly and justly, and that they will enjoy peace and prosperity under our protection. I must convince these leaders to see reason and accept Roman rule. Failure is not an option.

My dear friends, I come to you today not as a conqueror, but as a liberator. The might of Rome has triumphed over the forces of barbarism, and it is time for us to move forward together as partners in peace and prosperity. I know that many of you may be hesitant to submit to our rule, but I assure you that you have nothing to fear. We will treat you with the respect and dignity that you deserve, and we will work together to build a brighter future for all of us.

We have seen the might of Rome, and we know that we are no match for your armies. But why should we submit to your rule? We have always governed ourselves, and we have no desire to become slaves to your empire.

I understand your concerns, my friend. But I assure you that our rule will be fair and just. You will have the opportunity to participate in the governance of your people, and your rights and traditions will be respected. In return, you will enjoy the protection and benefits of Roman citizenship. Together, we can create a better future for all of us.
But what of our gods and our culture? Will they be respected under Roman rule?

Of course, my friend. We have a long tradition of respecting the beliefs and traditions of the people we conquer. You will be free to worship as you please, and your cultural heritage will be preserved. We are not here to destroy your way of life, but to enrich it with the benefits of Roman civilization.
But what if we refuse to submit to your rule? What then?

I hope it does not come to that, my friend. But if you refuse our offer of partnership, we will have no choice but to subjugate you by force. It is a path that I would prefer to avoid, but one that I will take if necessary. I urge you to see reason and accept our offer of peace and prosperity.
And what of our people who fought against you? Will they be punished?

I harbor no ill will towards those who have fought against us. They were merely defending what they believed in, and I respect that. I will pardon all those who surrender to us, and they will be given the opportunity to live under Roman rule. Those who continue to resist, however, will be dealt with harshly. It is up to you to decide the fate of your people.

I can see that my words have had an effect on these Gallic leaders. They are starting to understand that their best hope for survival lies in submitting to Roman rule. I must continue to press my advantage and convince them that their future lies with us. Failure is not an option.
We will consider your offer, Caesar. But we must consult with our people before we make a decision. We cannot simply surrender without their consent.

Of course, my friend. I understand that this is a difficult decision for you to make. Take all the time you need to consult with your people. But remember, the longer you delay, the greater the risk to your people. I urge you to make a decision quickly, before it is too late.
We will take your words into consideration, Caesar. But we cannot promise anything at this time.
I understand, my friend. But I hope that you will see the wisdom of our offer. Together, we can build a better future for all of us. May the gods guide your decision.
We will pray on it, Caesar. And we will let you know our decision in due time.
Very well, my friend. I look forward to hearing from you. Until then, may the gods watch over you and your people.

I have done all that I can for now. The rest is up to the Gallic leaders. But I am confident that they will see the wisdom of our offer and choose to submit to Roman rule. It is the only logical choice.

setting: The scene is set in the Roman Senate. Politics in Rome is tense, with violent street clashes between Clodius and two tribunes who were friends of Cicero, now supporting the allies. Caesar has sent news of his victories in Gaul to Rome, along with the claim of total victory and pacification. The senate at Cicero's motion voted him an unprecedented fifteen days of thanksgiving. Caesar needs these reports to prevent the senate from reassigning his command in Transalpine Gaul, even if his position in Cisalpine Gaul and Illyricum was guaranteed by the lex Vatinia until 54 BC.

dialogue.content: As I stand before the Roman Senate today, I cannot help but feel a sense of pride and accomplishment. My victories in Gaul have secured Rome's borders and expanded her dominance in the region. Yet, I know that there are still those who oppose me, who seek to undermine my authority and challenge my command. I must use all of my skills as an orator and politician to win the support of these senators and secure my position in the Republic.

Senators, we are here today to hear from our esteemed general, Julius Caesar, on matters of great importance to the Republic. Caesar has achieved great victories in Gaul and has secured our borders against our enemies. His leadership and bravery have been an inspiration to us all. I move that we hear from him now and give him the respect that he deserves.

Senators, I bring you news of my victories in Gaul. The Gallic Wars were long and difficult, but we have emerged victorious. The Gauls are now our allies, and Rome's borders are secure. We have expanded our territory and our influence, and we must continue to do so if we are to maintain our dominance in the region. I urge you, Senators, to support me in this endeavor, to give me the resources and the men I need to continue to expand Rome's power.

Caesar, we have heard of your victories in Gaul, and we congratulate you on your success. But we must also consider the cost of these wars. The lives lost, the resources expended, the damage done to the people of Gaul. Is it worth it to continue this expansion at any cost? Shouldn't we be focusing on the needs of our own people, on improving their lives and their prospects, rather than on conquest and domination?

Brutus, I understand your concerns, and I share them. But we must also consider the long-term benefits of this expansion. By securing our borders and expanding our territory, we ensure the safety and prosperity of our people. We create new opportunities for trade and commerce, for cultural exchange and intellectual growth. We build a legacy that will last for generations, that will be remembered long after we are gone. Is that not worth the cost?

Caesar, we have heard your arguments before. You speak of expansion and conquest, of securing our borders and building a legacy. But what of the cost to our Republic, to our democracy, to our very way of life? You seek to amass power and authority, to become a king or a tyrant, to rule over us rather than to serve us. We cannot allow that to happen. We must resist your attempts to undermine our democracy and our freedoms.

Cato, I assure you, I have no desire to become a king or a tyrant. I seek only to serve Rome and her people, to secure our borders and expand our influence. I do not seek power for its own sake, but for the good that it can do. I urge you, Senators, to trust me, to support me, to work with me to build a better future for all of us.

setting: The scene is set in the Rome Senate, where Julius Caesar is proposing his plan to restore his family's public monuments. The Senate is voting on this proposal, and there are objections from Catulus. This is happening four years after Caesar's aunt Julia's funeral, in 65 BC, when he served as curule aedile and staged lavish games that won him further attention and popular support. Caesar has also restored the trophies won by Marius, and taken down by Sulla, over Jugurtha and the Cimbri. According to Plutarch's narrative, the trophies were restored overnight to the applause and tears of joy of the onlookers.

dialogue.content: I cannot let Catulus and his objections hinder my plan to restore my family's public monuments. It is my duty as a member of the aristocracy to uphold the virtue of pietas and maintain my family's legacy. I must convince the Senate of the importance of this restoration and gain their support.
Caesar, I object to your proposal. It is not appropriate for you to use public funds to restore your family's monuments. The state should not be responsible for your personal matters.

Respected members of the Senate, I understand Catulus's concerns, but I must remind you all that my family has a long history of serving the Republic. It is only right that we restore our public monuments to their former glory. I have already restored the trophies won by Marius, which were taken down by Sulla. The people were overjoyed to see these symbols of our past glory returned to their rightful place. I believe that restoring my family's public monuments will have a similar effect. It will remind the people of the great deeds my family has accomplished in service to the Republic and inspire them to continue in that tradition.
But Caesar, you are a man of great wealth. Surely you could afford to restore your family's monuments without the help of the state?

Indeed, I could afford it. But it is not just about the money. It is about the symbolism of restoring these monuments. It is about upholding the virtue of pietas and showing the people that their leaders care about the past as well as the future. I believe that this restoration is a necessary step in ensuring the continued greatness of the Republic.
Caesar makes a compelling argument. We should not let personal animosity get in the way of doing what is right for the Republic. I support this proposal.

I have successfully convinced the Senate of the importance of this restoration. It is a small victory, but it is a step towards cementing my place as a leader of the Republic. I will continue to work towards the betterment of the state and the people.

setting: It is 57 BC, and the relations between Caesar, Pompey, and Crassus have broken down. One of Pompey's allies challenged Caesar's land reform bill, and the allies performed poorly in the elections that year. Caesar faces a real threat to his command and acta, and he needs his allies' political support. Pompey and Crassus also want military commands and they pooled their political resources again. They plan to draw in the support of Appius Claudius Pulcher and his younger brother Clodius for the consulship of 54 BC. They plan second consulships with following governorships in 55 BC for both Pompey and Crassus, along with a five-year extension of Caesar's command.

dialogue.content: This is an extremely precarious situation. I cannot afford to lose the support of my allies, yet I cannot let them overpower me either. The threat to my command and acta is real, and I need to act fast. I must convince Pompey and Crassus to support me and extend my command, but I must also ensure that I maintain my power and influence. The Pulchers can be useful allies, but they may also pose a threat to my position. I need to tread carefully here and plan my moves strategically.

Caesar, we are willing to support you, but we also have our own interests to consider. We want military commands, and we want them soon. We have pooled our resources to help secure the consulship of 54 BC for us both and to extend your command for five more years. But we need your assurance that you will not stand in our way.

Pompey is right, Caesar. We need to work together to achieve our goals. We have the support of the Pulchers, and we plan to use it to our advantage. But we need your support as well. We cannot afford to be divided at this crucial juncture.

I understand your concerns, Pompey and Crassus. I am willing to support your military commands, but we need to work out the details carefully. I also need your support to extend my command. The Pulchers can be useful allies, but we need to be careful not to give them too much power. We must work together to maintain our positions of influence and power.

Gentlemen, I am pleased to offer my support to your cause. My brother and I are willing to work with you to secure the consulship of 54 BC and to extend Caesar's command. But we also have our own interests to consider. We want to ensure that we have a say in the affairs of Rome, and we want to use our influence to further our own goals.

I agree with my brother, Appius. We are willing to work with you, but we also want to ensure that our interests are protected. We want to use our influence to help the people of Rome, and we want to ensure that their voices are heard. We believe that Caesar's land reform bill is a step in the right direction, and we are willing to support it.

The Pulchers can be useful allies, but they are also ambitious and can be a threat to my position. I need to be careful not to give them too much power, but I also need to maintain their support. I must find a way to balance their interests with mine and ensure that I remain in control. The extension of my command is crucial, and I must do everything in my power to ensure that it is granted.

Caesar, we need to finalize our plans soon. The elections are coming up, and we need to ensure that we have the support of the people. We have the support of the Pulchers, and we have your support as well. But we must also ensure that we have the support of the other senators. We cannot afford to be divided at this crucial juncture.

Pompey is right, Caesar. We need to start working on our campaigns and securing the support of the people. We have the resources and the influence to make it happen, but we need to act fast. The future of Rome depends on our success.

I agree, Pompey and Crassus. We need to start working on our campaigns and securing the support of the people. We have the support of the Pulchers, and we have the resources and the influence to make it happen. But we must also ensure that we maintain our positions of power and influence. We cannot afford to be divided at this crucial juncture.

Gentlemen, I am confident that we can work together to achieve our goals. We have the support of the people, and we have the resources and the influence to make it happen. But we must also be careful not to overstep our bounds. We must work together to ensure that the interests of Rome are protected.

I agree with my brother, Appius. We must work together to ensure that the interests of Rome are protected. We have the support of the people, and we have the resources and the influence to make it happen. But we must also be mindful of the other senators. We cannot afford to alienate them at this crucial juncture.

The Pulchers can be useful allies, but I must be careful not to give them too much power. I need to work with Pompey and Crassus to ensure that we maintain our positions of power and influence. The extension of my command is crucial, and I must do everything in my power to ensure that it is granted. The future of Rome depends on our success, and I cannot afford to fail.

setting: The Roman Forum was filled with tension as Caesar and his rivals sparred over the allocation of state funds for his growing army. With politics in Rome falling into violent street clashes between Clodius and two tribunes who were friends of Cicero, the atmosphere was charged with animosity and trepidation. Caesar had sent news of his victories in Gaul along with the claim of total victory and pacification to prevent the senate from reassigning his command in Transalpine Gaul. His success had been recognized when the senate voted state funds for some of Caesar's legions, which until this time Caesar paid for personally. However, his opponents remained skeptical and were determined to undermine his power and influence.

dialogue.content: The tension in the air was palpable as I stood before the senate, my rivals eyeing me with suspicion and contempt. I knew that they were determined to undermine my power and influence, to strip me of my command in Transalpine Gaul and leave me vulnerable to their attacks. But I was not afraid. I had proven myself on the field of battle, and I knew that I had the support of the people. All I needed was to convince the senate of the importance of my mission, to persuade them to allocate the funds necessary to continue my campaign in Gaul. And I was confident that I could do just that.

Caesar, we appreciate your service to Rome, but we cannot continue to fund your campaign in Gaul indefinitely. The state has other priorities, other needs that must be addressed. We cannot simply give you a blank check and trust that you will use the funds wisely. We need assurances, guarantees that our money will not be wasted.

I agree with Cicero. We cannot allow one man to have so much power, so much influence over the affairs of Rome. We must ensure that our resources are used for the good of the state, not for the glory of Caesar.

But we must also consider the consequences of denying Caesar the funds he needs. He has proven himself to be a capable leader, a skilled general. If we cut off his funding, we risk losing all that he has gained in Gaul. We risk leaving ourselves vulnerable to the barbarian tribes who would surely take advantage of our weakness.

I understand your concerns, my esteemed colleagues, but I assure you that the funds I request are necessary for the continued success of my campaign. I have already achieved great victories in Gaul, victories that have brought honor and glory to Rome. But there is still much work to be done. The barbarians are not yet fully pacified, and there are still pockets of resistance that must be dealt with. If we do not act now, if we do not provide the necessary resources, we risk losing all that we have gained.

But how can we be sure that you will not misuse the funds, that you will not use them for personal gain? We have seen too many times how power corrupts even the most noble of men. We cannot simply take your word for it.

I understand your skepticism, Cicero. But I have never given you reason to doubt my loyalty to Rome. I have always put the interests of the state first, even when it meant risking my own life. I pledge to you now that I will use these funds for the good of Rome, for the continuation of our glorious republic. I will not let you down.
But what of your growing army, Caesar? How do we know that you will not use it to seize power, to become a tyrant like Sulla before you?

My army is a necessary tool for achieving victory in Gaul, nothing more. I have no desire for power, for wealth, for glory. All I want is to serve Rome, to make her great again. And I can only do that with your support, with the funds necessary to continue my campaign in Gaul.

I believe that Caesar speaks the truth. He has proven himself to be a loyal servant of Rome, a capable leader who has brought honor and prestige to our great nation. We must trust in him, in his vision for the future of Rome. We must provide him with the funds he needs to continue his campaign in Gaul.

I am not convinced, but I will defer to the wisdom of my colleagues. If the senate votes to allocate the funds to Caesar, I will not oppose it. But I will be watching, Caesar. I will be watching very closely.

As I left the senate, I breathed a sigh of relief. I had done it. I had convinced them to allocate the funds I needed to continue my campaign in Gaul. But I knew that the battle was far from over. My rivals would continue to plot against me, to undermine my power and influence. I would have to stay vigilant, to remain ever watchful for any signs of treachery or deceit. But I was ready. I was Caesar, the greatest general Rome had ever known. And I would not be defeated, not by my enemies, nor by my own doubts and fears.

setting: Julius Caesar, a member of the aristocracy, was co-opted into the pontifices in 73 BC while absent from Rome. He returned shortly thereafter and was elected one of the military tribunes for 71 BC. Caesar had great future prospects in his political career and was well-accepted by the aristocracy.

dialogue.content: I must continue to build my reputation and gain support from the people. The aristocracy's acceptance is not enough. I need to advocate for the people to gain their favor.

Greetings, Caesar. I heard about your advocacy for the removal of Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate and pardoning the Lepidan exiles. It was a wise move to gain the support of the people.
Thank you, Pompey. I believe it is essential to advocate for the people's rights and show them that we, as their leaders, care for their welfare.
I agree with Caesar. We must do what we can to gain the people's support. Without them, we have nothing.
Pompey and Crassus are powerful allies. Their support will be beneficial in my future political endeavors.
Caesar, thank you for supporting the legislation to pardon the Lepidan exiles. I am forever grateful for your help.
It was the right thing to do, Lepidus. We must show mercy and compassion, even to those who have made mistakes.
I couldn't agree more. Your actions have earned my loyalty, Caesar.
Lepidus' loyalty will be valuable in the future. It's essential to build alliances with those who can benefit me in the long run.
Caesar, I heard about your advocacy for the people's rights. I must say, I am impressed.
Thank you, Cicero. I believe it's crucial to show the people that we, as their leaders, are fighting for their welfare.
I couldn't agree more. We must lead by example and show the people that we are worthy of their support.
Cicero is a powerful orator and a well-respected member of the Senate. His support will be beneficial in gaining the people's favor.
Caesar, I must say, I don't agree with your advocacy for the plebeian tribunate and the Lepidan exiles.
I understand your concerns, Brutus. But we must show compassion and mercy to those who have made mistakes. It's essential to lead by example and not be ruled by vengeance.
I see your point, Caesar. But I fear that showing mercy will only lead to weakness.
Compassion and mercy are not a sign of weakness, Brutus. They are a sign of strength and leadership.
Brutus is a powerful ally, but his disagreement with my advocacy may cause problems in the future. I must tread carefully and not let our differences get in the way of our alliance.

setting: Julius Caesar, the Roman dictator, is sitting in the Roman theater with actors and playwrights. They are discussing the incorporation of the new Julian calendar system into their performances. The year is 45 BC, and the calendar has just been introduced to align with the seasons.

dialogue.content: The new calendar system is a significant achievement for me and my empire. It will bring order and stability to the chaos that existed before. However, I need to ensure that everyone understands how important this change is and how it affects them. The theater is a perfect platform to convey this message to the people.
Your highness, we are honored to be here with you today. We understand that the calendar system has changed, but we are not sure how it affects our performances. Can you please explain it to us?

Of course, my dear actor. The new Julian calendar has 365 days, with an extra day added every four years. This system will help align the calendar with the seasons, making it easier for farmers to know when to plant and harvest their crops. It will also help in scheduling our festivals and events. Therefore, I want all of you to make sure that the new calendar system is incorporated into your plays and performances.
Your highness, we will make sure that the new calendar system is a part of our plays. However, we are not sure how to do it. Can you give us some ideas?
I need to come up with some innovative ideas to help them incorporate the new calendar system into their plays. Let me think.

I have an idea. Why don't you start your plays by mentioning the date and the month? For example, you can say, 'It is the Ides of March, 45 BC.' This will help the audience understand the timeline of the play and how it aligns with the new calendar system.
Your highness, that is an excellent idea. We will make sure to include the date and month in our performances.
I am pleased with their response. But I need to make sure that they understand how important this change is for the empire.

I want all of you to understand that this calendar system is not just a change in the way we keep track of time. It is a significant achievement for our empire. It shows the world that we are ahead of our time, and we are capable of making changes that will benefit our people. I want all of you to convey this message to your audience. Make them understand how important this change is for our empire.
Your highness, we understand. We will make sure that our plays convey this message to the audience.
I am pleased with their response. They understand the importance of this change, and I am confident that they will convey this message to the people.
I am glad that we are all on the same page. I want to thank all of you for your time and effort. Let us work together to make our empire great.

setting: In 73 BC, Caesar's relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta passed away. Caesar, who was absent from Rome at the time, was co-opted into the pontifices in place of his deceased relative, marking him as a well-accepted member of the aristocracy with great future prospects in his political career. Caesar decided to return shortly thereafter and on his return was elected one of the military tribunes for 71 BC. There is no evidence that Caesar served in war during his term.

dialogue.content: The death of my relative Gaius Aurelius Cotta was a great loss to me. However, his passing allowed me to take his place in the pontifices, which has only further solidified my position in the aristocracy. It is important for me to continue to climb the political ladder and gain more power and influence. I must carefully consider my next move to ensure that I am making the right decisions to further my career.

I believe it is time to agitate for the removal of Sulla's disabilities on the plebeian tribunate. It is a common and uncontroversial advocacy that will show my support for the people and help me gain more favor in the political sphere.
I agree with Caesar. It is time to restore the plebeian tribunate's rights and show the people that we are willing to work for their benefit.
I also support this legislation. It is crucial that we work together to ensure that the people's voices are heard and that their rights are protected.
With Caesar's support, I am bringing forth legislation to pardon the Lepidan exiles. It is time for them to return to Rome and live their lives without fear of persecution.

By supporting the restoration of the plebeian tribunate's rights and the pardon of the Lepidan exiles, I am further ingratiating myself to the people and showing them that I am on their side. This will only serve to increase my power and influence in the political sphere. I must continue to carefully consider my actions and make decisions that will benefit me and further my career.

setting: The forum is filled with tension as opposition to Caesar and Metellus Nepos' proposals are disputed by their supporters. Caesar attempted to deprive his enemy Catulus of the honour of completing the rebuilt Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus, accusing him of embezzling funds and threatening to bring legislation to reassign it to Pompey. This proposal was quickly dropped amid near-universal opposition. He then supported the attempt by plebeian tribune Metellus Nepos to transfer the command against Catiline from the consul of 63, Gaius Antonius Hybrida, to Pompey. After a violent meeting of the comitia tributa in the forum, where Metellus came into fisticuffs with his tribunician colleagues Cato and Quintus Minucius Thermus, the senate passed a decree against Metellus.

dialogue.content: This is not going according to plan. I had hoped to gain the support of the people and further cement my position of power. But it seems that my proposals have been met with fierce opposition. I must find a way to regain the favor of the people and repair my relations with the aristocracy. The Bona Dea affair has also caused me much trouble. I had to divorce my wife to avoid being implicated in Clodius' sacrilegious actions. But I cannot let this setback deter me. I must find a way to come out on top.

My fellow Romans, I implore you to support my proposal to transfer the command against Catiline to Pompey. As you all know, Catiline is a threat to the very fabric of our society. We must act swiftly and decisively to quell this rebellion. Pompey is the man for the job. He has proven himself time and time again on the battlefield. Do not let personal politics get in the way of doing what is best for our Republic.

Nepos, your proposal is nothing but a thinly veiled attempt to further Caesar's ambitions. We all know that Caesar is behind this. He seeks to gain even more power and influence by aligning himself with Pompey. This must not be allowed to happen. We must stand firm and oppose this proposal at all costs.

Cato is right. Nepos, you are nothing but a pawn in Caesar's game. Do not let yourself be used in this way. We must stand up to Caesar and his cronies. We must protect the Republic from those who seek to undermine it.

My fellow Romans, I understand your concerns. But I assure you that my only goal is to serve the Republic. The transfer of command to Pompey is necessary to ensure the safety and security of our people. Let us put aside our differences and work together for the greater good. Together, we can overcome any obstacle.

Caesar, your proposal to reassign the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus to Pompey is a blatant abuse of power. The people of Rome will not stand for this. We demand that you withdraw your proposal immediately.

Catulus, I understand your concerns. But I assure you that my only goal is to ensure that the temple is completed in a timely manner. Pompey has the resources and expertise to make this happen. Let us work together to achieve this goal.
Caesar is right. We must put aside our personal politics and work for the good of the Republic. Let us support this proposal and ensure that Catiline is defeated once and for all.
Nepos, you are a fool. Don't you see that Caesar is using you to further his own ambitions? We must stand up to him and protect the Republic from his tyranny.
Cato is right. We cannot let Caesar and his cronies take control of our Republic. We must oppose this proposal and protect our democracy.

These fools do not understand the necessity of my proposals. They are blinded by their own ambitions and fail to see the bigger picture. But I will not be deterred. I will find a way to gain their support and further my own ambitions. The Republic will be mine.

setting: The Roman Forum is filled with the sound of clashing factions as politics in Rome turn violent. The two tribunes who were friends of Cicero now support the allies, while Clodius leads his own supporters. All the while, Caesar and his rivals clash over the administration of provinces and the role of military leaders in civilian politics. Caesar has sent news of his victories in Gaul along with the claim of total victory and pacification. The senate, at Cicero's motion, has voted him an unprecedented fifteen days of thanksgiving. Caesar's success is recognised, and the senate has even voted state funds for some of his legions, which until this time he paid for personally. However, despite his successes, Caesar's position in Transalpine Gaul remains under threat from senatorial opponents, and he must wield all his political power to prevent them from reassigning his command.

dialogue.content: This is the moment I have been waiting for. The senate recognises my achievements in Gaul, but their recognition is not enough. I need to cement my position as one of the most powerful men in Rome. The senate is filled with my enemies, and they will not hesitate to try and strip me of my command. I need to use every trick in the book to prevent them from doing so. I must show them that I am not just a military leader but a political one too. Cicero is on my side, but I need to convince the rest of the senate that I am indispensable. My victories in Gaul have given me the power to do just that.

Senators, I implore you to recognise the achievements of our great leader, Caesar. His victories in Gaul have been nothing short of miraculous. He has pacified the region and brought peace to our borders. We owe him a great debt of gratitude, and I propose that we do not just recognise his achievements but also reward him. The state funds that have been granted to some of his legions are a good start, but we must do more. We must show him that he is valued and that his command in Gaul is secure.

I must disagree with Cicero. Caesar has been given more than enough recognition for his achievements. We cannot forget that he is a military leader and not a political one. His command in Gaul must be reassigned to a more capable and politically astute leader. We cannot allow a military leader to wield too much power in our republic.

I agree with my colleague. Caesar's victories in Gaul have been impressive, but we must remember that he is not the only capable general in our republic. We have other leaders who can take his place and even do a better job. We cannot allow one man to hold too much power. It goes against the very principles that our republic is built upon.

I understand your concerns, my fellow senators. But I must remind you that I am not just a military leader. I am also a politician. My victories in Gaul have given me the power to do great things for our republic. I have brought peace to our borders and expanded our territories. I have also shown the people of Gaul that Rome is a great nation that they should not oppose. My position in Gaul is secure, and I will not allow anyone to take it away from me. I implore you to recognise my achievements and support me in my command.

Caesar, your words are convincing, but we cannot ignore the fact that you are a military leader. Your position in Gaul must be reassigned to someone who is politically astute and has the interests of our republic at heart.

I agree with my colleague. We must not allow one man to hold too much power. It is dangerous for the stability of our republic. We must reassign your command in Gaul to someone who is more capable and politically astute.

These senators do not understand the power that I wield. They think that they can strip me of my command, but they are wrong. I have the loyalty of my legions, and they will follow me wherever I go.
